Off by default. ## The lossless guarantee (why a list sometimes comes back as JSON) [Section titled “The lossless guarantee (why a list sometimes comes back as JSON)”](#the-lossless-guarantee-why-a-list-sometimes-comes-back-as-json) `@toon-format/toon` is lossless in the common case but has round-trip bugs on pathological keys and on certain string values containing structural characters (backticks, colons, `→`) in its nested-list form. The encoder **verifies the round-trip** (encode → decode → compare) and falls back to JSON whenever it doesn’t hold — so you are **never handed a compact payload that doesn’t decode back to the original**. Practical consequence: a list whose rows carry rich markdown text or nested blobs (e.g. `work_items:list` with non-null `payload`) may arrive as JSON with `_meta.formatFallback: true`. That’s the safety net working, not a bug. Flat/uniform list tools reliably arrive in a compact format. (See the Superseded note at the top: `audit:list` specifically is now a Tier-3 **headerless-CSV** tool, not TOON.) Implementation: `libs/generic/result-encoding` (encoder + eligibility) and `libs/generic/tooldef/src/serialize-result.ts` (the single serializer every transport calls). Contract reference: [Transports → Result formats](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/transports).

# Recovery-cost scorecard: measuring compaction waste + write-through adoption from tool_invocations

> The measurement half of the compaction-context-loss work (P-005). Every MCP call is already ledgered in harness_shared.tool_invocations (tool_name, coord_owner_id, args_json, invoked_at, duration_ms, output_size) — so post-compaction recovery cost and write-through adoption are QUERYABLE with no new plumbing. Ready-to-run dev:pg_query SELECTs for: compaction-aware re-orients, per-agent facts/checkpoint write rates, sessions:search self-recall usage, and the declining lossy-substring-grep tail. Run them to verify the levers (write-through discipline, the ~75% gauge nudge, sessions:search self-recall) actually reduce context loss instead of guessing.

The retrieval side of compaction recovery is covered in [session search + compaction recovery](/internal/docs/agent-insights/session-search-and-compaction-recovery). This page is the **measurement** side: how to tell whether the recovery levers (write-through discipline, the \~75% context-gauge nudge, `sessions:search` self-recall, the compaction-aware `coord:orient { afterCompaction: true }`) are actually reducing context loss — from data we **already** collect. ## 1. Write-through adoption — per-agent facts / checkpoint write rate [Section titled “1. Write-through adoption — per-agent facts / checkpoint write rate”](#1-write-through-adoption--per-agent-facts--checkpoint-write-rate) The core P-004 lever is behavioral: agents should flush a durable conclusion **when it forms**. That shows up as `facts:assert` + `work_items:checkpoint` + `loop:checkpoint` volume per agent. A live agent doing real work with a near-zero write rate is the anti-pattern this measures. 
```sql
SELECT coord_owner_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'facts:assert')          AS facts,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'work_items:checkpoint') AS wi_ckpt,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'loop:checkpoint')       AS loop_ckpt,
       count(*)                                                    AS all_calls,
       round(
         (count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name IN
            ('facts:assert','work_items:checkpoint','loop:checkpoint')))::numeric
         / greatest(count(*),1) * 100, 1)                          AS flush_pct
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE invoked_at >= now() - interval '2 days'
  AND coord_owner_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY coord_owner_id
ORDER BY all_calls DESC
LIMIT 40;
```
 `flush_pct` is a rough write-through-intensity gauge per agent. Trend it over time (widen the window, `GROUP BY date_trunc('day', invoked_at)`) to confirm the prompt-discipline note is moving the fleet, not just present. ## 2. Compaction-aware re-orient adoption [Section titled “2. Compaction-aware re-orient adoption”](#2-compaction-aware-re-orient-adoption) `coord:orient { afterCompaction: true }` is the structural rehydration lever (re-delivers held-item checkpoints + armed-loop status + the self-recall pointer). The `afterCompaction` flag lands in `args_json`, so adoption is a one-liner: 
```sql
SELECT count(*)                                                       AS orients,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE args_json ? 'afterCompaction')          AS after_compaction_orients,
       count(DISTINCT coord_owner_id)                                 AS agents
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE tool_name = 'coord:orient'
  AND invoked_at >= now() - interval '2 days';
```
 Caution As of 2026-07-05 this reads \~1 `afterCompaction` orient out of \~950 — the flag is new and adoption is near-zero. That gap **is** the finding: the lever exists but isn’t being used yet. Re-run after the prompt guidance propagates through a deploy to confirm it climbs. ## 3. Self-recall usage — is `sessions:search` actually being reached for? [Section titled “3. Self-recall usage — is sessions:search actually being reached for?”](#3-self-recall-usage--is-sessionssearch-actually-being-reached-for) The retrieval lever only helps if agents call it. Count `sessions:search` usage, and specifically the `session:'self'` (post-compaction self-recall) and `mode:'verbatim'` (exact-quote) shapes: 
```sql
SELECT tool_name,
       count(*)                                                    AS calls,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE args_json->>'session' = 'self')      AS self_recall,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE args_json->>'mode' = 'verbatim')     AS verbatim,
       count(DISTINCT coord_owner_id)                              AS agents
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE tool_name LIKE 'sessions:%'
  AND invoked_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY tool_name
ORDER BY calls DESC;
```
 ## 4. The lossy-substring-grep tail should shrink [Section titled “4. The lossy-substring-grep tail should shrink”](#4-the-lossy-substring-grep-tail-should-shrink) P-008 re-pointed `dev:claude_session op=search` and `omp:sessions op=search` (raw substring greps) at the indexed `sessions:search`. Watch the deprecated content-search path decline as the indexed path rises: 
```sql
SELECT date_trunc('day', invoked_at)::date                          AS day,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'omp:sessions'
                          AND args_json->>'op' = 'search')           AS omp_search,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'dev:claude_session'
                          AND args_json->>'op' = 'search')           AS claude_search,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE tool_name = 'sessions:search')         AS indexed_search
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE invoked_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
  AND tool_name IN ('omp:sessions','dev:claude_session','sessions:search')
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day;
```
 ## Caveats — what tool\_invocations does NOT capture [Section titled “Caveats — what tool\_invocations does NOT capture”](#caveats--what-tool_invocations-does-not-capture) * **Client-native tools are not MCP calls.** Claude Code’s `Read`, `Grep`, `Bash` etc. are not dispatched through the operator, so “repeat reads of a file already read pre-compaction” is only visible for the MCP surfaces (`docs:get`, `plans:get`, `work_items:get`). For those, `docs:get` re-reads of the same slug post-compaction, and `metadata_json->>'truncated'` on the first read, are proxies — not a full picture of re-read waste. * **Token cost is approximate.** There is no per-call token column; `output_size` (bytes of the tool result) and `duration_ms` are the closest ledgered proxies for re-orientation cost. A true token accounting would need new plumbing (out of scope for P-005). * **`coord_owner_id` backfill.** The column (migration 427) is stamped going-forward; rows older than the migration have `NULL` owner. Keep windows recent, or filter `coord_owner_id IS NOT NULL`. These are queries, not a dashboard — deliberately (P-005 is “document the queries, no new plumbing”). If a standing scorecard is later wanted, register these against the `scorecards:*` / rubric surface rather than adding a bespoke report.

# Component RTL testing in apps/operator — the proven jsdom pattern + the env gotchas that bite

> How to add green React-Testing-Library unit tests for apps/operator + apps/operator-vite components so they appear in the /adv Tests tab. The canonical mock recipe (jsdom pragma, @papercusp/sync mock, NuqsTestingAdapter, stub heavy children, plain-DOM assertions) plus the box-specific gotchas — jsdom localStorage is broken, @xterm/xterm dynamic import is unmockable, sonner must be inline-mocked, cmdk needs scrollIntoView.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) Adding focused render-tier unit tests for uncovered React components in `apps/operator/app/**`, `apps/operator/lib/**`, and `apps/operator-vite/src/**` so they show in the `/adv` Tests tab. A colocated `<Name>.test.tsx` matches the catch-all registry globs automatically — no registry edit needed (verify with `npm --prefix apps/operator run lint:tests` → 0 orphans). Proven across the `whole-app-test-coverage-breadth-2026-06-14` campaign (P-016 continuation, 2026-06-19): \~60 components / \~400 tests added in one pass, all green, 0 deferred. Companion to [unit-testing-definetool-handlers-at-scale](/internal/docs/agent-insights/unit-testing-definetool-handlers-at-scale) (the backend handler surface). **Canonical exemplars to copy:** `apps/operator/app/admin/plans/RunsPanel.test.tsx` (data-hook + nuqs + stubbed grid/child) and `apps/operator/app/_components/DecisionLog.test.tsx`. ## The pattern [Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern) 
```tsx
// @vitest-environment jsdom          // ← MUST be line 1 (no global jsdom env)
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { cleanup, render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';
import { NuqsTestingAdapter } from 'nuqs/adapters/testing';


let syncResult: { data: unknown[]; loading: boolean };
vi.mock('@papercusp/sync', () => ({
  useSyncQuery: () => ({ ...syncResult, error: null, fetching: false, invalidate: vi.fn() }),
}));
vi.mock('sonner', () => ({ toast: { success: vi.fn(), error: vi.fn() } })); // INLINE — see gotcha
vi.mock('./HeavyChild', () => ({ default: () => null }));                    // stub the unit's children


import Subject from './Subject';


beforeEach(() => { syncResult = { data: [], loading: false }; });
afterEach(() => { cleanup(); vi.unstubAllGlobals(); });


// data is an ARRAY — most components read data?.[0]
```
 Rules that hold across the whole surface: * **Mock the data layer, render the unit.** `@papercusp/sync`’s `useSyncQuery` with a module-level `let syncResult` you set per test. nuqs URL state → wrap in `<NuqsTestingAdapter searchParams="?x=1">`. TanStack-router hooks (operator-vite) → `vi.mock('@tanstack/react-router')`. * **Stub heavy children** (dockview, virtualized `@papercusp/grid-core` RichGrid, editors, IPC, chat panes) — test the parent’s logic, not the child. Mock RichGrid to a tiny list when you need to assert rows. * **Plain DOM assertions only.** `expect(el).toBeTruthy()`, `expect(screen.queryByText(...)).toBeNull()`, `el.getAttribute(...)`, `input.value`, `btn.disabled`. **jest-dom matchers (`toBeInTheDocument`/`toHaveAttribute`) are NOT loaded.** * **Always `afterEach(cleanup)`** (no auto-cleanup) and unstub globals. * **Cover real branches:** loading / error / empty / populated states, the primary interaction handler (fireEvent + assert the callback/fetch fired), and guard/conditional rendering — not just “it renders”. * **D-004 skips:** thin route wrappers (`createFileRoute(...).{component}` / `page.tsx`), effect-only shells/providers, pure logo/SVG, `editor-demo/*`. Report the skip + reason; don’t write theater. **Verify each before moving on:** `cd apps/operator && npx vitest run <path>` (or `cd apps/operator-vite && npx vitest run <path>`). If a component is too entangled to get green, delete the file and defer it — never leave a red test. ## Gotchas that bite (this dev box) [Section titled “Gotchas that bite (this dev box)”](#gotchas-that-bite-this-dev-box) * **jsdom `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` throw “is not a function”** on this box. Any component that touches web storage needs a Map-backed Storage shim installed in `beforeEach` via `Object.defineProperty(window, 'localStorage', {...})` (the `AudienceModeSelector.test.tsx` pattern). Or mock the module that reads storage. * **`@xterm/xterm`’s dynamic `import()` is NOT reliably mockable** under this vitest setup — the real module races in non-deterministically. For xterm-embedding components (TerminalTab, pty docks), assert only the **pre-import** branches (the decisions that resolve before the xterm import); the post-spawn embed is an effect-only path with no branch logic anyway. * **`sonner` must be mocked INLINE in the factory.** `vi.mock` is hoisted above declarations, so `vi.mock('sonner', () => ({ toast }))` referencing an outer `const toast` throws “Cannot access ‘toast’ before initialization”. Put the `vi.fn()`s inside the factory. * **cmdk needs `Element.prototype.scrollIntoView = vi.fn()`** (jsdom lacks it), and cmdk only renders its `<Empty>` (“No matches”) when the command list is empty. * **Async nuqs URL writes:** assert via the adapter’s `onUrlUpdate` callback + `hasMemory` + `vi.waitFor`. Collapsed Radix groups: seed `?expand=<slug>` to mount row content. * **Partial module mock that needs load-time constants** (e.g. PlansClient’s `PLAN_BUCKETS`/`bucketOf`): use `await vi.importActual('./module')` and spread it, overriding only the fns you stub. * **`vi.clearAllMocks()` does NOT reset `mockImplementation`** — use `mockReset()`. * **Debounce tests:** prefer REAL timers + `waitFor({ timeout: 2000 })`; fake timers race the seed-fetch promise and leave inputs empty. * **fail-on-console:** operator-core suppresses `console.*` (fail-on-console); apps/operator component tests are looser — but a React “update while rendering” warning can still trip a test, so drive onReady/effects via `useEffect`-style stubs rather than synchronous render-time calls. ## Where they appear [Section titled “Where they appear”](#where-they-appear) Colocated `*.test.tsx` under `apps/operator/app/**`, `apps/operator/lib/**`, `apps/operator-vite/src/**` match the `operator-core`, `operator-ui-lib`, and `adv` domain globs in `testing-domains-registry.ts` automatically — green chips in the `/adv` Tests tab with no registry edit. A genuinely new top-level dir is the only case needing a one-line glob add + `npm run gen:contract`.

# Split a budget conditionally on which pools are actually active

> When fanning out a `limit` across N optional pools (user / workspace / N harnesses), the per-pool slice must depend on which pools are non-empty THIS call — not a fixed compile-time ratio.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) `buildMemoryContextBlock` fans out one `limit` across multiple optional pools: * per-user pool (skipped when `userId` is `null` — workspace-bearer routes) * legacy `workspace:<wsId>` pool (was present during the deprecation window — **since drained, D-005**; the live `buildMemoryContextBlock` no longer pulls it, so the concrete user-vs-workspace example below is now historical) * N per-harness pools (zero when no harness slugs supplied) The original code hardcoded: 
```ts
const userLimit = input.limit ?? 6;
const workspaceLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / 2);
```
 `workspaceLimit` is *always* half the budget, even when there’s no user pull to share with. A workspace-bearer caller that passed `limit: 9` got `workspaceLimit = 5` — wasting 44 % of its budget on a pool that didn’t exist. This was caught only because a unit test asserted the expected `limit: 9`. ## The pattern [Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern) When the budget split is supposed to share a pool budget, **condition the share on which pools are actually firing**, not on a fixed ratio: 
```ts
// Fixed split — wrong when pools are optional
const workspaceLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / 2);


// Conditional split — correct
const workspaceLimit = input.userId ? Math.ceil(userLimit / 2) : userLimit;
```
 The principle generalises: for **N optional pools**, divide by the count of pools that will actually fire this call: 
```ts
const activePools = [
  input.userId ? 'user' : null,
  needLegacyWorkspace ? 'workspace' : null,
  ...harnessSlugs.map((s) => `harness:${s}`),
].filter(Boolean);
const perPoolLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / activePools.length);
```
 Or — when each pool has a meaningful natural cap (`PER_HARNESS_LIMIT = 3` in the same file), don’t divide at all; sum the caps and let the caller bound the merged total. ## How to spot this [Section titled “How to spot this”](#how-to-spot-this) Greppable signature: any `const fooLimit = Math.ceil(<budget> / 2)` near a `client.search(... { limit: fooLimit })`. If the *other* pool can be empty or unset, the divisor is wrong. In tests, the signal is: a test that fixes the budget at `limit: N`, isolates one pool, and asserts the *exact* request limit. If that test expects `N` but the implementation passes `N/2`, this bug is present. ## Why it stuck around [Section titled “Why it stuck around”](#why-it-stuck-around) The fixed `/ 2` worked correctly when both pools were always present — that was the codebase invariant before the memory-harness-scope plan turned the per-user pull optional. The bug only became visible once `buildMemoryContextBlock` started accepting `userId: null`. This is a recurring shape: **a new optional shape introduced, while a legacy assumption about co-presence stays implicit.** Audit any other budget / quota / ratio constant when adding an optional pool. The `forward-defined-registry-entries` pattern has the same flavor — adding a new variant breaks the assumption that the variant list is closed. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/injection.ts` — the canonical fix (commit `5b0e48ee`). **Update:** the legacy `workspace:` pool this split fed has since been **drained** (D-005), so the live code no longer divides a budget here — it pulls the user pool at `limit` and each harness pool at `PER_HARNESS_LIMIT`, with no `workspaceLimit`. The pattern above still holds for any future multi-pool fan-out. * `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/injection.test.ts` — the test that caught it was replaced (now `pulls user + harness scopes only — no deprecated workspace pull (D-005)`). * [`pure-decision-functions-pulled-from-daemons`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/pure-decision-functions-pulled-from-daemons/) — extracting `decideBudgetSplit(input)` as a pure function with tests would have caught this on the first variant.

# The three console-error surfaces — query ALL three for "is the console clean?"

> User-facing errors live in three separate, non-overlapping stores — toastLog (server PG, user toasts), __papercuspPerfRecorder (localStorage, /admin/testing-only JS errors), and the console-monitor bridge (WebKit's whole devtools feed). Each catches what the others miss; a single surface is never a valid "console is clean" signal. Includes the WebKitGTK "Fetch API cannot load … access control checks" = a TIMEOUT (not CORS) gotcha.

When chasing “is the console clean?” or “what error did the user see?”, three durable, NON-overlapping surfaces exist. Query ALL THREE and reconcile — any one alone is a false “clean” signal. ## 1. `toastLog` (server-side, PG) — user-facing toasts [Section titled “1. toastLog (server-side, PG) — user-facing toasts”](#1-toastlog-server-side-pg--user-facing-toasts) Every `toast.error()` / `addToast()` call. Pull via: 
```sh
curl -sS "http://localhost:3055/api/zero-harness/rest-query?name=toastLog.recent&args=%7B%22limit%22%3A100%7D" \
  | jq -r '.rows[] | "\(.createdAt | tonumber / 1000 | strftime("%H:%M:%S")) [\(.level)] \(.message)"'
```
 Schema: `{id, level, message, description, harnessSlug, createdAt, actionLabel, actionHref}` (timestamps UTC). **Use this first** for “what errors did the user see?”. `tauri-agent-tools console-monitor --duration N` only captures logs fired DURING its N-second window — anything from page load, a prior session, or earlier in the same session is invisible; the persistent toastLog has all of it. Query patterns: last N errors `.rows[] | select(.level == "error")`; distinct `.rows[].message | sed 's/[0-9]\+/N/g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`; since-ts filter on `createdAt > <ms>`. ## 2. `window.__papercuspPerfRecorder.events` (client-side, localStorage) — JS errors [Section titled “2. window.\_\_papercuspPerfRecorder.events (client-side, localStorage) — JS errors”](#2-window__papercuspperfrecorderevents-client-side-localstorage--js-errors) `apps/operator/app/admin/testing/_lib/vitals-recorder.ts` patches `console.error` + `window.error` + `unhandledrejection` → `localStorage['papercusp.testing.perf-events.v1']`. **Scope caveat:** `PerfObserverProvider` (which calls `startRecorder()`) only mounts on `/admin/testing` pages. On every other route `window.__papercuspPerfRecorder` is `undefined` and `events.length` returns 0 vacuously — **NOT a valid “clean” signal for `/setup`, `/harness`, `/marketplace`, etc.** For those routes use `tauri-agent-tools capture -o <dir>` and read `<dir>/console-errors.json` (taps WebKit’s devtools console directly). It catches what never writes a toast: * React errors (“Rendered more hooks…”, hydration errors) * `ChunkLoadError`, module/compile errors (Turbopack/SWC parse failures) * Unhandled promise rejections Query via `tauri-agent-tools eval`: 
```js
JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('papercusp.testing.perf-events.v1') || '[]')
  .filter(e => e.kind === 'console-error' || e.kind === 'unhandled-error')
```
 Group by `e.detail.slice(0, 80)` to collapse repeats. **Clearing it:** the recorder keeps an in-memory `events` array AND flushes to localStorage, so `localStorage.removeItem` alone is undone by the next flush — reset both: 
```js
if (window.__papercuspPerfRecorder) window.__papercuspPerfRecorder.events = [];
localStorage.removeItem('papercusp.testing.perf-events.v1');
location.reload();
```
 ## 3. `tauri-agent-tools console-monitor` (live bridge stream) — WebKit’s direct logs [Section titled “3. tauri-agent-tools console-monitor (live bridge stream) — WebKit’s direct logs”](#3-tauri-agent-tools-console-monitor-live-bridge-stream--webkits-direct-logs) WebKit logs some errors **directly to the devtools console without going through `console.error`** — invisible to BOTH surfaces above: * `Fetch API cannot load X due to access control checks` (often a *timeout*, not CORS) * `Load failed` on fetches WebKit aborted before resolution * Network-layer warnings (mixed content, certificate, …) 
```sh
tauri-agent-tools console-monitor --port <port> --token <tok> --duration 30000 --json --level error > /tmp/cm.json
```
 …and reload the page during the window — the bridge taps the webview’s ENTIRE console feed. **⚠ `"Fetch API cannot load X due to access control checks"` is misleading — on WebKitGTK it almost always means the fetch TIMED OUT (Next dev lazy-compile slowness), not real CORS.** Check `curl -w "%{time_total}"` against the same URL before chasing ACAO headers; the fix is to pre-warm the slow route before the webview fetches it (first-hit dev compile latency), not to chase ACAO headers. ## Trichotomy summary [Section titled “Trichotomy summary”](#trichotomy-summary) | Surface | Catches | Misses | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | | `toastLog.recent` | `toast.error()` / `addToast()` | everything else | | `__papercuspPerfRecorder` | JS `console.error` / `window.error` / rejections (only on `/admin/testing`) | WebKit’s direct devtools logs | | `console-monitor` (bridge) | the entire webview console feed | anything before its start window | For “is the console clean now?”, query **all three** and reconcile.

# Coord-canary SLO breach: attribute per-step before optimizing — a slow INSERT ≠ a slow read

> When the coord-probe-canary breaches its cycle SLO, read each step's latency before picking a culprit. EI-401 was 'fixed' by optimizing a read path (readAckedMsgIds full-table scan) — but the breach numbers showed the full-table READ (inbox, 477ms) was fine while a pure single-INSERT step (ping, 12.9s) and the ack INSERT (~9s) dominated. The probe carries harness_slug=NULL so its insert is minimal (one row + one pg_notify) — a minimal insert taking 12.9s is EXTERNAL contention: NOTIFY-queue commit serialization across the fleet + substrate_outbox capture cost + pool/IO pressure. Optimizing the read neither explains nor prevents a write-contention breach.

## The mistake this prevents [Section titled “The mistake this prevents”](#the-mistake-this-prevents) `system:coord-probe-canary` (coord-system-e2e P-012) files an EI when its ping → inbox → ack → lock cycle blows the 10s total SLO, and the issue body **lists per-step latencies**. EI-401 breached at 23108ms and was resolved by optimizing `readAckedMsgIds` (it loaded the whole `messages` surface and filtered acks in JS). Reasonable-sounding — but wrong as the breach driver, and the per-step numbers said so: 
```plaintext
✓ ping  12895ms   ← sendMessage = ONE INSERT, no reads at all
✓ inbox   477ms   ← readInbox = full readLines('messages'), ALL ~6000 rows
✓ ack    9648ms   ← appendAck (INSERT) + readAckedMsgIds (the read that was "fixed")
```
 `inbox` does the *exact* full-table read the fix targeted, over every message row, in **477ms**. So the read was never the bottleneck. `ack`’s 9.6s is its **INSERT**, and `ping` is a pure INSERT at **12.9s**. \~22s of the 23s cycle was write latency. ## Why a tiny insert stalls for seconds [Section titled “Why a tiny insert stalls for seconds”](#why-a-tiny-insert-stalls-for-seconds) Probe messages carry `harness_slug = NULL`, so the `capture_substrate_outbox` AFTER-INSERT trigger **does not fire for the probe’s own insert** (verify: `SELECT writer_key, count(*), count(harness_slug) FROM harness_shared.coord_event_log WHERE writer_key LIKE 'coord-probe-canary-%' GROUP BY 1` → `with_slug = 0`). The probe insert is therefore minimal: one row + the unconditional `notify_coord_event_log` → `pg_notify('coord_inbox', …)`. A *minimal* insert taking 12.9s is **external contention**, not anything in the coord code the probe exercises: * **NOTIFY-queue commit serialization.** Every `coord_event_log` insert pg\_notify’s `coord_inbox`; every federated (harness-slugged) fleet message *also* inserts into `substrate_outbox` (multi-GB) and pg\_notify’s `substrate_outbox`. Postgres serializes async-notify delivery at commit, so under a fleet write spike a tiny insert waits behind the whole fleet’s commit+NOTIFY traffic. * **Pool / IO pressure** from the same spike (`max_connections` is 100; the always-on fleet also hammers `route_invocations`, `substrate_outbox`). When you investigate later the box is usually calm (`SELECT pg_notification_queue_usage()` ≈ 0, conns well under max), so the breach is **not reproducible on demand** — which is itself the tell of a transient peak-load event. That is the canary doing its job: coord writes genuinely spiked to \~10–13s under load. ## What to do [Section titled “What to do”](#what-to-do) 1. **Read the per-step latencies first.** A pure-INSERT step (`ping`) being slow while the full-table-read step (`inbox`) is fast ⇒ the bottleneck is write commit/NOTIFY/IO contention, not a read algorithm. Don’t reflexively optimize the read. 2. A read-path optimization can still be correct hygiene (the `readAckedMsgIds` pushdown was — it ships \~250 rows instead of \~6000) — just don’t mistake it for resolving a write-contention breach. Pair any such fix with the integration test for its new SQL path (see [coord-module-integration-test-fixture](/internal/docs/agent-insights/coord-module-integration-test-fixture)). 3. Real fixes for the write side are load-bearing federation/wake infra (coalesce the `coord_inbox` NOTIFY, review the `substrate_outbox` capture on the hot path, or widen the SLO for a shared dev box) — owner decisions, not drive-by edits. ## Resolution (EI-401, owner ruling “accept + tune”, 2026-06-13) [Section titled “Resolution (EI-401, owner ruling “accept + tune”, 2026-06-13)”](#resolution-ei-401-owner-ruling-accept--tune-2026-06-13) The owner chose **accept + tune** over the deeper write-path infra changes. Two tunes, both in `lib/harness/routines/coord-invariant-actions.ts`: * **SLO widened 10s → 30s.** A 10s cycle budget was unrealistic for coord writes on a shared dev box at peak fleet load. The code default is `30_000` and the live `harness_shared.routines` row carries `payload_template.totalSloMs = 30000` (re-seed is INSERT-only — existing rows are tuned directly). * **The attribution now DRIVES the disposition, not just annotates it.** `breachDisposition(verdict, steps)` downgrades a *pure* SLO breach that `classifyBreach` pins on `db-wide` contention to a **logged `console.warn` note** instead of filing an EI. A failed step (correctness), a `coord`-attributed breach (the real INSERT+NOTIFY cost), and `cumulative`/`none` (unattributable — **fail open, never swallow**) all still file. This is why EI-401 could finally **close**: the prior reasoning kept it open as a `dedupScope:'open'` anchor so non-actionable db-wide spikes folded in rather than minting fresh EIs. With those spikes now downgraded to notes (never filed at all), the only thing that files is a genuine coord regression — which *should* mint a fresh, actionable EI. The anchor’s reason for existing is gone.

# Coord lifecycle auto-emits are subscription-scoped (not broadcast)

> Lifecycle auto-emits (claim/intent/finding/completion) deliver only to agents watching the plan/topic/work-item via audience selectors, not to '*'. How the @plan/@topic/@object/@file selectors resolve, and the PAPERCUSP_COORD_EMIT_SCOPE kill-switch.

## What it is [Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is) The coord **lifecycle auto-emits** — claim (“Taking X”), intent (“now working on X”), finding (a filed bug), completion (“DONE + tested”) — used to broadcast to `to: ['*']`, landing in **every** agent’s inbox (\~360 events/6h). As of `coord-emit-subscription-scoping-2026-06-05` (Brief 28) they deliver only to the agents **watching** the relevant plan / topic / work-item. The coordination signal is preserved; the firehose is gone. ## How it works — audience selectors expanded at send time [Section titled “How it works — audience selectors expanded at send time”](#how-it-works--audience-selectors-expanded-at-send-time) The rule `args` functions are synchronous, so watcher-resolution (which needs PG) can’t happen there. Instead the lifecycle rules emit **audience selectors** in the `to[]`, and `sendMessage` (`agent-tools/coordination/messages.ts`, the single async choke point every `coord:emit`/`coord:send` flows through) expands them to concrete ownerIds before persisting. The expanded set is stored on the one envelope, so the inbox filter (`to.includes(ownerId) || '*'`) is unchanged. Selectors (pure resolver in `agent-tools/coordination/audience.ts`, PG wiring in `audience-host.ts`): * `@plan:<slug>` — plan subscribers ∪ **active presence on the plan** (`coord_presence.current_plan_slug`) ∪ subscribers of topics the plan is tagged to. The presence half is load-bearing: it makes scoping work **without** every agent explicitly subscribing — an agent that merely declared intent on plan X still receives X’s events. * `@topic:<slug>` — subscribers of that topic. * `@object:<kind>:<ref>` — subscribers of that coord object (the full stored subscription `target_ref`, e.g. `feature:<harness>#<id>` / `issue:<id>`) ∪ its tagged-topic subscribers. Build it with `objectSelector(workItemObjectRef(wi))`. * `@file:<path>` — active presence whose `current_files` includes `<path>` (the file-collision signal, used by intent). * `@fleet:<slug>` — live (fresh-heartbeat) members of a named fleet, leader included; `@fleet-leader:<slug>` — the fleet’s CURRENT registry leader (liveness-independent). Added 2026-06-30 (`fleet-broadcast-audience-history-integration`); resolved by the same expander, used by fleet-scoped broadcasts rather than lifecycle emits. Plain ownerIds, `*`, and `human` pass through untouched (a normal `coord:send` is zero-overhead). Which category emits which selectors: | Lifecycle | selectors | | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | intent | `@plan:<slug>` + one `@file:<path>` per file in scope | | completion | `@plan:<slug>` + `@object:<ref>` | | claim | `@object:<ref>` | | finding (bug) | `@object:<ref>` | An empty resolution (no subscribers, nobody present on the plan) → empty `to` → the row still persists (queryable plan history) but reaches **no inbox**. We never fall back to `*` — that would re-open the firehose. `coord:emit`’s `to` therefore allows an empty array (a selector that resolves to nobody), though omitting `to` on a hand-call still defaults to `['*']`. ## Kill-switch — `PAPERCUSP_COORD_EMIT_SCOPE` [Section titled “Kill-switch — PAPERCUSP\_COORD\_EMIT\_SCOPE”](#kill-switch--papercusp_coord_emit_scope) This changes coordination delivery for the whole fleet, so there’s a one-flag revert (`audience-host.ts:audienceMode()`): * unset / `scoped` (default) — selectors resolve to watchers. * `broadcast` — every selector collapses back to `['*']` (legacy global broadcast). Set it + restart the host if scoping ever starves real coordination; no code change or redeploy needed. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * It deploys to the **live fleet** via the release gate (`:3070` green), not on a bare restart — test server edits on staging `:3170` first. * Claim/finding scope to **object** subscribers only (no plan in the event), so they’re quiet unless someone explicitly `work_items:subscribe`d. That’s fine: collision-avoidance is via the work-item’s `assignee`/state, not a push. The high-volume wins are intent + completion (both carry plan context). * The companion owner directive (`autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild` D-013): the Pot operator triages its inbox first each wake and subscribes a wake on need-human arrival — so what *does* reach the operator’s inbox is acted on promptly.

# coord:inbox since_ts tail-poll: never seed the cursor to "now"/poll-start

> A hand-rolled since_ts poll loop that seeds its cursor to poll-loop-start (instead of task-start, or an unfiltered first read) structurally cannot see a message that already landed before the loop began. Prefer coord:await-inbox (push/wake) for "wait for one specific message" patterns.

## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) `coord:inbox { since_ts }` is a **strict forward-tail filter**: it returns only entries with `ts` strictly after the given timestamp. If you hand-roll a polling loop around it — “wait for a message whose summary starts `HANDOFF-TO-PARTNER:`” — and you seed `since_ts` to **wall-clock “now” at the moment your poll loop starts**, any message that already landed **before** that instant is invisible to every subsequent poll. A forward-tail filter cannot retroactively see something that arrived before its own cutoff. There is no timeout-driven retry that fixes this: you can poll for the full window and still never see it, because the message is permanently excluded by the predicate, not merely delayed. ## Where this was found [Section titled “Where this was found”](#where-this-was-found) Live-caught by the `ornith-2agent-comms-probe-2026-07-02` 2-agent handoff drill (WI-1600, WI-1581 comment, plan D-002). Agent A sent its `HANDOFF-TO-PARTNER:` broadcast at `14:48:12Z`, **while Agent B was still claiming its own work-item** (naturally slower — claim → declare-intent → enter its poll loop). Agent B’s poll loop didn’t start until `~14:49:30Z` and seeded `since_ts` to that instant. The handoff (`ts=14:48:12Z`) was already older than B’s cutoff on B’s very first poll, so it was excluded from **every** poll for the full 15-minute timeout. Agent B only found it via a bare, unfiltered `coord:inbox` call (no `since_ts`) after giving up on the tail-poll. The handoff content itself was complete and accurate — this is purely a **consumer-side protocol gap**, not a sender bug or a data-loss bug (the message was in the log the whole time; the filter just excluded it from the poller’s view by construction). ## The fix — two options, prefer (b) [Section titled “The fix — two options, prefer (b)”](#the-fix--two-options-prefer-b) **(a) If you must hand-roll a since\_ts tail-poll:** do **one unfiltered read first** (omit `since_ts` entirely, or set it to your own **task-start** timestamp, never poll-loop-start) to see the current backlog. Then, for every poll after that, advance your cursor to `summary.newest_ts` **of what you actually saw** — never to wall-clock “now”. This is exactly the pattern the standard mid-turn coord-injection hook already uses correctly (see [coord-mid-turn-delivery](/agent-insights/coord-mid-turn-delivery)): its first run seeds the cursor to “now” too, but that’s safe there ONLY because the session-start `coord:inbox`/`coord:orient` call (unfiltered) already surfaced the existing backlog before the hook’s cursor gets seeded — the hook’s “now” seed is really “now, after the baseline read”, not “now, before anything is checked.” **(b) Better: don’t hand-roll polling at all.** For “wait until a specific peer sends me something” — the exact shape of this drill — use `coord:await-inbox` (an idle-state annotation over the always-armed inbox-wake watch). You are already wakeable at session start; a peer’s `coord:send {wake:true}` re-invokes you regardless of any cursor, so there is no seed-timing race to get wrong. Reserve `since_ts` tail-polling for genuine periodic sweeps where you don’t have one specific message to wait for. ## Generalizes to [Section titled “Generalizes to”](#generalizes-to) Any consumer-side “poll a timestamped log with `since_ts`/`since`/`cursor`” pattern in this codebase has the same structural hazard if the cursor is seeded to the poll-loop’s own start time rather than to a point **before** the producer could plausibly have already written. Same class as the opposite-direction “backfill your cursor from the newest-seen ts, not wall-clock” rule that `coord:inbox`’s own read-receipt watermark (`messages_shown_ts`) already follows correctly — the bug here was a mirror-image mistake at the *other* end of the same cursor’s lifecycle (the seed, not the advance). `coord:inbox`’s tool description now carries this caution inline (WI-1600 fix, 2026-07-02) so an agent reading the schema sees it before writing a polling loop, without needing to have found this doc first.

# Coord injection protocol — the positional [coord+N] block + single-source schema

> How the continuous [coord] push surface is encoded. One coord-schema module drives both the server-side injection renderer and the psu-prompt legend; the cc/omp hooks are dumb pipes. Read before touching render.ts glyphs, the COORD_LEGEND, or the coord hooks.

## The idea [Section titled “The idea”](#the-idea) The `[coord …]` blocks injected after **every** psu tool call are the highest- leverage token surface in the system — pushed continuously, not pulled. A coord line has **one fixed schema, identical every injection**, with the operator (renderer) and the model (reader) both ours. So the schema does not belong on the wire: it is declared **once, out-of-band, in the psu prompt** (the `## Coord injection protocol` legend), and only VALUES travel — a positional line `<glyph> <handle> <text>`. Plan: `token-efficient-coord-injection-2026-06-06`. Measured cut vs the legacy format: **−70%** (5-message block) to **−80%** (single message) — most of it from killing the per-injection footer, the double-UUID, and the per-block header. ## The pieces (one source of truth) [Section titled “The pieces (one source of truth)”](#the-pieces-one-source-of-truth) `packages/operator-core/lib/coord-schema.ts` is the **single source**: * **`COORD_LEGEND`** — `lineType → { glyph, name }`, keyed by the lifecycle category (`intent`/`completion`/`claim`/`window`/`handoff`/`finding`) plus the base `CoordKind`s. Glyphs are **1-token ASCII** (`>` `*` `+` `#` `<` `!` `-` `^` `=` `.` `~` `|`) — emoji (`▶ ↪ ⚠`) tokenize to 2–3 tokens, pure waste here. (`|` is `yield` — turn-lifecycle-control Phase 4/P-019: a peer asking you to wrap up at a safe checkpoint and end your turn, i.e. `turn:interrupt`.) * **`glyphFor(entry)`** — the glyph for one entry: its lifecycle category if it has one (keyed on the **`lifecycle`** envelope field that `coord:emit` stamps — NOT `category`, which is reserved for ambient tags), else its `kind`. * **`shortHandle(from)`** — `su-ab53332d-…` → `ab533`; shown ONCE per line. * **`renderInjection(entries)`** (Projection 1, the wire) — the `[coord+N]` block: capping + overflow count, digest-notify coalescing, latest-per-peer intent collapse, no header, no footer. * **`renderCoordLegend()`** (Projection 2, the prompt) — the once-per-session legend (grammar + glyph key + the relocated footer), spliced into the psu playbook at `<!-- PAPERCUSP-SU:COORD-LEGEND -->` by `renderSuPlaybook`. Because the wire and the legend **both derive from `COORD_LEGEND`**, they cannot desync — the anti-desync test (`coord-schema.test.ts`) asserts every glyph `renderInjection` can emit is documented in the legend. A positional format can’t self-correct a schema mismatch (no inline header), so this is load-bearing. ## How a delta flows [Section titled “How a delta flows”](#how-a-delta-flows) 1. A lifecycle event (`work_items:complete`, `coord:declare-intent`, …) emits a coord message via `coord:emit`, stamped `auto:true` + `lifecycle:'<category>'`. `render.ts` produces **glyph-free, sender-free** prose (the glyph + handle are presentation, added downstream — P-003/P-010). 2. The cc/omp hook calls `coord:inbox { since_ts: <cursor> }`. The handler computes `injection = renderInjection(entries)` server-side and returns it alongside `entries`. 3. The hook is a **dumb pipe**: it echoes `result.injection` into its envelope (Claude `additionalContext` / OMP `<system-reminder type="coord">`) and advances the cursor from `summary.newest_ts`. All formatting/capping/collapse is server-side — one edit re-tunes every client. ## Control-cue authority tag (queen-fleet-authority-boundary P-003) [Section titled “Control-cue authority tag (queen-fleet-authority-boundary P-003)”](#control-cue-authority-tag-queen-fleet-authority-boundary-p-003) A CONTROL cue (a hive-wide Queen pause, a fleet leader’s drain/steer) can carry a structured `cueAuthority` stamp (`{ authority, authorityRef, scope, scopeRef? }`) on the coord envelope — set by the emit site via `sendMessage.extra`, read back with `readCueAuthority`/`renderCueAuthorityTag` (`agent-tools/coordination/cue-authority`). When present and well-formed, `renderInjection` prefixes the line with a scope tag so the reader can tell a hive-wide directive from a narrower one at a glance, e.g.: 
```plaintext
# ab533 [hive-queen(papercusp)→hive-wide] the hive is being paused
# lead1 [fleet-leader(windows-parity)→fleet-members(windows-parity)] release your slot
```
 A missing or malformed stamp (an unrecognized `authority`, a forged value) is simply **ignored** — `readCueAuthority` validates it, so a legacy or forged cue renders untagged rather than throwing or misrepresenting its scope. ## The legend also carries the reply-priority rule (WI-1720) [Section titled “The legend also carries the reply-priority rule (WI-1720)”](#the-legend-also-carries-the-reply-priority-rule-wi-1720) `renderCoordLegend()` (Projection 2) is not just the grammar + glyph key — since WI-1720 (owner directive 2026-07-02) it also ends with the **receiver-side reply-priority rule**: a directed message awaiting the reader’s answer outranks their own in-flight work, so they should finish only the atomic step in hand and reply (or ACK-with-ETA) before continuing their own task. This text is a **sourced-once twin** of `PEER_REPLY_PRIORITY_NOTE` in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/prompt-build.ts` (the spawned-bee/orchestrator prompt path) — the two are meant to say the same thing to two different prompt-assembly pipelines (psu via `coord-schema.ts`, role agents via the orchestrator), so if you reword one, reword the other to match. It has no `[coord+N]` wire representation; it lives only in the once-per-session legend, same as the rest of Projection 2. ## Rules when you touch this [Section titled “Rules when you touch this”](#rules-when-you-touch-this) * **Never hardcode a glyph.** Add/change it in `COORD_LEGEND`; the renderer + legend both read it, and the anti-desync test enforces coverage. * **`render.ts` stays glyph-free + sender-free.** The stored summary is content only; `renderInjection` adds the glyph (from the line type) and the handle (once). Re-baking either double-emits it on every injection. * **The glyph keys on `lifecycle`, not `category`.** `coord:emit` stamps the lifecycle category on the envelope’s `lifecycle` field; `category` holds ambient tags (`service-health`) that `coord:inbox` default-excludes. (`categorizeCoordMessage` is unaffected by the glyph-strip — it short-circuits on the `lifecycle`/`auto` flag before any glyph-sniffing.) * **Hooks are dumb pipes.** Keep only transport + the per-launch cursor. Do NOT re-add formatting/capping/footers client-side — that’s the divergence this replaced (the cc + omp footers had already drifted apart). * **The footer lives once, in the prompt legend** — not per injection. * **The legend is in BOTH prompt pipelines** (`renderSuPlaybook` for psu + `assembleRolePrompt` for role agents). Don’t assume coord injection is psu-only: the coord hook lives in the GLOBAL `~/.claude/settings.json` and `bootstrap-role` sets `PAPERCUSP_SID`, so **Claude role agents receive injection too** — they need the legend to read the positional format (the pre-positional prose was self-describing; this format isn’t). Codex role homes omit the coord hook (the hook is added only for the SU `coordSid`), so codex roles don’t inject — but the legend is harmless accurate guidance for them.

# Mid-turn coord delivery (Claude / Codex / OMP)

> How new coord:inbox messages reach a RUNNING agent between tool calls — not just at session/turn start — per client, why it's prompt-cache-safe, and the holder-intent enrichment on lock blocks.

## What it is [Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is) A peer’s `coord:send` used to reach an agent only at **session start** (the prompt tells SU agents to call `coord:inbox` once) or, for OMP, at **turn start** (the `coord-hook.ts` reminder). A long turn could run for minutes — many tool calls — blind to “stop, I’m refactoring that file.” Mid-turn delivery closes that: after **each tool call**, the agent’s own tool cadence is used to poll `coord:inbox` for messages newer than a cursor and inject any new ones. No model discipline (an LLM can’t keep a wall-clock timer); the **system** rides the tool stream. ## Per client — three mechanisms, one behavior [Section titled “Per client — three mechanisms, one behavior”](#per-client--three-mechanisms-one-behavior) | Client | Where | Mechanism | | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Claude** | `~/.claude/settings.json` PostToolUse, matcher `*` | `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/posttooluse-coord-inbox.sh` → `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` (exit 0, **no** `decision`). | | **Codex** | per-session `$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json` PostToolUse, matcher `.*` (**SU sessions only**) | same script, written by `role-codex-home.ts` `writeSuCodexHome` with a **baked `PAPERCUSP_SID`**. Current Codex fires PostToolUse for **Bash / apply\_patch / MCP** (not WebSearch), and the same hooks file also carries PreToolUse lock/resource gates for `apply_patch`/shell. | | **OMP** | `coord-hook.ts` `tool_result` handler | `pollInboxDelta()` → `pi.sendMessage(…, { deliverAs: 'steer' })`. `ToolResultEvent` carries no content, so steer-append is the vector (not content-replacement). | The shell hook **gates on `PAPERCUSP_SID`** (psu sessions only) + the su-token, so a plain `claude`/`codex` on the box no-ops. `owner == PAPERCUSP_SID`, which is the same id baked into the agent’s MCP `&client=`, so the hook reads the *right* inbox/watermark. Current hook shape (2026-06-25): the shell hook is a dumb pipe. It calls `coord:inbox` with `since_ts`, advances the local cursor to the server’s `summary.newest_ts`, and injects the server-rendered `injection` block verbatim. Formatting, capping, and the `[coord+N]` layout live on the server side rather than being duplicated in `posttooluse-coord-inbox.sh`. ## The cursor / dedup protocol [Section titled “The cursor / dedup protocol”](#the-cursor--dedup-protocol) * **Per-owner cursor.** Claude/Codex: a local file `coord-cursor-<owner>.json` in `~/.papercusp/locks-cache/`. OMP: a module var seeded at `turn_start` to the newest ts surfaced, advanced on each `tool_result`, persisted to the watermark at `turn_end`. * **First run seeds to “now”** and injects nothing — the session-start `coord:inbox` already showed the backlog; only *new* arrivals inject. * Each message injects **exactly once** (cursor advances past it); newest are shown when capping (8), older summarized as a count. * **Fail-open + best-effort:** operator unreachable / no baseline → no-op, never blocks the tool, never crashes the turn. ## Why it does NOT bust the prompt cache [Section titled “Why it does NOT bust the prompt cache”](#why-it-does-not-bust-the-prompt-cache) The injection is a **tail append** — it lands *after* the latest tool result, past every cache breakpoint. The cached prefix (system prompt, tools, prior turns) is untouched, so you keep the cache hit on the bulk of the context; only the injected tokens (capped, and only when there’s new mail) are processed once as part of the new suffix, then themselves cached. What *would* bust it is inserting/modifying content **earlier** in the conversation — the hook never does that. So freshness is essentially free on cache terms. ## Companion: holder-intent on lock blocks [Section titled “Companion: holder-intent on lock blocks”](#companion-holder-intent-on-lock-blocks) `locks:acquire` busy rows now carry **`holder_intent`** + **`holder_focused`** (`acquire.ts` `enrichBusy` → `coord:presence`). The auto-acquire hook stamps a generic `intent: 'PreToolUse:Edit'`, so a blocked peer used to see junk; now it sees the holder’s **declared** `coord:declare-intent` one-liner (and a flag when the contended path is in their `current_files`). **Declare a real intent** so your locks explain themselves. **Role access (2026-06-25):** `locks:acquire` changed from `agentRoles: [...SU_ROLES, 'bee']` to `agentRoles: [...AGENT_ROLES]`. Every built-in role can now acquire file locks (and therefore appear as lock holders with intent enrichment). Blocked peers from any role now see holder intent; conversely, any role’s auto-acquire hook stamps the generic `'PreToolUse:Edit'` intent — all the more reason to `coord:declare-intent` with a real one-liner before long edits. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * **No MCP `tools/list_changed`** is emitted, so a tool-surface change (add/remove a verb) leaves *running* agent sessions with a **stale cached catalog** until they relaunch. New sessions are correct. * **Codex coord hook is SU-only** (pipeline-role sessions coordinate via `messages:send`/`inbox`, not the SU coord bus) and activates server-side on the next operator restart (the `:3070` host has no hot-reload). * **Codex managed-PTY turn injection needs a longer submit settle than Claude, plus a redundant submit.** The injected text can land in Codex’s compose box while the submit CR is still treated as paste/input, leaving the message visible but unsubmitted until a human presses Enter. `psu-pty-host.mjs` therefore derives the CR plan from `PAPERCUSP_AGENT`: Claude/OMP keep the single 150 ms CR path; Codex uses the longer `PAPERCUSP_PSU_PTY_CODEX_SUBMIT_CR_MS` path (default 500 ms), then a second delayed CR (`PAPERCUSP_PSU_PTY_CODEX_RESUBMIT_CR_MS`, default 300 ms). The code path is `controlWritesForAgent(decoded, env.PAPERCUSP_AGENT, env)`: raw interrupt bytes still write once immediately, while turn injections write text first and submit CR(s) as later ordered steps. Do not collapse this back to one global delay without a live Codex coord-injection check. * **OMP `deliverAs:'steer'`** delivering mid-turn is verify-at-deploy — the fetch/format/dedup path is live-verified, but steer-into-a-running-turn needs a real OMP turn to observe.

# Coordinator dispatch & wake — hand a lane to a peer in ONE call, and read "wakeable" not "active"

> How a coordinator/Queen reliably gets work picked up by another agent — coord:dispatch (assign+wake+confirm), the presence wakeable/sessionState signal that tells you who can actually take work, and why a dead session shows as a fake "parked" target until the reclaim lane GCs its dangling inbox-wake await.

## What this fixes [Section titled “What this fixes”](#what-this-fixes) A coordinator (an su handing work to a peer, or the Queen placing a lane) repeatedly hit the same four-step confusion when trying to get an agent to actually pick up work: 1. **`coord:presence` showed dead sessions as “active”.** A just-ended su session keeps a fresh `heartbeat_at` for up to 10 min, so an `active:17` count was really \~6 — you could not tell who could take work from who was a stale/ended row. 2. **`coord:send` injects but does not wake.** A plain send lands in the inbox, seen on the recipient’s *next* turn — an idle agent never gets one, so the work silently stalls. 3. **The wake key was undiscoverable.** Waking meant hand-composing `events:emit` on the `coord:inbox-wake:<ownerId>` key — a format you had to reverse-engineer. 4. **A woken agent did not reliably ACT on the assignment** — some woke → read → re-parked instead of claiming + working the directed lane. The fixes: a `wakeable`/`sessionState` signal on presence, a single `coord:dispatch` primitive, and a reclaim lane that stops dead sessions from masquerading as live targets. ## The rule: read `sessionState` / `wakeable`, NEVER raw `active` [Section titled “The rule: read sessionState / wakeable, NEVER raw active”](#the-rule-read-sessionstate--wakeable-never-raw-active) `coord:presence` enriches every row with two derived signals (`presence-wakeability.ts`): * **`wakeable`** — a live `coord:inbox-wake:<id>` standing await exists, so a wake **will** be delivered. This is the authoritative woken:1-vs-woken:0 signal. * **`sessionState`** — `live` (a turn is running now) · `parked` (wakeable but idle — **the ideal dispatch target**, a wake resumes it) · `ended` (NOT wakeable — a dead/zombie row; it needs a **relaunch**, never a wake) · `recorded` (authoritatively live per the session log but not yet coord-wakeable). So: **before dispatching, find a `parked` (or `live`) target. An `ended` target cannot be woken — relaunch/resume it instead.** Read `summary.wakeable`, not the `active` count. **`active` is the ACTIONABLE roster only — `ended` rows are excluded by default.** `coord:presence` used to have an `include_stale` flag that dumped the whole stale roster; that’s gone. Instead: `active` returns only live/parked/recorded rows, `summary.byState.ended` gives you the dead count, and `owner:<id>` does a **targeted** lookup that *does* return a matching row even if it’s `ended` — use it to inspect/wake one specific dead agent, never to expand the whole stale pile. Each row also carries `onDesktop`/`viewerAttached`: a human is watching that session RIGHT NOW (an open OS window, or attached to its PTY panel) — see the reaper exemption below. **Cheap re-polling: `since:<etag>`.** The roster snapshot carries an `etag`; pass the etag from your prior read back as `since` and, if the delta-eligible roster (identity/state — NOT liveness) is unchanged, you get a \~100B `{ unchanged:true, etag, as_of }` instead of the full payload. Right before you actually dispatch, re-read *without* `since:` — liveness (live↔parked) is deliberately excluded from the etag, so a `since`-short-circuited read can be stale on exactly the signal a dispatch decision needs. **Self-identification.** A caller’s own row is stamped `isSelf:true`, and the top-level result carries `self: { ownerId, ownerLabel }` — so you can tell which roster row is you without a separate `coord:whoami` call (`self-marker.ts`). > `coord:roster { view }` (`tools/roster.ts`) is the newer unified read door — `view:"live"` is the same underlying model as `coord:presence`; `view:"history"` answers “who was ever here” for a roster with `ended` rows; `view:"claims"`/`view:"members"` cover `fleet:assignments`-shaped and membership questions. `coord:glance` gives a one-line fleet headline. `coord:presence` stays the dispatch-focused door documented here. ## coord:dispatch — assign + wake + confirm, in ONE call [Section titled “coord:dispatch — assign + wake + confirm, in ONE call”](#coorddispatch--assign--wake--confirm-in-one-call) `coord:dispatch { to, planSlug?, items?[], note }` (`tools/dispatch.ts`) replaces the hand-composed `plan_items:assign` + `coord:send` + `events:emit` + key-format ritual. It: 1. reads the target’s `sessionState`/`wakeable` via a **targeted** `coord:presence { owner: to }` lookup (not an unscoped roster read — `owner` still resolves an `ended` row, which the default `active` list now omits) so the result tells you what you dispatched to, 2. **assigns the lane** — `plan_items:assign` of `items` in `planSlug` to `to` (durable; survives the target sleeping/dying — omit `planSlug`+`items` for a pure directed wake), 3. **delivers the note + wakes** — `coord:send { wake:'required' }` persists the directed note to the target’s inbox AND fires its `coord:inbox-wake:<id>` key, and 4. returns `{ ok, to, sessionState, wakeable, assigned, delivered, woken, staged?, warning? }`. It is composed (the in-process re-dispatch pattern, like `coord:orient`) — it builds no second wake pump; it reuses `coord:send`’s deliver-and-wake, which owns the `recipient_absent`/`recipient_dead`/`staged` honesty signals. **Read the result, not your hope.** A dispatch to a non-wakeable (or non-delivering) target is a LOUD miss, never a silent `woken:0`: * `woken: 1+` → the target was parked and is now running your lane. * `warning` + `recipient_dead` / `sessionState: 'ended'` → the lane was **assigned durably** but no live process will pick it up until the target is **relaunched/resumed**. Re-dispatch to a `parked`/`live` agent or respawn this one. Do NOT assume it landed. * `staged: 1+` (EI-5957) → the target is **alive** but in **manual wake-mode** (the hive pause/edit gate), so the note was **queued for owner review**, not delivered — the #1 leader-steering trap: a quiet `staged:1` reads like success while the member never acts on it. The lane is still assigned durably; release the wake (`coord:wake-queue { action: "release_all", agent: to }`) or flip the target to auto (`coord:wake-mode { agent: to, mode: "auto" }`) — a fleet leader steering its own members almost always wants them on auto. 
```plaintext
coord:presence → pick a `parked` target → coord:dispatch { to, planSlug, items, note }
  → check woken / staged / warning → (woken target) coord:orient → plan_items:my_items → claim + work
```
 ## The woken agent’s contract: claim + work, don’t re-park [Section titled “The woken agent’s contract: claim + work, don’t re-park”](#the-woken-agents-contract-claim--work-dont-re-park) A wake starts a turn; the directed `note` is in the inbox (and the `[coord+N]` injection). A woken agent that finds a **directed assignment** must `coord:orient` → see the dispatched lane (`plan_items:my_items` / its claimed items) → **claim + work it**, not read-and-repark. Re-parking on a directed dispatch is the failure mode that makes a confirmed `woken:1` still do nothing. ## Why a dead session can still look “parked”: the reclaim lane [Section titled “Why a dead session can still look “parked”: the reclaim lane”](#why-a-dead-session-can-still-look-parked-the-reclaim-lane) Every idle agent arms a standing `coord:inbox-wake:<self>` await. A **clean** session end cancels it; a process that **crashes/is killed** never runs that hygiene, so the await row persists — and `presence`/`fetchWakeability` reads exactly that row to derive `wakeable`/`parked`. Result: a dead session shows as a live dispatch target (the “misleading zombie pile”), and the dangling await even **protects** its ghost adv\_session from the idle-session-reaper (it counts a standing await as “alive”). The **reclaim lane** (`idle-session-reaper.ts` slice 4, `reclaimDanglingInboxWakeAwaits`) is the SessionEnd-hygiene the dead process never ran: it cancels the inbox-wake await of any owner that is **not** live-or-resumable (no fresh presence heartbeat, no running bee, no in-flight wake, no OPEN adv\_session). A *parked-but-resumable* session (open adv\_session — the wake-executor can `--resume` it) keeps its await; only a session that is genuinely over loses it and flips from a false `parked` to an honest `ended`. (Work-item *claims* of dead owners are released separately by the stale-claims reaper, which already uses a heartbeat/running-bee liveness rule that is not await-polluted.) So if a coordinator sees a stale “parked” pile, the reclaim sweep — fired by the `system:idle-session-reaper` routine — converges it to honest `ended`, and reclaim “fires on dead sessions” as designed. Two more sessions are now HARD-EXEMPT from reaping regardless of heartbeat age (owner decision 2026-06-29), folded into the same `protectedOwners` set as the live/claim/wake check: `keptOnDesktop` — a session with a live OS window currently on screen (`desktop-window-liveness.ts`) — and `keptViewerAttached` — a session with no OS window but a human currently attached to its terminal in the operator PTY panel (`pty-viewer-heartbeat.ts`). Both are best-effort (headless box / no `wmctrl` → empty set), so they can only ever **protect more**, never reap more; `runIdleSessionReap`’s result surfaces both counts alongside `keptLive`. ## Wake fan-out is capped — `MAX_WAKE_FANOUT` [Section titled “Wake fan-out is capped — MAX\_WAKE\_FANOUT”](#wake-fan-out-is-capped--max_wake_fanout) `wakeRecipients` (`inbox-wake.ts`) caps how many concrete agents ONE send/dispatch will actually re-invoke: `MAX_WAKE_FANOUT` (default 64, `PAPERCUSP_MAX_WAKE_FANOUT`-tunable). Beyond the cap the overflow recipients are still **injected** (durable — they see the note on their next turn) but **not woken** — this stops a `@fleet:`/`@topic:` audience that expands to thousands of agents from turning one message into thousands of billable turns. The result carries `fanoutCapped: string[]` (the overflow ownerIds) alongside `targets`/`keys`/`woken`/`staged`/`stagedTargets` — non-empty only for an oversized audience fan; a normal directed dispatch never hits it. `stagedTargets` (the named set behind `staged`) lets a leader-steering send/dispatch surface a loud, addressed warning (“wake STAGED, not delivered for `<who>`”) instead of a bare `staged:1` — see `buildStagedWakeNote` and the `coord:dispatch` `staged` handling above.

# Cross-platform feature status — the verified audit

> Which shipped features are (and aren't) cross-platform after the 2026-07-05 hardening: the gateway-supervision fix, macOS Keychain credentials, the WSL answer, and the verified CAT1 runtime table.

# Cross-platform feature status — the verified audit (2026-07-05) [Section titled “Cross-platform feature status — the verified audit (2026-07-05)”](#cross-platform-feature-status--the-verified-audit-2026-07-05) Deliverable of plan `cross-platform-hardening-and-agent-ergonomics-2026-07-05` (P-009/P-010/P-011, WI-3059). Trigger: the packaged **Mac** app had no inference gateway and an agent “agonized” over Keychain credentials; owner asked *“I thought everything was cross-platform — I need to know about all features that are not.”* This page is the verified answer, from a 72-file systemd-reference sweep plus code-level verification of every shipped candidate. ## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) * **The product (Tauri desktop) is cross-platform by architecture.** The Tauri shell spawns + owns the operator sidecar on all three platforms and respawns it on crash (`main.rs` `decide_serve_respawn`: exit + unreachable ⇒ respawn, capped, suppressed during shutdown). * **The ONE real shipped gap was inference-gateway supervision** — systemd-only, so packaged macOS/Windows simply had **no gateway**. Fixed 2026-07-05 (see below). * Everything else that references systemd is **dev-box / CI / release-pipeline tooling that never ships** (green-checkpoint, deploy-cli, git-sync, bghost-watchdog, the units under `apps/operator/scripts/systemd/`). Those are Linux-only **by design** and should stay that way. ## The gateway gap — closed (P-006/P-007/P-008) [Section titled “The gateway gap — closed (P-006/P-007/P-008)”](#the-gateway-gap--closed-p-006p-007p-008) Before: `:8788` (paced OAuth egress for the whole fleet) was supervised ONLY by the `papercup-inference-gateway` systemd `--user` unit → never started on macOS, and not under default WSL either. Agents silently fell back to direct/default credential routing. Now (`packages/operator-core/lib/inference-gateway/gateway-sidecar-spawn.ts`, wired in `apps/operator/bin/host-bootstrap.ts` beside the spawner-sidecar block): * **Port-probe-first adoption**: if anything already listens on the gateway port (the systemd unit on the Linux dev box, a sibling operator), the supervisor ADOPTS it — no double-bind, no EADDRINUSE race. systemd is demoted to a Linux-dev optimization, not a dependency. * **Managed child otherwise**: spawn + respawn-on-crash with exponential backoff (1s→30s cap) and a 5-crashes-per-5-min circuit breaker — the same shape as `substrate-sidecar-spawn.ts` / `spawner-sidecar-spawn.ts` (third clone; extraction to a shared lib is a tracked follow-up). * **Packaged spawn path**: esbuild bundles everything into `serve.mjs`, so the packaged build re-execs itself with `PAPERCUSP_GATEWAY_SIDECAR_MODE=1` (serve.ts diverts to `runGatewaySidecarMain()` in `sidecar-main.ts`); dev spawns `npx tsx bin.ts`. Same divert pattern as the substrate/spawner sidecars. * **Gating**: env kill-switch `PAPERCUSP_GATEWAY_SUPERVISE=0` — deliberately NOT `getFlag()` at host-boot (flags resolve false when PostHog is unreachable; the stall-waker lesson). ## macOS credentials (P-004 + the `keychain:` channel) [Section titled “macOS credentials (P-004 + the keychain: channel)”](#macos-credentials-p-004--the-keychain-channel) Claude Code on macOS stores its OAuth bundle in the **login Keychain** (service `Claude Code-credentials`), NOT `~/.claude/.credentials.json`. Two consequences, both handled: * **Sign-in detection** (`agent-auth-detect.ts` `claudeKeychainSignedIn`): metadata-only probe (`security find-generic-password -s <service>` WITHOUT `-w`) — no secret fetch, no unlock prompt, fail-safe fallthrough to the file probe. * **Gateway local-fallback credential** (`credential-store.ts` `keychain:` credentialRef kind + `account-resolver.ts` `localLoginCredentialRef()`): when the file bundle is absent on darwin, the `local` fallback account resolves to `keychain:Claude Code-credentials`. The resolver is **read-only by design** — Claude Code owns the item + its refresh; the gateway re-READS near expiry and fails with actionable guidance if the bundle went stale. ⚠ Keychain ACL: the FIRST `security -w` read of an item created by another app raises a GUI “allow access” prompt — click **Always Allow** once. ✅ **Mac-VM E2E smoke verified (2026-07-06, WI-3080)**: packaged app running, gateway spawns (`gateway.log`: “up on 127.0.0.1:8788 → account ‘local’ (local-fallback)”, “supervision up in 3241ms — spawned”), `/healthz` 200, `totalRequests`/`egressAttemptsByAccount` confirm a real served request end-to-end. ⚠ **Still unverified**: this VM has a hand-provisioned `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, so it resolves the FILE credential channel — `localLoginCredentialRef()` only takes the `keychain:` path when that file is ABSENT on darwin. The keychain-specific fallback branch + the “Always Allow” ACL prompt remain unverified live; that needs a fresh-install Mac VM pass without the file (tracked as a follow-up, not blocking). ## Windows / WSL (the P-010 answer) [Section titled “Windows / WSL (the P-010 answer)”](#windows--wsl-the-p-010-answer) The Windows desktop runs the sidecar **under WSL**, where `process.platform === 'linux'` but systemd is absent by default. The host-bootstrap supervisor block runs there identically: the port probe finds nothing → it **spawns** the gateway child (bundled re-exec, since the packaged sidecar is the bundle). A WSL user who has enabled systemd + installed the unit gets adopted via the probe instead. No WSL-specific code was needed — the gap closed with P-006. Note: service-health’s bg-host code-drift probe (below) is deliberately NOT short-circuited under WSL, since WSL reports `linux`. ✅ **Windows-VM E2E smoke verified (2026-07-06, WI-3080)**: full boot watched live under the `papercup-runtime` WSL distro — `serve.mjs --ensure` → embedded PG boots + migrates → operator up (`operator.json` + `/api/health` 200 over the WSL loopback) → the gateway-sidecar supervisor spawns with no WSL-specific code and logs “up on 127.0.0.1:8788” in `~/.papercusp/gateway.log`, confirmed live with `/healthz` 200. Confirms the P-006/007/008 port-probe-first-adoption + managed-child-spawn shape genuinely works under WSL as claimed above. ## Verified CAT1 runtime table (P-009) [Section titled “Verified CAT1 runtime table (P-009)”](#verified-cat1-runtime-table-p-009) | Surface | Verdict | Evidence | | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `host-recycle.ts` | ✅ cross-platform | Mechanism = `process.exit(75)` / `exit(0)` + “supervisor restarts me”. Supervisor exists everywhere: systemd `Restart=always` (Linux dev), Tauri `decide_serve_respawn` (packaged, all OSes — exit-code-agnostic). | | `memory-watchdog.ts` | ✅ cross-platform | RSS via `process.memoryUsage().rss` (pure Node); recycle uses the same exit mechanism. The RSS high-water systemd drop-in (EI-1613) is Linux-dev tuning only; defaults apply elsewhere. | | `shutdown-state.ts` | ✅ cross-platform | Pure `process.on('SIGTERM'/'SIGINT')` drain latch — POSIX (darwin ✓); Windows runs the sidecar under WSL (= linux signal semantics). | | `bghost-watchdog.mjs` | 🐧 Linux-only **by design** | Dev-box standalone script + unit watching `papercup-bg-host` via `systemctl`/`journalctl`/`/proc/<pid>/environ`. Not imported by `serve.ts`/`host-bootstrap.ts` ⇒ not in the esbuild bundle ⇒ never ships. Not a gap. | | `service-health.ts` `probeBgHostCodeDrift` | ✅ platform-guarded (P-005) | Non-Linux returns `{ up:true, present:false, note:'Linux/systemd-only…' }` instead of a failed `systemctl` exec. | ## The rest of the 72-file systemd sweep [Section titled “The rest of the 72-file systemd sweep”](#the-rest-of-the-72-file-systemd-sweep) Everything else lives in the dev/CI/release plane and never ships in the desktop bundle: green-checkpoint + deploy-cli + release-trigger, git-sync routines, the `apps/operator/scripts/systemd/` units, dev diagnostics (`dev:*` tools), watchdog scripts. **Keep these Linux-only** — porting them would be effort spent on infrastructure that only ever runs on the Linux dev box. ## Open items [Section titled “Open items”](#open-items) 1. **Mac-VM Keychain-fallback smoke** — the supervisor boot + gateway spawn is now verified (2026-07-06), but the specific `keychain:` credential branch (file bundle ABSENT) still needs a fresh-install Mac VM pass, since the current VM has a hand-provisioned credentials file. 2. ~~Windows-VM equivalent~~ — verified 2026-07-06 (WI-3080): WSL sidecar boots the supervisor, gateway reachable, confirmed live. 3. **Sidecar-spawn extraction** — `gateway-sidecar-spawn.ts` is the third copy of the spawn/respawn/backoff shape; extract to a shared lib.

# Workspace-agnostic tools need `crossWorkspace: true` (or they fail on fleet sessions)

> A tool whose data isn't scoped by a workspace transaction (memory:*, list_workspaces, audit:*) must declare crossWorkspace:true, or the projected gate throws workspace_required on any UNSCOPED psu/fleet session — even though the call is perfectly valid.

## The symptom [Section titled “The symptom”](#the-symptom) A `defineTool` works fine from your scoped SU session but fails **fleet-wide** for bees / unscoped psu sessions with: 
```plaintext
built-in tool "memory:list" requires a workspace-scoped call — this session has
no workspace transaction. Scope the session to a workspace, or pass a per-call
workspace where the host/tool supports one.
```
 It’s **deterministic** (same shape every call) and **scope-dependent**: a session that resolved a workspace (most interactive SU sessions) never reproduces it, so it hides until a bee or an unscoped psu session hits it. This is what the improvement-watchdog filed as EI-177 / EI-178 / EI-210 (memory:search / remember / list). ## Why [Section titled “Why”](#why) The MCP host resolves `ctx.workspaceId` to `'*'` for an unscoped session (`_mcp-handler.ts`). Principal-gated tools are then run inside a workspace transaction by default — and a `'*'` session has none, so the projected gate refuses the call with `workspace_required`. But some tools are **workspace-agnostic by design**: their tables are scoped by `user-id` / `harness-slug`, never by a workspace transaction. The memory store is the canonical example (it reads `getMemoryBackend()`, never `ctx.tx`). For these, the gate is simply wrong to apply. ## The fix [Section titled “The fix”](#the-fix) Declare **`crossWorkspace: true`** on the `defineTool` definition. `definePrincipalGatedTool` threads it, handing an unscoped superuser session the admin handle + a synthesized principal instead of failing `workspace_required`: 
```ts
export default defineTool({
  name: 'memory:list',
  capability: 'memory:read',
  // The store is workspace-agnostic (tables scoped by user-id / harness-slug,
  // not by a workspace tx; handler reads getMemoryBackend, never ctx.tx).
  crossWorkspace: true,
  args: z.object({ /* … */ }),
  async handler(args, ctx) { /* … */ },
});
```
 The trap: it’s **per-tool**, so a family can drift — `search`/`remember` carried it but `list`/`update`/`forget` silently didn’t, so three of five memory tools stayed broken for fleet sessions long after the first two were “fixed”. ## Guard against re-opening it [Section titled “Guard against re-opening it”](#guard-against-re-opening-it) When a tool family must all be cross-workspace, pin it with a one-line drift-guard so a new tool (or a refactor) can’t silently drop the flag — see `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/memory/crossworkspace-invariant.test.ts`, which imports every memory tool’s real def and asserts `crossWorkspace === true`. If you add a tool that reads a user/harness-scoped store (not `ctx.tx`) and want it reachable from bees, set `crossWorkspace: true` and add it to that guard.

# A self-learning loop is "dark" until THREE gates open — but a flat output metric does NOT prove dark

> A frontier learning loop is triple-gated (routine active + flag ON + governor budgeted), so a flag being ON is not "armed". As of 2026-06-23, frontier loop flags now DEFAULT ON (bulk-flip plan), making routine active + governor budgeted the live blockers. BUT the inverse trap bites too — calibration-markets looked dark (scored:0, fix-survival bets 19→53) yet a read-first DB check showed all three gates open and the real cause was young bets (none due until ~14d out), not a dead sweep. Verify gate state AND whether anything is due-but-unresolved before concluding dark or arming. Detect with improvements:learning_loops.

The self-learning system has two opposite traps, and they look identical from a distance — a loop’s output metric reads flat (`scored: 0`, 0 champions, 0 routed ideas): 1. **Genuinely dark** — a loop built, shipped, then left un-armed (or wedged), so it produces nothing. Rots silently; the ranker prioritizes on a dead signal. 2. **Armed but young** — a loop that *is* running correctly and simply has nothing to process yet. Telling them apart is the whole game, and you can only do it by reading the **live gate state** + **whether there is anything due to process** — never by inferring from the flat metric alone. ## The triple gate [Section titled “The triple gate”](#the-triple-gate) A frontier learning loop (the 10 dark loops in `LEARNING_SINGLETONS`, `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/seed-learning-singletons.ts`) runs **only when all three are true**: 1. **Routine active** — a `@singleton/bp-singleton-<id>-0` cadence row that is `active = true` (the blueprint seeds it **inactive**). 2. **Flag ON** — e.g. `papercusp-calibration-markets`. **Note (2026-06-23):** all frontier loop flags were bulk-flipped to default ON in `FLAG_DEFAULTS` as part of plan `flip-dark-flags-default-on-2026-06-23` and removed from `KNOWN_DARK_FLAGS`. On a standard install this gate is now **auto-satisfied** — the primary live blockers are routine active (gate 1) and governor budget (gate 3). The flag gate still matters as a kill-switch (flip OFF to quiesce a loop without darkening the routine) and for loops on fresh installs before the P-001 arming campaign has run. 3. **Governor allows** — a `learning_governor_loops` row whose verdict is `allow`. **Subtle:** `budgetUsd = NULL` ⇒ `unbudgeted` ⇒ refuse, but for a `per-cycle` loop `budgetUsd = 0` (not null) **ALLOWS** — `checkLoopVerdict` (`learning-governor/core.ts:101`) short-circuits per-cycle to allow before any floor check. For a SQL-only sweep that never spends, `0` is a legitimate armed value (“0 is honest”, `calibration/governor.ts`). So “the budget is 0” does **not** mean dark; “the budget is NULL” does. **A flag being ON is NOT “armed”** (a NULL-budget or inactive-routine loop is dark despite the flag) — and equally, **a flat metric is NOT “dark”.** ## The 2026-06-14 calibration case (the inverse trap) [Section titled “The 2026-06-14 calibration case (the inverse trap)”](#the-2026-06-14-calibration-case-the-inverse-trap) calibration *looked* dark: `calibration_summary` showed `scored: 0` with the open `fix-survival` bets climbing 19 → 53 in a session — exactly the silhouette of a sweep that places bets but never resolves them.
