Complements `tool-call-batching-wrappers-2026-06-21` (hand-curated fixed-ritual wrappers) — shared `dev:tool_cooccurrence` signal + shared catalog labeling. ## Reuse: coord:orient wrapper adoption (tool-call-batching-wrappers P-013) [Section titled “Reuse: coord:orient wrapper adoption (tool-call-batching-wrappers P-013)”](#reuse-coordorient-wrapper-adoption-tool-call-batching-wrappers-p-013) The same seam measures **compound-WRAPPER** adoption, not just `code:run`. The wrapper `coord:orient` (folds the 6-call session-bootstrap into one) gets the identical A/B: * **Scenarios:** `su-S17-orient-bootstrap` (reach-for-the-bundle at wake) + its guard `su-S18-orient-not-for-single` (don’t wrap a lone inbox read). Same pair for `harness:overview` (`su-S19` / `su-S20`). * **Arms:** baseline (orient available) vs `orient-no-bundle` (`{configDelta:{excludeTools:['coord:orient']}}`, committed at `lib/llm-testing/variants/orient-no-bundle.json`) — the without-bundle cost. * **Run:** `cd apps/operator && PAPERCUSP_ANTHROPIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8788 PAPERCUSP_LLM_TEST_SKIP_CLAIM=1 LLM_TEST_SUT_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_JUDGE_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_SIM_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 npm run llm-test -- --scenario su-S17-orient-bootstrap [--variant @<repo>/packages/operator-core/lib/llm-testing/variants/orient-no-bundle.json] --no-matrix` **⚠ Prerequisite the smoke surfaced:** the SUT only sees the curated **`SU_CATALOG`** (`lib/llm-testing/targets/su-catalog.ts`), NOT the live tool registry — so a NEW wrapper must be ADDED there or the SUT reports *“I don’t have a `coord:orient` tool in my catalog”* and the reach-assert can never pass. (coord:orient + harness:overview added 2026-06-21 — the smoke caught it.) **Finding (haiku, N=1 — directional):** with `coord:orient` in the catalog the engineer **reached for it at Turn 0** (the `reaches-for-orient` assert passed); the `no-orient` arm fanned coord:presence + coord:inbox + plans:search and took **6 turns / $0.042 vs the bundle’s 4 turns / $0.036** — the same turns/cost reduction availability buys `code:run`. Both arms flopped the *helpfulness* judge (haiku’s capability ceiling — it orients, then stalls on empty payloads), so the CLEAN task-completion win is model-gated: **re-run on sonnet** (drop the `LLM_TEST_*_MODEL` overrides) for the definitive adoption + turns/cost deltas — same caveat as the code:run A/B above. ## Bulk-arg adoption (bulk-endpoint-standardization P-007) [Section titled “Bulk-arg adoption (bulk-endpoint-standardization P-007)”](#bulk-arg-adoption-bulk-endpoint-standardization-p-007) The same seam measures the **bulk-arg** path — a simpler “collapse N calls into one” optimization that doesn’t require a script runtime. Many multi-arity tools now accept `{ ids:[…] }` in addition to `{ id }` (every repeated-call read is dual-arity). When the engineer needs the same detail for every item in a collection, does it fire ONE `work_items:get { ids:[…] }` instead of `work_items:get { id }` once per item? * **Scenarios:** `su-S21-bulk-read-not-hand-loop` (reach for `{ ids:[…] }` on a 6-item collection; load-bearing assert: at most ONE `work_items:get` call total) + its guard `su-S22-bulk-not-for-single` (single known id → `{ id }` directly, no collection machinery — the over-application guard). The earlier **`su-S16-code-run-batch-write`** (a HOMOGENEOUS *write*: same state applied to every item) was retargeted onto this same bulk-arg path (`version: 2`, D-004) rather than code:run’s write/confirm-gate — reach for `work_items:set_state { ids:[…], state }` in ONE call, not a script. * **Arms:** same variant seam (excludeTools / promptOverlay / variantId) as the code:run A/B. * **Key difference from code:run:** no script needed — the bulk call IS the tool call. The adoption bar is lower (no language-model capability ceiling on scripting), but the model must still recognize the pattern and prefer the single bulk call over issuing separate per-id calls. ## Newer test dimensions (S23–S27) — correctness and behavioral compliance [Section titled “Newer test dimensions (S23–S27) — correctness and behavioral compliance”](#newer-test-dimensions-s23s27--correctness-and-behavioral-compliance) Scenarios beyond S22 cover **different axes** from adoption — correctness of a specific protocol and behavioral compliance with shared-base policies. They use the same `SU_RUBRIC` + assert infrastructure but are NOT A/B arms in the adoption sense. * **S23–S25 (delta-merge, agent-tool-delta-protocol P-007):** Correctness of applying a semantic delta response — does the agent merge the incoming delta against the base snapshot it still holds in context (S23: happy path when base is present; S24: fallback when base was compacted; S25: correctly ignores a wrong-merge attempt)? * **S26 (take-charge-dont-wait):** Behavioral compliance with the `CONCURRENCY_FIRST_NOTE` “never wait for a calm window; a non-resource block is a BUG to fix” policy in `prompt-build.ts`. The presence test (`prompt-build.test.ts`) asserts the note is IN the prompt; S26 asserts the agent actually BEHAVES on it (force-deploys rather than ending a turn asking “want me to verify once it propagates?”). * **S27 (woke-to-dispatch-claims):** Behavioral compliance with the `PEER_WAKE_NOTE` in `prompt-build.ts` (added 2026-06-24, step 3j of `buildPromptParts`). The note teaches: a parked agent does nothing until re-invoked; when woken by a directed dispatch, CLAIM + WORK the lane that turn — never read-and-repark. S27 asserts this: the engineer claims the dispatched items in the same turn it was woken rather than acknowledging and re-parking (`coord:await-inbox` / ending without claiming). The presence test for both S26/S27 policies is `prompt-build.test.ts` (every role’s compiled prompt CONTAINS the note); S26/S27 are the behavioral complements — proving the in-prompt policy changes actual agent decisions, not just prompt content. ## Production telemetry — the live waste + adoption metrics (2026-06-25 baseline) [Section titled “Production telemetry — the live waste + adoption metrics (2026-06-25 baseline)”](#production-telemetry--the-live-waste--adoption-metrics-2026-06-25-baseline) The A/B above measures adoption inside the llm-testing harness. To track the SAME levers on the **live fleet** — and to confirm plan `agent-tooling-token-efficiency-2026-06-25` actually moved them — query `harness_shared.tool_invocations` directly (`dev:pg_query`). Three metrics; re-run weekly and compare to this baseline. **⚠ Denominator: measure agent traffic on the `mcp` transport ONLY.** The raw call total is dominated by **UI HTTP polling** — `plans:list` + `plans:attention` alone ran **\~25 calls/sec** (45,943 in a 30-min sample, each a distinct `run_id`) over the `http` transport, which is *not* agent LLM tokens. Agent-authored work is the `mcp` transport (\~13k calls/6h). Every adoption ratio below filters `transport='mcp'`, or it is meaningless (raw code:run share looks like 0.0004% only because of the polling-inflated denominator; against `mcp` the honest figure is \~0.006% — still \~zero, but measure it right). ### 1. String-limit failure rate — did the validation-limit work land? [Section titled “1. String-limit failure rate — did the validation-limit work land?”](#1-string-limit-failure-rate--did-the-validation-limit-work-land) 
```sql
-- too-long-string validation failures by tool, last 14d (baseline: ~1,000+; top fleet:place_batch.brief=412)
SELECT tool_name, count(*) AS errs, max(invoked_at) AS last_seen,
       (array_agg(error_message ORDER BY invoked_at DESC))[1] AS sample
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status <> 'ok' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '14 days'
  AND (error_message ILIKE '%must contain at most%' OR error_message ILIKE '%Too big%'
       OR error_message ILIKE '%expected string to have <=%' OR error_code ILIKE '%too_big%')
GROUP BY tool_name ORDER BY errs DESC;
```
 Target after the fix: advisory-field tools (loop:arm.goal, coord notes, fleet briefs, …) drop to \~0 (they now *truncate* instead of reject); the rest fall sharply (caps raised 4–8×). ### 2. code:run adoption share (mcp transport) [Section titled “2. code:run adoption share (mcp transport)”](#2-coderun-adoption-share-mcp-transport) 
```sql
-- baseline 2026-06-25: code:run 9 / 3d, code:tools 1 — ~0.006% of mcp agent calls
WITH mcp AS (SELECT * FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
             WHERE transport='mcp' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '3 days')
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:run')   AS coderun,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:tools') AS codetools,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp)                              AS mcp_total,
       round(100.0*(SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:run')
             /NULLIF((SELECT count(*) FROM mcp),0),4)          AS coderun_pct;
```
 **Since 2026-07-03 the canonical opportunity-based metric (`dev:code_run_adoption` / `CODE_RUN_ADOPTION_SQL`) carries the same denominator discipline built in** — `transport='mcp' AND spawn_id IS NOT NULL`, plus poller tools (`activity:recent`) excluded from opportunity classification: a UI poller firing the same read twice is not a batchable agent flow (it manufactured \~87k fake opportunities/7d and made fleet adoption read 0.26% when the honest figure was \~22%). If you hand-roll an adoption query, copy those filters or your number is fiction. **Nudge→conversion funnel (2026-07-03):** every inline batch-hint fire is now recorded (migration `482`, `harness_shared.code_run_nudge_fires`) and `dev:code_run_adoption` returns `nudge: { nudgedSessions, convertedSessions }` — the direct measure of whether a nudged session then called `code:run`/`recipes:run`. Details + the structural-lockout finding (kits/caps/surface gate adoption before wording does): [code-run-adoption-metric](/agent-insights/code-run-adoption-metric/). **The structural-lockout finding, closed (`code-run-self-state-adoption-2026-07-03` P-001/P-003):** the lockout the metric above documented — `code:run` scoped to `SU_ROLES` only, so BEE/QUEEN-kit agents (the bulk of fleet adoption opportunity) could never reach it no matter how the nudge was worded — is now fixed at the root. `prompt-build.ts`’s `CODE_RUN_NUDGE` self-gate comment used to read “self-gated … since the tool is SU\_ROLES-scoped, so roles without it ignore it”; since P-001 it instead self-gates on “roles whose surface/envelope still lacks it”, because the BEE/QUEEN kits * the CORE spine now carry `code:run` and the self-gate resolves **TRUE fleet-wide** — SU\_ROLES scoping was the lockout signature, not a wording problem. P-003 closed the same class one layer down: `role-principal-caps.ts` had **drifted behind** several roles’ own seeded kits (a role’s kit advertised a tool its principal caps then denied — measured via 14d of `role-not-allowed` telemetry: the herald’s `memory:search`/`recipes:search` denied at wake every time, the queen’s `memory:search` denied 106×, bees denied on their own kit’s `capability:git`/`capability:read`/etc. dozens of times). **Practical effect for this A/B methodology:** the in-process `su` target’s `excludeTools`/kit simulation was always accurate for the SU surface, but any fleet-wide adoption number pulled from `harness_shared.tool_invocations` (§ Production telemetry below) measured against the OLD lockout baseline — re-run metric #2 post-P-001/P-003 before trusting a “still \~0%” adoption read; a role that structurally couldn’t reach `code:run` before now can, so the honest floor moved. ### 3. Redundant-bootstrap rate — orient duplication (the bigger leak) [Section titled “3. Redundant-bootstrap rate — orient duplication (the bigger leak)”](#3-redundant-bootstrap-rate--orient-duplication-the-bigger-leak) The win is agents NOT re-calling what `coord:orient` already returned. Baseline: orient co-fires with `coord:plan-events`/`memory:search`/`coord:inbox`/`coord:declare-intent` at \~1.0 confidence (lift 450–660 in `dev:tool_cooccurrence`). The precise per-spawn form: 
```sql
-- of spawns that called coord:orient, how many ALSO re-called a call orient already subsumed?
WITH s AS (
  SELECT spawn_id,
         bool_or(tool_name='coord:orient') AS oriented,
         bool_or(tool_name IN ('coord:plan-events','memory:search','coord:inbox','coord:declare-intent')) AS redundant
  FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
  WHERE transport='mcp' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '24 hours' AND spawn_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY spawn_id)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented) AS oriented_spawns,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented AND redundant) AS also_redundant,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented AND redundant)
             /NULLIF(count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented),0),1) AS pct_redundant
FROM s;
```
 Target after the orient-dedup guidance (orient.ts + the MCP instructions) + the soft re-call nudge: `pct_redundant` trends down from \~100%. (`dev:tool_cooccurrence { hours, orderBy:'confidence' }` is the quick read; this query is the precise one.) Wire all three into a weekly check (a scorecard row or a `dev:` rollup) so a regression — a new tool shipping a tight cap, or adoption sliding back — surfaces without a manual audit. **WI-839 — each metric is a first-class read** (mirrors `dev:code_run_adoption`’s pattern for metric #2 above): * **Metric #1** (string-limit failure rate) → **`dev:limit_failure_rate { sinceDays? }`** (`packages/operator-core/lib/limit-failure-rate.ts`) — a fleet total + per-tool breakdown + a graded rating (`healthy` < 10 errs/window, `broken` ≥ 100). * **Metric #3** (orient-dedup / redundant-recall rate) → **`dev:orient_dedup_rate { sinceHours? }`** (`packages/operator-core/lib/orient-dedup-rate.ts`) — oriented-spawn count, redundant-recall count, `pctRedundant`, and a graded rating (`healthy` < 25%, `broken` ≥ 60%). * Both are pure + unit-tested (injected `RunQuery`, no PG in tests) exactly like `code-run-adoption.ts`; each exports its canonical SQL (`LIMIT_FAILURE_RATE_SQL` / `ORIENT_DEDUP_RATE_SQL`) so it is also directly runnable via `dev:pg_query` if a caller wants the raw rows instead of the rolled-up read. **WI-839 — now ALSO a recurring measurement, not just an on-demand `dev:` read.** The dev: tools above are manual (someone has to remember to call them); the item’s real ask (“so a regression surfaces without a manual audit”) needed a periodic surface. `system-health/compute.ts`’s `collectToolEfficiency` folds all 3 grades (adoption + limit-failure + orient-dedup) into ONE new Health-tab panel (`PanelKey: 'toolEfficiency'`, `types.ts`) computed on every `computeSystemHealth` tick (the same \~30s cadence every other panel runs on) — surfaced on the read-only Health tab (flag `papercusp-system-health-tab`) with zero bespoke UI code (the tab renders generically off `PANEL_ORDER`/`health.panels[key]`). Panel status: `crit` if any leg graded `broken`, `warn` if any is `degraded`, `unknown` only when every leg’s window is too small to grade, else `ok` (`toolEfficiencyStatus`, pure + unit-tested in `compute.test.ts`). So a regression in any of the 3 now greys/reds a Health-tab card automatically, on the existing tick — no manual `dev:` call or `dev:pg_query` needed to notice one.

# mem0 entity store leaked COMPOUND fragments into memory recall — the collectionName the canonical store ignores

> 84% of memory_canonical was mem0 entity-linking junk ("ticks with", "s interactive session") surfacing in memory:search — mem0 separates its entity store ONLY by a *_entities collectionName suffix, and our patched CanonicalVectorStore ignored collectionName, so both stores shared one pool. Fix at the store, not the read seam.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) `memory:search` (and pre-turn injection candidates) returned junk fragment rows at near-zero scores — `"ticks with"`, `"s interactive session"`, `"second watchdog added to"` — each carrying `metadata: { entityType: 'COMPOUND', linkedMemoryIds: [...] }` (EI-366). At the 2026-06-12 audit, 6 of the top-10 hits for a representative query were fragments, and **1,829 of 2,170 rows (84%) in `harness_shared.memory_canonical` were entity rows** — only 341 real memories. The Learning tab’s `totalMemories` counted all of them. ## Root cause — a collection contract our store patch silently dropped [Section titled “Root cause — a collection contract our store patch silently dropped”](#root-cause--a-collection-contract-our-store-patch-silently-dropped) mem0ai 3.x’s `Memory.add()` runs entity extraction (proper nouns, quoted strings, compound noun phrases) and writes each entity as a row in a **second vector store**, created by `getEntityStore()` in `mem0ai/oss` via the same VectorStoreFactory with the same config except `collectionName` suffixed `_entities`. Entity payloads are `{ data, entityType, linkedMemoryIds, user_id }`. At search time mem0 reads that store back for its entity-boost pass — the machinery is legitimate. Our `CanonicalVectorStore` (patched into mem0’s factory — `libs/generic/memory/src/mem0-client.ts`) **deliberately ignores `collectionName`** so canonical rows survive embedder-mode switches. That design choice silently erased the ONLY thing distinguishing mem0’s entity store from its memory store: both instances wrote to the same `memory_canonical` + vec tables, and semantic search over the memory pool returned entity fragments as memories. ## Fix — segregate at the store, not the read seam [Section titled “Fix — segregate at the store, not the read seam”](#fix--segregate-at-the-store-not-the-read-seam) `libs/generic/memory/src/canonical-store.ts` now derives a store kind from the collectionName suffix (`*_entities` → entity store) and partitions `search()`/`list()` by **payload shape**: entity payloads always carry `entityType`; real memory payloads never do (`payload ? 'entityType'` / `NOT (payload ? 'entityType')`). Why this layer (the brief’s read-seam-vs-indexer investigation): * A read-seam filter (in `Mem0Backend.search` or the tool) would hide the junk from us but leave mem0’s OWN entity-boost pass broken — its entity-store searches were matching real memory rows too (and its ≥0.95-similarity dedupe could link entities onto memories). * The store-level partition fixes BOTH directions with no migration and no backfill: the 1,829 pre-fix entity rows become invisible to memory recall and correctly visible to the entity store, retroactively. * Top-K is no longer wasted: pre-fix, fragments consumed most of the candidate slots before the score floor. `readMemoryHealth` (knowledge-read.ts) now counts `totalMemories` excluding entity rows and reports `entityRows` separately; recall telemetry (`memory_recall_stats`, migration 240) carries a `fragment_count` regression canary surfaced on the Learning tab memory-health card — it must stay 0. ## Watch out for [Section titled “Watch out for”](#watch-out-for) * **Any vector-store impl handed to mem0 must honor collection separation** — by name, by table, or by a payload discriminator. If a future backend ignores `collectionName`, it has this bug. * The discriminator is payload shape. Never write `entityType` into a real memory’s metadata via `memory:remember` — it would be segregated out of recall. * Tests: `libs/generic/memory/src/canonical-store.test.ts` pins the SQL partition; the live proof is the audit query returning zero `entityType` rows in its top 10.

# mem0 extraction rides the Claude session — and the OAuth cache must never live forever

> Fact extraction's cascade rung

## The path (mem0-extraction-via-claude-session-2026-06-06) [Section titled “The path (mem0-extraction-via-claude-session-2026-06-06)”](#the-path-mem0-extraction-via-claude-session-2026-06-06) mem0’s fact-extraction LLM (the model that distills `remember(raw)` into facts and decides ADD/UPDATE/DELETE) resolves through a **three-rung cascade** (`resolveExtractionLlmConfig`, `libs/generic/memory/src/mem0-client.ts`): 1. **claude-session** — `SessionExtractionLlm` (`packages/operator-core/lib/memory/session-extraction-llm.ts`): `claude-haiku-4-5` direct to api.anthropic.com, authenticated with Claude Code’s own OAuth token (`~/.claude/.credentials.json` → `claudeAiOauth.accessToken`, header `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20`). Probe-validated at client build (models-endpoint GET — only an explicit 401/403 disqualifies; network blips pass so an offline box keeps its extractor). Strict-JSON output with ONE repair retry, then a throw that the cascade serves from the next rung — mem0 never sees unparseable text. 2. **Anthropic API key** (probe-validated, `LLM_MODEL` Haiku). 3. **OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`** (the understudy the whole fleet ran on while the Anthropic key was stale — and the extractor behind the scorecard’s misleading 0/6 near-dup result; under Haiku it’s 4/6, see `.papercusp/bench-reports/memory-dedup-haiku-2026-06-07T00-44-05-016Z.md`). The session rung is injected through the host seam (`MemoryHost.getExtractionLlm`, wired in `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/configure.ts`) — `libs/generic/memory` stays domain-free and only knows the mem0ai custom-LLM interface + a generic `FallbackExtractionLlm` primary→fallback wrapper. ## The gotcha: a forever-cached OAuth token in a long-lived process [Section titled “The gotcha: a forever-cached OAuth token in a long-lived process”](#the-gotcha-a-forever-cached-oauth-token-in-a-long-lived-process) `resolveStatelessTransport()` caches the Claude token **per process** (`_claudeTokenCache`). Fine for a short-lived CLI; in the long-lived operator the claude CLI **rotates the credentials file under you**, and a forever-cache eventually serves an expired token. The first time this class of failure hit (a stale Anthropic *API key*, pre-session-rung), mem0 swallowed the 401s inside `Memory.add()` and returned `{results: []}` — **every write a silent no-op for weeks** (“stillborn”, memory-backend-benchmark D-007). The session rung closes the class structurally (D-004): * On 401/403: invalidate the token cache → re-read `~/.claude/.credentials.json` → retry **once**. * Still failing: throw `ExtractionAuthError` → `FallbackExtractionLlm` **sticky-demotes** the rung for the process lifetime (re-probed next boot) and serves the call from the key rungs — with a `warnOnce` (`[mem0-session]` / `[memory]` prefixes). * No fallback available: the error **rethrows WITH the warning fired** — visible, never silent. The loudness contract is pinned by tests: a dead token must yield *successful writes via the next rung plus a fired warning* (`session-extraction-llm.test.ts` in operator-core; `extraction-llm.test.ts` in `libs/generic/memory`). Debugging 'memory writes nothing' Check the rungs in order. `PAPERCUSP_MEM0_SESSION_EXTRACTION=0` disables rung 1 entirely (escape hatch). A `[mem0-session] … auth-rejected by the probe` warning means the session token is dead → key rungs. If you see NO warning and no stored facts, suspect the embedder (‘disabled’ is a hard stop for the whole client) — not extraction. ## Verifying it live [Section titled “Verifying it live”](#verifying-it-live) * **Round-trip probe** (isolated schema; exit 2 = skip without a session): `npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/memory/session-extraction-live.ts` — also registered in the `/adv` Tests tab (Memory → Live). Proof-of-rung is the adapter’s own usage counters (`sessionExtractionUsage()`), not just a stored row. * **Telemetry**: every session-rung call lands a usage sample in `harness_shared.agent_usage_samples` (provider `anthropic`, class `haiku`) via the shared stateless usage sink — tokens are metered against the Max quota even though marginal cost is \~$0. * A staging (`:3170`) `memory:remember` whose stored text comes back **rewritten** (not your verbatim input) is extraction working; verbatim echo means the write skipped extraction (`verbatim: true`) or the client fell back to a degraded path. ## Two test-side gotchas (from the Phase 1/2 build) [Section titled “Two test-side gotchas (from the Phase 1/2 build)”](#two-test-side-gotchas-from-the-phase-12-build) 1. **mem0ai’s `memory` vector-store provider is NOT in-process-only.** It persists to `~/.mem0/vector_store.db` (+ `vector_store_entities.db`) by default, so a “hermetic” test pollutes the homedir — and later runs **hash-dedup against the stale rows, silently returning `[]` on add**. Pass `dbPath: ':memory:'` in `vectorStore.config` (see the comment in `libs/generic/memory/src/extraction-llm.test.ts`). 2. **`getMemoryClient()` cannot run under vitest** — the bundler-dodging `new Function('return import(...)')` dynamicImport has no import callback in vitest’s runner. That’s why the loudness test composes `SessionExtractionLlm` + `FallbackExtractionLlm` + a real `Memory` manually, and why live verification is a **tsx runner**, not a vitest file (`mem0-client.test.ts` header documents it).

# `mem0_unavailable` can be a swallowed bug, not just an outage

> The memory:* tools return { ok:false, reason:'mem0_unavailable' } whenever getMemoryClient() returns null — which happens for env gaps (no LLM key / no embedder / unreachable PG) AND when the mem0 Memory constructor throws and is caught. Don't read it as "not a regression"; check the warning, or round-trip the store.

## The symptom [Section titled “The symptom”](#the-symptom) Every `memory:*` tool (`remember` / `search` / `list` / `forget` / `update`) can return: 
```json
{ "ok": false, "reason": "mem0_unavailable" }
```
 It is tempting to treat this as a benign environmental outage. **Do not.** It means exactly one thing — `getMemoryClient()` returned `null` — and one of the ways that happens is a **real bug that got swallowed**. Danger A real defect (a mem0ai version incompatibility) made the memory subsystem **100% non-functional** while showing only this same clean `mem0_unavailable`. The fix is commit `879fc733`. An earlier version of this very insight wrongly claimed the symptom is “almost always an outage, not a regression.” It isn’t. Treat `mem0_unavailable` as unknown until you’ve read the reason. ## What actually produces it [Section titled “What actually produces it”](#what-actually-produces-it) The verb wrappers (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/memory/*.ts`) are simple: 
```ts
const client = await getMemoryClient();
if (!client) return { /* reason: 'mem0_unavailable' */ };
```
 So the real question is **why `getMemoryClient()` (→ `tryLoad()` in `libs/generic/memory/src/mem0-client.ts`) returns `null`.** Four causes, and only the first three are “outages”: | # | Cause | Outage or bug? | | - | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | | 1 | `resolveEmbedder()` → `{ mode:'disabled' }` (user disabled, or `auto` found no OpenAI key and `@huggingface/transformers` absent) | outage | | 2 | `pgFields()` throws — admin URL unreachable/unparseable | outage | | 3 | No Anthropic **and** no OpenAI key (mem0 needs an LLM for `add()` fact-extraction; creds are encrypted in `operator_credentials.payload_ct`) | outage | | 4 | **`new Memory(...)` THREW and was caught** (`tryLoad`’s try/catch) — a mem0ai API/version mismatch, a bad config, a missing patch | **bug** | Cause 4 is the trap: a genuine construction failure is caught and folded into the *same* `null` → `mem0_unavailable` as the benign cases. **The symptom alone cannot tell an outage from a regression.** ## The decisive diagnostic: read the warning [Section titled “The decisive diagnostic: read the warning”](#the-decisive-diagnostic-read-the-warning) `tryLoad()` calls `warnOnce(<reason>)` before every `null`. That string is the diagnosis: * `embedder unavailable: …` / `no Anthropic or OpenAI API key …` / `couldn't resolve PG connection: …` → **outage** (cause 1–3). * `Unsupported embedder provider: custom`, `fn is not a function`, `require is not defined`, or any other constructor error → **bug** (cause 4). Investigate, don’t shrug. A thrown **MCP error** (not a structured `mem0_unavailable`) — e.g. `@papercusp/memory is not configured…` — is a *third* category: broken seam wiring (`configureMemory()` never ran / a bad import). That one is unambiguously a regression. ## The mem0ai 3.x bug this insight was born from [Section titled “The mem0ai 3.x bug this insight was born from”](#the-mem0ai-3x-bug-this-insight-was-born-from) Two defects, both hidden behind `mem0_unavailable` (fixed in `879fc733`): 1. **Custom embedder unsupported.** The store builds mem0 with `embedder: { provider: 'custom', config: { embed } }`, but mem0ai 3.0.3’s `EmbedderFactory` only knows openai/ollama/lmstudio/google/ azure\_openai/langchain — it throws `Unsupported embedder provider: custom`. We patched `VectorStoreFactory` (for the `canonical` store) but never `EmbedderFactory`. Both are exported from `mem0ai/oss`, so patch both. **Gotcha:** the `custom` embedder must read a module-level fn, **not** `config.embed` — mem0’s `ConfigManager.mergeConfig` strips function-valued config fields during Zod validation (you’ll see `fn is not a function` at dimension auto-detect). 2. **`require('pg')` under ESM.** `@papercusp/memory` runs as ESM (not in Next’s `transpilePackages`), where `require` is undefined — the pgvector probe threw `require is not defined`, silently downgrading the store to mem0’s **volatile in-process** provider. Use `await import('pg')`. A **third** patched factory landed since (`mem0-client.ts` `patchLlmFactory`, same shape as the two above): mem0ai 3.x’s `LLMFactory.create` is also a hard-coded provider switch with no `custom` case, needed so session-backed extraction can route through the host’s own Claude/Anthropic session instead of a separately-configured LLM. It follows the identical module-level-fn pattern (`_currentExtractionLlm`, not `config`-carried, same Zod-stripping reason) and the identical swallow risk — `patchLlmFactory` failing throws `warnOnce('mem0 LLMFactory not patchable…')` down the same cause-4 path, not a loud error. Pinned against the real `mem0ai` module by `extraction-llm.test.ts` so an upstream interface change fails a test, not production silently. If you’re auditing “which mem0 internals does this repo monkey-patch”, it’s now three: `VectorStoreFactory`, `EmbedderFactory`, `LLMFactory` — check all three when mem0ai bumps its version. ## Prove the full path actually works [Section titled “Prove the full path actually works”](#prove-the-full-path-actually-works) Don’t trust a passing tsc or a mocked unit test — round-trip the real store. Decrypt the OpenAI key from `operator_credentials` via pgcrypto (`pgp_sym_decrypt(payload_ct, <~/.papercusp/db-encryption-key>)`), `configureMemory()` with `getAdminUrl`/`getCredentials`/`resolveEmbedder`, then `getMemoryClient()` → `add()` → `search()` → `getAll()` → `delete()`. A real OpenAI-backed round-trip against the canonical pgvector store takes seconds and is the only thing that proves cause 4 is clear. To exercise just the storage layer **without** an LLM, drive `CanonicalVectorStore` directly (it needs only PG + a pre-computed 384-dim vector) — see [`embedded-pg-discovery`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/embedded-pg-discovery/) for how `getHarnessAdminUrl()` resolves (the native fallback PG may be fully provisioned even with the desktop down). `memory_canonical.id` is a UUID column — use a valid UUID, scope to a throwaway `user_id`, delete after. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * [`live-pg-regression-sentinel`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/live-pg-regression-sentinel/) — the broader “verify against live PG, not just unit tests” pattern. * [`embedded-pg-discovery`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/embedded-pg-discovery/) — PG URL resolution + the native fallback.

# METR HCAST time-horizon bench — run it via taskhelper.py, not the private Inspect bridge

> The official inspect-metr-task-bridge (mtb) won't install (6 private METR PyPI deps). Drive the pre-built task images directly with the Task Standard's public taskhelper.py. Plus the human-time-baseline join and the two-arm horizon-lift framing.

The METR HCAST / time-horizon suite (`suite='metr-hcast'`, plan `benchmark-suite-metr-hcast-2026-06-17`) measures a **50%/80%-task-completion time horizon** — the human-expert task LENGTH at which an arm succeeds 50%/80% of the time — and reports the **hive-vs-single-opus horizon LIFT**. Integration lives under `packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/metr-hcast-*` + the horizon math in `libs/generic/bench-metrics/src/horizon.ts`. ## The load-bearing gotcha: the official Inspect bridge won’t install [Section titled “The load-bearing gotcha: the official Inspect bridge won’t install”](#the-load-bearing-gotcha-the-official-inspect-bridge-wont-install) METR’s README says to run tasks via the **Inspect Task Bridge** (`inspect-metr-task-bridge`, the `mtb` package). **It cannot install on a public box** — its `pyproject` pins six METR-internal packages that are not on public PyPI: `metr-task-artifacts`, `metr-task-assets`, `metr-task-aux-vm-helpers`, `metr-task-legacy-verifier`, `metr-task-protected-scoring`, `metr-task-standard`. `pip install` dies on `metr-task-artifacts`. (`inspect_ai` itself installs fine.) **Drive the task images directly with the Task Standard’s own `drivers/taskhelper.py`** — the public, dependency-free script the bridge merely wraps (vendored in `~/.papercusp/bench-harnesses/metr/task-standard`). That is what `dockerTaskStandardOps` (metr-hcast-live.ts) does. ### The container recipe (validated end-to-end) [Section titled “The container recipe (validated end-to-end)”](#the-container-recipe-validated-end-to-end) Pre-built images: `registry-1.docker.io/metrevals/public-tasks:<family>-<version>` (\~4 GB, anonymous Docker Hub pull). They ship the `TaskFamily` at `/root/<family>.py` + the unprivileged `agent` user (uid 1000) but **NOT** `taskhelper.py` — copy it in. 
```bash
docker run -d --name c --entrypoint sh "$IMG" -c 'tail -f /dev/null'
docker cp task-standard/drivers/taskhelper.py c:/root/taskhelper.py
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> start    # sets up + chowns /home/agent
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> setup    # → {instructions, ...}
#   ...agent works inside as `agent` user, produces a submission string...
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> score -s "<submission>"   # → float
docker rm -f c
```
 Output is the line `SEP_MUfKWkpuVDn9E` then a JSON result (`parseTaskhelperResult`). `score()` returns a float (binary tasks: `0.0`/`1.0`); `resolved = score >= threshold` (default `1.0`). ## The human-time baselines: join the open tasks to runs.jsonl [Section titled “The human-time baselines: join the open tasks to runs.jsonl”](#the-human-time-baselines-join-the-open-tasks-to-runsjsonl) The horizon fit needs a human-time baseline per task. The open `metr/public-tasks` repo ships **31 runnable tasks (10 families)** but the structured baselines live in `metr/eval-analysis-public/reports/time-horizon-1-*/data/raw/runs.jsonl` (field `human_minutes`, keyed by `task_id = <family>/<task>`). Joining the two yields only **18 horizon-eligible tasks** (16 `baseline` + 2 `estimate`), spanning \~2–95 min — the other 13 (clone\_game, complex\_payments, cowthello, crossword, several variants) are newer dangerous-capability families absent from METR’s released horizon dataset. The vendoring step writes `~/.papercusp/bench-results/metr-hcast/tasks.jsonl` with `horizonEligible`. ## The math + the honest framing (don’t skip) [Section titled “The math + the honest framing (don’t skip)”](#the-math--the-honest-framing-dont-skip) `fitHorizon` (bench-metrics) is a faithful port of METR’s reference (`eval-analysis-public/src/horizon`): **weighted logistic regression of success on `log2(human_minutes)`, horizon = `2^((logit(q) − intercept)/coef)`**, reg `1e-5`, hierarchical-bootstrap CIs. The golden test reproduces METR’s published Claude 3.7 Sonnet \~50–60 min horizon (we get p50 ≈ 63 min on their data). **The absolute horizon on \~18 short tasks is illustrative-only — NOT leaderboard-comparable** (METR’s real fit spans seconds→8 h over \~170 tasks). The **defensible headline is the LIFT**: treatment (hive, `papercusp`) vs baseline (single-opus, `baseline-a-ablation`) on the SAME tasks cancels much of the subset bias (plan D-002). `buildMetrHcastReport` emits three mandatory caveats — surface them. ## Running it (host-gated) [Section titled “Running it (host-gated)”](#running-it-host-gated) 
```bash
npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/_xbench_metr_hcast.ts \
  --task-set metr-hcast-horizon --arms baseline-a-ablation,papercusp \
  --samples 5 --account <quiet-acct> --concurrency 2 \
  --out ~/.papercusp/bench-results/metr-hcast/run.json
```
 **Gateway contention is the operational gotcha.** Each arm routes opus-4.8 through the gateway; under concurrent benches (tau2 / agentsnet / the fleet) the shared accounts **429 globally** — every account on both `:8788` and `:8799` returned the same synthetic `rate_limit_error`. `gatewayModelCall` retries transient 429s and supports `--account <id>` (the `x-papercusp-account` header) to pin a quiet account, but a clean multi-sample run still needs a genuinely quiet opus window. The 429→`infra-failed` fairness path (excluded from the fit, never a capability fail) is the same discipline as the rest of external-bench.

# Migrating a bespoke loop to a deterministic / hybrid blueprint

> The established pattern for deterministic-blueprints-migration — a learning loop becomes a program-mode blueprint whose steps are registered step-ops (deterministic capability ops + spawn-roles for agents), fired on a cadence by system:blueprint-run. Reuse the lib logic; don't rewrite.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The blueprint **program-mode spine** (`spine.steps` + optional `spine.gate`) is the deterministic-step substrate. A “deterministic step” is **not a new engine** — it is a registered typed function (a `CoordOp`: `name` + `argsSchema`/`resultSchema` * `run(args, ctx)`) that the program runner executes as a checkpointed step. The coord-op registry is the step-op registry; coordination ops are one family, deterministic capability ops (wrapping lib logic) are another. (Plan: `deterministic-blueprints-migration-2026-06-13`, P-010/P-011.) Two program shapes, discriminated by the gate (no schema field): * **deterministic pipeline** — `steps`, **NO gate**. Runs every step then resolves `done`. The migrated learning loops (negative-space, neologism, fleet-ekg, …). * **decision program** — `steps` + `gate` (must have a fallback). vote / deliberate. ## How to migrate a loop (the recipe) [Section titled “How to migrate a loop (the recipe)”](#how-to-migrate-a-loop-the-recipe) 1. **Reuse the lib logic — don’t rewrite (D-003).** Extract the loop’s flag → governor → tick orchestration into a shared `run<Loop>Mine`-style fn (one source of truth) with **injectable deps as parameters**. Example: `packages/operator-core/lib/negative-space/mine.ts` (`runNegativeSpaceMine`). The existing `system:<loop>` action then delegates to it (keeps its test seams), and so does the new op — provably behavior-neutral (D-004). 2. **Write the deterministic step-op** under `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/ops/<loop>.ts`: a `CoordOp` named `<domain>:<verb>` (e.g. `negative-space:scan`), declared `argsSchema`/`resultSchema` (the typed I/O — P-140), a module-level test-deps setter (`setXScanDeps`), and `run(args, ctx)` that calls the shared orchestration using `ctx.workspaceId` / `ctx.harnessSlug`. `registerCoordOp(op)` at the bottom, and `import './ops/<loop>.js'` in `blueprint-steps/index.ts`. The op carries the flag + governor gating (P-012) — so **dark stays dark**. 3. **Write the blueprint** at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/<loop>/blueprint.yaml`: `extends: base`, a `workItem`, a program spine with the step(s) and `triggers.schedule` (the loop’s existing cron). Pure-deterministic ⇒ **no gate**. Args interpolate `{{ payload.* }}` (an unset whole-string placeholder → `undefined` → the op’s optional arg defaults). 4. **Point the seed routine at the blueprint**: `target: 'system:blueprint-run'`, `payload_template: { blueprintId: '<loop>' }`. Keep the governor-loop registration. `system:blueprint-run` detects program-mode (`isProgramSpine`) and runs the program **inline as its durable step** via `runProgramCore` + `inlineRunOp` (behavior-neutral: the bespoke loops also ran inline in their step). 5. **Hybrid loops** (det → agent → det, e.g. regret / transfer / prompt-ablation / iq-battery): the agent leg stays **INTERNAL to the op** (Option A), NOT an `orchestrator:spawn-roles` step. Two reasons (D-009 / D-013): (a) those loops’ “agents” are governed `llmCall`s (regret/transfer/ablation) or fleet bees that already route through `spawnAgentInHarness → bee:spawn → spawnInvokeOnce` — **the one governed chokepoint** — so there is NO ungoverned second spawn path to “close”; (b) `spawn-roles` is for **role fan-out** (vote’s per-lens voters): its agents take a harness *role/persona*. A loop whose agent takes a *brief* (a corpus case, a transcript continuation) doesn’t fit that contract — keep the spawn inside the op. So “deterministic step” = deterministic *top level* (the gate logic), with internal governed spawns, NOT “no spawns.” iq-battery is the worked hybrid: `iq-battery:gen` op wraps `runIqBatteryGen` (cadence-tick + the gen-0 bee runner). ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * **Before migrating, check it isn’t ALREADY a blueprint role.** The worker chunk loop (`worker-chunk-loop.ts`) looked like a bespoke loop to migrate, but it IS the coding blueprint’s `worker` role body — already blueprint-integrated, running in the `invoke-once` subprocess with the subprocess’s `InvokeContext`. “Migrating” it is a cross-process durability RE-ARCHITECTURE (the op runs in the operator’s program workflow, a different context), not a gap. Don’t re-migrate the already-integrated. * **No top-level throwing computation in a wrapped lib** (the same class as the `__dirname` deploy incident). `change-ledger/scan-loop.ts` did `const x = promisify(execFile)` at module scope; a test that partially mocks `node:child_process` (only `spawn`) made `execFile` undefined → `promisify(undefined)` threw AT IMPORT, poisoning every test whose graph includes the module. Promisify / resolve lazily INSIDE the function. * **Workspace-singleton cadence: there is now a first-class trigger for it (D-018).** A migrated loop is a workspace SINGLETON (one routine per workspace), but the default `materializeBlueprintTriggers` mints one routine PER INSTALL (keyed `(install_slug, name)`) seeded ACTIVE — so naively declaring `triggers.schedule` would N-duplicate into N ACTIVE pulses (the D-010/D-012(b) objection that kept the bespoke SEED scripts as the live materializer). A schedule entry can now declare **`singleton: true`**: materialize upserts EXACTLY ONE routine per workspace, seeded INACTIVE/dark, under the reserved synthetic host-slug `SINGLETON_TRIGGER_HOST_SLUG` (`@singleton`), named `bp-singleton-<blueprintId>-<i>` (blueprint-unique under the shared slug). This is the CAPABILITY only (`packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/materialize-triggers.ts`); rewiring the \~13 loops onto it — retiring each bespoke seed + folding its `registerLearningLoop` governor registration — is the per-loop follow-on (D-018 step 2, reverses D-012(b) one loop at a time under the arming gates), NOT the capability. Until a loop is rewired, its bespoke seed stays the live materializer. * **The live `@singleton` cutover RACES the seed-based arming workflow — sequence it, don’t race it (D-023).** The cutover (`seed-learning-singletons.ts`: materialize the `@singleton` row + delete the legacy `papercup` row) is incompatible-while-concurrent with how loops get ARMED: an arming agent re-runs `seed-<loop>-routine.ts --active`, which RE-CREATES the `papercup` row ACTIVE. Run the cutover during a live frontier-arming campaign and you get a double-state (a dark `@singleton` row beside a re-armed `papercup` row → latent double-fire); this actually happened (calibration/deferral/neologism) and had to be reverted (all rows restored to `papercup`). **Correct sequence: (1) let arming settle; (2) RETIRE the bespoke seeds FIRST so arming can only target the `@singleton` row; (3) then run the cutover.** **DONE (D-026):** the full cutover of all 13 loops then completed cleanly by following exactly this sequence — seeds deleted first → no re-creation path → no collision. 5 dark loops via the dark CLI, 8 active loops via `--active-cutover` (the byte-identical copy: active+payload+timing preserved). NEW ARMING PATH (seeds gone): `UPDATE harness_shared.routines SET active=true WHERE install_slug='@singleton' AND name='bp-singleton-<loop>-0'`; re-materialize is active-preserving. * **Two hardenings the collision forced, now in the capability (D-024):** (a) singleton materialize is RE-RUN-SAFE — `upsertSingletonRoutine` seeds dark + `concurrency:'skip'` on first creation, but on conflict PRESERVES `active`/`next_fire_at`/`concurrency` and MERGES the payload (ensure `blueprintId`, keep owner tuning). The generic `upsertRoutine` overwrites those, so a naive re-materialize would DARKEN an armed loop + DROP tuning — never use it for singletons. (b) the cutover CLI is COLLISION-SAFE — it SKIPS any loop whose `papercup` row is ACTIVE (`skipped:'legacy-active'`) instead of minting a dark duplicate; an active loop needs the owner-watched ATOMIC active cutover (copy active+payload+timing → `@singleton`, delete `papercup`, one transaction), not the dark CLI. * **worker-chunk-loop → operator-hosted op (P-142/D-017, Option A) is NOT a thin op-wrap — it needs a NEW operator-side worker-spawn primitive.** `runChunkLoopCore` is cleanly extracted (stage a) and takes injected `ChunkLoopDeps`, so an op CALLING it is easy. The hard part is the deps: `planChunks` needs the worker’s RAW LLM output, `implementChunk` needs a worker run against a SCRATCH dir reporting its TOUCHED files, and the loop commits per chunk. The existing `ctx.caps.spawnRoles` (the `orchestrator:spawn-roles` op) is a CONVERSATION fan-out — it spawns role agents that post into a thread and exit; it has no cwd/scratch, no raw-output capture, no touched-files report. So an operator-hosted `worker:chunk-loop` op must build a new “run a worker against a scratch checkout, capture output + touched files” spawn primitive (plus repo checkout operator-side). That is the operator↔subprocess topology re-architecture D-015 flags as the coding HOT PATH — staged * owner-watched + monitored over weeks (dark-launch → 25→50→100% ramp → retire), NOT an overnight cutover. Don’t write a mock-only op shell and call P-142 “built”: its substance IS the spawn primitive. * `validateBlueprint` is called WITHOUT `knownOps` at every current call site, so a program op that doesn’t exist is caught at RUN time (`requireCoordOp` throws), not load time. Register your op (import the family index) wherever the program runs. * A deterministic op must **fail loud** on a missing `ctx.workspaceId` (a misconfigured fire), not silently mine the wrong scope. * `runProgramCore` maps a gateless completed run (`no-gate-match` from the generic runner) to a clean `done` — don’t reintroduce a gate just to terminate. * **Gating varies per loop** — replicate the ACTUAL gate: most are flag + learning- governor; change-ledger is flag-only (pure bookkeeping); scout is structural (cadence/fire-gate/claim/budget, no flag); iq-battery is owner-budget (refuse if no `budgetUsd`). Read the action; don’t assume flag+governor. * **A `system:blueprint-run` fire spawns into the FIRING install by default — override via a `launchInstallSlug`-family payload key when the routine must launch work into a DIFFERENT named install/hive than the one whose routine fired.** `handleBlueprintRun` builds its durable-spawn `installSlug` (and the idempotency key) from `ctx.installSlug` unless the routine’s `payload_template` sets one of `launchInstallSlug` / `hiveSlug` / `hiveInstallSlug` / `targetInstallSlug` (checked in that order; first non-blank string wins) — the DBOS no-first-step routineFire requeue guard surfaced this when a routine requeued after a reaper-cancelled fire and the replay needed to keep targeting the same install, not wherever it happened to be re-picked-up. Set the override key in the blueprint’s seeded `payload_template` for any cross-install program-mode blueprint; omit it and the fire targets its own firing install (the common case). * **Editing the seed `.ts` does NOT repoint the LIVE routine row — you MUST re-run the seed (step 4 is a runtime act, not just a source edit).** Changing `target` / `payload_template` in the seed script only affects FUTURE upserts. An already-seeded `harness_shared.routines` row — *especially one an owner ACTIVATED before the migration deployed* — still has `target_role = 'system:<loop>'` (now retired, no registered handler) and the old payload shape, so when it fires it hits a dead target and silently no-ops. After the migration lands, **re-run each loop’s seed against the live workspace DB** (`PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID=<ws> tsx lib/.../seed-<loop>-routine.ts [--active]`); the upsert’s `ON CONFLICT` repoints target + payload (and the well- written seeds preserve owner payload keys — change-ledger keeps `sinceDays`, iq-battery keeps `budgetUsd`). This bit **`iq-battery-gen`, `scout-cycle`, `change-ledger-scan`** — all active, all firing at a retired target (Scout + change-ledger loops were dead) until re-seeded 2026-06-13. **Corollary — the INACTIVE migrated rows are latent traps:** flipping `active=true` in the routines admin WITHOUT re-seeding fires the retired target. Arm a migrated loop by **re-running its seed with `--active`**, never by an admin active-flip alone. (Quick audit: `SELECT name,target_role,active FROM harness_shared.routines WHERE target_role <> 'system:blueprint-run'` — every row whose target isn’t a still-registered action is suspect.) ## Files (pilot A — negative-space, the reference) [Section titled “Files (pilot A — negative-space, the reference)”](#files-pilot-a--negative-space-the-reference) * Schema/validator: `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/validate.ts` (gate optional) * Runner: `packages/operator-core/lib/coord-ops/program-runner.ts` (gateless → done) * Scheduled fire: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/blueprint-run-action.ts` (`runScheduledProgram`) * Op family: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/` * Shared orchestration: `packages/operator-core/lib/negative-space/mine.ts` * Blueprint: `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/negative-space/blueprint.yaml` * Tests: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/negative-space-blueprint.test.ts`

# Migration-number collisions: use the reservation tool; the lint's FS checks are now gated

> Two agents racing `ls | tail` pick the same NNN-*.sql number. db:next-migration prevents this — an MCP agent-tool (also available as `npm run db:next-migration` since 2026-06-20) now open to ALL built-in roles, and (2026-07-03) with its fsMax read moved inside the advisory lock to close a TOCTOU race (EI-6852). lint:migrations catches dups + raw BEGIN/COMMIT + unreserved numbers; since 2026-07-04 (EI-6843) its two PG-free checks are gated — lint-migrations.test.ts runs them against the real sql/ dir on every test:affected / green-checkpoint run, after re-baselining ENFORCED_FROM 215→494 to grandfather already-applied ledgered history. Only the PG-backed reservation check still needs a manual run. Plus a two-dirs footgun: the canonical libs dir vs the gitignored sidecar mirror.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) When several agents add SQL migrations concurrently they collide on the leading `NNN`. While implementing PR-4 (WI↔PR producer, `2026-06-20`) I wrote `319-pr4-feature-pr-producer-identity.sql` and found a peer had **already** taken `319` (`319-pr-review-reports.sql`) and another had taken `320` (`320-autovacuum-high-churn-telemetry.sql`). My file had to be re-numbered to `321`, allocated through the reservation ledger to avoid a third collision. ### What a dup number actually breaks today (verify before you assume “silent dark”) [Section titled “What a dup number actually breaks today (verify before you assume “silent dark”)”](#what-a-dup-number-actually-breaks-today-verify-before-you-assume-silent-dark) `next_migration.ts`’s docstring warns “only one of the colliding files applies, so a table goes silently dark.” That is **not** how the current boot runner behaves: `applyPendingMigrations` (`libs/papercusp/packages/embedded-postgres-server/src/ migration-runner.js`) keys `harness_shared.schema_migrations` by **filename**, so `319-foo.sql` and `319-bar.sql` are distinct keys and **both apply** (in lexicographic filename order). The desktop sidecar path applies the same way (its serve boot runs the same runner over the `db-sql` mirror). So the cited single-apply/silent-dark is path/history-specific, not a property of today’s runner — don’t propagate it as a current fact. The **real**, verifiable damage from a dup number today: * **`lint:migrations` goes red** (its `duplicateNumberGroups` check). Since `2026-07-04` that check IS gated for enforced-era numbers (see gap #3’s resolution below): a new dup ≥494 fails `test:affected` / the green gate immediately; pre-494 historical dups are grandfathered (the runner keys by full filename, so they never collided at runtime). * **Coordination confusion** — two unrelated features both claim “319”; tooling and humans that key on the number get the wrong file. * **Possible loss at git-merge time** — when the two authors’ divergent branches reconcile, a careless merge can drop one of the same-numbered files (a VCS hazard, not a runner one). The fix layers are therefore **prevention at creation** (the reservation tool/CLI) + **detection at PR** (the existing lint dup-check) — NOT a change to boot-apply semantics. ## Why it keeps happening (three compounding gaps) [Section titled “Why it keeps happening (three compounding gaps)”](#why-it-keeps-happening-three-compounding-gaps) 1. **`db:next-migration` is the safe path, but was MCP-only until 2026-06-20.** The atomic allocator (advisory lock + `harness_shared.migration_reservations`, GREATEST(max-on-disk across the serving + staging trees, max-reserved, max-applied)+1) lives in `next_migration.ts` as a `defineTool` agent-tool. ~~There is **no `npm run db:next-migration`** script.~~ **Fixed (2026-06-20)** — see the “How to allocate a number now” section and item #1 in the Recommended fix section. An agent (or human) who isn’t wired into the harness MCP still does `ls | tail` and hand-picks — exactly the racing path the tool was built to replace. The lint error even says “use db:next-migration”, naming a command that (before the fix) didn’t exist as a script. **Role access (2026-06-25):** `db:next-migration` previously used `agentRoles: [...SU_ROLES, 'bee']` — only superuser-role agents and the generic bee could call it. Changed to `agentRoles: [...AGENT_ROLES]`: every built-in role (worker, validator, reviewer, architect, etc.) can now call the MCP tool directly and participate in collision-free allocation without falling back to the npm CLI. **fsMax TOCTOU race fixed (2026-07-03, EI-6852):** even after the advisory lock landed, both allocators read the filesystem max (`maxNumberOnDisk`) **before** entering `sql.begin(...)` — i.e. before acquiring `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. That left a window (a pooled-connection-acquire plus the lock-wait, which can run seconds under a busy fleet) during which a concurrent caller could write a higher-numbered `NNN-*.sql` to disk; the stale `fsMax` then failed to fold it in and the tool could hand out an already-used number. Both `next_migration.ts` (the MCP tool) and `scripts/next-migration.mjs` (the CLI) now compute `fsMax` **inside** the `sql.begin` callback, immediately before the `GREATEST(...)` read and the reservation insert, so all three GREATEST inputs (on-disk, reserved, applied) are read atomically under the same lock. `next_migration.ts` also now `export`s `ALLOC_ADVISORY_KEY` so the regression test (`next_migration.integration.test.ts`, case “EI-6852: the filesystem max is read INSIDE the advisory lock”) can hold the lock itself to reproduce the race. This closes the last remaining collision window in the “supported path” — the collisions this doc otherwise documents are all from agents who bypassed `db:next-migration`/the CLI entirely. 2. ~~**The MCP client is currently dropped.**~~ **Historical note (2026-06-20):** At the time of discovery the harness MCP client was dropped, so even MCP-aware agents couldn’t reach `db:next-migration` and fell back to hand-picking. The npm CLI (`npm run db:next-migration`) was added precisely to fix this (gap #1 fix). The MCP client drop is a session-specific transient; the systematic fix is the CLI + the per-role access expansion (see gap #1 update above). 3. **`lint:migrations` was not gated** (RESOLVED for the PG-free checks, `2026-07-04` — see below). `scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` already detects (a) duplicate `NNN`, (b) raw top-level `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;` (which would end the runner’s per-file wrapper txn early), and (c) numbers ≥`ENFORCED_FROM` absent from the reservation ledger. But it was **only an npm script** — referenced in neither `.github/` (CI) nor `.husky/` / `.git/hooks` — so the guard never ran automatically; the dup-number check (which is PG-free and runs fine in CI) never fired on a PR. As of `2026-06-20`, `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` exited **1**: 7 files carried raw `BEGIN/COMMIT` (`299, 300, 306, 307, 308, 312, 317`) and \~10 numbers ≥215 were unreserved (`293, 294, 298, 301, 303–307, 319, 320`). **Re-verified `2026-07-03` — the guard is still ungated and the violation count has grown, not shrunk** (confirming gap #3 is still open): `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` still exits **1**, now with **3 duplicate-number groups** (`357`, `375`, `460` — each has two distinct files sharing the same leading `NNN`, exactly the collision this doc is about), **34 files** carrying raw top-level `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;`, and **64 numbers ≥215** on disk with no reservation-ledger row. The tree has been shipping with the linter red for weeks with nothing catching it at PR time — direct evidence that gap #3 (below) remains unaddressed. **Resolved for the PG-free checks (`2026-07-04`, EI-6843):** the duplicate-`NNN` and raw-tx-control scans now run against the REAL `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/` directory inside `packages/operator-core/lib/lint-migrations.test.ts` (the “real … sql/ directory (gate wiring)” describe block), which `npm run test:affected` — and therefore the green-checkpoint gate — runs on every candidate. Because the tree was red (worse than at discovery), enforcement was re-baselined FIRST: `ENFORCED_FROM` moved 215→494, grandfathering the already-applied, ledgered history (editing/renaming an applied file would break its recorded checksum), and `duplicateNumberGroups` now takes an `enforcedFrom` boundary so historical same-number pairs don’t red the gate. A FUTURE violation (≥494) fails the suite immediately. The PG-backed reservation check (c) remains CLI-only — as of `2026-07-05` `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` still exits 1 with one live violation (migration `510` on disk with no reservation row), so “clean first, gate second” still applies to that check. ## The two-dirs footgun (bonus) [Section titled “The two-dirs footgun (bonus)”](#the-two-dirs-footgun-bonus) There are **two** migration directories and they are NOT the same role: * **`libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/`** — CANONICAL. The operator auto-applies these on boot (`migration-drift.ts` `resolveSqlDir()`), and `db:next-migration` scans this dir for the on-disk max. **Write new migrations here.** * **`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/sidecar/db-sql/`** — a build-time MIRROR, and it is **gitignored inside the `papercusp-desktop` submodule** (`git check-ignore` confirms). A file written only here is never committed and never applied. Both are submodules (`libs/papercusp`, `papercusp-desktop`). I initially wrote my migration into the sidecar mirror — it silently did nothing useful. Identical copies of `314–318` in both dirs make the mirror look authoritative; it isn’t. ## How to allocate a number now (the supported path) [Section titled “How to allocate a number now (the supported path)”](#how-to-allocate-a-number-now-the-supported-path) Use the CLI (added `2026-06-20` — works even with the MCP client down): 
```bash
npm run db:next-migration -- --name add-foo-index --intent "what it does"
# → reserves the next free NNN in harness_shared.migration_reservations and prints
#   the canonical path: libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/<NNN>-add-foo-index.sql
# Add --dry-run to see the number without reserving it.
```
 It scans BOTH dirs for the on-disk max **inside** the advisory lock (the `2026-07-03` EI-6852 fix — see above), allocates, and records the reservation — the same contract as the MCP `db:next-migration` tool. Then write the file to `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/<NNN>-<slug>.sql` (NOT the sidecar mirror). It auto-applies on the next operator restart. It refuses to hand out a number when PG is unreachable (an unreserved number re-opens the race). ## Recommended fix (plan) [Section titled “Recommended fix (plan)”](#recommended-fix-plan) Small, mostly additive; each item is independent: 1. ~~**Add `npm run db:next-migration`.**~~ **DONE (`2026-06-20`)** — `scripts/next-migration.mjs` + the `db:next-migration` npm script. Reservation now works without the MCP client (the highest-leverage gap — it kills the `ls | tail` path at the source). Mirrors the MCP tool via the shared ledger + advisory key. ~~A follow-up could DRY the two onto one exported core~~ — see item 4 below (still open). **Also DONE (`2026-07-03`, EI-6852):** both allocators now read the on-disk max **inside** the advisory-lock transaction instead of before it, closing the TOCTOU window described above. 2. ~~**Gate `lint:migrations`**~~ **DONE for the PG-free checks (`2026-07-04`, EI-6843)** — not via `.github/`/`.husky` but via the vitest suite: `packages/operator-core/lib/lint-migrations.test.ts` scans the real sql/ dir for duplicate numbers + raw tx-control on every `test:affected` / green-checkpoint run. The required “clean first” sequencing was honored by RE-BASELINING instead of editing history: `ENFORCED_FROM` 215→494 grandfathers the applied, ledgered legacy (immutable — recorded checksums), so the gate starts green and only a genuinely NEW violation reds it. Still open: the PG-backed unreserved-number check is not in the gate (needs a live PG; exercised only by the CLI) — backfill the missing reservation rows (e.g. `510` as of `2026-07-05`) before gating it. (Do NOT instead change the boot runner to abort on dup numbers: it currently applies both colliding files by filename, and altering boot-apply semantics — especially the `continueOnError` fleet path — is far riskier than catching the dup at PR time.) 3. **Mark the sidecar mirror.** Since the mirror dir is itself gitignored, a `README` placed in it wouldn’t be tracked — put the “this is a gitignored build mirror; author migrations in the canonical libs dir” note where it’s visible: the canonical dir’s own README, or `migration-drift.ts` (which already owns `resolveSqlDir`). 4. **DRY the allocator** (low priority). Export the allocation core from `next_migration.ts` and have both the MCP tool and `scripts/next-migration.mjs` call it, instead of the two mirroring the ledger contract independently. The `2026-07-03` EI-6852 fix had to be hand-applied to **both** files in lockstep (see above) precisely because they’re still two independent implementations of the same contract — live evidence for why this item matters, not just a hypothetical. Sequencing mattered for the gating item (#2) and was honored via the `2026-07-04` re-baseline; the same rule — clean first, gate second — applies to any future gating of the reservation check.

# Manually-applied migrations must be re-run-safe — guard DDL or the auto-deploy dies on lock timeouts

> The deploy pipeline re-applies every pending sql/<NNN> file on the live DB. A migration already applied by hand on the dev box re-runs at deploy time — and bare ALTER TABLE/CREATE POLICY/GRANT statements take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks that can hit the runner's lock_timeout and roll back the whole deploy. Wrap RLS/policy/grant DDL in existence-guarded DO blocks so a re-run takes zero locks.

## What happened (live, 2026-06-09) [Section titled “What happened (live, 2026-06-09)”](#what-happened-live-2026-06-09) Migration `208-scout-ticks-and-lens-weights.sql` was applied **manually** to the dev box’s native PG (the documented dev chore — native `:5432` has no auto-runner). The auto-deploy pipeline then tried to apply the same file on the live DB at 20:00/20:30/20:45 and **all three deploys failed with `canceling statement due to lock timeout` and auto-rolled back**, stranding the live operator \~5 hours behind staging. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` no-ops cheaply — but the rest of a conventional migration does NOT: * `ALTER TABLE … ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, **every run** * `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS … ; CREATE POLICY …` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, every run * `GRANT …` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, every run On a table that’s already live (because the manual apply created it and resolvers/routines are already reading it), any concurrent reader queues those locks past the runner’s `lock_timeout` → the migrate step dies → rollback. ## The rule [Section titled “The rule”](#the-rule) A migration that can ever be **re-applied on a DB where it already ran** (which is every migration on this project, because of the manual-dev-apply + deploy-re-apply pattern) must make its lock-taking statements conditional: 
```sql
DO $$ BEGIN
  IF NOT (SELECT relrowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'harness_shared.t'::regclass) THEN
    ALTER TABLE harness_shared.t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_policies WHERE schemaname='harness_shared'
                  AND tablename='t' AND policyname='t_workspace_isolation') THEN
    CREATE POLICY t_workspace_isolation ON harness_shared.t USING (…) WITH CHECK (…);
  END IF;
  IF NOT has_table_privilege('harness_app', 'harness_shared.t', 'INSERT') THEN
    GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON harness_shared.t TO harness_app;
  END IF;
END $$;
```
 Guarded = the re-run takes **zero** table locks; the fresh-migrate path (embedded-pg, the `fresh-migrate.integration.test.ts` gate) executes the statements normally. See `208-scout-ticks-and-lens-weights.sql` for the worked fix, and mirror it instead of the older bare-DDL pattern in `202-*.sql`. ## How to recognize it [Section titled “How to recognize it”](#how-to-recognize-it) * `/tmp/papercup-auto-deploy.log` shows `migrate: apply <NNN>-…` then `✖ deploy failed: canceling statement due to lock timeout` then a rollback. * `papercup-release` checkout SHA stops advancing while `origin/main` moves. * The live operator stays healthy (rollback works) — the failure is silent unless you look at the deploy log, so a stalled release SHA is the tell.

# Mobile endpoints are a defineRoute flag, not a separate router

> The mobile API moved off the bespoke _hono/mobile.ts router onto defineRoute under /api/device/* + a `cors: true` flag. Device JWTs resolve through requirePrincipal; isRevoked treats unknown devices as revoked, which bites synthetic test JWTs.

## What changed [Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed) The `/api/mobile/*` routes used to live in a bespoke Hono router (`_hono/mobile.ts`, \~1000 LOC, since deleted) with its own `cors()` block, its own `deviceAuth()` middleware, and lazy DDL. As of the endpoint-unification arc (`endpoint-unification-2026-05-21`) they are ordinary `defineRoute` modules under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/device/*.ts` — the URLs were renamed `/api/mobile/*` → `/api/device/*` (P2b) and the principal kind is `'device'`, not `'mobile'`. Making a route reachable from the paired phone is now one flag: 
```ts
defineRoute({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/device/whatever',
  auth: DEVICE_AUTH,  // = { kind: ['device'] } — gate on the device-JWT principal
  cors: true,         // mount the shared CORS allowlist
  handler(req, ctx) { /* ctx.principal is the device */ },
});
// (a query-token route adds `tokenIn: ['query']`, e.g. routes/device/sync.ts)
```
 `cors: true` mounts the shared CORS middleware (`corsFor` in `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/cors.ts` — tauri.localhost, localhost:\*, 127.0.0.1:\*, 10.0.2.2:\*) via `corsFor(def.cors?.origins)`. The device-JWT gate is the separate `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` requirement (the reusable `DEVICE_AUTH` constant in `routes/device/_shared.ts`). ## Gotcha 1 — the device JWT is just a bearer [Section titled “Gotcha 1 — the device JWT is just a bearer”](#gotcha-1--the-device-jwt-is-just-a-bearer) A device JWT arrives as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` — the same header shape as an agent’s `system`/`pi` bearer. The `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all resolves principals with a **composite** resolver: `resolveBearer` (token\_index → agent) first, then `principalFromDeviceJwt`. One hook reaches both. A phone can therefore call any built-in `defineTool` directly; it no longer needs the `/voice-tool/:name` proxy. ## Gotcha 2 — `isRevoked` treats an unknown device as revoked [Section titled “Gotcha 2 — isRevoked treats an unknown device as revoked”](#gotcha-2--isrevoked-treats-an-unknown-device-as-revoked) `principalFromDeviceJwt` (`packages/operator-core/lib/auth/principal/from-device-jwt.ts`) runs `isRevoked(claims.sub)` (parity with the old `deviceAuth()` middleware). `isRevoked` returns **`true` for any device not present in `harness_shared.mobile_devices`** — a valid signature is not enough; the device must be a known, paired, non-revoked row. Consequence for tests: a synthetic JWT minted with `signDeviceToken` for a device that was never `insertDevice`’d will (correctly) resolve to a **null principal**. Mock it: 
```ts
vi.mock('../device-store', async (orig) => ({
  ...(await orig<typeof import('../device-store')>()),
  isRevoked: async () => false,
}));
```
 ## Gotcha 3 — route-stack auth needs a DB; handler-direct tests don’t [Section titled “Gotcha 3 — route-stack auth needs a DB; handler-direct tests don’t”](#gotcha-3--route-stack-auth-needs-a-db-handler-direct-tests-dont) Driving a `requirePrincipal`-gated route through `registerAllRoutes` + `app.request()` exercises the real resolver chain, which touches PG. In a no-DB test that throws (or flakily 500s). Either mock the auth/DB layer (the `auth.test.ts` pattern) or test the handler directly with a hand-built `RouteContext` (the `agent-tools-catchall.test.ts` pattern) — the latter is cleaner for verifying port fidelity.

# Driving a multi-agent build: the write-capable pivot when fleet bees can't write

> The coordinator runbook for building a whole plan via spawned workers when conditions are degraded. Fleet bees may be READ-ONLY (EI-524 capability confinement) — they draft, they can't write; the 'lift' can be announced-but-not-effective. Org-wide API rate-limiting kills parallel agent BURSTS but serial main-loop work survives. Pivot to write-capable Agent (Task) subagents + serial; place waves at ≤3 concurrency; ALWAYS verify bee/subagent drafts before applying.

## Current behavior (2026-07-03) [Section titled “Current behavior (2026-07-03)”](#current-behavior-2026-07-03) **Wall 1 below is CLOSED — fleet bees are now write+bash capable, not read-only.** The “OWNER-PRIORITY FIX (2026-06-15)” (`bee-capability-expansion -2026-06-08` D-005/P-004) granted `capability:fs-write` + `capability:bash` (plus `fs-read` / `git` / `net` / `code-inspect`) to the `bee` role principal in `role-principal-caps.ts`, closing the “two-gate desync” this doc’s Wall 1 describes (the ENVELOPE-layer deny had been lifted, but the principal CAPABILITY grant lagged — bees still 100%-failed with `lacks capability 'capability:fs-write'` until this landed). A `system:bee` today CAN `Edit` / `Write` / run bash directly — do **not** assume a bee report of “read-only” is still the EI-524 confinement; verify against `role-principal-caps.ts`’s current `bee: [...]` grant list (and `bee-tool-boundary.test.ts`) before re-diagnosing it as Wall 1. See `agent-spawning/allowlist-and-caps.mdx` for the current, maintained capability/allowlist model. **Everything past Wall 1 — Wall 2 (rate-limit bursts), verify-before-apply, migration safety, and the monitor loop — is still generically useful runbook knowledge** for a degraded/high-load build (a bee CAN now write, but a genuinely capability-confined or otherwise-blocked agent still benefits from the write-capable-subagent + serial pivot). Read the body below as historical context for *why* that pivot pattern exists, not as “bees are read-only today.” ## When this applies [Section titled “When this applies”](#when-this-applies) You are an SU coordinator driving a `ready` plan to completion by **spawning workers** (the “assign a bunch of agents + monitor on a loop” ask). The happy path is: decompose the plan into lanes → `fleet:place_batch` bees → flip plan items + place the next wave as deps clear. This page is the **degraded path** — the two infra walls that path hit in practice, and the pivots that got through. ## Wall 1 — fleet bees can be READ-ONLY (EI-524 capability confinement) [Section titled “Wall 1 — fleet bees can be READ-ONLY (EI-524 capability confinement)”](#wall-1--fleet-bees-can-be-read-only-ei-524-capability-confinement) A `system:bee` spawned via `bee:spawn`/`fleet:place_batch` may lack `capability:fs-write`. It can read, diagnose, and produce an excellent **draft** (exact migration SQL, code diffs), but its `Edit`/`Write` fails: > `Principal 'system:bee' lacks capability 'capability:fs-write'` * **Detect it, don’t fight it.** If a bee reports the fs-write error (or two of them do), stop re-placing bees into the same wall. * **A capability “lift” can be announced-but-not-effective.** A broadcast that “bees are now write+exec capable” did NOT immediately grant fs-write to bees spawned right after — the change was in-flux. **Verify empirically** (spawn one, watch for the error) before trusting a capability flip; multiple fleet agents hit the same wall after the “lift.” * The working fleet pattern while bees are read-only: **bee drafts → a write-capable actor verifies + applies.** But that funnels every write through a few write-capable SUs — a real throughput bottleneck. ## The pivot — write-capable execution [Section titled “The pivot — write-capable execution”](#the-pivot--write-capable-execution) Two write-capable mechanisms the coordinator owns directly: 1. **Your own Agent (`Task`) subagents** — they inherit your full tool access, so they CAN `Edit`/`Write`/`Bash` + reach MCP tools. Launch with `run_in_background: true`; you’re notified on completion (your monitor loop). This is the parallelism the read-only fleet can’t give you. 2. **Serial main-loop work (you)** — the most reliable path; it consistently got through when both fleet bees and parallel subagents were blocked. Stand the read-only bees down (`fleet:cancel` + close their work-items so the autoloop doesn’t re-place them) and re-route the lanes to subagents/serial. ## Wall 2 — org-wide API rate-limiting kills parallel BURSTS [Section titled “Wall 2 — org-wide API rate-limiting kills parallel BURSTS”](#wall-2--org-wide-api-rate-limiting-kills-parallel-bursts) Under heavy fleet load the Anthropic API returns `Server is temporarily limiting requests (not your usage limit) · Rate limited`. Observed shape: **parallel subagents die \~2 min / \~20 tool-calls in with tiny output** (a 3-way burst is what trips it), while **serial main-loop work survives** — the rate-limit punishes concurrency spikes, not steady single-stream work. * **Reduce concurrency under rate pressure.** Place waves at **≤3** write-capable subagents, not a big fan-out. Do the critical-path / privileged steps (DB migrations) **serially yourself**. * Fleet bees route through the **rate-governor** (paced), so they degrade more gracefully than raw parallel Agent subagents — prefer them once the confinement is fixed. * A rate-limited kill leaves **partial work**: check `git status` + a targeted `tsc` for an island of new files (they may be complete-but-unwired, or broken). A self-contained new-file island that nothing imports won’t break the build — finish the wiring + tests serially. ## ALWAYS verify a draft before applying it [Section titled “ALWAYS verify a draft before applying it”](#always-verify-a-draft-before-applying-it) Read-only bees (and rushed subagents) produce **unverified** drafts. In one build this caught **three real bugs** before they landed: a backfill `CROSS JOIN harness_shared.harnesses WHERE kind='hive'` (no such table/column — hives are a registry entry with `harness_kind='hive'`), a join on `engineer_issues.harness_slug` (no such column — the slug is in the federation outbox jsonb, mig 197), and a `DROP TABLE … CASCADE` rebuild where a `safe-to-truncate` cache only needed `ADD COLUMN` + truncate + repoint-PK. **Verify every schema/table/symbol assumption against the real files; correct, then apply + test.** ## Migration safety under a concurrent, rate-limited build [Section titled “Migration safety under a concurrent, rate-limited build”](#migration-safety-under-a-concurrent-rate-limited-build) * Reserve the number with **`db:next-migration`**, never a guess — `288` was taken between a draft and its apply; the reserver hands out the real next number. * **Don’t `db:migrate` a coupled schema change ahead of its code deploy.** A `NOT NULL`/PK change that the still-deployed (green) code violates will break on the live DB. Write the migration file (it **boot-applies** with the code on the next deploy) and validate it in a **fresh testcontainer** (any integration test applies all migrations) instead of hand-applying to the shared dev DB. * A **best-effort write path** (the writer wrapped in try/catch) makes a schema↔code split **degrade gracefully** (warn + skip) instead of breaking — which removes the “must land atomically” pressure during a flaky build. ## The loop [Section titled “The loop”](#the-loop) Monitor with **completion wakes** (background `Task` notifications + the bees’ `coord:send {wake:true}` on done) plus an **`events:await` heartbeat** fallback for stalls. On each wake: flip the landed plan items (`plans:set-status`), place the next wave as deps clear, re-`coord:declare-intent { items }` to keep your lane visible (the claim-discipline watch nudges if you declare a plan but hold no items). Stop placing waves when only **owner-gated** (outward-facing: live PR / Comb publish / credentials) or genuinely-optional items remain — don’t auto-cross the outward-facing line, and don’t manufacture low-value churn to satisfy a “continue” loop.

# multi-peer-convergence.test.ts green-blocker is a box-weather flake, NOT a convergence bug

> When `lib/harness/git-sync/multi-peer-convergence.test.ts` reds the green-checkpoint with `git cat-file -e <hash>^{commit} failed (128): not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git`, do NOT investigate it as a convergence / submodule logic bug. The convergence logic is sound — the file passes deterministically in isolation, under 12× concurrent self-execution, and under a forced sub-second testTimeout.
