The red is a rare load/teardown artifact under extreme full-suite box load (~135): the heavy real-git test is torn down past its timeout while git subprocesses are still in flight, and a late `git()` call hits the just-`rm`'d temp tree, rejecting as an unhandled rejection that reds the WHOLE vitest run. It self-clears — the next green-checkpoint run advances main right past it.

## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) If the green-checkpoint (or a hive bee’s `test:affected`) goes red on: 
```plaintext
lib/harness/git-sync/multi-peer-convergence.test.ts
Test: "the losing peer conflicts INSIDE the submodule, does NOT publish a broken
       gitlink, then the fleet converges"
Error: git cat-file -e <hash>^{commit} failed (128):
       fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
```
 **Do not re-diagnose it as a submodule / gitlink / convergence logic bug.** At least four SU sessions have now traced it (su-1897a, su-aaee9, su-ca91b, and the session that wrote this page) and reached the same verdict: **the convergence LOGIC is correct; this is a non-deterministic box-weather flake.** `main` self-advances past it on the next checkpoint run — confirm with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <blocker-sha> origin/main` before spending any time on it (on 2026-06-13 the blocker held main at `6d044f9b`; the next run advanced it 18 commits to `b55e1a5f4`). ## Why it is NOT a logic bug (the evidence) [Section titled “Why it is NOT a logic bug (the evidence)”](#why-it-is-not-a-logic-bug-the-evidence) The file passes **deterministically** under every condition that isn’t extreme full-suite load: * `npx vitest run …/multi-peer-convergence.test.ts` in isolation — 6/6 green, repeatably (every prior diagnoser confirmed this). * **12× concurrent** self-execution at box load \~30 — all 12 exit 0, zero git errors. (The flake is not simple inter-process `/tmp` contention.) * Forced **`--testTimeout=1200`** (sub-2s) — still 6/6 green in \~8s, because even the heavy submodule test completes in well under a second of wall-clock git work on a quiet box. A genuine convergence/gitlink defect would fail in isolation. This one cannot be made to fail except under the real full-`test:affected` shard at pathological load — exactly the “box weather” the unit config’s own comment documents (`libs/test-config/src/vitest-config.ts`: green-checkpoint went red twice “purely on 20\_000ms timeouts … ALL passing in isolation … with the box at load \~135”). ## The mechanism (most-consistent hypothesis) [Section titled “The mechanism (most-consistent hypothesis)”](#the-mechanism-most-consistent-hypothesis) The error text is unambiguously this file’s own `git()` helper throwing at the **last** assertion of the submodule test (`cat-file -e <pointer>^{commit}` in the submodule’s bare origin). The selectivity puzzle — the two `git` calls on the same bare repo *immediately before* (`rev-parse main`, `ls-tree main`) succeed — rules out an env leak (`GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`: no operator-core test mutates them) and rules out a sibling test (this is the only git-sync test with both the `failed (<code>)` throw-helper format and a `cat-file …^{commit}`). The remaining mechanism that fits *“passes in isolation + flakes only under load + surfaces as an unhandled rejection that fails the whole run”*: 1. Under extreme load the heavy real-git test (clones super+sub, N peers, `convergeFleet` up to 20 rounds × per-peer `runGitSync` × `resolveScope` up to 8 push passes — many real `git` subprocesses) overruns the 60s unit timeout. 2. vitest marks the test timed-out and tears the **file** down, but JS cannot cancel the in-flight async — the test body keeps running and its `finally { await rm(tmpRoot, { recursive, force }) }` deletes the temp tree. 3. A `git` call that is still in flight (or runs just after) now resolves against a **deleted** working/temp dir → `git()` throws `not a git repository` in an async chain vitest is no longer awaiting → **unhandled rejection** → vitest reds the *entire* run, attributing the git error to whatever test is “current.” So the confusing part — a `cat-file` “not a git repository” that looks like a broken gitlink — is a **teardown artifact**, not a published-pointer defect. The “published superproject pointer is unreachable on the submodule origin” reading is a red herring. (Not fully reproduced: forcing the exact stranded-rejection sequence needs the real \~135 box load, which a quiet box can’t manufacture. The *negative* claim — “not a convergence logic bug” — is what’s proven, and it’s the one that matters.) ## What to do [Section titled “What to do”](#what-to-do) * **Nothing urgent.** It self-clears; `main` advances on the next green run. Don’t hand it to a merge-resolver, don’t edit the convergence assertions, don’t “fix the gitlink.” * **Do NOT weaken the assertions.** The `maxRounds: 20` / 8-pass resolver bounds ARE the no-ping-pong proof (P-004) — shrinking them to dodge the timeout would delete the property the test exists to verify. * A real fix (owner / B-02 lane, `shared-hive-hardening-2026-06-13`) would make the heavy real-git tests **not strand an unhandled rejection on teardown** — so a load timeout fails cleanly as *itself* instead of reddening the whole run and mis-pointing the next investigator at a phantom convergence bug. That needs a repro under genuine extreme load, which is why it’s gated on the owner’s rig, not a blind edit. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * [git-sync absorbs history rewrites](/internal/docs/agent-insights/git-sync-history-rewrite-absorbed) — the P-005 sibling semantics in the same test file. * [spawn env leaks into vitest](/internal/docs/agent-insights/spawn-env-leaks-into-vitest) — the other “passes locally, reds the green-checkpoint” class (env pollution, scrubbed by `setup-hermetic-env.ts`). * [vitest threads pool Node 25 coredump](/internal/docs/agent-insights/vitest-threads-pool-node25-coredump) — why the unit layer is `pool: 'forks'`, and another non-deterministic whole-run red that isn’t a test-logic defect.

# Green health check but memory handlers hang (native-addon ABI mismatch)

> /api/health is 200 but memory:* / MCP calls hang forever. Root cause class: a native addon (e.g. better-sqlite3) built for the wrong Node ABI fails at LOAD, mem0 never comes up, and every memory-touching handler awaits a promise that never resolves — invisible behind a shallow health probe. Diagnosis + the 4 shipped guards.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) * `/api/health` returns **200** (fast) but the operator is effectively down: `memory:search` / `memory:remember` (and any MCP/HTTP handler that touches memory) **hang forever** — the MCP client eventually 55s-times-out; coord wakes stop flowing; systemd still shows the unit `active`. * The host can look healthy to every shallow probe while no real work completes. ## Root cause class [Section titled “Root cause class”](#root-cause-class) A **native addon built for the wrong Node ABI** fails at *load* time, not install time. The 2026-06-19 `:3070` outage: `papercup-release`’s `better-sqlite3` was built for Node 22 (ABI 127) while the service runs Node 25 (ABI 141) — it threw `Module did not self-register`, **mem0 never loaded**, and every memory call awaited a promise that never resolved. Two independent gaps combined: 1. **Nothing rebuilt/verified native addons against the runtime Node** → the broken binary shipped to green undetected. The unit PATH carried BOTH nvm Node 22 *and* linuxbrew Node 25 — that drift is what produced the mismatch. 2. **The memory call path had no effective deadline, and the health probe exercised no subsystem** → the load failure became a silent infinite hang behind a green check. ## Diagnose (fast) [Section titled “Diagnose (fast)”](#diagnose-fast) 1. `curl :3070/api/health` (200, fast) **vs** `curl :3070/api/health/deep` — the deep probe round-trips PG + memory; a 503 with `memory.status: "down"` (or a `latencyMs` near the 3s deadline) points straight at a wedged memory subsystem. (`/api/health/ready` only reflects DBOS boot — a green `ready` does NOT mean memory works.) 2. Confirm the ABI: `node -e "console.log(process.versions.node, process.versions.modules)"` on the SERVICE’s Node (ABI = `modules`). Then `npm run preflight:addons --root <install>` — a `FAIL` on a required addon (e.g. `better-sqlite3`) is the smoking gun. 3. `node -e "require('better-sqlite3')"` under the service Node reproduces the load throw directly. Distinct from [event-loop saturation](/agent-insights/agent-mcp-slow-but-health-fast-event-loop-saturation/) (MCP slow but health fast because the loop is *busy*) — here the loop is fine; a specific subsystem never loaded. ## Immediate fix (the incident) [Section titled “Immediate fix (the incident)”](#immediate-fix-the-incident) Rebuild the addon for the runtime Node ABI and restart: `prebuild-install` (or `npm rebuild better-sqlite3`) against the **pinned** Node, then restart `papercup-dev-api.service`. Verify with `npm run preflight:addons` and `/api/health/deep` (both should pass). ## Prevention now in code (infra-fail-fast-build-integrity-2026-06-19) [Section titled “Prevention now in code (infra-fail-fast-build-integrity-2026-06-19)”](#prevention-now-in-code-infra-fail-fast-build-integrity-2026-06-19) The class is closed from four angles: * **B1 — memory tools deadline, never hang.** `lib/memory/op-deadline.ts` (`withMemoryToolTimeout`) wraps every backend call in all five `memory:*` tools (incl. the `available()` probe, which itself hangs). A wedged mem0 now returns `{ ok:false, reason:'memory_timeout' }` instead of hanging — the silent-hang *symptom*. Shared latch with the pre-turn inject path. Env: `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_TOOL_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 10s). * **A1 — deploy gate.** `npm run preflight:addons [--root <install>]` (`lib/native-addon-preflight.ts`) test-LOADS each required addon via its real package entry (NOT a raw `.node` scan — that false-alarms on the \~60 benign alternate-platform prebuilds) under the pinned Node and exits non-zero on failure, so a bad binary fails the promotion. `bare-*` (Bare-runtime) packages are skipped. Required set: `PAPERCUSP_PREFLIGHT_ADDONS` (default `better-sqlite3`). * **A2 — boot self-check.** `runBootAddonPreflight()` in `host-bootstrap.ts` logs LOUDLY at boot if a required addon won’t load (visible error, not silent hang). Safe by default; set `PAPERCUSP_ADDON_PREFLIGHT_FATAL=1` to exit non-zero so `Restart=always` surfaces a crashloop instead of a green-but-dead host. * **B4 — deep readiness.** `GET /api/health/deep` (`lib/endpoint-route/routes/misc/health-deep.ts`) round-trips PG (`SELECT 1`) + memory (`available()`) under a 3s deadline. A *hang* → `down` → 503; a clean “memory disabled” (NoopBackend host) stays healthy (no false alarm). ## Still open / owner-gated [Section titled “Still open / owner-gated”](#still-open--owner-gated) * **A3** — drop nvm Node 22 from the service unit PATH + pin linuxbrew Node 25 (`.nvmrc`/`engines`, `npm rebuild` on every release refresh) to kill the drift at the source. Live systemd edit — owner-gated. * Flip `PAPERCUSP_ADDON_PREFLIGHT_FATAL=1` once A2’s required set is validated against every host shape (e.g. memory-disabled utility hosts). Full audit: `BRIEF-infra-fail-fast-build-integrity-2026-06-19.md` (repo root).

# Native-scheduler lockout — one scheduler of record for agents

> Agent sessions (bees, Queen, role panes, wake resumes) are denied every client-native and OS scheduling surface, so a wake can only live in the harness routines table. The variadic --disallowedTools gotcha and the per-backend enforcement map.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The hive’s liveness contract is **“a wake is always armed in `harness_shared.routines`”** (`hive:declare-wake` → the one-shot `hive-wake` row). That table is the single scheduler of record read by `hive:status`, Pause, the wake-mode gate, and the liveness backstop. A wake scheduled anywhere else — claude-code’s `CronCreate`/`ScheduleWakeup`/`/schedule`/`/loop`, or `crontab`/`at`/`systemd-run` through any backend’s shell — is invisible to all of it: the backstop double-fires, Pause can’t stage it, and a cron job outlives the hive as a zombie. So every **agent** launch is locked out of those surfaces (plan `native-scheduler-lockout-2026-06-09`). The owner’s own `psu su` sessions are untouched. ## The enforcement map [Section titled “The enforcement map”](#the-enforcement-map) | Layer | Mechanism | Where | | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | claude T1 (its scheduler tools + skills) | `--disallowedTools=…` at launch | `invoke.ts` extraFlags (every headless spawn) · `wake-executor.ts` resume leg · `psu-launcher.mjs` `roleLaunchArgs` + brain legs | | claude T2 (OS schedulers via Bash) | `Bash(crontab:*)`-style deny patterns in the same flag (works hook-less, i.e. for headless bees) + the bash-resource-gate hook (catches compound forms) | canonical list: `@papercusp/orchestrator/native-scheduler-deny` · hook: `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh` | | omp (no T1 surface — toolset audited 2026-06-09) | coord-hook `tool_call` block on OS-scheduler commands | `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/omp/coord-hook.ts` (`OS_SCHEDULER_CMD_RE`) | | codex (no T1 surface — toolset probed 2026-06-09) | gate hook wired into the role home’s `hooks.json`; current Codex supports `PreToolUse` matchers for Bash and `apply_patch`/`Edit`/`Write` | `role-codex-home.ts` `writeCodexLockHooks({ agentSession: true })` | | All backends, intent layer | explicit prohibition in the prompts | `queen.md` wake section · `bee.md` Don’ts | The hook layers key off **`PAPERCUSP_AGENT_SESSION=1`**, set by every agent launch path (orchestrator spawn env, wake-executor resumes, psu role panes, the brain) and never by human sessions — the guard fails open for the owner. ## Gotchas (all verified live, 2026-06-09) [Section titled “Gotchas (all verified live, 2026-06-09)”](#gotchas-all-verified-live-2026-06-09) * **`--disallowedTools` is variadic** (`<tools...>`): the space form greedily eats every following token — in the wake-executor’s case the positional wake text itself became “deny rules” and the run errored with no prompt. **Always use the single-token `=` form** (`--disallowedTools=A,B,C`). * **The deny holds under `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`** — the tool is removed from the model’s toolset, not merely permission-gated. * **`ScheduleWakeup` is present even in headless `claude -p` sessions**, so this is a live exposure for bees, not an interactive-only concern. * **Headless claude spawns load NO hooks** (minimal `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, creds symlink only) — that’s why the T2 Bash deny-patterns ride the launch flag instead of relying on the PreToolUse gate. * Bash prefix deny-patterns can’t match compound commands (`cd x && crontab …`) — the hook layer covers those; `at` is hook-only (a bare prefix rule would false-positive `atuin`/`attach`). * CLI flags don’t persist into resumes: **every resume leg must re-apply the flag** (the wake-executor does; that’s the leg that wakes the Queen). ## Residual gaps (accepted, documented) [Section titled “Residual gaps (accepted, documented)”](#residual-gaps-accepted-documented) * Headless **omp** bees load no `-e` extension (auto-discovery dir is empty on this box), so their shell is prompt-governed only. Default bees are claude, which is fully covered. * **codex** relies on the managed per-session `hooks.json` actually being installed. If `papercusp-diagnostics.json` reports `hooks-missing`, the scheduler gate falls back to prompt discipline until the local hook install is repaired. * Anything remote (`ssh host 'crontab …'`) is out of scope for local hooks. * `psu --resume` of a role session by the OWNER doesn’t re-apply the flag (owner-supervised; OQ-2 of the plan).

# A new learning-singleton blueprint ships its DEFINITION but does NOT auto-create the routine — materialize it post-deploy

> Adding a learning loop (blueprint + LEARNING_SINGLETONS entry + op) ships code only; the `@singleton/bp-singleton-<id>-0` routine ROW is never created on deploy/boot — there is no boot-time materializer. Until you run `materializeLearningSingletons` (the seed CLI) for the workspace, the loop has no routine, never fires, and never shows in improvements:learning_loops — even with singletonActive:true and the flag ON. This is the 0th gate, before the three in dark-learning-loops-are-triple-gated.

You added a new learning loop the right way — a `blueprints/<id>/blueprint.yaml` with `singleton: true` (and maybe `singletonActive: true`), a deterministic op registered in `blueprint-steps/index.ts`, an entry in `LEARNING_SINGLETONS`, a flag defaulting ON. It type-checks, the blueprint test passes, it ships to green. And then… nothing fires. It is not in `improvements:learning_loops`. Its output table stays empty forever. **Why:** adding the blueprint ships only the loop’s *definition*. The actual `harness_shared.routines` row — `@singleton/bp-singleton-<id>-0`, the thing the routine engine ticks — is **never created on deploy or operator boot**. There is no boot-time materializer that walks `LEARNING_SINGLETONS` and upserts rows. `materializeLearningSingletons` / `materializeBlueprintTriggers` is called only from: * the **seed CLI** (`packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/seed-learning-singletons.ts`), run by hand, and * `enable-platform-mode.ts` (when the owner first enables platform mode — it flips the `PLATFORM_IMPROVEMENT_LOOPS` flag ON **first**, then calls `materializeLearningSingletons` so Class-C singletons actually get written), and * `harness:create` / `hive:create` (for that harness’s own blueprint, not the workspace singletons). **P-070 deployment-mode gate (added 2026-06-14):** `materializeLearningSingletons` now has a skip condition for Class-C platform-improvement loops: if the `PLATFORM_IMPROVEMENT_LOOPS` flag is OFF (a public release or a fresh install before the owner enables platform mode), the seed CLI prints: 
```plaintext
SKIP <id>: platform-improvement loops are OFF (PLATFORM_IMPROVEMENT_LOOPS) — release/non-platform mode (P-070)
```
 and creates **no `@singleton` row** — not even a dark/inactive one. `--execute` returns without an error; the loop is simply not materialized. In dev/self-host the flag defaults ON so this gate is transparent, but on a clean install or a release image it is the silent barrier. Fix: enable platform mode first (`enablePlatformMode` / the owner’s platform-mode toggle) — that flips the flag ON, then materializes all Class-C singletons atomically. If you are seeding manually on a release box, verify the flag is ON before running `--execute`. So the existing live loops (calibration, scout, iq-battery, …) got their `@singleton` rows from a **past owner-run seed campaign**, not from their code landing. A brand-new loop inherits none of that. **Fix — materialize it once, AFTER your code is deployed to the operator that runs the routine engine** (the routine fires `system:blueprint-run`, which loads your blueprint + op on the *running* operator; do it before the code is there and the first fire fails to resolve): 
```sh
# dry-run first (prints the plan, writes nothing)
PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID=<ws> DATABASE_URL=… \
  npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/seed-learning-singletons.ts --only <id>
# then create the @singleton row
… --only <id> --execute
```
 `singletonActive: true` makes it seed **active** (always-on monitoring, e.g. iq-battery / memory-precision); `false` (the frontier default) seeds it **dark**, still needing the three arming gates afterward. Either way the ROW must exist first. This is the **0th gate**, before the three in \[\[dark-learning-loops-are-triple-gated]]: routine row exists → routine active → flag ON → governor budgeted. A flag default-ON and a green deploy are necessary but **not sufficient** — without the materialize step the loop has no heartbeat at all. (Two smaller traps seen alongside, 2026-06-18: the `papercup-staging-api` :3170 instance runs `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ROUTINES=0` and does **not** boot-apply migrations — restarting it won’t apply a new `sql/NNN-*.sql`; that happens on the main operator’s boot after the file reaches its checkout. And when you build a bench to MONITOR an already-floored metric, replay the gold set **with** the production floor — `runGoldSet(…, { minScore, minLexScore })` — not the unfloored `runBench`, or you measure raw-recall FP\@5 (\~100%) instead of the floored production number (\~17%).)

# A new package in a CJS family must not set type:module (and needs main+types, not just exports)

> Two packaging traps that bite when you add a workspace package to the src-as-entry tooldef family. (1) Setting "type": "module" on a package that CJS siblings re-export from breaks the operator's tsx host with 'does not provide an export named X' — vitest/esbuild mask it, so unit tests stay green while the real host would fail on reload. (2) A package.json with only "exports" and no top-level "main"/"types" is unresolvable under classic moduleResolution: node. Both surfaced during the @papercusp/tooldef extraction.

Superseded (2026-06-04) — verify against current code The premise of **Trap 1** no longer holds. The whole tooldef re-export chain moved to ESM together on 2026-06-04: `@papercusp/tooldef`, `@papercusp/tooldef-http`, `@papercusp/tooldef-mcp`, `@papercusp/agent-mcp`, **and** `@papercusp/chat-protocol` all now carry `"type": "module"`. So a new sibling should now **match the family by setting `"type": "module"`** — the opposite of the rule below. (The page’s own escape hatch — “if you genuinely need ESM, move the whole re-export chain together” — is exactly what happened.) Note the build configs still emit CJS (`tsconfig.build.json`: `"module": "CommonJS"`), which is now mismatched with the package `"type"`; the runtime that matters is `tsx`, which honors `"type"`. **Trap 2** is also weakened: the operator + operator-core now compile under `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` (not classic `node`), so the `exports` map *is* honored. The top-level `main`/`types` belt-and-suspenders is still present and harmless, but the “classic node ignores exports” rationale no longer describes these consumers. The “verify under real `tsx`/Node, not just vitest” advice at the bottom still stands. When you scaffold a **new** workspace package and wire it into the `@papercusp/tooldef` family (src-as-entry packages — `main`/`types`/`exports` all point at `./src/index.ts`, consumed via a direct `node_modules/@papercusp/<pkg>` symlink), two `package.json` fields decide whether the **operator host** can load it at runtime. Both default to the wrong thing, and both are **masked by the test runner**, so green unit tests are not proof the host works. ## Trap 1 — `"type": "module"` in a CJS family [Section titled “Trap 1 — "type": "module" in a CJS family”](#trap-1--type-module-in-a-cjs-family) `@papercusp/tooldef` and `@papercusp/agent-mcp` are **CommonJS** (their `tsconfig.build.json` emits CJS; no `type` field → Node treats `.js`/`.ts` as CJS). The operator’s `:3070` Hono host runs under **`tsx`**, which honours `type`. If you give a new sibling (`@papercusp/tooldef-http`, `@papercusp/tooldef-mcp`, …) `"type": "module"`, then importing a **named** binding across the CJS↔ESM boundary throws under tsx: 
```plaintext
SyntaxError: The requested module '@papercusp/tooldef' does not provide an
export named 'dispatchProjectedTool'
```
 — the classic CJS↔ESM named-export interop break (the named binding isn’t statically visible across the boundary). **Observed directly:** the standalone `examples/standalone-http.ts` proof failed with exactly this under both node 22 and node 25 while the packages carried `"type": "module"`. **Why it hides:** `vitest`/`esbuild` transpile everything to a single module graph and don’t enforce the CJS/ESM boundary, so the package’s own test suite passes 100%. The break only appears under real Node/tsx module resolution — a `npx tsx examples/…` script, or the operator’s `:3070` Hono host, which runs under the same tsx runtime and imports these packages (via `agent-mcp`’s re-export) — so the host is exposed to the same break. During the extraction the bug was invisible until the standalone example ran it under tsx. **Verified after the fix (2026-05-31, live host):** with `"type"` removed, the operator’s `:3070` Hono host (`bin/hono-host.ts` under tsx, node 22) boots clean on the fixed packages and serves both transports end-to-end — a live HTTP projected-tool call returns `200` + the `{content}` envelope (`tooldef-http`), and MCP `tools/call` dispatches projected tools through `tooldef-mcp`. (The caveat the examples teach still stands: only `tsx`/real-Node resolution exercises this boundary; the bundled test suite won’t.) **Rule:** a new package that any CJS package re-exports from (or that the tsx host imports) must **not** set `"type": "module"`. Match the family — omit `type` (CJS). If you genuinely need ESM, the whole re-export chain has to move together, which the family deliberately hasn’t done. ## Trap 2 — `"exports"` without top-level `"main"`/`"types"` [Section titled “Trap 2 — "exports" without top-level "main"/"types"”](#trap-2--exports-without-top-level-maintypes) The operator + several consumers compile under **classic `moduleResolution: node`** (not `node16`/`bundler`). Classic resolution **ignores the `exports` map** and looks only at top-level `"main"`/`"types"`. A `package.json` like: 
```jsonc
{ "exports": { ".": { "types": "./src/index.ts", "import": "./src/index.ts" } } }
```
 resolves fine under `tsx`/bundler but fails a consumer’s `tsc` with `Cannot find module '@papercusp/<pkg>'`. This is exactly why `@papercusp/chat-protocol` “didn’t exist” until its submodule `package.json` gained top-level `main`/`types`. **Rule:** every src-as-entry package ships **both** — top-level `"main": "./src/index.ts"` + `"types": "./src/index.ts"` **and** the `exports` map. Belt and suspenders covers both resolver modes. ## How to actually verify (don’t trust the test suite) [Section titled “How to actually verify (don’t trust the test suite)”](#how-to-actually-verify-dont-trust-the-test-suite) The package’s own `vitest` is necessary but **not sufficient**. Before claiming a new package works in the host: 1. Write a `examples/standalone-*.ts` that imports only the package(s) under test and run it with `npx tsx examples/<x>.ts`. This exercises real Node/tsx resolution and the CJS/ESM boundary the bundler hides. 2. If it’s on the host’s import path, reload the Tauri shell (server-side code has no hot-reload) and exercise the route — a green tsc + green vitest can still ship a host that won’t boot. See also [`generalizing-a-lib-host-seam-pattern`](/agent-insights/generalizing-a-lib-host-seam-pattern) for the src-as-entry + symlink recipe these packages follow, and the plan `papercusp-tooldef-extraction-2026-05-29` (P-051) for the commit that fixed it.

# Add a non-diff (in-container / interactive) bench suite as a fleet arm — makePoolBacklogDriver

> The shared pool-orchestration shell so a non-M1 suite (METR HCAST containers, tau2 interactive sims) runs through the same HiveBacklogDriver contract + fleet metrics as the SWE-bench diff arms, supplying ONLY a per-task work fn.

The SWE-bench-Pro fleet arms (`su-independent-backlog.ts`, `hive-backlog-realqueen.ts`) and the non-diff suites (METR HCAST containers, tau2 interactive sims, TheAgentCompany) share ONE orchestration skeleton — a bounded concurrency pool + a live-occupancy `ConcurrencyTimeline` + the never-throw drain — and differ only in the per-task **work surface** (M1 = clone a host worktree → spine bee via :3170 → `git diff`; M2 = run an agent inside a Docker container / drive an agent↔sim conversation → score in place). Don’t fork the orchestration per suite. ## The shared shell [Section titled “The shared shell”](#the-shared-shell) `packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/hive-backlog-utilities.ts`: * `makeConcurrencySampler(startedAtMs, now)` — the `ConcurrencyTimeline` accounting (enter/exit/sample/peak/finalize). * `runConcurrencyPool({ backlogLength, cap, now, deadlineMs, perTask, onEntered, onExited, onResult })` — the bounded, never-throw worker pool (≤cap live, drains in waves, stops at the deadline). * **`makePoolBacklogDriver(deps): HiveBacklogDriver`** — the whole pool-topology driver shell. It owns the sampler + pool + the canonical `HiveBacklogResult` projection. A suite supplies ONLY its `perTask`. ## Adding a suite = one `perTask` [Section titled “Adding a suite = one perTask”](#adding-a-suite--one-pertask) 
```ts
export function myBacklogDriver(ops, opts = {}): HiveBacklogDriver {
  return makePoolBacklogDriver({
    now: ops.now,
    concurrencyCap: () => ops.concurrencyCap(),
    perTask: async ({ task, index, arm, seed, budget }) => {
      // arm (FleetArmId) selects the agent loop — {baseline-opus | hive | su}; identical pool → causal isolation.
      // Run the agent on ONE task → ONE FleetTaskResult. NEVER THROW: on infra failure RETURN a result with
      // attempt.stopReason='error'|'infra-failed' (downstream isScoredStopReason excludes it).
      const r = await runOneMyTask(ops, { task, arm: myArmId(arm), seed, budget });
      return toFleetTaskResult(r);            // carry suite-specific score on attempt.armMeta
    },
    collectCoordEvents: () => [],             // hive arm → placement events; pool/independent → []
  });
}
```
 `metr-hcast-backlog.ts` is the live \~12-line example (perTask = pull container → driveArm → taskhelper `score()` → `toFleetTaskResult`). Its `metrHcastTaskResultsFromFleet(result)` round-trips the canonical output back to the suite-specific report (one run → both the standard fleet metrics AND the horizon fit) — carry the suite score on `attempt.armMeta` and read it back. Copy this shape for an interactive suite (tau2): the `perTask` body is the per-turn `TurnGenerator` (agent↔sim conversation → reward score). ## Why the canonical contract matters [Section titled “Why the canonical contract matters”](#why-the-canonical-contract-matters) The shell returns `HiveBacklogResult` (`FleetTaskResult[]` + `ConcurrencyTimeline` + `CoordEvent[]`), so the new suite flows straight through `runHiveBacklog()` → `toFleetRunSummary()` → `@papercusp/bench-metrics` `buildHiveReport` (throughput / value / autonomy) + MAST coordination — identical to every SWE-bench arm. The suite driver + its per-turn loop live in **external-bench**; keep `@papercusp/bench-metrics` domain-free (pass-k / horizon / fleet aggregation only). ## The one honest gap (M1 vs M2) [Section titled “The one honest gap (M1 vs M2)”](#the-one-honest-gap-m1-vs-m2) This shares the POOL topology. The REAL Queen-over-backlog (`hive-backlog-realqueen`) places bees onto host **worktree** member harnesses — a spine bee cannot literally operate inside a Docker container / a sim loop without generalizing the spine to a “container/interactive work-surface.” So a non-diff suite’s “hive” version is the in-container/interactive **coordination** arm (e.g. lead + delegate), labelled as such — NOT the real Queen placing over the backlog. Generalizing the spine work-surface is the deeper, separate change.

# nuqs ↔ TanStack Router search params — number coercion + the stock-adapter clobber

> Why ?dock=1 / ?switch=1 were unreachable, and why nuqs writes dropped TanStack-native search params. Normalize flag params to the number 1; use a functional-search nuqs adapter.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) `/harness/<slug>?dock=1` always redirected to `/adv` (the dock shell was unreachable), and `/login?switch=1` never entered switch-account mode — even though the URL clearly carried the param. Diagnostic logs showed `window.location.search = "?dock=1"` while the route’s `validateSearch` saw `search.dock === undefined`. ## Two independent root causes (both Next → TanStack-Router migration regressions) [Section titled “Two independent root causes (both Next → TanStack-Router migration regressions)”](#two-independent-root-causes-both-next--tanstack-router-migration-regressions) ### 1. TanStack coerces `?dock=1` to the **number** 1; `=== '1'` is false [Section titled “1. TanStack coerces ?dock=1 to the number 1; === '1' is false”](#1-tanstack-coerces-dock1-to-the-number-1--1-is-false) TanStack Router’s default search parser JSON-parses each value, so `?dock=1` becomes `dock: 1` (a **number**). The migrated `validateSearch` kept the Next check `search.dock === '1'` (Next gave a **string**) → `1 === '1'` is `false` → `dock` resolves to `undefined` → the loader redirects. **Do NOT “fix” it by normalizing to the string `'1'`.** TanStack’s default *stringifier* JSON-encodes strings, so `dock: '1'` serializes to `?dock="1"`, which then re-parses/re-stringifies and **drifts** (`"1"` → `"\"1\""` → …) until the value is the quoted string `"1"` and the `=== '1'` check fails again — intermittently, which is maddening to debug. **Fix:** normalize flag params to the **number** that the URL naturally parses to. `dock: 1` round-trips as `?dock=1` with no quoting and is stable: 
```ts
validateSearch: (search): { dock?: 1 } => ({
  dock: search.dock === 1 || search.dock === '1' ? 1 : undefined,  // accept '1' too, self-heal
}),
// consumers: if (search.dock === 1) …   // number, not '1'
```
 ### 2. The stock `nuqs/adapters/tanstack-router` clobbers + double-encodes [Section titled “2. The stock nuqs/adapters/tanstack-router clobbers + double-encodes”](#2-the-stock-nuqsadapterstanstack-router-clobbers--double-encodes) When this app mixes nuqs (`useQueryState('ws')`, tabs, …) with TanStack-native typed search (`validateSearch` + `useSearch` for `dock`/`switch`/`slug`), the stock adapter is hostile to the native params. Its `updateUrl` does: 
```ts
navigate({ to: pathname + renderQueryString(search) })  // search = WATCHED keys only, as a STRING
```
 Two failures fall out: * **Clobber:** it rebuilds the whole query string from only the nuqs-*watched* keys, so any TanStack-native param (`?dock=1`) is **dropped on every nuqs write**. The WorkspaceSwitcher mount effect writes `?ws=<active>` on load → that single write wipes `?dock=1`. * **Encoding loop:** because it hands TanStack a `to` string, TanStack re-stringifies it with its own JSON encoder, so already-encoded values get re-encoded and params duplicate (`?tab=x&tab=x`). **Fix:** a custom adapter (built on `nuqs/adapters/custom`’s `unstable_createAdapterProvider`) whose `updateUrl` uses TanStack’s **functional search updater** so TanStack owns serialization exactly once and non-nuqs params survive: 
```ts
updateUrl: (nuqsSearch, options) =>
  navigate({
    to: pathname,
    search: (prev) => applyNuqsToSearch(prev, watchKeys, nuqsSearch), // {...prev minus watched, ...nuqs}
    replace: options.history === 'replace',
  });
```
 See `apps/operator-vite/src/lib/nuqs-tanstack-router-adapter.tsx` (+ its unit test) and `src/routes/__root.tsx` (imports the custom `NuqsAdapter`, not the stock one). ## How to recognise it [Section titled “How to recognise it”](#how-to-recognise-it) * A search param is in `window.location.search` but `Route.useSearch()` / `validateSearch` reports it `undefined` → suspect number/string coercion. * A nuqs write (often a mount-effect sync like `?ws=`) makes an unrelated search param vanish, or params start duplicating / gaining `%22` quotes → suspect the stock tanstack adapter. Instrument `updateUrl`’s `to`/merge. Only 5 of \~84 operator-vite routes use `validateSearch`; the rest pass search through, so nuqs params survive there — the clobber only bit routes that mix both systems.

# Octokit 7+ changed the `auth:` API — use `hook.before('request')` instead of an async factory

> The async-factory `auth: async () => token` pattern that worked in @octokit/rest v3-v5 throws `Token passed to createTokenAuth is not a string` on v7. Set the Authorization header in a `before('request')` hook instead.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) The v3-v5 docs (and most random snippets you’ll find via search) tell you to lazy-resolve tokens like this: 
```ts
import { Octokit } from '@octokit/rest';


const oc = new Octokit({
  auth: async () => {
    const result = await getMyToken();
    return result.token;
  },
});
```
 In **@octokit/rest 7+** that throws immediately on construction: 
```plaintext
[@octokit/auth-token] Token passed to createTokenAuth is not a string
```
 The `auth:` option’s contract changed: v7 expects either a string literal or a structured `{ strategy, ... }` object. Functions are no longer accepted as a shortcut for “I’ll give you a token when asked.” The error message blames `@octokit/auth-token`, which masks that the real culprit is your factory shape. ## The fix [Section titled “The fix”](#the-fix) Don’t pass `auth:` at all. Use the request lifecycle hooks to set the `Authorization` header on every outgoing request: 
```ts
import { Octokit } from '@octokit/rest';


const oc = new Octokit({});


oc.hook.before('request', async (options) => {
  const result = await getMyToken();
  if (result.kind !== 'ok') {
    throw new Error('not authenticated');
  }
  if (!options.headers) options.headers = {};
  options.headers.authorization = 'token ' + result.token;
});
```
 You keep the same per-request async resolution. You keep your token’s cache layer hot. You don’t fight the v7 type system. ## Bonus: 401-retry without infinite-looping [Section titled “Bonus: 401-retry without infinite-looping”](#bonus-401-retry-without-infinite-looping) Pair the `before` hook with a `wrap` hook to handle revoked tokens gracefully: 
```ts
oc.hook.wrap('request', async (request, options) => {
  try {
    return await request(options);
  } catch (err) {
    if (isUnauthorizedError(err)) {
      const wasRetried = (options as { __retried?: boolean }).__retried;
      if (!wasRetried) {
        await refreshMyTokenCache();
        return request({ ...options, __retried: true });
      }
    }
    throw err;
  }
});
```
 The retry flag short-circuits the second 401 so a genuinely revoked token doesn’t loop forever. `before('request')` runs again on the retry (it always does for `request()` calls), so the refreshed token gets picked up automatically. ## Why the v7 surface is structurally better [Section titled “Why the v7 surface is structurally better”](#why-the-v7-surface-is-structurally-better) The v3-v5 async-factory pattern conflated two concerns: 1. *How* to authenticate (token, OAuth, JWT, app installation). 2. *When* to resolve the credential (lazy, cached, refreshed). The new `authStrategy` option owns (1). Request hooks own (2). If you only need (2) — which is the common case — you don’t have to build a strategy object. `hook.before('request')` also runs for *every* request including ones the strategy layer can’t see (e.g. `oc.request('GET /custom')`). Setting the header in the hook means no path silently bypasses your auth. Caution The test you write to verify the wiring will be the thing that catches this. A unit test that just calls `oc.hook.before(...)` and asserts on the hook object will pass; a test that actually issues `oc.users.getAuthenticated()` (with `gh auth status` succeeding locally) will throw the `createTokenAuth` error and force the rewrite. Lean on live integration smokes for SDKs with breaking auth changes. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * `packages/operator-core/lib/identity/octokit-client.ts` — the canonical wrapper in this repo. Uses both `before('request')` for auth and `wrap('request')` for 401-retry. Also wires a `makeTimeoutFetch` wrapper (default 20 s, tunable via `PAPERCUSP_GITHUB_TIMEOUT_MS` env or the `CreateOctokitOpts { timeoutMs?, fetch? }` arg to `createOctokit()`) into `Octokit`’s `request.fetch` option — the single app-wide guard against a stalled socket blocking the caller indefinitely (root cause: dogfood hive-join froze at 5% because `resolveLocalAnnounceIdentity`’s GitHub calls never resolved or rejected on a hung socket). The `fetch` option also lets tests inject a fake fetch for deterministic timeout coverage. (The repo now pins `@octokit/rest ^22`; the v7 `auth:`-shape break this page documents persists unchanged in v22, so the `before('request')` fix is still the right one.) * `packages/operator-core/lib/identity/gh-token.ts` — the token cache the Octokit wrapper consumes (see also [`forward-defined-registry-entries`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries/) for the pattern of placing helpers ahead of their primary consumer). * [Octokit migration guide v6→v7](https://github.com/octokit/octokit.js/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) — the upstream changelog.

# OMP eval tool has no tools proxy — use mcp__papercusp_su_* directly

> Why omp agents calling MCP tools via `tools.invoke()` in Python eval get NameError.


# OMP eval tool has no `tools` proxy [Section titled “OMP eval tool has no tools proxy”](#omp-eval-tool-has-no-tools-proxy) When an OMP agent runs Python code via `mcp__papercusp_su_tools:invoke { name: "tools:invoke", args: { ... } }` in the eval context, the `tools` object is **not available** in that Python runtime. ## Symptoms [Section titled “Symptoms”](#symptoms) * `NameError: name 'tools' is not defined` * Agent tries to call MCP tools (e.g. `tools.invoke()`, `tools.find()`) from inside a Python `eval`/`exec` block * Works fine from the OMP agent’s native prompt context, fails only inside eval ## Root Cause [Section titled “Root Cause”](#root-cause) OMP’s `eval` tool runs Python code in an **isolated Python runtime** that has no access to: * The OMP agent’s `tools` proxy (the `mcp__papercusp_su_*` namespace) * Any Node.js/TypeScript objects * The agent’s call context (no `ctx`, no `tools`) The Python runtime is a **pure Python sandbox** — it can run any Python code, but it doesn’t have the MCP tool proxy available as a Python variable. ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) **Call MCP tools directly from the OMP agent’s native context, NOT from inside eval.** ### Wrong: Inside eval [Section titled “Wrong: Inside eval”](#wrong-inside-eval) 
```python
tools.invoke({ name: "tools:find", args: { query: "X" } })  # NameError
```
 ### Right: Native OMP context [Section titled “Right: Native OMP context”](#right-native-omp-context) 
```plaintext
mcp__papercusp_su_tools:find { query: "X" }  # Works — native tool call
```
 If you need to **pass Python results TO MCP tools**, capture them in a variable and use them as args: 
```python
# In Python eval:
result = some_python_computation()
```
 Then call the MCP tool from OMP’s native context: 
```plaintext
mcp__papercusp_su_tools:find { query: "X", extra_arg: result }
```
 ## Why This Exists [Section titled “Why This Exists”](#why-this-exists) The `tools` proxy lives in the **OMP agent’s TypeScript runtime**, not in the Python eval sandbox. They are separate execution contexts — Python eval cannot import or reference the agent’s tool namespace. ## See Also [Section titled “See Also”](#see-also) * `agent-insights/tool-delta-base-presence-contract` — tool contract docs * `agent-insights/token-efficiency-production-scorecard` — when to use eval vs native tools *** *Written 2026-07-03 by Ornith behaviour-test batch (P-011).*

# OMP (pi) inference-gateway routing via a session models.yml

> How an OMP/pi agent is account-pinned + routed through the Papercusp inference gateway — a per-session models.yml that defines a dedicated `papercusp-gateway` provider (baseUrl → gateway, x-papercusp-account header). The OMP peer of codex's CODEX_HOME config.toml writer. Verified end-to-end on real omp.

OMP (the `pi` / `@oh-my-pi/cli` backend) reaches Tier-1 parity with Claude and Codex for **inference-gateway routing + account-pinning**. Plan: `omp-account-pinning-gateway-2026-06-29`. ## The mechanism (no new gateway protocol) [Section titled “The mechanism (no new gateway protocol)”](#the-mechanism-no-new-gateway-protocol) pi reads its model config from `<HOME>/.omp/agent/models.yml` (legacy `models.json` auto-migrates). A per-provider entry supports `{ baseUrl, apiKey, api, auth, headers, models }`. So routing an OMP session through the gateway is a **config write**, not a protocol — the OMP peer of codex’s per-session `CODEX_HOME/config.toml` `[model_providers.*]` writer. `ompGatewayModelsConfig()` (`omp-models-config.ts`) emits a **dedicated `papercusp-gateway` provider**: 
```yaml
providers:
  papercusp-gateway:
    baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:8788"     # gateway root (anthropic) or /v1 (openai)
    apiKey: "papercusp-gateway"           # inert; the gateway strips+reinjects the account OAuth
    api: anthropic-messages               # or openai-responses for an OpenAI/codex account
    auth: apiKey
    headers:
      "x-papercusp-account": "<acct>"     # the account pin the gateway routes on
      "x-papercusp-owner": "<spawnId>"
    models:
      - id: "claude-sonnet-4-6"             # a VALID dated id — bare `claude-sonnet-4` 404s
        api: anthropic-messages
        # ...
```
 …and the session selects `--model papercusp-gateway/<model>` (the helper returns this as `modelSelector`). omp then POSTs `/v1/messages` to the gateway carrying the pin header, in the exact wire shape the existing **anthropic** (or **openai-compatible**) gateway adapter expects — reusing the shipped Claude/Codex gateway infrastructure. There is **no bespoke “omp” protocol**; `provider-adapters.ts`’s `omp` row is a diagnostics view that delegates to the anthropic adapter (the gateway dispatches by request *path*, never by a per-backend omp adapter). Use a DEDICATED provider id, not a bare \`anthropic\` override pi’s canonical-model equivalence resolves a built-in id like `claude-sonnet-4` to cloud gateways (amazon-bedrock / cloudflare-ai-gateway) **before** a built-in-provider `baseUrl` override applies. A unique provider id (`papercusp-gateway/...`) is selected deterministically. Overriding `providers.anthropic.baseUrl` does **not** reliably capture the traffic. ## Two delivery paths [Section titled “Two delivery paths”](#two-delivery-paths) The `omp` CLI reads models config **user-level only** from `os.homedir()/.omp/agent` — there is no `--models` flag and no agent-dir env var, so a session override must ride `HOME`. * **Power-user connect (shipped):** `/api/agent-bundle` computes the models.yml (`resolveOmpGatewayModels`, gated on the gateway flag + a pool account + the capability matrix) and ships it in `omp_gateway_models`. The `@papercusp/omp` client (`connect.ts` `installOmpModelsConfig`) **temp-installs** it at `~/.omp/agent/models.yml` — backing up any existing `models.yml`/`models.json` and **restoring on exit** (incl. SIGINT/SIGTERM), so there is no permanent `~/.omp` edit — and selects `--model papercusp-gateway/<model>`. * **Fleet / autonomous spawns (shipped):** `resolveSpawnGatewayEnv` (operator-core) emits the models.yml **bytes** + selector as env — `PAPERCUSP_OMP_MODELS_YML` + `PAPERCUSP_OMP_MODEL_SELECTOR` alongside `PAPERCUSP_ACCOUNT_ID` — so the canonical builder stays in operator-core (no orchestrator duplication; the orchestrator package can’t import operator-core, and OMP has no `CODEX_HOME` equivalent — its only config-home lever is `HOME`). The orchestrator spawn path (`invoke.ts`) reads `process.env.PAPERCUSP_OMP_MODELS_YML` and, for an omp spawn, mints a per-spawn HOME via `writeSpawnOmpHome` (the peer of `writeSignedSpawnCodexHome`): a fresh `mkdtemp` HOME whose `.omp/agent` **symlinks** the source essentials (`auth.json`, `agent.db`, `config.yml`, `mcp.json`, `extensions/` — no credential copy) and **authors** the gateway `models.yml`, then sets `spawnEnv.HOME` to it (overriding `resolveSpawnHome`) and force-selects `--model papercusp-gateway/<model>` (it must win over any role/AGENT\_CMD `--model`, per the dedicated-provider gotcha above — stripped via `stripExplicitModelFlags`). Cleaned up on spawn close/error. Per-spawn HOME isolation is collision-free under concurrent pins and leaves no persistent `~/.omp` mutation; git identity comes from the injected `gitConfigNoPushEnv`, not HOME’s `.gitconfig`, so a fresh HOME is fine for autonomous spawns. ## Account pinning [Section titled “Account pinning”](#account-pinning) `accountProviderForInteractiveBackend('omp')` resolves to `'claude'` — an OMP session pins to a **Claude/anthropic** pool account (the dominant case; OpenAI-account OMP is a later extension). For omp, `resolveSpawnGatewayEnv` / the bootstrap-su resolver emit `PAPERCUSP_ACCOUNT_ID` **plus** the per-session `PAPERCUSP_OMP_MODELS_YML` (the gateway provider config) + `PAPERCUSP_OMP_MODEL_SELECTOR` — never the claude-CLI `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`/`ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS` env, which pi does not read. The models.yml exposes the writer’s **default** model per wire (`claude-sonnet-4` for a Claude account); per-role model fidelity through the gateway is a tracked follow-up (the chokepoint that builds the models.yml does not resolve the role’s configured model, and the orchestrator can’t regenerate it — it can only pass the bytes through). ## The third surface: the `psu` interactive `omp-su` launch (global config) [Section titled “The third surface: the psu interactive omp-su launch (global config)”](#the-third-surface-the-psu-interactive-omp-su-launch-global-config) The two delivery paths above both inject a **session-scoped** models.yml. The **`psu` interactive `omp-su` launch** (`apps/operator/scripts/psu-launcher.mjs` → raw `omp --approval-mode yolo --append-system-prompt <playbook> -e <coord>`) does **neither** — it runs against the **global `~/.omp/agent/`** config and the owner’s own in-OMP model selection. Per the owner steer (2026-06-29) this surface must **not** force a model; the fix is to make the global config’s providers *work*, not to inject routing. Two ways an interactive OMP session reaches real Claude: 1. **Native / direct (claude-parity):** pi’s built-in `anthropic` provider + the owner’s own OMP login in `~/.omp/agent/auth.json` → `api.anthropic.com` directly — the same direct-subscription path claude uses (no shared pool). An expired stored token degrades silently to local ollama; an `omp` re-login restores it. 2. **Managed gateway:** a persistent `papercusp-gateway` provider in `~/.omp/agent/models.yml` carrying **`x-papercusp-priority: interactive`** and **no account pin** — so the gateway picks an available pool account and admits at **tier-1**, ahead of the bee fleet. Selected as `papercusp-gateway/claude-sonnet-4-6`. (When the fleet has saturated the whole pool, even a tier-1 interactive request gets a `rate_limit_error`; that is a transient pool condition, not a routing fault — the native/direct path or local ollama is the fallback.) Defunct local 'Meridian' router gotcha A box can carry a **stale** `providers.anthropic.baseUrl: http://127.0.0.1:3456` (header `x-meridian-agent: pi`) pointing at a local LLM router that is **no longer running** (e.g. host `:3458` reassigned to an unrelated container). Every Claude selection then silently routes nowhere and OMP falls back to a local ollama model — and `ornith:fast` is **32k + text-only**, so it overflows the SU tool/prompt context (\~33k) on the very first turn: `request … exceeds the available context size (32768)` + `snapcompact needs a vision-capable active model` + `Operation aborted`. Remove the dead override; the only live model egress is local ollama + the inference gateway (`:8788`). Valid Anthropic model ids — bare \`claude-sonnet-4\` 404s The gateway forwards the model id **verbatim** to `api.anthropic.com`, which rejects the bare alias: `404 not_found_error — model: claude-sonnet-4`. Use the dated ids `claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-opus-4-8` (or `-4-7`), `claude-haiku-4-5`. **`omp-models-config.ts` `DEFAULT_MODELS` still ships the bare `claude-sonnet-4` / `gpt-5-codex` fallback** — any caller that does not pass `opts.models` inherits an id that 404s against a real account (the shipped verification used a local probe “model”, so it never surfaced). Fix the default to a valid dated id. ### MCP discovery is inherited from Claude [Section titled “MCP discovery is inherited from Claude”](#mcp-discovery-is-inherited-from-claude) OMP discovers MCP servers from `~/.claude.json` **and `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json`** (a `ClaudePlugins` discovery helper) **and** the cwd `.mcp.json`. Two consequences for a `psu` SU omp session: * The `github` / `cloudflare:*` / `context7` **failures are shared Claude plugins** — `github` uses `Bearer ${GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}` (unset → “Authorization header is badly formatted”); the cloudflare-api/bindings/builds/observability servers need an un-done OAuth flow (→ `invalid_token`); only public `cloudflare-docs` connects. These fail **identically in claude** — **not** an OMP-specific gap. * A **role-scoped** cwd `.mcp.json` (a signed role URL → a per-role MCP host on `:9071`) left behind by a prior role session in the launch dir **leaks into the SU session** and produces a 30s `Connection to MCP server "papercusp" timed out`. An SU omp session needs only the user-level `papercusp-su` and should not load a role-scoped cwd `.mcp.json`. ## Gotcha (RESOLVED in omp 16.2.5): omp headless boot + `proxy-agent` [Section titled “Gotcha (RESOLVED in omp 16.2.5): omp headless boot + proxy-agent”](#gotcha-resolved-in-omp-1625-omp-headless-boot--proxy-agent) Headless `omp -p` on omp **15.5.13** crashed at boot with `Cannot find package 'proxy-agent'` from `@puppeteer/browsers@2.13.2/.../httpUtil.js` — that version eagerly imported `proxy-agent@^6.5.0`, which the install only hoisted nested under `pi-voice`. A symlink to the top level was the temporary stopgap. **Resolved by the omp 16.2.5 upgrade (WI-934, verified live):** `@puppeteer/browsers@3.0.5` no longer eagerly imports `proxy-agent` (it is now an OPTIONAL peer), and `proxy-agent@8.0.1` is hoisted as a real top-level dep — so headless omp boots with no symlink. Recurrence guard: `packages/operator-core/lib/omp-headless-boot.test.ts` boots `omp -p` against an isolated empty HOME and fails if the crash signature regresses; it self-skips where `omp` is not on PATH (CI has no omp binary — the regression only manifests on a dev/release box with the real install, e.g. after a release node\_modules swap). ## Verification [Section titled “Verification”](#verification) The routing was **verified end-to-end on real omp 15.5.13** with a local probe “model” (no real Claude account/quota, per the owner steer): the exact `ompGatewayModelsConfig` output drove omp to `POST /v1/messages` carrying `x-papercusp-account`. Verified for **both** delivery paths — the connect path (D-006) and the **fleet path from a home produced by the real `writeSpawnOmpHome` + `ompGatewayModelsConfig`** (D-008), which additionally carries the `x-papercusp-priority` tier pin. Unit coverage: `spawn-mcp.test.ts` (the `writeSpawnOmpHome` seeder — symlinks + authored models.yml * cleanup), `resolve-spawn-gateway-env.test.ts` (the omp branch emits the models.yml + selector + tier pin), `omp-models-config.test.ts`, `provider-adapters.test.ts`, the `backend-parity-smoke-matrix` `gateway-account-pin` row, and the omp-plugin `omp-gateway-models-install` test (proves restore = no permanent `~/.omp` edit). The full **real-quota** fleet smoke through the live gateway + pool (P-010) is deferred: it needs an owner-authorized **isolated** pool account, because an unknown `x-papercusp-account` falls back to the gateway’s `active()` account — which would spend real quota against the owner’s “local models only” steer. The gateway’s header-consumption + account-routing (the consumer side of the pin) is independently covered by the operator-core gateway / account-routing test suite.

# "On-desktop" sessions — reaper hard-exemption + presence flag

> A session whose OS window is currently open on the user's screen (derived live via wmctrl + adv_sessions.window_id) is "on the desktop". Such sessions are HARD-EXEMPT from every idle-session-reaper slice (the user kept losing windows they were looking at to the live-idle terminate), and coord:presence + /adv/sessions now expose an `onDesktop` flag so you can "assign these to the agent on the desktop".

## The problem [Section titled “The problem”](#the-problem) The idle-session reaper is armed in production (both `papercusp-idle-session-reaper` **and** the destructive `papercusp-idle-session-reaper-terminate` default to `true`). Slice 2 (live-but-idle terminate) Ctrl-C → SIGKILLs any *alive* session that has done no genuine activity for 4h — **including a session the user has open on screen but hasn’t typed in**. The owner kept losing windows they were actively watching. ## What “on the desktop” means (owner decision 2026-06-29) [Section titled “What “on the desktop” means (owner decision 2026-06-29)”](#what-on-the-desktop-means-owner-decision-2026-06-29) A session is **on the desktop** iff its OS window is *currently present* — a live `wmctrl -lp` enumeration of open windows, matched against the launch-recorded `adv_sessions.window_id` (with the unique `[adv:<id>]` window-title tag and the recorded pid as fallbacks). Purely **derived** — no new column, no migration, recomputed each read. A minimized window still counts (it’s still a window). This deliberately covers the **console / terminal-window** launch population (`console-launch.ts` opens a real terminal emulator and stores its `window_id`). It does **not** cover the operator web / Tauri PTY *panel* (that attaches over a PTY WebSocket with no OS window) — by design; the owner chose the OS-window definition over a viewer-attach heartbeat. `desktop-window-liveness.ts` is the whole mechanism: * `parseWmctrlList` / `selectOnDesktopSessions` — **pure**, unit-tested without an X server. * `listOpenWindows` — wmctrl spawn, **async `execFile`** (NOT `spawnSync` — this runs on the single `:3070` operator loop via the presence path; a blocking spawn on a hung X server would freeze the operator), short-TTL cached. * `gatherOnDesktopSessions()` → `{ owners, sessionIds, advSessionIds }`, the three keyings the callers need, short-TTL cached, **best-effort → empty** on any failure. **Box-local + fail-safe:** wmctrl talks to *this* host’s X server, so a headless fleet box returns no windows → nothing is on the desktop → the reaper/presence behave exactly as before. Every failure path yields empty sets, so a hiccup can only **over-protect** (skip a reap) or omit the flag — never crash a read/sweep and never cause an *extra* kill. ## The exemption (hard, all slices) [Section titled “The exemption (hard, all slices)”](#the-exemption-hard-all-slices) In `idle-session-reaper.ts` the on-desktop owners/sessionIds are folded in: * **Slice 1** (dead-process ghost reap): `gatherOnDesktopSessions().owners` ∪ the protected set → an on-desktop owner is never a “ghost” however long its heartbeat lapsed. Counted as `keptOnDesktop` in the result + routine log. * **Slice 2** (live-idle terminate): on-desktop owners ∪ the *busy* set → an on-desktop session is never in the terminate cohort, however idle. * **Slice 3** (zombie `--resume` reap): `planZombieReap(procs, ended, onDesktop)` excludes on-desktop session ids — belt-and-braces atop the existing foreground-TTY spare in `discoverResumeProcs` (a console terminal’s claude proc is already foreground), covering minimized/backgrounded edge cases. The pure plan functions are unchanged — the sets they receive just get bigger — so the slice-1/2/3 unit tests still hold; new tests cover the exclusions. ## Surfacing (so you can target it) [Section titled “Surfacing (so you can target it)”](#surfacing-so-you-can-target-it) * **`coord:presence`** — every local roster row carries `onDesktop` (LIVENESS lane in `presence-payload.ts`, so it never churns the byte-stable \[coord+N] delta channel), and `summary.onDesktop` is the count. To act on *“the agent on the desktop / on my screen”*, filter rows where `onDesktop:true`. Federated rows are `null` (their windows live on their home box). * **`/adv/sessions`** — each row gets `onDesktop`; the UI shows a `🖥 desktop` chip. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * It’s **live**: close the window and the session drops out of `onDesktop` within the TTL, and normal reaping resumes — that’s intended (hard-exempt only *while* on the desktop). * A false-positive pid match only **over-protects** (safe). The reliable keys are `window_id` and the `[adv:<id>]` title tag.

# One account runs ~15 agents — never read rate flags as "no headroom"

> The inference gateway paces ~15 concurrent agents per account. Do not treat healthyAccounts=1 / sustainedlyLimited / utilization7d=1.0 as "no capacity" or refuse to launch a fleet — that is a fabricated wall.

**Owner directive (Avi, 2026-07-06):** *“AVIYNW HAS HEADROOM. DON’T MAKE UP THAT THERE IS NO HEADROOM. WE CAN RUN 15 SIMULTANEOUS AGENTS ON 1 ACCOUNT.”* ## The mistake this prevents [Section titled “The mistake this prevents”](#the-mistake-this-prevents) When a fleet launch is capacity-clamped (e.g. `fleet:launch-on-plan` opens 2 members for a `count:10` request) it is tempting to read `accounts:status` and conclude “the account pool is exhausted, there is no headroom, I can only run 2 agents.” **That conclusion is wrong.** It fabricates a capacity wall that does not exist and strands the owner’s request. ## The reality [Section titled “The reality”](#the-reality) * **One Anthropic account paces \~15 simultaneous agents** through the inference gateway (`:8788`). The rate **governor** cap is `maxSimultaneousAgents: 16` (`dev:rate_governor_status` → `config.maxSimultaneousAgents`). Account count is **NOT** a per-agent cap — the gateway spaces/queues calls so many concurrent sessions share one account without tripping its per-window limit. * The launch advisory says this itself: *“ONE account paces many concurrent Claude sessions through the gateway, so account count is NOT a per-member cap. All N members WILL still launch.”* ## Flags that do NOT mean “cannot launch” [Section titled “Flags that do NOT mean “cannot launch””](#flags-that-do-not-mean-cannot-launch) From `accounts:status`, none of these should stop you launching the requested count: | Field | What it actually means | What it does NOT mean | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | | `healthyAccounts: 1` | The launcher’s conservative pre-flight count | ”Only capacity for \~2 agents” | | `sustainedlyLimited: true` | Recent rate penalties / near a rolling window | ”This account is unusable” | | `utilization7d: 1.0` | The 7-day rolling usage window is full | ”No calls will succeed” | | `recommendedHeadroom: 2` | An advisory, deliberately conservative clamp | ”The hard ceiling is 2” | `utilization7d` and `sustainedlyLimited` are **advisory rate signals**, not hard gates. The gateway still routes through these accounts and paces the load. ## How to actually launch the full count [Section titled “How to actually launch the full count”](#how-to-actually-launch-the-full-count) `fleet:launch-on-plan` applies the `recommendedHeadroom` clamp (a 10-ask can open 2), and has a **300s cooldown** before a re-call opens any new members. To reach the requested count now, open the remaining members with **`capability:terminal`**, which runs the raw `psu` command and **bypasses the clamp entirely**: 
```plaintext
capability:terminal {
  fleet: '<fleet-slug>',            // color only — the --fleet flag below is what joins
  terminals: [
    { command: 'psu --no-picker --fleet=<slug> --agent=claude --harness=<h> --plan=<plan> --account=auto --model=sonnet:high --launch-context=<composed-brief-path>', label: 'bd-N' },
    // …one entry per remaining member (max 12 per call)
  ]
}
```
 * The `--fleet=<slug>` flag **inside the psu command** is what actually joins the member to the fleet (`capability:terminal`’s own `fleet` arg is window-color only). * Reuse the fleet-composed launch-context path that `fleet:launch-on-plan` reported (`…/launch-context/fleet-<slug>-launch-context.md`) so the raw members get the same brief layered under the member baseline. * `--account=auto` lets the gateway pace + fail over across the pool. ## When capacity IS genuinely constrained [Section titled “When capacity IS genuinely constrained”](#when-capacity-is-genuinely-constrained) True exhaustion is rare and must be **verified**, not assumed — and even then the answer is “the gateway paces it,” not “refuse to launch.” If you truly suspect a wall, check `accounts:status` + `dev:rate_governor_status` for whether the **governor** (`fleet.effective` / `maxSimultaneousAgents`) is the limit, not the per-account rate flags. Launch the count the owner asked for and let the gateway do its job.

# One Sentinel voice pipeline — EL relay, says-pump, deep delegation

> The pane Sentinel is the ONE brain for every modality: EL Conv-AI is a relay front-end (instant ack), pane voice:say lines are synthesized server-side and fanned over the voice bus, and hard thinking goes to ephemeral background agents whose answers re-enter the pane. Includes the single-consumer drain gate and the EL prompt-override requirement.

## The design in one paragraph [Section titled “The design in one paragraph”](#the-design-in-one-paragraph) Since `voice-unified-sentinel-pipeline-2026-07-01` (owner-ratified D-001..D-004), the **zellij pane’s psu Sentinel is the ONE brain of record for every modality**. Typed text and voice both enter through `writeToSentinelPane` (`sentinel/sentinel-pane-input.ts` — the shared mechanics behind `POST /operator/sentinel-input`), and every Sentinel answer leaves both **written** (pane text) and **spoken** (`voice:say` → `sentinel_says` FIFO → the says-pump). ElevenLabs Conv-AI is deliberately **demoted to a voice front-end**: STT, the Herald voice, turn-taking, barge-in — never a brain. ## The relay (voice-in) [Section titled “The relay (voice-in)”](#the-relay-voice-in) `operator-voice-session.ts` relays **every final `user_transcript` event** to the pane deterministically — in our code, NOT dependent on the EL agent’s LLM choosing to call a tool. The EL `ask_operator` client tool no longer runs a brain: it returns only `VOICE_RELAY_ACK` (“On it — I’ll come back to you in a moment”) for EL to speak, or a spoken failure line (`relayFailureLine`) when the relay is known to have missed (no dock / exited pane / write failure). A tool call with no preceding transcript is a fallback relay, deduped against an identical same-turn transcript relay. The old second brain — `askOperator` → `${role}:converse` in `operator-voice-session-deps.ts` — is **deleted**. That path was the modality split-brain: voice answered from an in-process converse turn while typed text went to the pane, so the two modalities had different conversation state. ## The says-pump (voice-out) [Section titled “The says-pump (voice-out)”](#the-says-pump-voice-out) While a voice session is LIVE, `voice-node/sentinel-says-pump.ts` drains the pane’s `voice:say` lines from PG (`harness_shared.sentinel_says`, migration 390) server-side, broadcasts each as a **response transcript** (clients display it) and synthesizes it into **bus audio** via the same `speakIntoSession` seam the proactive sweep uses (`synthesize` → WAV → PCM → `broadcastOpVoice`), then persists it to the shared thread. Every attached client (webview, TUI) sees + the elected player hears the same answer. **The single-consumer gate is the load-bearing subtlety.** The FIFO has TWO possible consumers: this pump, and the webview’s legacy local-mode poll (`VoiceAppBridge` → `GET /operator/sentinel-output`). Exactly one may drain at a time: * pump: gated on `sessionLive()` — it never touches the FIFO without a live session; * webview poll: gated OFF while `micOwnedByFullAgent` (a session is live). The PG drain (`DELETE … RETURNING`) is atomic, so a transition race delivers a line to exactly one consumer — worst case it is spoken by the wrong engine once, never twice and never lost. If you add a third consumer you must extend this gate, not race it. ## The deep-delegation lane [Section titled “The deep-delegation lane”](#the-deep-delegation-lane) Hard thinking (an answer expected back in conversation) must not block the conversational pane and must NOT go to the Queen (her wake loop places work; she is not an answer channel — D-003). Two entry points, one core (`sentinel/sentinel-deep-delegate.ts`): * pane runtime: the `voice:delegate_deep` MCP tool (`agent-tools/voice/delegate-deep.ts`); * converse runtime: the `<delegate_deep summary brief>` tag (parsed in `operator-converse-tags.ts`, dispatched from `converse.ts`). `delegateDeep` mints a `research-task` work-item **already claimed by the pre-minted spawn id in the same write** (so it never sits unclaimed in the placement frontier — no double-execution race), spawns an ephemeral deep-tier `bee` with the question as its brief (cap 2 in flight, 15-min timeout, claim released back to `todo` if the launch is refused), and the agent answers by COMPLETING the item — `completion.summary` IS the answer. On settle, `sentinel/sentinel-deep-watch.ts` (fired from the work-items settled-events seam) injects `[deep-answer WI-NNN] <summary>` back through `writeToSentinelPane`, with a hindsight fallback when the pane is down. The Sentinel never spawns anything itself — the SN-H04 no-spawn contract holds; the tool/watch is the accountable, capped indirection. ## Traps [Section titled “Traps”](#traps) 1. **The EL agent must be relay-shaped.** `resolveConfig` pushes `EL_RELAY_PERSONA` as a `conversation_config_override` — but EL only honors it when the agent’s dashboard security settings allow prompt overrides. If the dashboard rejects it, the session silently runs the dashboard persona; keep THAT persona relay-shaped too, or the EL LLM will chat from its own knowledge and the split-brain returns at the edges. 2. **Do not “fix” the pump to run without a session.** With no session there is no elected player to render audio, and the webview local-mode poll owns the FIFO. 3. **The relay types real turns into the one dock.** Every voice utterance consumes a pane Claude turn, lands in the user-visible sentinel pane, and rides the warm-up/exited-pane guards. Live testing therefore touches the user’s dock — the full round-trip E2E is a coordinated (owner-present) run, not a silent CI job. 4. **Scenario coverage:** `sn-D01`/`sn-D02` enforce the three-way routing (answer / delegate / handoff); the host relay semantics are unit-tested in `operator-voice-session.test.ts`; the pump in `sentinel-says-pump.test.ts`.

# The :3070 operator host has no hot-reload — restart to pick up lib/** edits

> The Hono host on :3070 (MCP tools + endpoint-route handlers + the lib/** they import) runs under tsx with no file-watch. Server-side edits don't go live until it restarts; probe where a write lands to tell if you're on stale code.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) You edit `packages/operator-core/lib/**` (or `apps/operator/lib/**`) — an MCP tool, an endpoint-route handler, a `coordLog`/store seam — reload the operator UI, exercise the tool — and it behaves like your change isn’t there. It isn’t: the **`:3070` Hono host** (`apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts`) runs under `tsx` with **no file-watch**. It loaded the old module graph (including module-level singletons like `coordLog`) at startup and won’t pick up `lib/**` edits until the process restarts. The `:3055` Vite dev server (`@papercusp/operator-vite`) *does* hot-reload its own routes/components — so a frontend change goes live while an identical-feeling server-side change silently does not. That asymmetry is what makes this confusing. (Next.js is retired for the operator; `:3055` is the Vite SPA, not a Next dev server.) ## Restart it [Section titled “Restart it”](#restart-it) Two-port model since staging→main (2026-06-06) On the standing dev box, `:3070` (`papercup-dev-api`) is now the **GREEN/stable** operator — it runs from the **separate release checkout** (`papercupai-workspace/papercup-release/apps/operator`), pinned to the green `main` branch. **Restarting it reboots the same green snapshot; your `staging` edits are invisible to it** until the auto-serve pipeline carries them (green-checkpoint FFs `main`, then release-trigger deploys). To test a server-side `staging` edit live, restart the **staging** operator on `:3170` instead: `systemctl --user restart papercup-staging-api.service` (runs `bin/hono-host.ts` from the staging tree at `papercup/apps/operator` with `PAPERCUSP_HONO_PORT=3170`), then probe `:3170`. The Tauri dev shell still spawns its own operator from the staging tree, so reloading the desktop window picks up staging edits there. See the root `CLAUDE.md` “Running the operator” section. * **Tauri dev shell:** reload the desktop window (it respawns the host from the staging tree), or * **Staging operator on the dev box:** `systemctl --user restart papercup-staging-api.service` (that unit runs `npx tsx bin/hono-host.ts` on :3170 from the staging tree). The unit name is this dev box’s local supervision — not a repo invariant. Other setups have the Tauri shell spawn the host; restart it however it’s supervised there. ## The tell: probe where the write lands [Section titled “The tell: probe where the write lands”](#the-tell-probe-where-the-write-lands) A passing typecheck proves nothing about whether the *running* host has your code. Before trusting a live result, **probe where a write actually lands**: See also the user-level memory note `verify-server-pid-before-measuring` and the engineer playbook’s CLAUDE.md pointer.

# operator-core `lint:tsc` is a COUNT gate — vitest-green != tsc-clean

> npm run lint:tsc gates packages/operator-core on a TOTAL tsc-error count vs .tsc-baseline.json, hard-fails TS1xxx syntax errors, and hard-blocks green-checkpoint when it rises. vitest (esbuild) does NOT typecheck, so a vitest-green test edit can add tsc errors that tip the count over baseline. Run lint:tsc after operator-core edits — not just test:affected.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `npm run lint:tsc` (`scripts/lint-tsc.mjs`) runs `tsc -p packages/operator-core/tsconfig.json --noEmit` and compares the **total parsed error count** against `packages/operator-core/.tsc-baseline.json` (a single number, `operatorCoreErrorCount`). Don’t trust any literal value cited here as current — run `npm run lint:tsc` for the live count vs baseline. As of this writing (2026-07-03) the baseline is **PINNED at `224`** (deliberately the *higher* of a known `223`/`224` flap — see below), ratcheted down repeatedly since the `262` figure this doc originally cited — but the baseline file’s own change history shows the true count **flapping between `223` and `224` within the same day** under unrelated concurrent-edit noise (a pre-existing deep-instantiation/test- fixture ripple, e.g. `inference-gateway/observability.test.ts`’s `GatewayStats`), not a real regression each time. Pinning the higher value makes the gate pass at both 223 and 224 instead of false-redding the fleet every time it shuffles back up. If you see a lone ±1 shift with no attributable new error, that’s the known flap — verify across a few clean runs on a quiet tree before treating it as either a real improvement or a real regression, and **don’t** bare-run-ratchet a transient dip (that happened twice on 2026-07-03 and had to be manually re-restored to 224 — see the baseline file’s own `note` field). The gate: * **count > baseline ⇒ HARD FAIL** — and it runs in green-checkpoint, so a single net-new error **blocks the whole fleet’s deploy**, not just yours. * **count < baseline ⇒ ratchets down, but ONLY on an explicit `npm run lint:tsc -- --update`** (audit P-073 / EI-104, fixed 2026-07-03 — this reverses the prior “auto-ratchet on every bare run” behavior). A **bare** run (CI, or a peer’s plain `npm run lint:tsc`) never rewrites the baseline file — it only checks and hard-fails above baseline; auto-ratcheting on every bare run turned out to lock in transient dips in this shared, concurrently-edited tree and then false-red the gate for the whole fleet the next time the count shuffled back up. `--update` still only ever *lowers* the baseline (or no-ops at parity) — raising it remains a deliberate human JSON edit, never automatic. This `--update`-only policy now lives in the **pure `decide()`** function (a bare run below baseline returns `ok-below` and `main()` never writes; only `--update` yields `ok-ratchet`) and is locked by `lint-tsc.test.ts` — so a `main()` refactor can’t silently reintroduce the auto-ratchet flap. (EI-104 shipped in `main()` first but left the invariant in untested imperative code while `decide()` + its test still encoded the old auto-ratchet; WI-1822 folded the policy into `decide()` and added the guard.) * **any TS1xxx parse error ⇒ HARD FAIL** — syntax-broken files fail regardless of the total count because `tsc` under-reports the errors behind a parse failure. * It is **position-independent**: only the count matters. Adding lines above a pre-existing baselined error doesn’t “create” it, but any *net-new* error (yours, or one a refactor newly exposes) tips the total over. This is a different mechanism from the apps/operator “scope to touched files” baseline (\[\[tsc-baseline-vs-next-build]]) — there the move is per-file; here it’s a hard count gate on one package. ## The trap: vitest is green, lint:tsc is red [Section titled “The trap: vitest is green, lint:tsc is red”](#the-trap-vitest-is-green-linttsc-is-red) `npm run test:affected` runs **vitest**, which transforms with **esbuild** and does **NOT typecheck**. So a test file can be fully vitest-green while carrying tsc errors that only `lint:tsc` sees. You commit, vitest passes, and a peer (or green-checkpoint) finds the count over baseline minutes later — now everyone’s deploy is blocked. The recurring test-specific cause: a `vi.fn(async () => …)` mock infers a **zero-parameter** call signature, so `mock.calls[0]` is the empty tuple `[]`. `mock.calls[0][0]` then trips **TS2493** (“Tuple type ’\[]’ has no element at index ‘0’”), and the `as {…}` cast on the resulting `undefined` trips **TS2352**. Give the mock a typed parameter (`vi.fn(async (spec: CardSpec) => …)`), or read the first arg through a typed accessor. Concrete (B-10, 2026-06-13): a new describe block in `ask_choice.test.ts` was 15/15 vitest-green, but six existing `vi.fn(async () => …)` mocks’ `mock.calls [0][0]` casts tipped operator-core 455 → 466 and blocked green-checkpoint. Fix was a one-helper `firstSpec(askUser)` typed accessor → 0 errors in the file → count back to baseline. ## How to verify [Section titled “How to verify”](#how-to-verify) After **any** edit under `packages/operator-core` (source *or* test): 
```bash
npm run lint:tsc        # the authoritative gate — count vs baseline
```
 * If it prints `> baseline`, your touched files added tsc errors — fix them. **Do not** raise the baseline to absorb your own new errors (the script only ratchets *down*; raising is a reviewed human act with a justification). * If it reports TS1xxx syntax-broken files, fix those files first.
