The same deletion-commit pattern had already bitten once before: the endpoint-IPC server start ALSO lived only in instrumentation-node.ts and had to be ported to `host-bootstrap.ts` (see the long comment there). The registration call was the second side effect in that file, and it was missed. ## The rules [Section titled “The rules”](#the-rules) 1. **Deleting a “dead” entry file: enumerate its side effects, not its importers.** “Zero importers” proves nothing for a file whose job was to RUN things (registrations, server starts, watchers). Diff the file body against `host-bootstrap.ts` and port every effect, or state per-effect why it’s vestigial. 2. **A `registerX()/getX()` seam needs one test that fails when no host registers.** Unit tests mocking the seam keep the consumers green forever; the only honest check is at the host level (a bootstrap test, or a live probe). If you add such a seam, add the tripwire in the same PR. 3. **Verify on the running host, not in vitest.** The probe that found both bugs (bearer = any `kind='system'` row from `harness_shared.token_index`): 
   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3170/api/mcp \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
     -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"prompts/get","params":{"name":"agent:role","arguments":{"role":"architect"}}}'
   ```
 Note: `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` does NOT resolve on this surface (`invalid_bearer`) — the prompts/resources paths resolve bearers via `token_index`, not the superuser bypass. ## The second bug a first bug can mask [Section titled “The second bug a first bug can mask”](#the-second-bug-a-first-bug-can-mask) With registration fixed, the same probe failed differently: `render_error: The "paths[0]" argument must be of type string`. `import.meta.dirname` is **undefined** when the operator host runs agent-mcp through tsx’s CJS transform (apps/operator has no `"type": "module"`), while under vitest (real ESM) it works — so tests pass and the host crashes. `import.meta.url` IS shimmed there. Portable helper: `packages/agent-mcp/src/prompts/module-dir.ts` (`dirname` → `fileURLToPath` fallback, null-safe). If you write `resolve(import.meta.dirname, …)` in code any operator host loads, use `moduleDir(import.meta)` instead — and remember the hosts run with **cwd `apps/operator`**, so cwd-relative fallbacks need a `../../` candidate too. Fixed in: host-architecture-2026-05-20-v2 P-001..P-003 (D-002 has the full phase-by-phase re-baseline).

# Deploys crash-loop :3070 on MODULE_NOT_FOUND — an in-place node_modules rebuild under the live operator

> ':3070 connection refused on all pages' in recurring ~1–35 min windows: a deploy's setup-release-checkout.sh refreshed node_modules with `rm -rf $dest; cp -al` IN PLACE while the live operator kept serving from it, so for the ~minute the root copy took the tree was deleted/half-populated → the 32 cluster workers respawned mid-copy, hit MODULE_NOT_FOUND (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @papercusp/plugin-loader), exhausted the 160-respawn budget → 0 workers → connection refused, until the copy finished and it self-recovered. Root fix: atomic sibling-temp swap (two renames) so the live tree is only ever complete. Defense-in-depth: a workspace-resolution gate (step 3c, EI-2118) that aborts before restart if any workspace symlink is dangling, a boot-integrity preflight (fail fast + named), and a cluster boot-failure backstop (halt the respawn storm) so an inconsistent tree degrades to a fast, loud, self-correcting fail instead of an hour-long all-pages outage.

## The symptom [Section titled “The symptom”](#the-symptom) `:3070` (the operator that serves every page over SSE/sync) goes **“connection refused on all pages”** in recurring windows — the client shows **“Operator connection lost”** then reconnects (“Welcome back, User”), sometimes seconds apart, for anywhere from \~1 to \~35 minutes, then self-recovers. The operator journal during a window: 
```plaintext
[hono-host] fatal unhandledRejection — exiting: Error: Cannot find module
  '.../papercusp-release/node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/cjs/types.js'  code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'
[cluster] worker N exited (code=1 signal=null); respawn budget exhausted (160) — NOT respawning
[cluster] SIGTERM — draining 32 worker(s) + exiting primary
```
 `NRestarts=0` at the systemd level can hide it — the storm is the **cluster primary respawning workers**, not systemd restarting the service. ## The mechanism (root cause) [Section titled “The mechanism (root cause)”](#the-mechanism-root-cause) `:3070` runs the `papercusp-release` checkout. A deploy shells `setup-release-checkout.sh`, whose step 3 historically refreshed node\_modules **in place**: 
```sh
[ -e "$dest" ] && rm -rf "$dest"      # deletes the LIVE root node_modules
cp -al "$nm" "$dest"                  # then slowly (~a minute, 100k+ files) re-hardlinks it
```
 This tree “never `npm install`s” — it **hardlink-copies** node\_modules from the integration tree. For the whole \~minute the root `cp -al` runs, the live operator’s node\_modules is **deleted or half-populated**. Any worker that (re)boots in that window — a `lag-self-restart`, a crash respawn, a deploy restart racing the copy — `require()`s a module that isn’t there yet → `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` → it exits → the primary respawns it → it crashes again → **the 160-respawn budget (workers×5 = 32×5) burns out → 0 live workers → connection refused on every page**. When the copy finishes the next restart boots clean and it self-recovers — which is why it looks transient and recurs on (dep-changing) deploys. `PAPERCUSP_CLUSTER=32` maximizes the blast radius: one inconsistent tree crash-loops all 32 workers at once. ## The fix — four layers [Section titled “The fix — four layers”](#the-fix--four-layers) **1. Atomic node\_modules swap (root cause removal)** — `setup-release-checkout.sh` `sync_one_node_modules()`. Hardlink-copy into a **sibling** temp (`$dest.deploy-tmp.$$`, same depth so the workspace packages’ relative `../../packages/X` symlinks resolve identically), then swap with **two fast renames** (`mv dest old; mv tmp dest; rm old`). The live tree is only ever **complete**; the exposure shrinks from \~a minute to the microseconds between two `rename(2)`s. `set -e` aborts a failed `cp` *before* any swap, so a partial copy can never replace the live tree. **2. Workspace-resolution gate — step 3c (EI-2118)** — `setup-release-checkout.sh` step 3c. A related but distinct failure mode: the `need_node_modules()` heuristic compares entry **names** via `ls`+`diff`, which cannot detect a dangling symlink (it exists by name but the target is absent). Before EI-2118, a dangling `@papercusp/<pkg>` symlink in the release tree slipped through that check, the deploy skipped the re-copy, and the operator crash-looped on `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at the restart cutover (2026-06-20 `@papercusp/plugin-loader`). The fix: `unresolved_workspace_pkgs()` walks `@papercusp`/`@papercup` in both trees using `-e` (which **follows** symlinks), so a dangling link fails the test. `need_node_modules()` in `auto` mode now also calls it and forces a re-copy when any package is unresolved. After the copy, step 3c runs `unresolved_workspace_pkgs()` once more: if any package still doesn’t resolve, the script **exits 1 before any restart** — the old process keeps serving, zero downtime. **3. Boot-integrity preflight (fail fast + named)** — `boot-integrity-preflight.ts`, run as the **first import** of `hono-host.ts` via `boot-integrity-first.ts` (so it evaluates before the heavy import graph). It `require.resolve`s a manifest of load-bearing modules; on a broken/partial tree it logs one **named** diagnostic and exits `78` (distinct, `EX_CONFIG`) instead of a deep `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` stack. The module is **dependency-free** (only `node:module`) so it can’t be a victim of the inconsistency it checks. Manifest entries are **resolve-verified against a healthy tree** — naïve `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and `mem0ai/package.json` FAIL even when installed (exports-map quirks), so the manifest uses the forms that actually resolve. **4. Cluster boot-failure backstop (no respawn storm)** — `cluster-fork.ts`, opt-in via `onUnbootable`. A worker that exits within `bootGraceMs` (10s) of fork never came up; if a **whole generation** fails that way and **none was ever healthy**, the build is unbootable → halt the respawn storm and call `onUnbootable` (→ exit the primary clean/fast/distinct so the supervisor/deploy rolls back) instead of burning all 160 respawns. A worker that crashes **after** surpassing the grace window is a normal runtime crash and still respawns — `onUnbootable` never fires once any worker has been healthy. Layers 1–2 prevent inconsistent trees from reaching the live operator (either by making the swap atomic or by aborting before cutover); layers 3–4 turn any *remaining* inconsistency (a botched rollback, a non-manifest module) into a fast, loud, self-correcting fail instead of an hour-long all-pages outage. ## Diagnosing / recovering a live incident [Section titled “Diagnosing / recovering a live incident”](#diagnosing--recovering-a-live-incident) * `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3070/api/health` → `000`/connection-refused = down; the journal grep above confirms the MODULE\_NOT\_FOUND crash-loop. * It usually **self-recovers** once the in-place copy finishes; if wedged, the documented recovery is `systemctl --user stop papercup-dev-api.service` then re-run the deploy (`PAPERCUSP_ALLOW_DEV_RESTART=1 npx tsx apps/operator/lib/release/deploy-cli.ts --execute --no-drain`) or `npm ci` in `papercusp-release` to complete node\_modules. * Confirm `papercusp-release/node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/cjs/types.js` and `@papercusp/plugin-loader` resolve (`cd papercusp-release && node -e "require.resolve('@papercusp/plugin-loader')"`). ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `cluster-workers-exhaust-inotify-watches.mdx` — a *different* 32-worker crash-loop (per-process inotify exhaustion); already fixed by gating watchers on `cluster.isPrimary`. * `deploy-pipeline-is-async-self-healing.mdx` — why `:3070` serves green `main`, not your staging edit.

# Replay-consumer loops must not re-ledger battery spend

> runGovernedReplay already ledgers every battery dollar on frontier:replay-harness — a consumer loop (regret/transfer/ablation) that also records the returned totalCostUsd on its own governor loop double-counts it on the one visible spend number.

**The trap.** The frontier consumer loops (regret mining FB-07, transfer harness FB-08, shadow ablation FB-09) run student/counterfactual batteries through `runGovernedReplay` (`packages/operator-core/lib/replay/governed.ts`). That wrapper ALREADY calls `recordLearningSpend` with the battery’s `totalCostUsd` on loop `frontier:replay-harness` (accumulate:true, origin=‘replay’). The returned `ReplayBatteryResult.totalCostUsd` is there for *reporting* — if your loop also ledgers it on its own governor loop, the same dollar lands twice in `summarizeLearningSpend().totalSpentUsd` (D-004’s “one visible number”), and your loop’s lifetime budget exhausts at half its real allowance. **The rule.** A consumer loop ledgers on its own loop id ONLY the spend it generates *outside* the battery (the transfer harness: distillation LLM calls). Battery spend belongs to `frontier:replay-harness` — that loop’s owner-set budget is the chokepoint for ALL replay consumers, by design (FB-06). Surface battery cost in your tick report from `totalCostUsd`, don’t re-record it. **How FB-08 wires it** (`lib/transfer/tick.ts` testLeg + `replay-adapter.ts`): the tick’s `recordSpend` port is called for distillation refs only; the adapter routes batteries through `runGovernedReplay` and returns the cost purely for the log line. **Corollary for arming (P-001).** A consumer loop needs BOTH budgets set to actually run: its own loop (distillation/selection spend) AND `frontier:replay-harness` (battery spend) — plus both flags. An armed consumer with a dark/unbudgeted replay loop fails its tests with “governed replay refused (replay-dark)” — that’s the designed refusal, not a bug.

# Replication-liveness detector: live debugging + the per-join counter blind spot

> How to read the WI-1840 replication-liveness registry on a live sidecar (RPC, socket path, PG creds), and the detector blind-spot class that made it silent on its first live proof: per-join swarm-connection counters cannot see sockets that pre-date their registration.

Written 2026-07-04 (su-b5d1c, plan `shared-hive-p2p-release-readiness-2026-07-03` P-004 / WI-1840, WI-183 class). Two things live here: the **diagnostic recipe** for the replication-liveness detector on a live frame, and the **blind-spot class** its first live proof exposed. ## The one-line lesson [Section titled “The one-line lesson”](#the-one-line-lesson) **A detector’s own liveness must be live-proven.** WI-1840’s `connected_never_replicated` axis was 17/17 green in-process and completely silent on a live rig with a genuine stall in front of it (run `m1783120511`). In-process green ≠ live green applies to the watchdog, not just the watched. ## The blind-spot class: per-join counters on shared event emitters [Section titled “The blind-spot class: per-join counters on shared event emitters”](#the-blind-spot-class-per-join-counters-on-shared-event-emitters) `joinHarnessSwarm` (operator-core `lib/sync/hyperbee/swarm.ts`) hand-rolled a `liveConnectionCount` (`++` on `'connection'`, `--` on socket `close`). Two mechanisms make such a counter read 0 while a peer is demonstrably replicating: 1. **Shared-swarm dedup** — one Hyperswarm instance serves every topic and emits `'connection'` ONCE per peer socket. A join registered AFTER the socket exists never sees the event (the interface doc on `HyperswarmLike.connections` states exactly this). 2. **Rekey reset** — the hive first-join `rekey()` replaces the handle with a fresh join whose counter starts at 0; live sockets don’t re-emit. Result: the merge-pass sampler fed `swarmConnections: 0` → the axis treated the node as offline (never alarms, by design) → silence in exactly the zombie-connection scenario the axis exists for. **Fix (landed):** the handle getter prefers the swarm’s OWN live set — `swarm.connections.size` — with the counter only as a fallback for minimal test fakes. Generalize: when a shared emitter exposes authoritative live state, **read the state, don’t shadow it with event arithmetic**. Regression pins in `__tests__/swarm.test.ts` (“shared-swarm late join”) and the b8 matrix scenario (a red-SLA soak now asserts the detector line exists — a silent detector on a real stall self-announces as `DETECTOR REGRESSION`). ## Diagnostic recipe: read the live registry on a frame [Section titled “Diagnostic recipe: read the live registry on a frame”](#diagnostic-recipe-read-the-live-registry-on-a-frame) The registry lives in whichever process runs the merge loop — under `papercusp-substrate-sidecar` (default-ON on rig frames, WI-1994) that is the sidecar child, and its console output lands in `serve.log` prefixed `[substrate-sidecar]` / `[substrate-sidecar-err]`. 1. **Grep the fire line** (what the b8 scenario pins): 
   ```plaintext
   grep "replication-liveness" /home/pcusp/serve.log
   # [replication-liveness] replication_stalled (connected_never_replicated) harness=… swarm has N live connection(s) …
   ```
 2. **Read the registry** — JSON-RPC 2.0, newline-framed, over the sidecar’s unix socket (`/tmp/papercusp-substrate-<spawner-pid>.sock`); no auth: 
   ```plaintext
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"substrate:getReplicationLiveness","params":{},"id":1}
   ```
 Key fields per log: `verdict` (`live` / `never_connected` / `no_replicator` / `frozen` / `sampling_stale` — a FIRED connected-never latch derives `no_replicator`), `peersCount`, `msSinceSampled` (\~1s when the merge poll is healthy — a big value means the merge loop itself is dead), and **`lastSwarmConnections`** — the exact value the axis saw on the last sample. `null` = the sampler never passed one (axis disabled at the source); `0` while a peer is connected = the counter blind spot above. 3. **Durable escalation** — EIs land in `harness_shared.engineer_issues` (`psql 'postgresql://harness_admin:harness_admin_pwd@localhost:39532/papercusp'` on a rig frame; note the id column is `issue_id`, not `id`). One open EI per (harness, log, kind); rows federate to peers once replication heals. 4. **Admin HTTP route** (`/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-status`) is trust-gated: bare loopback curl gets 403 `unverified-loopback`. Bearer the frame’s superuser token (`/home/pcusp/.papercusp/superuser-token`, the `rig_ban_member` pattern in `deb-hetzner-rig.sh`). The RPC socket needs none. ## Grace/churn semantics (why the axis is quiet when it should be) [Section titled “Grace/churn semantics (why the axis is quiet when it should be)”](#gracechurn-semantics-why-the-axis-is-quiet-when-it-should-be) * Fire requires `swarmConnections > 0` samples accumulating ≥ 3min (`DEFAULT_LIVENESS_GRACE_MS`) on a log with **zero replicator attach this process lifetime**. Zombie connections churn (\~10s lives), so swarm=0 resets the window only after 60s sustained (`SWARM_CHURN_TOLERANCE_MS`). * Edge-triggered once per latch; recovery (a real replicator attach) re-arms. * The axis never fires when the substrate/swarm never came up (`swarmConnections` undefined) — genuinely-offline peers must not page. Related: the WI-183 stale-DHT-announce zombie-window mechanism (root cause the detector exists to catch) is written up on WI-183 / ledger row 13 of `shared-hive-release-testing/RELEASE-READINESS.md`.

# Repo-less hive data layer: member-repo resolution, per-hive outbox-drain, dead-executor reaper

> A kind:'hive' harness can be repo-LESS — its code lives in a MEMBER repo (e.g. papercusp's member is papercup). Three facets must resolve that correctly or the hive looks broken: (1) repo-backed surfaces (Docs/Tests) must read the member repo, not the empty hive dir; (2) the hive must arm its OWN cross-hive-outbox-drain on create or its substrate_outbox grows unbounded; (3) the DBOS routine scheduler must survive dead-executor dedup wedges (the reaper) or NOTHING fires — including the drain. All three were the root of papercusp looking half-broken on 2026-06-19.

## The shape [Section titled “The shape”](#the-shape) A `kind:'hive'` harness can be **repo-less**: it has no git working tree of its own; its code/docs/tests live in a **member** repo. papercusp (the operator-home hive, `PAPERCUSP_HIVE_HOME_SLUG`) is repo-less — its member is **papercup**, which carries the actual checkout. Anything that resolves a harness to on-disk files or runs its automation must account for this, or the hive looks broken even though its data is intact. Three facets, all fixed 2026-06-19: ## 1. Repo-backed surfaces resolve the MEMBER repo [Section titled “1. Repo-backed surfaces resolve the MEMBER repo”](#1-repo-backed-surfaces-resolve-the-member-repo) Docs and Tests read a harness’s on-disk repo. For a repo-less hive the registry `project.path` is the (near-empty) hive state dir → blank tabs. **Fix:** `resolveHarnessContentPath(reg, slug)` in `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-registry.ts` returns, for a `kind:'hive'` harness, its **member repo’s** path (else `project.path` for a normal repo harness). Applied at every repo-backed resolver: * docs MCP tools — `agent-tools/docs/{outline,search,get}.ts` * docs HTTP endpoint — `harness/docs/harness-repo.ts` `resolveHarnessRepoRoot` (feeds `buildMergedDocs` / the Docs tab) * testing endpoints — `endpoint-route/routes/harness/testing.ts` `resolveCtx` (Tests tab + `/file-status`, `/health-strip`, `/domain-detail`) Result: papercusp’s Docs (426 pages) + Tests (36 domains) now match papercup. The fallback is exact for non-hive harnesses, so this is additive. ## 2. A hive arms its OWN cross-hive-outbox-drain on create [Section titled “2. A hive arms its OWN cross-hive-outbox-drain on create”](#2-a-hive-arms-its-own-cross-hive-outbox-drain-on-create) Every federated-table write enqueues a `harness_shared.substrate_outbox` row, drained per-install by the `cross-hive-outbox-drain` routine. `hive:create` provisioned the learning loop but **never armed the drain**, so a new hive’s outbox grew unbounded (papercusp hit \~24k undrained before this was caught — only the operator-home install had ever been seeded, via a manual script). **Fix:** `harness/routines/arm-hive-cross-hive-drain.ts` (`armHiveCrossHiveDrainRoutine`), called from `agent-tools/hive/_create.ts` step 6d and mirrored in `teardownHiveLearningLoop` (dissolve). The manual `seed-cross-hive-drain-routine.ts` now delegates to it so the seeded row can’t drift. (Clearing an existing inert backlog is lossless **only if** the hive has no remote replicas — check `contributors=0` AND `cross_hive_outbox=0`; mark `drained_at` rather than delete.) ## 3. The dead-executor reaper keeps the scheduler alive (EI-455) [Section titled “3. The dead-executor reaper keeps the scheduler alive (EI-455)”](#3-the-dead-executor-reaper-keeps-the-scheduler-alive-ei-455) The deepest one — and the shared root of BOTH the deploy-pipeline stalls and the outbox not draining. A `routineFire` workflow stuck `PENDING` on a **dead** DBOS executor pins its `deduplication_id` forever (the `uq_workflow_status_dedup_id` unique index is status-INDEPENDENT; DBOS frees a dedup only on dequeue). Every future fire of that routine then collapses on the held dedup, and the routine scheduler silently halts — no routine fires at all, including the drain. **Fix:** `dbos/dbos-executor-reaper.ts` (`reapDeadExecutorWorkflows` + `startExecutorReaper`), started from `dbos/bootstrap.ts` right after `DBOS.launch()`: a boot reap + a **2-min process-level `setInterval`**. It is deliberately a process-level interval, **NOT** a DBOS scheduled routine — a scheduled reaper would queue on the very executor that wedges and so couldn’t fire when most needed; the process-level loop un-wedges even a frozen routine engine. It NULLs the `deduplication_id` and CANCELs `PENDING`/`ENQUEUED` rows on any executor with no `workflow_status` activity in >5 min. Kill-switch `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_EXECUTOR_REAPER=0`. The deeper diagnosis + the manual-clear runbook is [the dead-executor dedup wedge](/internal/docs/agent-insights/deploy-pipeline-silent-stall-dead-executor-dedup); `dbos-workflow-gc` (default-on) prunes terminal rows so the table stays small. A sibling process-level sweep, `release/green-stall-watchdog.ts` (started right after the reaper in `dbos/bootstrap.ts`), closes the DETECTION half: it alarms when an `active` green-checkpoint routine stops firing (`last_fired_at` > 3h) or stops greening (`lastGreenAt` > 12h), independent of the routine itself — the in-routine `trackGateStall` is blind to “the routine never fired.” EI-455 bug #2. ## Operational invariant [Section titled “Operational invariant”](#operational-invariant) For any shared/repo-less hive: it must resolve its member repo for repo-backed reads (#1), arm its own outbox-drain (#2, now automatic at create), and the operator must run the dead-executor reaper (#3). Miss any one and the hive looks broken — blank tabs, an unbounded outbox, or a silently dead scheduler — while its data is perfectly intact. Still open under EI-455: only an optional dedup-TTL safety valve for a hung-but-live executor (the “no-green-verdict-in-N-hours” alarm, EI-455 bug #2, is now shipped — see facet #3 above).

# Repro tests must be *.repro.integration.test.ts — the deploy-gate naming contract

> A *.repro.test.ts reproduces an UNFIXED bug and fails BY DESIGN; named as a bare unit *.test.ts it runs in the green-checkpoint's unit gate and red-gates every deploy. Repro/heavy-sidecar tests MUST be *.repro.integration.test.ts; findMisroutedReproTests + repro-test-naming-guard.test.ts enforce it.

## The contract [Section titled “The contract”](#the-contract) A `*.repro.test.ts` reproduces an **unfixed** bug — it **fails by design** until the bug is fixed. If you name it as a plain unit `*.test.ts`, it lands in the unit suite the hourly **green-checkpoint** gates deploys on. A fail-by-design test in the unit gate reds the gate, and a red gate blocks **every** fleet deploy. **Rule:** a repro test MUST be `*.repro.integration.test.ts` (integration layer — run by `test:affected:integration`, kept **out** of the unit deploy-gate). More broadly: any test that reproduces an unfixed bug, or that spawns real peers / sidecars / a real swarm / outbound network, belongs in the integration layer (`*.integration.test.ts` or `*.repro.integration.test.ts`), never a bare `*.test.ts`. ## Why the “misnamed test fails at import” guard rail does NOT catch this [Section titled “Why the “misnamed test fails at import” guard rail does NOT catch this”](#why-the-misnamed-test-fails-at-import-guard-rail-does-not-catch-this) The [testing-doc §1.6](/internal/docs/testing) naming guard rail says a misnamed integration test “fails at module-import time because the pure-Vitest (unit) config doesn’t load the testcontainers global setup.” That’s true **only for tests that import the testcontainers setup**. A spawned-sidecar / real-swarm repro test spawns child processes (the `serve.mjs` sidecar spawner) — it does **not** import testcontainers, so under the unit config it doesn’t fail at import: it just **runs**, and fails-by-design. That is the WI-1053 incident: 8 federation `*.repro.test.ts` files (`federation-{all-content-types,multimember,restart-durability,revocation-kcut,security-drops,reconnect-catchup}-sidecar`, `sidecar-joiner-owner-bootstrap-admit`, `federation-issues-assignments-matrix`) red-gated **all** fleet deploys for \~73h before anyone noticed the naming was the cause. ## The guard (WI-1091) [Section titled “The guard (WI-1091)”](#the-guard-wi-1091) Enforcement is **naming-based** (no import-scan needed), in two pieces: * `libs/test-config/src/vitest-config.ts` exports `MISROUTED_REPRO_TEST` (a `/\.repro\.test\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/` regex that matches `.repro.test.ts` but **not** `.repro.integration.test.ts`) and `findMisroutedReproTests(files)`. * `packages/operator-core/lib/repro-test-naming-guard.test.ts` is a gated **unit** meta-test that (a) fixture-tests `findMisroutedReproTests`, and (b) walks the whole monorepo and fails if any `*.repro.test.ts` reappears — with an actionable “rename to `*.repro.integration.test.ts`” message. Net effect: re-introducing a misrouted repro test now reds **that one unit meta-test** with a clear rename instruction, instead of silently red-gating deploys. `guardLayeredTestPathUnderUnit` (same file) only catches the **reverse** direction — a correctly-named integration test run *by path* under the unit config — so the two guards are complementary. ## Rule of thumb [Section titled “Rule of thumb”](#rule-of-thumb) Reproduces-an-unfixed-bug, or spawns real peers/sidecars/network → `*.repro.integration.test.ts` (or `*.integration.test.ts`). Never a bare `*.test.ts`. If unsure, integration is the safe default — the unit gate is the one that blocks deploys.

# A `require()` in a "type":"module" package crashes only fresh tsx/ESM consumers — not the long-running operator, and vitest can mask it

> A bare CommonJS `require('node:os')` inside a `"type":"module"` package throws `ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope` at IMPORT time — but only in a fresh tsx/ESM process. The already-running operator (loaded the module earlier, or via a CJS path) and a vitest run that mocks the module both stay green, so the bug passes review + the green-checkpoint while crashing every tsx launcher (e.g. external-bench runners) at startup. Fix with createRequire(import.meta.url), the repo's house pattern.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) A `"type": "module"` package (check its `package.json`) is pure ESM. A bare CommonJS `require(...)` anywhere in its runtime code throws at the point it executes: 
```plaintext
ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope, you can use import instead
```
 This bit `libs/generic/resource-profile/src/index.ts`, which had: 
```ts
// inside a "type":"module" package
const os = require('node:os') as typeof import('node:os');
```
 `getResourceProfile()` is called by the `rate-limit-config.maxSimultaneousAgents` getter **at module-import time**, so *any* fresh tsx/ESM process that imports anything pulling in `rate-limit-config` (every `packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/_xbench_*.ts` launcher) died at startup with the stack ending in `detectResourceSignals`. ## Why it hid (passed review + the green-checkpoint) [Section titled “Why it hid (passed review + the green-checkpoint)”](#why-it-hid-passed-review--the-green-checkpoint) The crash is **import-time and process-fresh**, so the usual safety nets miss it: * **The long-running operator stays up.** `:3070`/`:3170` loaded the module (or reached it via a CJS/bundled path) *before* the bad line landed, so they keep serving with the old code in memory. No hot-reload → no crash there. “Works on the running server” ≠ “works in a fresh process.” * **vitest can be green.** If a test mocks the module, or the suite never drives the real `detectResourceSignals` under the ESM loader, the unit run passes. The green-checkpoint went green while every tsx launcher was broken. * **It’s the inverse of the more famous trap.** The existing insight *new-package-cjs-family-type-module-trap* is about a new package wrongly *setting* `type:module`; this is about CJS `require` left *inside* a package that is already `type:module`. So the only thing that surfaces it is **running the real thing under tsx** — which an agent benchmark launcher does and a `vitest run` may not. ## The fix [Section titled “The fix”](#the-fix) Use `createRequire(import.meta.url)` — the repo’s established pattern (6+ call sites, e.g. `plugin-host-runtime.ts`). It is ESM-valid (a `type:module` package always has `import.meta.url`) and keeps the lazily-loaded builtin **out of the static import graph**, preserving a “pure derivation + types usable in a non-Node bundle” contract that a static top-level `import 'node:os'` would break: 
```ts
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
// ...
const os = createRequire(import.meta.url)('node:os') as typeof import('node:os');
```
 (If the function may be async and the call chain tolerates it, `await import('node:os')` is the other ESM-correct option. Here the whole `maxSimultaneousAgents` getter chain is synchronous, so `createRequire` is the right tool.) ## How to spot it [Section titled “How to spot it”](#how-to-spot-it) * A tsx script dies at **startup/import** with `require is not defined in ES module scope`, stack pointing into a `libs/generic/*` or other `"type":"module"` package. * The same code “works” when probed against the already-running `:3070`/`:3170` (stale process) — don’t trust that; restart-or-fresh-process is the real test. * Before trusting “tests are green,” confirm the failing path actually runs under a real ESM/`tsx` process, not only a mock-heavy vitest run.

# Retiring (or adding) a peer-log federated table — the six surfaces three drift guards force in lockstep

> A sync:'peer-log' table is wired across six files. Three independent drift guards each enforce a different pair, so you cannot touch one surface without the others — change them together or the green gate reds one guard at a time. The exact map, learned removing the orphan harness_feature_prs projection (EI-479).

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) A `sync:'peer-log'` table (the cross-machine Model-B federation set) is wired across **six** surfaces. Three independent drift guards each pin a **different pair** of them, so adding or retiring a federated table is an all-or-nothing edit: change one surface and you red a guard; change the right six together and the gate stays green. The guards are good — they make the omission *fail CI* instead of silently dropping writes — but they fire one at a time, so it’s easy to play whack-a-mole if you don’t know the full set up front. This is the map, reverse-engineered while retiring the orphan `harness_feature_prs` projection (it was classified `sync:'peer-log'` with a read projection but **no producer** — the poll daemon was never built, so it never federated; EI-479 reclassified it `sync:'none'`). ## The six surfaces [Section titled “The six surfaces”](#the-six-surfaces) For a table `T` with Hyperbee tag `tag` and key prefix `tag/`: 1. **Registry classification** — `harness-state/table-registry.ts`: `T` in `PEER_LOG_LIVE` (or `PEER_LOG_WORKSPACE_OWNED`). Removing it lets `T` fall through to `DEFAULT_SPEC` = `{ key:'slug-shared', sync:'none' }`. 2. **Read projection tag → table map** — `harness-state/projection-engine.ts`: `PEER_LOG_TAG_TO_TABLE[tag] = 'T'`. 3. **Projection registration** — `sync/hyperbee/projections/register-all.ts`: `tag` in `REGISTERED_PROJECTION_TAGS` **and** `buildTProjection(opts)` in `buildHarnessProjections` (+ the import). 4. **The projection itself** — `sync/hyperbee/projections/<tag>.ts` (`tableTag`, `composeKey`, `writeToPg`/`deleteFromPg`). 5. **Hyperbee key shape** — `harness/hyperbee-key-types.ts`: `tag` in `HYPERBEE_TABLE_TAGS`, both prefix maps, the `keyX` composer, the `ParsedHyperbeeKey` union variant, and the `parseHyperbeeKey` branch. 6. **Write-side producer** — `sync/hyperbee/capture-coverage.ts`: a CDC trigger (`CDC_CAPTURED_TABLES`), a log-first append (`LOG_FIRST_PRODUCED_TABLES`), **or** a documented `ACCEPTED_UNFEDERATED_TABLES` carve-out. ## The three guards and which pair each enforces [Section titled “The three guards and which pair each enforces”](#the-three-guards-and-which-pair-each-enforces) * **`checkPeerLogConsistency`** (projection-engine, pinned by `projection-engine.test.ts`) ties **#1 ↔ #2+#3**: every `PEER_LOG_TABLES` entry needs a registered projection tag mapping to it, and every registered tag must map to a still-`sync:'peer-log'` table. Drop #1 but keep #2/#3 → `orphanTag`; drop #2/#3 but keep #1 → `missingProjection`. * **`checkCaptureCoverage`** (projection-engine, pinned by `capture-coverage.test.ts`) ties **#1 ↔ #6**: every federated table needs exactly one producer; a producer pointing at a non-federated table is an `orphanProducer`. So you can’t drop `T` from the registry while leaving its `ACCEPTED_UNFEDERATED_TABLES` entry. * **The superset invariant** in `register-all.test.ts` ties **#3 ↔ #5**: `REGISTERED_PROJECTION_TAGS ⊇ HYPERBEE_TABLE_TAGS` (minus `features-by-status`). So you cannot remove a tag from #3 without also removing the key shape from #5 — and vice versa. This is the surface agents miss: retiring the projection forces editing `hyperbee-key-types.ts`, which isn’t obviously part of “the federation wiring.” ## So [Section titled “So”](#so) To **retire** a federated table: remove it from all six (delete the projection file + its test; empty/keep the `ACCEPTED_UNFEDERATED_TABLES` mechanism). The table itself **stays in PG** — `sync:'none'` just means PG is the local store-of-record and it never crosses machines. **No migration** is needed (you are not dropping the table), and **independent PG read paths stay**: the sync-resolver `table-to-query-names` invalidation map + any read route / `useSyncQuery` are about PG→client reads, not federation — leave them. To **add** one: do the same six in reverse, and pick #6 deliberately — a PG-first table uses a CDC trigger; a log-first table appends directly. A table must have **exactly one** producer (a CDC + log-first double-capture is the EI-117 echo-storm shape and `checkCaptureCoverage` rejects it). Run the affected suites together: `npx vitest run` over `harness/hyperbee-key-types.test.ts`, `sync/hyperbee/__tests__/capture-coverage.test.ts`, `harness-state/projection-engine.test.ts`, `harness-state/table-registry.test.ts`, `sync/hyperbee/projections/__tests__/register-all.test.ts`.

# Retiring an fs-watcher mirror — re-audit the consumer first; most "mirrors" are dead orphans, not producer-migrations

> The fs-watcher-retirement plan framed each remaining mirror as needing a supervised "producer-time POST migration." In practice 3 of 4 (summary, branch_actions, phases) had NO live consumer and a REST route that recomputes on demand — dead orphans, retired mechanically like git_log. Only pending-reviews was a real migration (already shipped, P-077). The decisive consumer test + the full wiring map, learned retiring 4 mirrors in one session.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-fs-watcher.ts` mirrors a handful of `.papercusp/*` files into `harness_shared.*` tables so panels can read them over the sync push. The `fs-watcher-retirement-2026-05-10` plan framed each remaining mirror as a **supervised producer-migration** (“build a producer-time POST endpoint, migrate the producer, live-verify the panel, then remove the mirror leg”). That premise was **wrong for 3 of 4**. Re-auditing code truth before touching anything (the `git_log` step-1 pattern) showed: | Mirror | Reality | Retirement | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | | `summary` | no producer writes the file; no consumer reads the table (UI summary comes from `harness_text_artifacts`, mig 035) | **dead orphan** → drop | | `branch_actions` | marked “KEPT mirror” but the `/branch/:branch/actions` REST route recomputes on demand; no sync subscriber | **dead orphan** → drop | | `phases` | only consumer (HealthBadge) read `alive`, which the watcher **hardcoded `false`** — an always-dark dot; the `/phases` REST route recomputes | repoint consumer → drop | | `pending-reviews` | the watcher leg was REDUNDANT — `promote.ts`/`resolveReview` already write PG directly (audit P-077) | remove leg, **keep table** | Only `pending-reviews` was a “migration” — and it had **already happened**; the watcher leg was leftover dead weight (its orphan-delete sweep was even a latent hazard to the PG-only rows). ## The decisive test (do this before assuming a producer-migration) [Section titled “The decisive test (do this before assuming a producer-migration)”](#the-decisive-test-do-this-before-assuming-a-producer-migration) For each mirror table, answer two questions: 1. **Does anything READ it?** Grep the camelCase queryName across real source (`apps/**`, `libs/**` — exclude `node_modules`, `src-tauri/target`, `_retired`, `public/`, `libs/zero-harness`). Also check for a direct REST read and an MCP tool. Check the live DB row count — a stale/empty table is a tell. 2. **Is there a REST route that recomputes the same data on demand?** (git\_log → `/git/log`; branch\_actions → `/branch/:branch/actions`; phases → `/phases`.) These shell out / scan fs every call with a short TTL cache. **No reader + a recomputing REST route ⇒ dead orphan.** Retire it mechanically — there is no producer to migrate and no panel to live-verify. If there IS a live consumer, repoint it to a live, non-watcher source first (phases → `harnessLanes.byHarness`, the PID-swept lane tracker), *then* drop. ## The full wiring map (every surface a mirror touches) [Section titled “The full wiring map (every surface a mirror touches)”](#the-full-wiring-map-every-surface-a-mirror-touches) 1. **Watcher** (`harness-fs-watcher.ts`): the `upsert*`/`delete*` fn, the `watchedPaths()` entry, the dispatch block in `classifyAndDispatch`, the reconcile/bootstrap sweep, and the `const x = generated.*InHarnessShared` import (drop it once unused). 2. **Sync resolver** (`sync-resolver/index.ts`): the `'name.byHarness'` entry. 3. **Table→query map** (`sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts`): the `'harness_shared.<table>': [...]` line (this + the PG `emit_change_notify` trigger are what make a KEPT table still push live — leave them if you keep the table). 4. **Resolver test** (`sync-resolver/index.test.ts`): the batch `toContain` list (the `≥ floor` count assertion absorbs the drop). 5. **If git-synced** (`harness_phases` was): remove from `table-registry.ts` `GIT_DOCS`, `git-export/serialize.ts` `PROSE_TABLES` (prose tables only), and `git-export/ensure-git-outbox.ts` `GIT_KEY_COLS`. `detachStaleGitCaptureTriggers` drops the capture trigger on next boot; the boot-hydrate skips the table once it leaves `GIT_TABLES` (no crash). Committed `.papercusp/state/<table>/*.json` files go **inert** — harmless dead-debt, not auto-deleted. 6. **Drop migration** + schema codegen: remove the table block from `generated.ts` **and** `schema.ts` only (the git\_log precedent leaves `generated.reference.sql` / `zero-reference.json` — they’re not consumed by the live drizzle schema). Do **not** run a full `pull-schema` — it sweeps in unrelated peer drift; hand-remove the one block. ## Gotchas that cost real time [Section titled “Gotchas that cost real time”](#gotchas-that-cost-real-time) * **Reserve the migration number via `db:next-migration`, never hand-pick.** I hand-picked 280/281 and collided with **three** concurrent peer migrations; renumbering + backfilling `migration_reservations` was avoidable churn. `≥215` on disk without a reservation row reds `lint:migrations`. * **A “consumer” can be reading a dead field.** `harness_phases.alive` was hardcoded `false` by the only writer, so HealthBadge’s liveness dot was always dark — the repoint to `harness_lanes` was a *fix*, not a swap. * **Verify against code truth, not the plan.** This is the load-bearing meta- lesson: in a busy fleet, documented “remaining work” goes stale fast. The same session, the entire `EI-444` brief (adopt-event-rules `MatchMap` convergence) was **already shipped** — the plan was status=`shipped` (D-010) and the `custom:` hatch already retired. Re-audit the source before executing any plan step / brief / issue. See `fs-watcher-retirement-2026-05-10` for the per-mirror record and [retire-or-add-a-federated-table](/internal/docs/agent-insights/retire-or-add-a-federated-table) for the *peer-log federated* (not fs-watcher mirror) variant.

# Extend a multi-entry route with a body-discriminator + a helper-per-entry + a shared error vocabulary

> POST /harness/projects now accepts 3 entry shapes (Entry 1/2/3). The pattern that scales — discriminate on body, delegate to a per-entry helper, surface errors with a shared .code vocabulary the UI handles uniformly.

## The pattern [Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern) `POST /harness/projects` started as a single-shape handler: `{ slug, path }` for “register an existing folder.” It now accepts three shapes (Entry 1/2/3 from the dogfood v5 §3 spec): 
```ts
// Entry 1 — new local dir   (init-local-dir.ts helper, P-010)
{ slug, parentDir, folderName }


// Entry 2 — GitHub URL      (clone-github.ts helper, P-008)
{ slug, githubUrl, shallow? }


// Entry 3 — existing folder (in-route path resolve)
{ slug, path }
```
 Three rules made this scale cleanly: ### 1. Discriminate on body, not on a `kind:` field [Section titled “1. Discriminate on body, not on a kind: field”](#1-discriminate-on-body-not-on-a-kind-field) The handler picks the entry by which fields are present: 
```ts
if (parentDir && folderName) {
  // Entry 1
} else if (githubUrl) {
  // Entry 2
} else if (rawPath) {
  // Entry 3
} else {
  return Response.json({ error: 'one of `parentDir+folderName`, `githubUrl`, or `path` required' }, { status: 400 });
}
```
 No `body.kind === 'local_init'` discriminator. Why: callers can paste a `{ githubUrl }` body without remembering to set `kind: 'github'`; the shape *is* the kind. Less ceremony, fewer bugs. The trade-off: the body must be unambiguous (you can’t paste both `path` and `githubUrl` and expect a predictable winner). The handler enforces this implicitly by check-order — if you do mix them, Entry 1 → Entry 2 → Entry 3 priority applies. Document the priority in the route’s leading comment; callers shouldn’t rely on it. ### 2. Each entry has a dedicated helper module [Section titled “2. Each entry has a dedicated helper module”](#2-each-entry-has-a-dedicated-helper-module) Entry 1 → `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/init-local-dir.ts` exports `initLocalHarnessDir({parentDir, folderName})`. Entry 2 → `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/clone-github.ts` exports `cloneGithubRepo(url, opts)`. Entry 3 → in-route path resolve (small; no helper warranted). The route handler is thin: it picks the entry, calls the helper, handles errors, falls through to the shared scaffold path. The helpers are independently testable (init-local-dir: 20 tests; clone-github: 65 tests) without the HTTP layer. When Entry 4 lands (harness link via Hyperswarm, Phase 1b P-009), it’ll be `lib/harness/join-shared-harness.ts`. Same pattern. ### 3. Errors share a `.code` vocabulary [Section titled “3. Errors share a .code vocabulary”](#3-errors-share-a-code-vocabulary) Both helpers throw a structured error class: 
```ts
class InitLocalDirError extends Error {
  code: 'invalid_path' | 'parent_missing' | 'dest_exists' | 'git_missing' | 'unknown';
  detail?: string;
}


class CloneGithubError extends Error {
  code: 'invalid_url' | 'dest_exists' | 'auth_required' | 'not_found' | 'git_missing' | 'unknown';
  detail?: string;
}
```
 Overlapping codes (`dest_exists`, `git_missing`, `unknown`) map to the *same* HTTP status across entries. New codes (`invalid_path` vs `invalid_url`, `parent_missing` vs `auth_required`) cover the entry-specific cases. The route’s error mapping is a single switch: 
```ts
const httpStatus =
  e.code === 'invalid_url' || e.code === 'invalid_path' ? 400 :
  e.code === 'parent_missing'                          ? 400 :
  e.code === 'dest_exists'                             ? 409 :
  e.code === 'auth_required'                           ? 401 :
  e.code === 'not_found'                               ? 404 :
  e.code === 'git_missing'                             ? 500 :
                                                          502;
```
 The UI’s error handler (P-012 picker, when it lands) reads `response.code` and renders the matching copy — no per-entry switch needed because the codes overlap where the meaning overlaps. ## Why this scales [Section titled “Why this scales”](#why-this-scales) A new entry (Entry 4, 5, 6 …) adds: * One helper module + its tests. * One `if` branch in the route handler discriminator. * Maybe one new error code if it has a genuinely novel failure mode. It does NOT add: * Per-entry route paths (they all live at `POST /harness/projects`). * Per-entry response schemas (one shared `{ ok, project, provisioning, init?, clone? }`). * Per-entry UI error switches (the shared `.code` vocabulary covers it). The handler’s complexity grows linearly with entry count; the rest of the system doesn’t grow at all. ## When NOT to use this pattern [Section titled “When NOT to use this pattern”](#when-not-to-use-this-pattern) If your entries have *fundamentally different response shapes* (e.g. one is a streaming response, one is sync JSON), don’t try to unify them into one route. Split into `POST /harness/projects/stream-clone` vs `POST /harness/projects/create`. The body-discriminator approach only works when the success shape is shared. If your entries have *security boundaries* (Entry A is public, Entry B requires admin), don’t discriminate on body — discriminate on auth. The route’s `auth:` declaration should match the most-restrictive entry, with looser entries enforcing their own checks. Mixing auth modes in one route is a privesc hazard. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/projects.ts` — the canonical example, three entries. * `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/init-local-dir.ts` — Entry 1 helper + structured error. * `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/clone-github.ts` — Entry 2 helper + structured error. * [`verification-signal-on-the-row`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/verification-signal-on-the-row/) — sister principle: signals belong on the entity they describe; the same instinct applied to error shapes here.

# A "routine is failing" EI is usually a reaper self-heal phantom

> Triage runbook: a routine-failure watchdog EI whose last_error_source is dbos-executor-reaper is a self-heal breadcrumb, not a genuine failure — check source + active before treating it as real.

The self-improvement watchdog files a `bug` EI titled **“Background routine `\<name>` is failing”** whenever a routine carries a non-empty `metadata.last_error` (`collectRoutineFailureSignals`, `watchdog.ts`). Most of these are **phantoms**, and multiple auto-implement workers have each independently re-diagnosed the same class (EI-5950, EI-6061, EI-6081, EI-6083, … 25+). Read this before touching one. ## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) `dbos-executor-reaper.ts` recovers a stuck `routineFire` and, as a **self-heal breadcrumb**, stamps the routine with: 
```plaintext
metadata.last_error        = "DBOS routineFire produced no DBOS operation output;
                              executor reaper cancelled the stuck fire and requeued the routine"
metadata.last_error_source = "dbos-executor-reaper"
```
 This marker means *“I recovered this routine”* — **NOT** that the routine failed. But `collectRoutineFailureSignals` alarms on **any** non-empty `last_error` regardless of source, so the self-heal note is misread as a failure and an EI is minted. `clearStaleReaperLastError` only wipes the marker on the routine’s **next successful fire**, so a low-cadence or **deactivated** routine carries it (and the phantom) indefinitely. ## Triage in one query [Section titled “Triage in one query”](#triage-in-one-query) 
```sql
select active, metadata->>'last_error_source' as src, last_fired_at,
       metadata->>'last_error_at' as err_at
  from harness_shared.routines where name = '<routine-name>';
```
 It is a **phantom** (resolve `fixed`, evidence-it’s-gone) when any of: * `src = 'dbos-executor-reaper'` (a self-heal marker, not an action failure), **and** * `active = false` — `collectRoutineFailureSignals` filters `WHERE active = true`, so an inactive routine can never re-file; the EI is structurally dead, **or** * `last_fired_at > last_error_at` — the routine already fired successfully after the marker. `loop-su-*` routines are per-session self-wake loops (`loop:arm`); when the session ends the loop goes `active=false, next_fire_at=infinity` — a normal lifecycle, not a wedge. ## When it is NOT a phantom [Section titled “When it is NOT a phantom”](#when-it-is-not-a-phantom) * `last_error_source` is absent (git-sync `recordOutcome`) or `'runner'` (a system action that **threw**) → a genuine failure; treat it as real. * `metadata.reaped_count` is high (≥3 consecutive reaps, never self-heals) → a genuinely wedged routine the reaper keeps cancelling; the `git-sync-stall-watchdog` alarms on this on purpose. ## The durable class fix is a STOP surface [Section titled “The durable class fix is a STOP surface”](#the-durable-class-fix-is-a-stop-surface) Making the collector source-aware (skip `dbos-executor-reaper` markers unless `reaped_count >= N`) lives in `watchdog.ts` / `dbos-executor-reaper.ts` — both auto-implement **protected surfaces**. Route that to a human (tracked via EI-6061); resolve the individual phantom instances `fixed` with the query evidence above.

# Routines that "fire" but never run — the dedup-ID + dead-executor wedge

> A routineFire PENDING on a dead DBOS executor holds its deduplicationID forever, silently collapsing every later cron fire while claimDueRoutine keeps bumping last_fired_at — the routines table looks healthy while the routine is dead. gym-cycle lost 7.5h this way.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) A cron routine’s `routines.last_fired_at` advances on schedule, but the routine’s *effect* never happens. For `gym-cycle` (2026-06-12, 06:28→14:00): `harness_shared.autoloop_state` frozen at `gym-cycle:dispatch`, `gym_autoloop_config` stuck `running` for 7.5h (far past the 45-min stale-reclaim — which never ran, because the reclaim lives INSIDE the action that never executed), zero `[gym-cycle]` lines in the host journal. The Queen surfaced it as “P-001 autoloop discrepancy”. ## Mechanism [Section titled “Mechanism”](#mechanism) `routinesTickImpl` (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/routines-workflow.ts`) enqueues each due fire with `deduplicationID: routine:<id>` and swallows `Duplicate…` errors as back-pressure. DBOS holds a dedup ID until the workflow reaches a terminal state — and **recovery is per-executor**: a fire PENDING on an executor that died is never recovered by the surviving hosts. So one dead executor holding one fire = that routine’s dedup ID is occupied FOREVER; every later tick claims the routine (bumping `last_fired_at` — the misleading part) and then silently collapses the enqueue. How a foreign executor got the fire at all: any ad-hoc host (here `executor_id='repro-debug'`, an incident-repro session) sharing the live DB with the same DBOS app version joins the workflow queues and steals work; if it exits mid-run, everything it held is orphaned. ## Diagnosis recipe [Section titled “Diagnosis recipe”](#diagnosis-recipe) 
```sql
select workflow_uuid, status, executor_id, to_timestamp(created_at/1000)
from dbos.workflow_status
where name='routineFire' and status='PENDING';
```
 A PENDING row whose `executor_id` no longer exists is the wedge. Cross-check `harness_shared.routines.last_fired_at` (advancing) vs the routine’s actual effect table (frozen). ## Fix (2026-06-12) [Section titled “Fix (2026-06-12)”](#fix-2026-06-12) * Immediate: cancel the phantom — and note the dedup is enforced by a unique index with NO status predicate (`uq_workflow_status_dedup_id` on `(queue_name, deduplication_id) WHERE deduplication_id IS NOT NULL`), so a status flip alone does NOT free it (verified live: the next tick still collapsed). DBOS’s own terminal transition clears the column; a manual cancel must too: 
  ```sql
  UPDATE dbos.workflow_status
     SET status='CANCELLED', deduplication_id=NULL
   WHERE workflow_uuid=… AND status='PENDING';
  -- and clear any lingering queue row:
  DELETE FROM dbos.workflow_queue WHERE deduplication_id='routine:<id>';
  ```
 * Structural: `startWorkflow(..., { timeoutMS: ROUTINE_FIRE_TIMEOUT_MS })` (2h) — DBOS cancels a wedged fire at the deadline, so the worst case is one ceiling window, not forever. * Prevention (open, EI-396 residual): per-host `DBOS__APPVERSION`/`DBOS__VMID` discipline for ad-hoc/repro hosts so they never join the live hosts’ queues (the staging unit already isolates itself this way). ## Update: no-first-output routineFire rows (2026-06-25) [Section titled “Update: no-first-output routineFire rows (2026-06-25)”](#update-no-first-output-routinefire-rows-2026-06-25) The same user-visible symptom can happen on a live executor: DBOS creates a `routineFire` workflow row, assigns `started_at_epoch_ms`, and pins `deduplication_id='routine:<id>'`, but the workflow never records its first `dbos.operation_outputs` checkpoint. A later recovery pass may refresh both `updated_at` and `started_at_epoch_ms`, so those clocks can make the dead fire look newly active even though the routine has not produced any durable DBOS operation output. Use immutable `created_at` for the no-first-output stale check. Diagnosis: 
```sql
select ws.workflow_uuid, ws.status, ws.deduplication_id,
       to_timestamp(ws.started_at_epoch_ms/1000.0) as started_at
  from dbos.workflow_status ws
 where ws.name='routineFire'
   and ws.status in ('PENDING','ENQUEUED')
   and not exists (
     select 1 from dbos.operation_outputs op
      where op.workflow_uuid = ws.workflow_uuid
   );
```
 Structural fix: `dbos-executor-reaper` now treats a `routineFire` whose `created_at` is older than a longer first-output window with zero operation rows as stale, NULLs its dedup, sets it `CANCELLED`, and pushes the owning `harness_shared.routines.next_fire_at` back to `now()`. That window is deliberately longer than the scheduler-tick window because `operation_outputs` is a checkpoint table: a legitimate long first step has no row until it completes or records its own timeout/error. Scout’s cycle timeout is the live proof. It also cancels no-first-output `routinesTick` rows by `created_at`, because a stuck scheduler tick is the upstream version of the same failure. The requeue is intentionally limited to the no-first-output `routineFire` safety-valve class; routine bodies that did checkpoint a DBOS step still rely on their explicit workflow deadline/backoff rather than being retried immediately. ## Update: the fix itself caused a NEW wedge — over-eager reaping of healthy fires (WI-1415 → WI-1416, 2026-06-30–07-01) [Section titled “Update: the fix itself caused a NEW wedge — over-eager reaping of healthy fires (WI-1415 → WI-1416, 2026-06-30–07-01)”](#update-the-fix-itself-caused-a-new-wedge--over-eager-reaping-of-healthy-fires-wi-1415--wi-1416-2026-06-3007-01) **Symptom (2026-06-30, `git-sync-stall-watchdog` incident).** git-sync kept firing every 3 min, but its DBOS fires got stuck — `metadata.last_error` repeatedly showed `"routineFire produced no DBOS operation output; executor reaper cancelled the stuck fire and requeued the routine"` — so no commit landed for \~6h while \~100 source files sat stranded uncommitted (and thus un-deployable). Nothing alarmed: the routine LOOKED active (`last_fired_at` advancing every 3 min, exactly the symptom this doc’s title describes), but every fire was being killed and restarted from scratch before it could commit — roughly one commit per 40 minutes instead of one per 3 minutes. **Root cause: the 2026-06-25 fast-orphan check above was built on the WRONG queue-row semantics.** It read “no live `dbos.workflow_queue` row” as “orphaned” — but this DBOS version deletes the queue row at **dequeue** time, so every actively-EXECUTING `PENDING` fire *also* has no queue row. The fast path was therefore reaping ANY fire whose first step ran past the 90s scheduler-silence window, healthy or not — a self-inflicted restart loop on git-sync specifically, because git-sync’s real first-step work (committing across the whole tree + every submodule) routinely takes longer than 90s. **Fix (`dbos-executor-reaper.ts`, verified live 2026-07-01):** * The fast-orphan path now only reaps a fire that is `ENQUEUED` (never dequeued at all — a genuine anomaly, e.g. a crash between the queue delete and the status flip) AND older than its own, separate, tunable window (`DEFAULT_STALE_ROUTINE_FIRE_ORPHAN_MS`, default 10 min; env `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_REAPER_FIRE_ORPHAN_MS`). A `PENDING` (i.e. executing) no-output fire is no longer eligible for the fast path at all — it falls back to the longer no-first-output window, now **60 minutes** (`DEFAULT_STALE_ROUTINE_FIRE_NO_OUTPUT_MS`), retuned above green-checkpoint’s suite runtime (grew to \~55m; see the constant’s own header comment for the tuning invariant chain against `GREEN_CHECKPOINT_SUITE_TIMEOUT_MS` and `CHECKPOINT_LOCK_STALE_MS`). * `routineFireImpl` (`routines-workflow.ts`) now runs a **multi-step** system action like git-sync’s internal steps as individual `DBOS.runStep` sub-steps of the workflow (`entry.ownSteps`, WI-1416 / `bg-host-freeze-eventloop-stall` P-006) instead of one opaque long step — so the reaper sees genuine incremental progress (`operation_outputs.function_id > 0`) as soon as any sub-step checkpoints, rather than waiting for the whole action to finish before it can prove it isn’t wedged. * A dedicated **`git-sync-stall-watchdog.ts`** (process-level `setInterval`, 15-min sweep, same “not a DBOS routine” reasoning as `dbos-executor-reaper` — a routine-based watchdog queues on the very engine that wedges) now closes the observability gap this whole doc originally called out (“the routines table looks healthy while the routine is dead”). It reads `harness_shared.routines.metadata` for git-sync specifically and alarms (owner page + escalation + fleet broadcast) on any of: HEAD staleness (tree hasn’t advanced while active — the PRIMARY signal, skipped on a legitimately clean/idle tree), fire staleness (scheduler not running it), a persistent `last_error` across ≥2 consecutive 15-min sweeps, or — the WI-1416-specific signal — `metadata.reaped_count` (consecutive executor-reaper cancels since the last completed fire, incremented by the reaper and reset on success) reaching 3, which catches exactly this reap→requeue→restart loop even while `last_error` is flipping null between reaps. Net effect: the `routineFire` no-output windows are now two-tiered by TRUE anomaly (never-dequeued `ENQUEUED`, 10 min) vs legitimate-long-first-step `PENDING` (60 min), and a persistent-reap counter + dedicated watchdog give this failure class its own alarm instead of relying on someone noticing `last_fired_at` looking healthy while nothing actually happens.

# Routines are claimed by WHICHEVER host's tick wins — green and staging race on one table

> Green (:3070, release tree) and staging (:3170, main) both run routinesTick against one harness_shared.routines table, so which CODE VERSION handles a fire is a lottery — new-code-only payloads fail intermittently until the release deploy.

## Current behavior (2026-07-03) [Section titled “Current behavior (2026-07-03)”](#current-behavior-2026-07-03) **The two-host race this doc describes no longer happens — the topology it was written against has been superseded.** Verified live against the running systemd units + journal: * `papercup-dev-api.service` (green, `:3070`, `papercusp-release` checkout) now runs with `PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=0` (drop-in `50-cluster.conf`). Its journal confirms: `[host] PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=0 — secondary host: skipping hyperbee substrate, git-export, and DBOS background machinery (EI-126)`. * `papercup-staging-api.service` (`:3170`, `main`/staging checkout) has carried the same `BACKGROUND_WORKERS=0` gate since **EI-126** (drop-in `10-background-workers.conf`) — also confirmed live in its journal. * The **sole** DBOS routines primary is now a dedicated third host, `papercup-bg-host.service` (`PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=1`, cut over 2026-07-03 per `operator-scalability-event-loop-2026-06-16` P1-3) — confirmed firing `routinesTick`’s sweeps live in its journal. It runs from the **staging/integration checkout** (`papercupai-workspace/papercusp`, same tree as `:3170`), **not** `papercusp-release`, and pins its own `DBOS__APPVERSION=bg-host-v1` / `DBOS__VMID=bg-host-3270`. Net effect: exactly ONE process claims `harness_shared.routines` rows now, and it always runs the current staging/`main` code — never the (older) green/release checkout. The version-lottery this doc documents is structurally gone for the current green+staging+bg-host topology. **This is a topology invariant, not a code guarantee** — nothing stops a future change from starting a second `BACKGROUND_WORKERS=1` host again (the underlying fact that `:3070`/`:3170` share the same default `PINNED_APP_VERSION` unless a host sets `DBOS__APPVERSION` is still true; `bg-host` is simply the only host that currently does). If you are re-introducing a second background-capable host, the failure mode and mitigations below still apply verbatim — read on. *** **What (historical, 2026-06-05).** Since the 2026-06-05 release-gate cutover the dev box runs TWO operators — green `:3070` from the `papercup-release` checkout (the `ready` ref) and staging `:3170` from `main` — and **both** register the DBOS `routinesTick` against the **same** `harness_shared.routines` table (they share `apps/operator/.env.local`, so both see `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ROUTINES=1`). The atomic claim in `claimDueRoutine` guarantees exactly ONE host fires a due routine, but **which one wins is a race** — so the code version that executes a routine’s payload is a per-fire lottery. **Why it matters.** A routine whose payload only newer code understands fails intermittently-to-always until the next release deploy. Observed live (autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild D-010): a `system:blueprint-run {blueprintId:'pot'}` wake was claimed by the green host, whose release tree had no `pot` blueprint — `fireLaunchBlueprint` threw, and (second, compounding bug fixed on `main` in `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/routines/claim.ts`) the old claim semantics left the one-shot row ACTIVE with `next_fire_at=NULL`, which means “due now” — an infinite 30s refire loop until the row was deactivated by hand. **How to apply.** * Don’t arm (activate) a routine whose `target_role`/payload needs code that hasn’t reached the **green** checkout yet — seed it INACTIVE and flip it after the release deploy, or verify green has the code first (`journalctl --user -u papercup-dev-api` paths name the serving tree). * A misfiring routine loop is stopped with `UPDATE harness_shared.routines SET active=false WHERE name='<name>'`. * If you change routine CLAIM/fire semantics on `main`, remember the live ticker is green’s until a deploy — your fix is not protecting production rows yet.

# `import { RRule } from 'rrule'` crashes DBOS boot (CJS-in-ESM)

> A static named import of the CommonJS `rrule` package throws at module load under the ESM/tsx operator host — taking down the whole routinesTick (git-sync, green-checkpoint, deploys, scheduled plans). Use createRequire. vitest does NOT catch this.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) The operator boots (HTTP `/api/health` responds, MCP works) but the **entire DBOS background system is silently dead**: no `routinesTick`, so **git-sync stops committing**, **green-checkpoint / release-trigger stop** (deploys freeze, `main` goes stale), scheduled-plan fires stop, and `fleet:place_batch` 500s. The boot log has the tell: 
```plaintext
[endpoint-ipc] failed to start: .../harness/routines/schedule-next.ts:14
import { RRule, RRuleSet } from 'rrule';
SyntaxError: The requested module 'rrule' does not provide an export named 'RRule'
[dbos] boot failed (non-fatal): The requested module 'rrule' does not provide an export named 'RRule'
```
 `[dbos] boot failed (non-fatal)` is the line that matters — “non-fatal” means the HTTP host stays up, so health/MCP look fine while every routine-driven subsystem is down. On 2026-06-17 this took prod (`:3070`) down for \~2h and stranded \~650 files of fleet work uncommitted (git-sync is itself a routine, so it died too). ## Root cause [Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause) `rrule` is a **CommonJS** package. Under the operator’s ESM/tsx host, a CJS module’s classes are exposed on the **default export**, not as statically-detectable named exports — so `import { RRule, RRuleSet } from 'rrule'` throws `does not provide an export named 'RRule'` **at module load**. Any module that statically imports the offender (here `claim.ts → schedule-next.ts`) fails to load, and because `routinesTick`’s import graph reaches it, the whole tick fails to register. vitest does NOT catch this The named import passes the unit + integration suites (vitest’s CJS interop resolves the named export) and the SPA build (Vite handles CJS). It only throws under **tsx**, which is what the operator runs. So a green test run + green deploy can still ship a DBOS-killing regression. Verify a backend `rrule` (or any CJS-only dep) consumer with a real tsx import, not just vitest. ## Fix — load CJS deps via createRequire [Section titled “Fix — load CJS deps via createRequire”](#fix--load-cjs-deps-via-createrequire) 
```ts
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
// rrule is CJS: its classes are on the default export, NOT statically-detectable
// named exports under ESM/tsx. createRequire resolves them at runtime.
const { RRule, RRuleSet } = createRequire(import.meta.url)('rrule') as typeof import('rrule');
```
 This is the repo’s ESM-safe CJS pattern (cf. `libs/generic/resource-profile`). The `as typeof import('rrule')` keeps the static types. **Frontend** code (operator-vite) can keep the named import — Vite bundles CJS fine; this is a **backend/tsx-only** trap. ## Verify before you ship a backend CJS consumer [Section titled “Verify before you ship a backend CJS consumer”](#verify-before-you-ship-a-backend-cjs-consumer) 
```bash
npx tsx -e "import('./packages/operator-core/lib/.../your-module.ts').then(m => console.log('loaded', !!m))"
```
 If it prints `loaded`, the module loads under the runtime the operator uses. A passing `vitest run` alone does not prove this. ## Recovery, if it already shipped [Section titled “Recovery, if it already shipped”](#recovery-if-it-already-shipped) The deadlock: git-sync (dead) can’t commit the fix; the routine tick (dead) can’t deploy it. Break it manually — minimal one-file commit of the fix + push `staging`, then the **sanctioned incident path** `tsx apps/operator/lib/release/deploy-cli.ts --deploy-commit <sha> --execute` (needs `PAPERCUSP_ALLOW_DEV_RESTART=1` to permit the restart). Once `:3070` reboots on the fix, DBOS relaunches and git-sync sweeps the backlog normally. See also [Scheduled plans](/internal/docs/spec/scheduled-plans) (the routine this import feeds) and the design [libraries](/internal/docs/design/libraries) note.

# RTK (Rust Token Killer) cross-platform integration matrix — Linux / macOS / Windows

> How the rtk 0.43.0 PreToolUse auto-rewrite hook was verified on each platform, the crates.io name-collision gotcha, the exact per-platform install, and the Windows caveats. Verified 2026-07-06 (su-d2654).

RTK (Rust Token Killer, `rtk-ai/rtk`, Apache-2.0) is a single Rust binary that compresses shell-command output 60–90% before it reaches the LLM. We integrate it as a **Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook** (`rtk hook claude`) that rewrites `<cmd>` → `rtk <cmd>` for compressible commands. This page is the verified cross-platform install + behavior matrix. ## ⚠️ Install gotcha: `cargo install rtk` gets the WRONG package [Section titled “⚠️ Install gotcha: cargo install rtk gets the WRONG package”](#️-install-gotcha-cargo-install-rtk-gets-the-wrong-package) `cargo install rtk` (crates.io) installs **“Rust Type Kit” v0.1.0** — a totally unrelated FFI-type-generation tool (verified 2026-07-06: it has no `hook` subcommand, its `--help` says “query Rust types and produce FFI types”). This is a real name collision. **Never `cargo install rtk`.** Use one of the correct sources below. ## Per-platform install (all yield the real `rtk … hook claude`) [Section titled “Per-platform install (all yield the real rtk … hook claude)”](#per-platform-install-all-yield-the-real-rtk--hook-claude) | Platform | Install | Version got | Notes | | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | **Linux** (dev box) | Homebrew bottle (`brew install rtk`) → `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/rtk` | 0.43.0 | Surface A, live | | **macOS** (x86\_64 Sonoma 14.8.5) | `brew install rtk` → `/usr/local/bin/rtk` | 0.43.0 | Verified 2026-07-06 | | **Windows** (prebuilt, PREFERRED) | Download `rtk-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` from the GitHub release, extract to `C:\tools\rtk`, add to PATH | 0.43.0 | Version-matches Linux/Mac | | **Windows** (from source) | `cargo install --git https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk` → `%USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin\rtk.exe` | 0.42.4 (tracks master) | Works; slightly behind the release | Release assets for v0.43.0: `rtk-{x86_64,aarch64}-apple-darwin.tar.gz`, `rtk-{x86_64-musl,aarch64-gnu}-unknown-linux.tar.gz`, `rtk-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip`, `.deb`/`.rpm`. (`gh release view v0.43.0 --repo rtk-ai/rtk --json assets`.) ## Behavior verified per platform (2026-07-06, su-d2654) [Section titled “Behavior verified per platform (2026-07-06, su-d2654)”](#behavior-verified-per-platform-2026-07-06-su-d2654) * **Linux — full e2e** through fresh `claude -p` sessions (claude 2.1.201): (1) `git status` rewrote to `rtk git status` + ledger row recorded; (2) `PAPERCUSP_AGENT_SESSION=1 git reset --hard HEAD` **DENIED** by the shared-tree guard in-engine (guard runs before rtk; deny wins); (3) failing `node --test` output byte-identical raw-vs-rtk, exit 1 both. * **macOS — full e2e**: fresh `claude -p` ran `git status`, the pasted-verbatim output was the rtk-**compressed** format (`* main` / `clean — nothing to commit`), NOT standard git format, AND the gain ledger incremented (2→3) — the two together prove the hook loaded + rewrote + compressed. Component checks 4/4 (hook JSON, compression, failing-verbatim + exit code, ledger). * **Windows — rtk binary verified** (both 0.43.0 prebuilt and 0.42.4 from-git): `rtk hook claude` reads PreToolUse JSON on stdin and emits the correct `{"hookSpecificOutput":{…,"updatedInput":{"command":"rtk git status"}}}`; `rtk hook check git status` → `rtk git status`. The **blog claim that native Windows has “no auto-rewrite hook, only a CLAUDE.md fallback” is outdated** — the `hook claude` subcommand is present and functional on the native Windows build. A full live Windows `claude -p` e2e was NOT run because Claude Code is not installed/authed on the Windows VM (and native Windows is not a fleet-spawn or interactive-su target — our agents run on Linux/macOS); the updatedInput-application is Claude Code’s platform-independent engine behavior, already proven on Linux + macOS. ## Ledger locations (for verifying a spawn actually rewrote) [Section titled “Ledger locations (for verifying a spawn actually rewrote)”](#ledger-locations-for-verifying-a-spawn-actually-rewrote) * Linux: `~/.local/share/rtk/history.db` (sqlite; table `commands`, cols `timestamp, original_cmd, rtk_cmd, saved_tokens, project_path, …`). * macOS: read it via `rtk gain` / `rtk gain -H` (the `bash -lc` login shell gives the right PATH; a non-login ssh shell may not find `sqlite3`). * The authoritative “did the rewrite execute” signal is a **new ledger row** (or the compressed output format), not the model’s paraphrase of the output. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * The deny-evasion this exposed + its fix: see `agent-insights/pretooluse-updatedinput-evades-deny-patterns` (WI-3159). * Surface-B fleet rollout checklist: WI-3164.

# Which schedulers deliberately stay OFF DBOS (and why)

> The audit (dbos-scheduler-consolidation-2026-06-03) moved every portable periodic job onto DBOS scheduled workflows. This is the catalog of the loops that deliberately did NOT move, with the one-line reason for each — so the next agent doesn't try to "finish the migration" by porting something that can't or shouldn't be a DBOS cron.

The scheduler-consolidation pass ported the portable periodic jobs (backup orphan-cleanup, push-credential refresh, telemetry/scratch-gc/memory/embed timers, test-runs prune) onto **DBOS scheduled workflows** (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/periodic-workflows.ts` — grep `DBOS.registerScheduled` for the live set). A set of recurring loops were **deliberately kept off DBOS**. If you’re tempted to “finish the migration,” check this list first — these are conscious keeps, not stragglers. > **Correction (EI-1622):** the original pass ALSO put a batch of high-frequency, no-durability-need checks on DBOS — `harnessStatusSweep` (the harness-status sweep), `completionRefVerify` (the completion-ref verifier), `systemHealth`, `connectionPressure`, `serviceHealth`, `spawnReclaimSweep`, `staleClaimSweep`, `learningInfraHealth`, `steeringChurnSweep`. Those were later converted **back off DBOS** to lightweight in-process intervals (`dbos/in-process-periodic.ts`, armed from `host-bootstrap`): they wrote \~200k `dbos.workflow_status` rows/day for zero durability gain (the recurring routine-engine freeze). So they are NOT in `periodic-workflows.ts` anymore — grep the symbol names in `in-process-periodic.ts` instead. This is the doc’s own rule of thumb in action: no durability need ⇒ don’t keep it on DBOS. ## The keep list (consolidation D-002) [Section titled “The keep list (consolidation D-002)”](#the-keep-list-consolidation-d-002) * **All Rust schedulers** (`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri`, `papercup-rust-server`, `papercup-native`, `papercup-rust-mobile`). DBOS is a Node/TS library — it cannot run a Rust `tokio`/thread loop. The work is runtime-bound: Axum SSE keepalives, PG `LISTEN` reconnect, PG/zero-cache process spawn+kill lifecycle, WebSocket/ EventSource reconnect. * **Per-connection / per-request / per-spawn loops.** `expert-dispatcher` (≈100ms result-file poll during one agent run), `pty-ws`/`pty-bridge`/`device-voice-ws`/ `voice-engines/deepgram` keepalives, `run-command-sse`, the `pty` route, `agent-tools/locks/acquire` wait-poll, `voice-engine-health`, and `provision/ runner`’s `drainFifo`. Each is bound to a live in-process handle (socket / child process / session) that a detached periodic cron has no reference to. Not crons. * **In-memory sweepers.** `expirable-registry` sweeps a process-local `Map` of TTL’d entries; `harness-fs-watcher`’s 60s tick is a reconcile **backstop** to its event-driven (chokidar) watcher. A detached DBOS cron can’t see in-process memory or the watcher’s view. (Each carries an inline `// not a DBOS candidate` note.) * **`sync/hyperbee/outbox-drain`** — native at-least-once draining is the right fit; DBOS is a worse fit here (prior DBOS plan D-006). * **UI** — `ui/use-ui-presence` is a client-side React hook. * **Infra / CI** — the systemd *services* (mac VM, cloudflared ×2, pg-tunnel) and the `.github` nightly Actions cron are OS/platform-level, not operator work. `llm-test-nightly.timer` stays systemd too (a heavy external test-suite runner needing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, \~90min — CI-shaped, not operator maintenance; D-004). ## Update (2026-06-28): off-DBOS ≠ invisible anymore [Section titled “Update (2026-06-28): off-DBOS ≠ invisible anymore”](#update-2026-06-28-off-dbos--invisible-anymore) These loops still deliberately stay OFF DBOS — but they are no longer runtime-INVISIBLE. The `schedule-inventory-and-ephemeral-tier-2026-06-26` pass routed **every** operator-host `setInterval` through `managedSetInterval` (`@papercusp/scheduled-registry`), so each off-DBOS keep here (`expirable-registry`, `harness-fs-watcher`, `outbox-drain`, the per-connection keepalives, the watchdogs) now appears in `schedule:inventory` / `/admin/schedules` with a name + category + last-fire — *visibility ≠ control* (registering does NOT move it onto a central scheduler). A bare `setInterval` is now a `lint:no-raw-setinterval` build failure. See [The scheduler layer model](/agent-insights/two-tier-scheduler-and-timer-visibility/) for the full two-tier model (DBOS durable / in-process `managedSetInterval` / the ephemeral blueprint cadence). ## The rule of thumb [Section titled “The rule of thumb”](#the-rule-of-thumb) DBOS scheduled workflows are for **periodic, durable, operator-process maintenance jobs that read/write Postgres**. If a loop (a) runs in another runtime (Rust), (b) is bound to a live in-process handle (socket/child/session/Map), (c) is genuinely event-driven with the timer only a backstop, or (d) is OS/CI infra — it stays where it is.

# npm-scope renames: import-grep misses the references that break fresh builds

> When migrating a package across npm scopes (e.g. @restart/* -> @papercusp/*), grepping for import statements finds the imports but MISSES bare-string references — next.config transpilePackages, astro noExternal, tsconfig path maps, and command/script tables. Those pass a running dev server (it cached the old config) so route-200 smoke checks give false confidence, then break a fresh build.
