> Step-by-step procedure for flipping PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE=1, what to expect at each stage, how to verify success, and how to roll back cleanly if something goes wrong.

Superseded: there is no flag to flip anymore (Model B / Stage 4d) The `PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE` opt-in gate **was removed** with the Model B substrate rewrite — the substrate now **always boots** in-process and no code reads the env var (it survives only in “the gate was removed” comments in `in-process-status.ts` / `share-finalize.ts`, and setting it in `.env.local` is a no-op). This whole “set the env var → restart → verify the flag took effect → roll back by unsetting it” procedure is therefore **obsolete**. What is still real and useful below: the diagnostic surfaces (`substrate:status` CLI, `/admin/dogfood-substrate`, `/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-health`, `/api/harness/<slug>/claim-attempts`, the boot-history table) and the boot-error troubleshooting table — read those as “verify the always-on substrate,” not “verify the flag.” (Note: step 5’s `<HarnessChromeHeaderBadges>` component does not exist; the live pills are `SubstrateHealthPill` / `BootstrapProgressIndicator` in `app/harness/insights/`.) For the current diagnostic walkthrough see [Substrate diagnostic stack](/internal/docs/agent-insights/substrate-diagnostic-stack). ## Before you start [Section titled “Before you start”](#before-you-start) * This is a **one-process toggle** — restart the operator after editing the env var. It is not picked up live. * Substrate boot opens real Hyperswarm peer connections + writes to local Hypercore stores under `~/.papercusp-workspaces/<workspace>/.papercusp/<harness>/hyperbee/`. Leaves disk artefacts after the first run; rolling back the flag does NOT delete them. * Native dependencies must be installed (corestore, hypercore, autobase, hyperswarm, b4a). If `npm install` skipped them (rare; usually `--no-optional` or similar) the boot fails fast in `boot-history` with a clear error. * Has **no effect** on the legacy single-writer claim path. The orchestrator only switches to the distributed path if your code calls `getClaimStrategy()` — see “Orchestrator wiring” below. ## Steps [Section titled “Steps”](#steps) ### 1. Set the env var + restart [Section titled “1. Set the env var + restart”](#1-set-the-env-var--restart) 
```bash
export PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE=1
# kill -HUP / restart the operator process so instrumentation-node.ts
# picks it up.
```
 ### 2. Verify the flag took effect [Section titled “2. Verify the flag took effect”](#2-verify-the-flag-took-effect) 
```bash
cd apps/operator && npm run substrate:status
```
 Or open `/admin/dogfood-substrate` in a browser. Expected: 
```plaintext
Substrate flag: ✓ ON   booted: 0 harnesses
  → flag is on but no handles in boot map yet.
```
 If you see `· off`, the env var didn’t propagate — check whether you restarted the right process. ### 3. Wait for harnesses to boot [Section titled “3. Wait for harnesses to boot”](#3-wait-for-harnesses-to-boot) `instrumentation-node.ts` boots harnesses in parallel during startup (typically `<30s` for a handful of harnesses on local disk). The boot table on `/admin/dogfood-substrate` populates as each one comes up. If a boot **fails**, the `boot-history` section at the bottom of the page shows the error message. Common causes: | Error pattern | Likely cause | | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | `corestore lock contention` | Two processes opening the same store. Kill the other one. | | `bootstrap timeout` | Hyperswarm can’t reach any peer (firewall / no internet). | | `schema_version mismatch` | A peer is on a newer Papercusp. Update or wait. | | `permission denied` | Disk perms on `~/.papercusp-workspaces/...`. | ### 4. Check the health verdict per harness [Section titled “4. Check the health verdict per harness”](#4-check-the-health-verdict-per-harness) 
```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:3070/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-health | jq
```
 Or look at the per-row `SubstrateHealthPill` on the admin page. Verdict should be `healthy` once boot completes and no claim attempts have errored. ### 5. (Optional) Surface in chrome [Section titled “5. (Optional) Surface in chrome”](#5-optional-surface-in-chrome) Drop `<HarnessChromeHeaderBadges slug={...} />` into the harness header to show the 3-pill row (status / health / bootstrap) live in-app. ### 6. (Optional) Wire orchestrator [Section titled “6. (Optional) Wire orchestrator”](#6-optional-wire-orchestrator) The distributed claim path is off until production code calls `getClaimStrategy()` + branches. This is a code change, not a runtime toggle — see `lib/orchestrator/distributed-claim.ts` for the pattern. ## What you’ll see when things go well [Section titled “What you’ll see when things go well”](#what-youll-see-when-things-go-well) * `/admin/dogfood-substrate` top bar: green “Substrate live” pill + green health pill with `N✓` count. * Per-harness row: green health pill + bootstrap “Up to date” pill. * Boot history: 1 boot\_start + 1 boot\_ok per harness. * `substrate:status` CLI exits 0. ## What you’ll see when things go wrong [Section titled “What you’ll see when things go wrong”](#what-youll-see-when-things-go-wrong) * Top bar: green “Substrate live” but yellow/red health pill. * Per-row: health pill in `degraded` or `unhealthy` state. Tooltip lists the reasons (e.g. `claim error rate 30% ≥ 25%`). * Boot history: `boot_fail` rows with the error message. * `substrate:status` CLI exits 1. ## Rolling back [Section titled “Rolling back”](#rolling-back) The flag is a no-op when unset. To disable: 
```bash
unset PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE
# restart the operator
```
 What happens: * Substrate boot is skipped on the next start. * The boot map stays empty. * `attemptDistributedClaim` returns `substrate-not-booted` for every call — production code falls back to the legacy single-writer path. * Health pill shows `disabled`. * The on-disk Hypercore stores from previous boots stay where they are (safe to leave; harmless when not opened). To wipe the on-disk substrate entirely (use only if rotating keys or starting fresh): 
```bash
rm -rf ~/.papercusp-workspaces/*/.papercusp/*/hyperbee/
```
 ## Telemetry checkpoint [Section titled “Telemetry checkpoint”](#telemetry-checkpoint) After the first 24h with the flag on, sanity-check: * `/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-boot-history?kinds=boot_fail` — should be empty or only show transient errors. * `/api/harness/<slug>/claim-attempts?stats=1` — `error` count should be < 5% of `total`. * `/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-health` — every harness `healthy`. If any of these stay degraded for hours, file an issue with the boot- history entries attached. ## Related docs [Section titled “Related docs”](#related-docs) * [Substrate diagnostic stack](/internal/docs/agent-insights/substrate-diagnostic-stack) * [Dogfood v5 readiness map](/internal/docs/agent-insights/dogfood-v5-readiness-map)

# Substrate federation — HLC was dead code, and the two-axis capture model

> Until P-010 the Model-B peer-log carried NO HLC (lwwPick always fell back to wall-clock ts); and a federated table reaches the log by one of two mechanisms (CDC trigger OR log-first append) — both now guarded.

## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) Two non-obvious facts about the Model-B substrate (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/*`), both surfaced + fixed by `shared-hive-hardening-2026-06-13` P-010/P-011: 1. **The HLC was vestigial.** `lwwPick`/`beatsStored` order same-key conflicts by Hybrid Logical Clock “when both ops carry one, else wall-clock `ts`”. The HLC primitives (`@papercusp/locks-core` `processHlc`/`encodeHlc`) existed and were tested — but **`sync/hyperbee` never imported them**. `PeerLogOp` had no `hlc` field and `toEnvelope` (read-merge) silently dropped it. So **no federated write ever carried an HLC**, and the HLC branch was dead on the live path — every cross-peer conflict resolved by raw wall-clock `ts` (a fast/stepped clock wins). “HLC-when-present” meant present=never. 2. **A federated table reaches the log by exactly ONE of two mechanisms** — and which is non-obvious. Don’t assume “every `sync:'peer-log'` table has a `capture_substrate_outbox` trigger.” ## The two-axis capture model (read this before adding a federated table) [Section titled “The two-axis capture model (read this before adding a federated table)”](#the-two-axis-capture-model-read-this-before-adding-a-federated-table) A table classified `sync:'peer-log'` (registry: `harness-state/table-registry.ts` `PEER_LOG_TABLES`) gets its LOCAL writes onto the peer-log by one of: * **PG-first (CDC):** a `capture_substrate_outbox` / `capture_hive_members_outbox` trigger enqueues writes into `substrate_outbox`; `outbox-drain.ts` appends them. The set is `CDC_CAPTURED_TABLES` (= keys of `feature-issue-op-keys.ts` `TABLE_NAME_TO_TABLE_TAG`). These projections set `skipOwnOps: true` (an own-log op is a replay of a row PG already authored — applying it back is the EI-117 echo-storm). * **Log-first (direct append):** application code appends the op straight to the own log; PG state is materialized purely from the read-merge. Currently `feature_claims` (orchestrator/feature-claim.ts), `feature_queue` / `feature_working_set` (write-\*.ts), `contributors` (write-contributor-row\.ts), `shared_presence` (presence-announce.ts). These do **not** set `skipOwnOps`. A table must be in exactly one set (a table that is both CDC + log-first echo-storms). A `sync:'peer-log'` table with NEITHER producer silently never federates — its writes drop on the floor (the EI-382 class at the data layer). `ACCEPTED_UNFEDERATED_TABLES` (`sync/hyperbee/capture-coverage.ts`) is the escape hatch for a table that stays `sync:'peer-log'` but is deliberately left unproduced with a documented reason — it is currently **empty**. `harness_feature_prs` used to be that one documented exception (a read projection with no producer, because PR state is GitHub-derived + re-polled per-machine), but EI-479 went further: it retired the orphan projection entirely and **reclassified the table `sync:'none'`** in `table-registry.ts`, so it’s no longer in `PEER_LOG_TABLES` at all and needs no accepted-unfederated entry. See [Retiring (or adding) a federated table](./retire-or-add-a-federated-table) for the full six-surface removal this took. ## The guards (so neither recurs) [Section titled “The guards (so neither recurs)”](#the-guards-so-neither-recurs) * **HLC, P-010:** `sync/hyperbee/hlc-stamp.ts` — `stampOpHlc` (SEND seam, called at the single choke point `boot.ts` `handle.append`) stamps every LWW write; `observeRemoteHlc` (RECV seam, called in `projection.ts` `applyOpVia` for remote ops) advances the process clock past the observed remote frontier → cross-machine happens-before. `toEnvelope` now carries `hlc`. The append-only claim path uses the raw `ownLog.append` and correctly carries no HLC (distinct-key per attempt, never LWW). Tests: `__tests__/hlc-coverage.test.ts`. * **Capture coverage, P-011:** `harness-state/projection-engine.ts` `checkCaptureCoverage` (pure, the write-side dual of `checkPeerLogConsistency`) + `sync/hyperbee/capture-coverage.ts` (`checkSubstrateCaptureCoverage`, the bound sets). It asserts `PEER_LOG_TABLES = CDC ∪ log-first ∪ accepted-unfederated`. Tests: `__tests__/capture-coverage.test.ts`. Adding a federated table without a producer now fails CI. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * `lwwPick` compares the **encoded** HLC string directly (`a.hlc > b.hlc`); that equals `compareHlc` ONLY because `encodeHlc` is fixed-width sortable (`<15-digit ms>:<5-digit count>`). Don’t store a non-encoded HLC there. * The HLC is stamped at **append (drain/helper) time**, not write time. That is correct: the log append IS the federation event, drain is serial per peer (monotone), and `ts` still carries write-time for display. The receive-side `recv` advance is what makes it causal across machines — without it, two peers’ clocks are independent and a skewed peer still wins. * The `fed_ts` PG-level LWW guard (`projections/__tests__/fed-ts-lww-guard.integration.test.ts`) is a SEPARATE, independent floor (a strictly-older op can’t clobber a row); HLC improves the *cross-peer concurrent* pick, fed\_ts prevents *stale* clobber. Both are needed.

# Substrate revocation — the trust model (read before touching admission)

> How peer revocation works in the Model B substrate — self vs owner, the GitHub-anchored authority, the re-verify enforcement, and why it's fail-open.

If you’re about to change substrate admission/revocation, or a security review flags something here as a “gap,” read this first — several of these are **intentional** trust-model decisions, not bugs. ## Two flavors of revocation (both enforced) [Section titled “Two flavors of revocation (both enforced)”](#two-flavors-of-revocation-both-enforced) 1. **Self-revocation** (`papercusp-substrate-revocation-v1-2026-06-01`). A contributor revokes their OWN device key (lost/rotated device). Mechanism: the device pubkey is added to that contributor’s own `revoked_pubkeys` (a `TEXT[]` on `harness_shared.contributors`, replicated via the substrate). Trigger: `revokeSelfDevice` / `POST /api/admin/substrate/revoke-self-device` / the `substrate:revoke_self_device` MCP tool — guarded by `not_your_key` (you can only revoke keys in your OWN `device_attestations`). Enforcement: `boot.ts` seeds the admission `revoked` Set from `loadRevokedPubkeys` at startup (unconditional, fail-open) AND refreshes it inside every `mergeNow`. 2. **Owner-revocation** (`papercusp-substrate-revocation-v2-owner-2026-06-01`, Component A — PASSIVE detection; plus Component B, now BUILT with a different design than originally planned, see below). Kicking out a different contributor (a bad actor). * **Component A (passive, unchanged):** a repo admin **deletes the contributor’s `user/<id>` branch** (the channel-2 artifact) directly on GitHub. Enforcement: `boot.ts` periodically **re-verifies admitted peers’ channel-2** (throttled inside `mergeNow`, default \~15 min) and drops any whose binding conclusively `fail`s. This drop does **not** blocklist the pubkey (see below). * **Component B (active, `substrate:revoke_contributor` — `non-collaborator-join-fork-pr -2026-06-02` D-001, supersedes the old branch-delete design):** an in-app OWNER trigger. **The original “delete the `user/<id>` branch via the GitHub API” design was dropped before shipping** — it would have been a silent no-op, because admission moved to being gated on the contributor’s attestation **gist** (`read-admission` → `verifyAttestation`), not a repo branch, and an admin can’t delete another user’s gist. The shipped design instead: the owner (gated on holding a GitHub token with **repo-admin** on the shared repo) adds the target’s device pubkeys directly to the **owner’s own** contributor-row `revoked_pubkeys` and publishes it — the same blocklist self-revocation uses (`revoke-contributor.ts` `revokeContributorViaGithub`). Every peer’s `read-admission` union honors it on the next re-verify. A **Hive-scope** variant (`shared-hive-federation-2026-06-08` P-006, `hive-revoke-contributor.ts` `revokeHiveContributor`) revokes the contributor from a WHOLE Hive’s federation (every member harness) in one call — its authority is **holding the Hive’s private key**, not GitHub repo-admin (a Hive may be repo-less); see the authority section below. The gap that motivated rev-v2 Model B verified a peer’s channel-2 binding ONCE at admission and re-checked only PENDING peers. An already-**admitted** peer was NEVER re-verified — so a deleted GitHub binding was not noticed. If you see admission logic that only checks at admit-time, that gap is back. ## Why GitHub-anchored authority (not a papercusp owner gate) [Section titled “Why GitHub-anchored authority (not a papercusp owner gate)”](#why-github-anchored-authority-not-a-papercusp-owner-gate) Deliberate, consistent with `papercusp-trust-model-2026-05-31` + the **no-collaborator-gate** decision + Phase-1b §8 / D-009: **GitHub is the real authority** for the thing that matters (merging code); peer-synced state is **advisory**. An owner-signed revocation list was considered and rejected — it reintroduces exactly the papercusp-side authority gate that decision avoided, and the P-068 “owner” is only *provisional*/contestable. Re-verifying channel-2 is **not** a collaborator gate; it re-applies the *same* check admission already requires, just periodically. **Update:** `substrate:revoke_contributor` (Component B, above) DOES now gate its harness-scope action on a papercusp-side check — but it’s still anchored in GitHub, not a papercusp-native owner: the gate is “does the caller’s GitHub token have **repo-admin** on the shared repo,” checked live via `octokit.repos.get(...).permissions.admin`, the same authority Component A’s branch-delete always assumed. The **Hive-scope** variant is the one genuine departure: its authority is **holding the Hive’s private key** (a Hive can be repo-less), not a GitHub permission at all — a deliberate, narrower keypair-native authority for the Hive-wide case. ## Intentional decisions a reviewer will want to “fix” (don’t, without re-deciding the posture) [Section titled “Intentional decisions a reviewer will want to “fix” (don’t, without re-deciding the posture)”](#intentional-decisions-a-reviewer-will-want-to-fix-dont-without-re-deciding-the-posture) * **Fail-OPEN on a revocation/re-verify LOAD failure** (rev-v1 D-006, rev-v2 D-004). If the PG read or the GitHub API fails, admission continues WITHOUT the (new) revocation rather than evicting peers. Rationale: advisory substrate + GitHub-is-authority → a transient blip must not self-inflict a federation outage. It’s **visible** (`merge_error`/`announce_error` events) and **self-healing** (re-checked next cycle). A channel-2-`fail` (conclusive) DOES drop; only transient (`pending`/api-down) keeps. Fail-secure (evict-on-failure) is the wrong trade here. * **A channel-2-fail drop does NOT blocklist the pubkey.** A re-published binding is re-admitted by normal admission; a still-deleted binding is rejected (`binding_invalid`) — no flap. (Self-revocation DOES persist via `revoked_pubkeys` — that’s the difference.) * **Revocation is non-retroactive.** Ops a peer already merged remain (advisory; GitHub is authority). True cryptographic removal isn’t a goal. ## Not built (intentional) [Section titled “Not built (intentional)”](#not-built-intentional) * **Multi-device per login** — see `phase1b-federation-limitations`. ## Built since this doc was first written (2026-07-03 update) [Section titled “Built since this doc was first written (2026-07-03 update)”](#built-since-this-doc-was-first-written-2026-07-03-update) * **Rev-v2 Component B is now BUILT** (`substrate:revoke_contributor`, see above) — but with a *different* design than the branch-delete this doc originally described as “not built.” The branch-delete trigger was dropped before shipping (it would have been a no-op once admission moved to gist-based attestation); the shipped trigger blocklists the target’s pubkeys directly. * **Un-revoke / re-instate is now PARTIALLY built** (`WI-193` “G8” fix in `boot.ts` `applyRevocationRefresh`) — this doc previously said it was YAGNI/append-only; that is no longer accurate for the *published-list* path. Any pubkey whose provenance is refresh-sourced (`revokedViaRefresh` — seeded at startup from `loadRevokedPubkeys`, or added by a later `applyRevocationRefresh` cycle) is **removed from `revoked`** the moment it disappears from the freshly-loaded published `revoked_pubkeys` set, re-admitting it on its next announce (a `peer_unrevoked` boot-history event records it). This can never silently undo an explicit **live** `revoke()` call (self-revoke or owner-revoke via the tools above) — `revoke()` evicts the pubkey from `revokedViaRefresh` too, so an explicit in-process revocation stays blocked for the life of that boot regardless of the published list. There is still no dedicated “un-revoke” MCP tool; the only way to un-revoke today is to edit the pubkey out of the relevant contributor row’s `revoked_pubkeys` column directly (and, for a pubkey revoked live in the current process, restart the boot so the seed no longer includes it).

# The substrate-sidecar relocation silently fell back to in-process in every packaged build

> papercusp-substrate-sidecar ON still ran hyperbee in-process off any bundle — a CWD-relative socket EACCES'd and the spawn used `npx tsx` a bundle can't run. Fix — absolute socket + re-exec the bundled serve.mjs in sidecar mode.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) With `papercusp-substrate-sidecar` flipped ON, the operator logged 
```plaintext
[substrate-boot] SUBSTRATE_SIDECAR on: spawning sidecar for relocated substrate boot
[substrate-boot] sidecar spawn failed, falling back to in-process: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '.papercusp'
```
 and ran the whole hyperbee substrate (corestore + merge + projections + swarm) **in-process** — exactly the event-loop saturation the relocation exists to remove. The flag was ON; the feature did nothing. The single-box unit suite was green the whole time. (Caught only by the P-006 live 2-machine rig verify, on a hand-deployed current-staging `serve.mjs`.) ## Why the tests missed it [Section titled “Why the tests missed it”](#why-the-tests-missed-it) `substrate-boot-wrapper.test.ts` **mocks** `./substrate-sidecar-spawn`, and the host tests use writable temp dirs. So the one thing that was broken — the *real* `spawnSubstrateSidecar` running from a packaged, root-owned CWD — was never exercised. “47 green” covered everything except the failure. The flag’s `DARK_FLAG_CASE: 'incomplete'` tag was, in hindsight, exactly right: the packaged spawn path was never finished. ## Root cause (two bugs, the first masked the second) [Section titled “Root cause (two bugs, the first masked the second)”](#root-cause-two-bugs-the-first-masked-the-second) 1. **CWD-relative socket.** The spawner, the entrypoint, and the IPC client all defaulted the Unix socket to `.papercusp/substrate.sock` — relative to `process.cwd()`. In a packaged deploy the operator’s CWD is the **root-owned install dir** (`/usr/lib/Papercusp/sidecar`), so the `tester` user’s `mkdir '.papercusp'` is `EACCES`. The spawn threw and `bootSubstrateWithFallback` swallowed it into the in-process fallback. 2. **`npx tsx <.ts>` from a bundle.** Even past the mkdir, the spawn ran `npx tsx apps/operator/bin/substrate-sidecar.ts`. The packaged operator ships a single esbuild bundle, `serve.mjs` — there is no `tsx` and no `.ts` on disk. So the relocation could only ever spawn from a **dev tree** (where the bg-host RSS win was measured); it was dead in the product. ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) * **`substrate-socket-path.ts`** (new): `resolveSubstrateSocketPath()` — honours `PAPERCUSP_SUBSTRATE_IPC_SOCKET`, else an **absolute** `os.tmpdir()` path keyed by the main operator pid (two operators on one box never collide). Never CWD-relative. The spawner pins the resolved path into `process.env` once so the parent IPC client and the spawned child agree. * **Bundled spawn.** esbuild bundles every module into `serve.mjs`, so `import.meta.url` in the spawner *is* `serve.mjs` in a packaged build. The spawner now re-execs **that artifact** under `process.execPath` with `PAPERCUSP_SUBSTRATE_SIDECAR_MODE=1`; `serve.ts` diverts to `runSubstrateSidecarServer()` before any operator boot. Dev (TS source) still uses `npx tsx`. * **`substrate-sidecar-server.ts`** (new): the JSON-RPC server extracted out of the bin into operator-core, with **no top-level side effects** — so `serve.ts` can import it without an auto-running bin guard firing (in the bundle a bin’s `import.meta.url === argv[1]` guard would resolve TRUE on every boot and start a stray sidecar). `apps/operator/bin/substrate-sidecar.ts` is now a thin dev shim. * **Pattern reused for spawner-sidecar (WI-344 ③, 2026-06-30).** The identical `serve.mjs` re-exec approach was applied to the agent-spawn sidecar (`packages/operator-core/lib/fleet/spawner-sidecar-server.ts`, plan `spawner-sidecar-offload-2026-06-30`): `serve.ts` now also diverts under `PAPERCUSP_SPAWNER_SIDECAR_MODE=1` to `runSpawnerSidecarServer()` before any operator boot. The no-top-level-side-effects rule and the absolute socket path are both enforced in the new sidecar from the start, closing both P-006 root causes for the spawner path before they could recur. ## Verifying it actually engaged [Section titled “Verifying it actually engaged”](#verifying-it-actually-engaged) On a host running the fixed `serve.mjs` with the flag ON, the boot log must show **no** “falling back to in-process”, and a real sidecar child must exist: 
```plaintext
fed.sh <a|b> ssh 'grep -i "spawning sidecar\|falling back\|PAPERCUSP_SUBSTRATE_READY" ~/*.boot.out'
fed.sh <a|b> ssh 'ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd | grep -i SUBSTRATE_SIDECAR_MODE | grep -v grep'
fed.sh <a|b> api GET /api/admin/dogfood-substrate-boot-history
```
 ## Lesson [Section titled “Lesson”](#lesson) A flag being ON is not the feature being on. When a code path only runs in a **packaged** deploy (different CWD, no dev toolchain, a single bundle), a mocked unit test proves nothing about it — verify on the real artifact before flipping the default. Anything that resolves a path/socket/binary relative to `cwd` or assumes `tsx`/source-on-disk is a packaging bug waiting for production.

# Substrate sidecar process seams: why federation bootstrap resolves fail there (and the deterministic fix)

> The substrate sidecar is a SEPARATE process where PG-backed default seams and process-local singletons (org-PG, operator-state reads, the live hive-directory instance) can be unconfigured or empty — and every failure is a silently-caught fail-closed null. The owner-bootstrap admit binding (hivePubkey → ownerDevicePubkey) depended on exactly such state, making owner→joiner federation directory-timing LUCK. Fix pattern: thread boot-resolved values into per-frame paths + carry verified bindings in the REGISTRY (the one store that resolves in every process).

## The trap in one sentence [Section titled “The trap in one sentence”](#the-trap-in-one-sentence) Code under `lib/sync/hyperbee/**` runs in the **substrate sidecar — a separate process** — where the operator’s PG-backed default seams and process-local singletons may be unconfigured or empty, and because every consumer wraps them in `catch(() => null)` / `catch(() => [])`, a missing dependency looks exactly like “no data”: **fail-closed, silent, and unreproducible in-process.** ## How it manifested (2026-07-01, Brief-3 live rig — a full day of INCOMPLETEs) [Section titled “How it manifested (2026-07-01, Brief-3 live rig — a full day of INCOMPLETEs)”](#how-it-manifested-2026-07-01-brief-3-live-rig--a-full-day-of-incompletes) The joiner’s **owner-bootstrap admit** must resolve `(hivePubkey → ownerDevicePubkey)` before it will admit the hive OWNER’s log (`resolveJoinedHiveOwnerDevice` in `boot.ts`; `loadHiveOwnerDevicePubkey` in `hive-membership-store.ts`). Until that resolves, the joiner **rejects every owner announce** (`[A-003] owner-admit …: ownerDevice=<null> match=false`) — no roster, no content, nothing federates. The binding’s two legs were BOTH process-local state: 1. **The live in-process hive directory** (`getHiveDirectory().listDiscoveredHives`) — a per-process singleton. The OPERATOR process’s directory heard the owner’s announce (and wrote the PG cache row); the SIDECAR’s instance had not. 2. **The PG offline cache** (`readOperatorState('hive_directory_cache', ws)`) — worked only when the row for exactly that workspace existed at read time; the descriptor arrived on the joiner \~18 minutes after publish (directory propagation), long after every scenario poll window expired. So whether owner→joiner federation worked at all was **directory-timing luck**: Brief 4 won the race and passed; Brief 3 lost it four consecutive runs. The in-process matrix could never catch this — in one process, the directory singleton is shared, so the binding always resolves. The same trap, second face: the fire-and-forget `admitAnnouncedPeerAsOwner` call re-resolved the harness’s hive-home **per inbound announce** through registry+PG defaults. In the sidecar/test contexts those defaults threw (`getOrgPg().sql` undefined → “reading ‘unsafe’”; `readOperatorState` → “sql is not a function”), and the catch turned every announce into a silent admit skip (live) or a `console.error` that failed the whole cross-peer suite 9/9 (tests). ## The fix pattern (two halves, both landed 2026-07-02) [Section titled “The fix pattern (two halves, both landed 2026-07-02)”](#the-fix-pattern-two-halves-both-landed-2026-07-02) 1. **Thread boot-resolved values; never re-resolve per frame.** The boot already knows its hive-home (`hiveHomeProjectionSlug ?? ownHiveHomeSlug`, kept current across rekey rebinds). `boot.ts` now passes it into `admitAnnouncedPeerAsOwner` via `deps.hiveHomeSlugForHarness` — deterministic, free, and independent of any process-local seam. 2. **Carry verified bindings in the REGISTRY** — the one store that demonstrably resolves in every process (the sidecar’s `joinerHiveHomeSlug` registry read works live; that is the existence proof). `joinHiveAsView` now stamps the verified `(hive_pubkey, owner_device_pubkey)` from the discovery descriptor onto the `remote_hive` view entry at JOIN time (idempotent re-join backfills pre-stamp views), and `loadHiveOwnerDeviceBindings` reads that as its first, deterministic leg. Both values trace to `verifyHiveAnnounce`-gated sources, so trust is unchanged — only availability widened. ## Rules for the next agent [Section titled “Rules for the next agent”](#rules-for-the-next-agent) * **Anything imported under `sync/hyperbee/**` must assume: no org-PG, no operator-state PG, no live directory, no operator singletons.** If it needs one, either take it as a dep threaded from boot opts, or read the registry. * **A `catch(() => null)` around a cross-process dependency is a silent fail-closed** — when debugging “X never happens” in the sidecar, suspect the seam before the logic. `PAPERCUSP_A003_TRACE=1` prints the admit/resolve decisions to `serve.log` and is the fastest live discriminator. * **In-process green ≠ live green, specifically BECAUSE of process seams**: the in-process matrix shares every singleton; only the 2-VM rig (or the sidecar repro tests) exercises the process boundary. * Debug flow that worked: run the rig scenario with `--keep-up` + the trace env → `grep -a 'A-003' /home/pcusp/serve.log` on the failing side → psql the frame’s PG directly to compare what each PROCESS believes → mutate the state live (inject a row, restart one sidecar) to discriminate hypotheses.

# Substrate federation self-heals without an operator restart (the two re-peer loops)

> The per-harness substrate swarm (joinHarnessSwarm) used to join its DHT topic ONCE and never re-announce/re-lookup, so a dropped peer or aged-out announce left federation DEAD until an operator RESTART (fed-a↔fed-b sat dead ~7h; WI-559/WI-752/FED-2). Two self-heal loops fix the whole class with no restart: (1) a two-speed discovery.refresh() loop in joinHarnessSwarm (fast post-join/post-peer-loss window + slow keepalive), mirroring the hive-directory gossip; (2) a bounded-backoff JOIN-retry in boot.ts for when the boot-time join itself failed (DHT/identity/gh-auth/keychain blip → local-only). Found + fixed 2026-06-24.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) Cross-machine federation (fed-a ↔ fed-b) goes **dead and stays dead** — peers stop seeing each other’s content/presence (e.g. `shared_presence` cross-rows go hours stale) — and the **only** thing that brings it back is an **operator restart**. WI-559 finding #1 / WI-752 / FED-2: the link sat dead \~7h with no self-heal. ## Root cause — the substrate swarm never re-announced [Section titled “Root cause — the substrate swarm never re-announced”](#root-cause--the-substrate-swarm-never-re-announced) `joinHarnessSwarm` (`swarm.ts`) is the per-harness **content-replication** swarm (`corestore.replicate` + the `papercusp/announce` channel). Pre-fix it called `swarm.join(topic, …)` **once**, fired the legacy `discovery.flushed()`, and **never re-ran `discovery.refresh()`**. On the current hyperswarm/hyperdht the first announce/lookup round reliably misses and nothing internal retries for minutes (see [standalone-hyperswarm-discovery-driver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/standalone-hyperswarm-discovery-driver)), so when an established peer connection died (idle / timeout / reset / mid-replication death) or the topic’s DHT announce aged out, the peer was **never rediscovered**. The `swarm-chaos` test only “proved” recovery because the **test harness** called `refresh()` itself (`forceReconnectAll`) — production had no such driver. The hive-**directory** gossip (`directory-swarm.ts`) already self-healed via a two-speed refresh loop; the substrate path was just never given the same loop. A **second**, distinct failure mode: the boot-time join is also one-shot. If `resolveLocalAnnounceIdentity` throws (gh-unauthed / keychain / DHT blip), boot’s catch keeps the harness **local-only** (`handle.swarm === null`) — and pre-fix it stayed local-only **forever until a restart**. (This was the live fed-a/fed-b dead-link cause: both VMs gh-unauthed → never announced.) ## The fix — two self-heal loops, both ON by default, no restart [Section titled “The fix — two self-heal loops, both ON by default, no restart”](#the-fix--two-self-heal-loops-both-on-by-default-no-restart) 1. **Re-peer loop** (`joinHarnessSwarm`, `swarm.ts`) — a two-speed `discovery.refresh({ client: true, server: true })` loop: * **FAST** (`DEFAULT_SUBSTRATE_REFRESH_MS` = 2.5s) inside the post-join window (`DEFAULT_SUBSTRATE_FAST_WINDOW_MS` = **120s**, widened from the original 30s — see “Update” below), **re-armed** whenever a peer socket `close`s (snappy reconnect — a fresh node needs several rounds); * **SLOW** keepalive (`DEFAULT_SUBSTRATE_SLOW_REFRESH_MS` = 60s) otherwise, so the topic stays announced (a *future* drop can always re-pair) without hammering the public DHT. * `unref()`’d; cleared in `close()`. 2. **Join-retry loop** (`bootHarnessSubstrate`, `boot.ts`) — when the boot-time join FAILED (`swarmHandle === null`), retry `joinForBinding` on a bounded exponential backoff (`DEFAULT_SWARM_JOIN_RETRY_MS` = 15s → `SWARM_JOIN_RETRY_CAP_MS` = 5m) until it succeeds, then stop. A **permanent** cause just backs off at the cap and self-heals the instant the cause clears (e.g. a gh token is restored — no restart). Self-rearming `setTimeout` chain (the P-022 pattern), `unref()`’d, cleared in `close()`. ## Why a dropped connection re-pairs [Section titled “Why a dropped connection re-pairs”](#why-a-dropped-connection-re-pairs) Hyperswarm dedups one socket per peer across all shared topics. The substrate’s `connection` handler is registered on the shared swarm, so when `refresh()` re-runs the DHT round and a new connection forms, the handler fires again → `corestore.replicate(newSocket)` re-replicates and the announce channel re-exchanges (a fresh per-connection announce, WI-559 issue-2) → the next `mergeNow()` picks up everything written while the link was down. ## Tests (the durable proof) [Section titled “Tests (the durable proof)”](#tests-the-durable-proof) * `swarm-self-heal.test.ts` — fake swarm + fake timers: fast cadence, slow keepalive, peer-`close` re-arm, `close()` stops the loop, `refreshMs: 0` disables. * `__tests__/swarm-self-heal-reconnect.test.ts` — REAL Hyperswarm over an offline testnet: federate a write, **kill the live connection with NO manual refresh**, and a post-drop write still crosses once the production loop reconnects (\~1s). * `__tests__/swarm-join-retry.test.ts` — a transient identity failure at boot → the retry loop joins on its own (no restart); `swarmJoinRetryMs: 0` disables. ## Update (D-045, shared-hive-member-content-federation): fast window widened 30s → 120s [Section titled “Update (D-045, shared-hive-member-content-federation): fast window widened 30s → 120s”](#update-d-045-shared-hive-member-content-federation-fast-window-widened-30s--120s) The original 30s fast window (above) turned out too short: a **freshly-spawned sidecar process** joining over the public DHT reliably misses the first several announce/lookup rounds (cold start), so the next re-announce after 30s fell straight to the 60s SLOW cadence — a \~90s dead zone where two genuinely-separate machines never `peer_connected` (seen live: run-12 “no peer in \~90s”; invisible to tests because local-testnet peers instantly). `DEFAULT_SUBSTRATE_FAST_WINDOW_MS` is now **120s** — 2.5s re-announces keep a cold node aggressively discoverable until it pairs, then it drops to the bounded SLOW keepalive. Still re-armed on last-peer-loss; still bounded (no forever-hammering). ## Update (2026-07-02, cross-machine-coord-parity-and-trust-2026-07-01 P-004/D-008): directory-swarm.ts is now a thin instantiation of the generic `topic-gossip.ts` chassis [Section titled “Update (2026-07-02, cross-machine-coord-parity-and-trust-2026-07-01 P-004/D-008): directory-swarm.ts is now a thin instantiation of the generic topic-gossip.ts chassis”](#update-2026-07-02-cross-machine-coord-parity-and-trust-2026-07-01-p-004d-008-directory-swarmts-is-now-a-thin-instantiation-of-the-generic-topic-gossipts-chassis) The hive-**directory** gossip’s two-speed refresh loop referenced throughout this doc no longer lives inline in `directory-swarm.ts` — it moved to a generic `createTopicGossip<Frame>()` chassis in the new `topic-gossip.ts`, which `directory-swarm.ts` now calls as a thin instantiation (`createDirectoryGossip` → `createTopicGossip({ protocol: HIVE_DIRECTORY_PROTOCOL, ... })`); the presence-gossip transport is the chassis’s second instantiation. The refresh defaults for the directory path are unchanged and still live as constants re-exported from `topic-gossip.ts` (`DEFAULT_REFRESH_MS` = 2.5s, `DEFAULT_FAST_WINDOW_MS` = **30s** — not widened, unlike the substrate path below — `DEFAULT_SLOW_REFRESH_MS` = 60s). Public API and existing callers/tests (`hive-directory-boot.ts`) are unchanged. The **substrate** swarm (`joinHarnessSwarm` in `swarm.ts`, the subject of the fix below) has **not** been migrated onto this chassis — it still runs its own bespoke `managedSetInterval`-based refresh loop with its own `DEFAULT_SUBSTRATE_*` constants (verified current as of 2026-07-04). Don’t assume “the same loop” means “the same source file” anymore: for the hive-directory side, read `topic-gossip.ts`; for the per-harness substrate side, read `swarm.ts` directly. ## Gotcha [Section titled “Gotcha”](#gotcha) `admission-pending-retry.test.ts > "…announce was built >5 min before retry fires (behavioral)"` is a **pre-existing flaky/broken** fake-timer test (fails on `vitest-fail-on-console` / nondeterministic teardown on the parent commit, with zero FED-2 code) — **not** caused by these loops. Don’t chase it as a self-heal regression.

# Substrate write-side stack — one shape per Hyperbee table

> The 7-layer pattern for shipping a new Hyperbee-backed write path (substrate write helper → PG projection → HTTP wrapper → polling read hook → pure UI → client wrapper → list integration). Shipped in batch for feature_queue (P-032) and contributors (P-033) on 2026-05-25; document so the next per-table pickup can replicate without rediscovering.

## When this applies [Section titled “When this applies”](#when-this-applies) You are adding (or wiring up) a Hyperbee-backed table that users can *write to* from the UI. The read-side projection probably already exists; the write path needs all 7 layers below. Skip this insight when you’re only consuming (read-only) — the projection writes to PG and a normal PG-read endpoint is fine. ## The 7-layer stack [Section titled “The 7-layer stack”](#the-7-layer-stack) Each Hyperbee write-table follows the same shape: 
```plaintext
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Substrate write helper                                  │
│    packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/write-<table>.ts│
│    Pure: takes BootedHarnessHandle + row, appends op.      │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. PG projection (existing)                                │
│    .../lib/sync/hyperbee/projections/<table>.ts            │
│    Substrate's applyHyperbeeOpToPg fans the op to here.    │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. PG reader                                               │
│    .../lib/sync/hyperbee/load-<table>-membership.ts        │
│    Pure: SELECT joined with `contributors` for UI.         │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. HTTP wrapper                                            │
│    .../lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/<table>.ts        │
│    GET membership; POST per write verb.                    │
│    substrate-off → 200 + reason='substrate-off'.           │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5. Polling read hook                                       │
│    use<Table>Membership.ts (UI layer)                      │
│    Polls every 8s; pauses when document.hidden.            │
│    Returns {map, membersFor, isQueued, refresh}.           │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 6. Pure UI primitives                                      │
│    <Table>AvatarCluster.tsx (read) / <Action>Button.tsx    │
│    No state; consumer feeds props.                         │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 7. Client wrapper                                          │
│    <Action>ButtonClient.tsx                                │
│    Optimistic flip + POST + revert on failure.             │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
        List integration (FeatureList.tsx, FeaturePage, etc.)
        — drops hook + UI + client into the row render.
```
 ## Cardinality + contract [Section titled “Cardinality + contract”](#cardinality--contract) * **One write helper module per table** — exports `enqueueX` / `dequeueX` / `publishXRow`. Both put-ops with semantic differences (e.g. dequeue is soft-delete `removed_at = now`, not a `del` op; the projection treats `del` as hard delete). * **One PG reader per table** — pure; injectable `runQuery`; returns `{}` when the substrate table doesn’t exist yet (not booted, flag off, etc.). * **One HTTP route file per table** with N tools (one GET + enqueue/dequeue/etc. POSTs). The route’s `parseWriteBody` exported so unit tests can hit it directly without spinning a fake Request. * **The hook + UI tests use vitest + @testing-library/react with `@vitest-environment jsdom`** and `afterEach(() => cleanup())` — the project’s house style. ## Substrate-off behavior contract [Section titled “Substrate-off behavior contract”](#substrate-off-behavior-contract) Every layer must handle “substrate not booted” cleanly: | Layer | substrate-off shape | | --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | | Write helper | Caller’s problem — helper assumes handle. | | HTTP write POST | `{ok: false, reason: 'substrate-off'}` 200. | | Client wrapper | Reverts optimistic flip on `ok: false`. | | PG read | `{}` when projection table doesn’t exist. | | Read hook | `loaded: true` with empty map. | | Avatar cluster | Renders em-dash for empty members. | The point: a flag-flip toggles the entire stack alive without route changes. The UI shows ”—” before flip, real data after. ## Worked example — feature\_queue [Section titled “Worked example — feature\_queue”](#worked-example--feature_queue) What was shipped on 2026-05-25 for P-031b → P-032: 1. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/write-feature-queue.ts` (enqueueFeature/dequeueFeature) 2. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/projections/feature-queue.ts` (was already there) 3. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/load-queue-membership.ts` (PG joined w/ contributors) 4. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/feature-queue.ts` (still mounted) 5. `useQueueMembership.ts` — **removed** (UI layer not carried to the Vite SPA) 6. `QueueAvatarCluster.tsx` + `PullToQueueButton.tsx` — **removed** 7. `PullToQueueButtonClient.tsx` — **removed** * list integration (`FeatureList.tsx` / `FeatureFilterChips`) — **removed**. (Layers 1–4 above are real; 5–7 are historical — see the Update note at top.) Commits: `2501088c` `c9861001` `139e6a7b` `310c87e2` `6a7dee42` `730119af` `7397a7ce` `1240532e` `2dd0b34b`. ## Worked example — contributors [Section titled “Worked example — contributors”](#worked-example--contributors) Same shape, fewer write verbs: 1. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/write-contributor-row.ts` (publishContributorRow) 2. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/projections/contributors.ts` (was already there) 3. PG read happens directly inside step8 — no separate `load-` module needed because `contributors` rows go to a dedicated PG table whose readers already exist (`/harness/:slug/contributors` route). 4. HTTP write happens inside the join-shared-harness orchestrator step8, not via a public route — bound to the join flow. 5-7. UI surfaces are P-048 ContributorsTab + ContributorRow (pre-existing). Commits: `1f53912e` (write helper), `ac7b99b7` (step8 wire-up). ## Bouncing the hono-host to pick up new routes [Section titled “Bouncing the hono-host to pick up new routes”](#bouncing-the-hono-host-to-pick-up-new-routes) `tsx` doesn’t auto-restart on new file additions. New route files need a host bounce: 
```sh
pkill -9 -f "tsx.*hono-host"; sleep 2
cd apps/operator
nohup env PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE=1 \
  PAPERCUSP_HONO_PORT=3070 PAPERCUSP_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 \
  npx tsx bin/hono-host.ts > /tmp/hono-host.log 2>&1 &
sleep 8
curl -sw '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:3070/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-status
```
 Live-substrate writes through Autobase can hang on a degraded corestore — if the POST never returns, the host is probably crashed. Bring it back up cleanly + skip live writes from curl. The unit tests cover correctness; live integration through Autobase needs a proper test rig. ## Anti-patterns to avoid [Section titled “Anti-patterns to avoid”](#anti-patterns-to-avoid) * **Don’t write to PG directly from a write-side endpoint** — bypasses the projection’s LWW conflict resolution + the substrate sync. The PG row is a *projection*, not the source of truth. * **Don’t `del` on dequeue** — the projection treats `del` as a hard delete and we lose the history. Use a `put` with the tombstone field set (e.g. `removed_at = now`). * **Don’t fetch per-row from the UI** — the hook fetches the whole membership map once at the list level + polls. Per-row HTTP would be N × pollMs requests. * **Don’t add a new field to a HarnessFeatureRow without adding it to `isHarnessFeatureRow`** — the projection drops rows that fail the predicate, so a typo here silently makes ops vanish. ## What’s still missing [Section titled “What’s still missing”](#whats-still-missing) **Update:** the clobber-toast delivery channel has since been built. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/clobber-events.ts` emits `clobber` events on the server, and `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/clobber-stream.ts` (`GET /api/harness/:slug/clobber-stream` → `text/event-stream`, Phase 5b P-035) now forwards each emission as an SSE `clobber` event to a browser-side `ClobberToast`. It emits all clobber events globally and relies on the browser-side per-row `hbKey` filter to scope what the user sees (per-harness filtering at the SSE side is deferred — the event doesn’t carry the source harness slug, and the operator boots one harness per process today).

# Surviving an operator wedge: your papercusp-su MCP severs and won't auto-reconnect — bridge over HTTP, and DON'T retry-storm

> When the :3070 operator event-loop wedges, your papercusp-su MCP client silently drops all 480 tools and never reconnects for the rest of the session — coord/plans/memory/work-queue all gone. Here's how to confirm it, reach the operator over a direct HTTP bridge instead, and why hammering it with retries makes the wedge worse.

## The signature [Section titled “The signature”](#the-signature) Mid-session, every `mcp__papercusp-su__*` tool vanishes — a system-reminder says “MCP server disconnected” and `ToolSearch` for them returns nothing. You’ve lost coord, plans, memory, work-queue, fleet — your entire coordination surface. It does **not** come back on its own: the client does not auto-reconnect, even after the operator recovers. You are stranded for the rest of the session. The root cause is upstream: the `:3070` operator’s **event loop is wedged** (see [`attributing-loop-saturation-via-cpuprofiles`](/agent-insights/attributing-loop-saturation-via-cpuprofiles/)). `papercusp-su` is an **HTTP MCP** (`POST http://localhost:3070/api/mcp`), so when the loop pegs, the MCP route stops being serviced and the client’s transport drops. ## Confirm it in 10 seconds [Section titled “Confirm it in 10 seconds”](#confirm-it-in-10-seconds) 
```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3070/api/health   # 200 = operator process alive
timeout 20 curl -s -X POST 'http://localhost:3070/api/mcp?...' ...           # times out = MCP route wedged
cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg                                               # context: host contention?
```
 `/api/health` **200 but `/api/mcp` times out** is the discriminator: the process is up, the event loop is saturated. (Health is \~2 hops; the MCP route is hop-heavy, so it starves first.) A wedge is single-thread saturation — it does **not** clear when host loadavg drops; it needs the worker to drain its backlog or a coordinated restart. ## The HTTP bridge (reach the operator without the MCP client) [Section titled “The HTTP bridge (reach the operator without the MCP client)”](#the-http-bridge-reach-the-operator-without-the-mcp-client) The MCP client is dead, but the HTTP endpoint it spoke to is still there. Your `papercusp-su` config in `~/.claude.json` has the URL + a superuser bearer token — POST JSON-RPC `tools/call` directly. **Use YOUR OWN session SID as `client=`** or you impersonate another agent and corrupt coordination (claims, messages, intent). 
```bash
SID="su-<your-own-session-id>"   # NOT another agent's
URL="http://localhost:3070/api/mcp?superuser=1&client=$SID&workspace=papercusp-workspace&profile="
curl -sS -m 60 -X POST "$URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token-from-your-own-config>" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"coord:whoami","arguments":{}}}'
```
 The response is SSE (`data:` lines); take the line with `result`/`error` and read `result.content[].text`. Tool names use the **colon** form (`coord:send`, `plans:set-status`, `work_items:create`), not the `mcp__papercusp-su__` form. DO NOT retry-storm the wedged route The wedge is **demand-driven**. When N stranded agents each fire retrying curls at the saturated `/api/mcp`, they ARE the load keeping it pegged — a thundering herd on a degraded service (the round-4 poll-storm dynamic, live). Restarting “barely helps” for the same reason: fresh workers re-peg in 40–70s under the reconnect storm (round-4 D-005). **Back off.** Fire ONE light probe per cycle to detect recovery; do your real writes in a SINGLE batched script the instant a window opens. Adding retries trades your own throughput for everyone’s. ## What to do while stranded (auto-mode) [Section titled “What to do while stranded (auto-mode)”](#what-to-do-while-stranded-auto-mode) 1. **Back off** the operator (one probe per tick, not a retry loop). 2. **Stage, don’t spray.** Write a single `flush.sh` that fires your critical writes in priority order (re-`declare-intent`, file work-items, sync plan status) so one execution lands everything when a window opens. Partial-success-safe + re-runnable. 3. **Keep doing operator-free work** — anything that commits via git-sync (code fixes verified under a package’s own tsconfig, docs, analysis) needs no MCP. Record findings to a local handoff note to replay through the bridge later. 4. **Don’t** solo-ship auth-critical or high-blast-radius changes you can’t verify while the operator is down (you can’t test, and you can’t be told if you broke it), and **don’t** restart `:3070` if it’s another lane’s responsibility. ## The underlying gap [Section titled “The underlying gap”](#the-underlying-gap) A server-side recovery does not heal the client: the MCP transport needs **client-side auto-reconnect with backoff + a periodic deferred-tools re-probe**, plus a degraded-MCP signal, so a transient operator wedge doesn’t strand an agent for hours. Until that lands, this bridge is the manual workaround.

# ≥3-Swarm decentralized claim-dispatch E2E — the harness, the PG-less seam, and the kill timing

> How the P-013 ≥3-Swarm work-item-claim E2E is built and run: each Swarm is a claim-agent.ts process exercising the REAL authority election + HTTP RPC + fail-open + reconcile, with only the claim STORE swapped for an in-memory one (the frames are PG-less) — parity-proven vs the SQL store. Plus the two gotchas that make or break a real run: the Hetzner 2-server account limit (→ 3 Swarms over 2 frames, authority isolated) and why the authority-kill must be progress-gated, not a fixed delay.

P-013 of [`decentralized-dispatch-scaling-2026-06-08`](/internal/docs/plans) asks for the one thing the unit/integration layers can’t give: **≥3 real Swarms, across instances, each claiming DIFFERENT items off one Hive backlog with no central dispatcher; kill the authority mid-run → fail-open reconcile; assert no double-completed work + no starvation.** This is the harness that proves it, and the two non-obvious things that decide whether a real run passes. ## The shape — reuse su-116e7’s Hetzner harness, add a claim scenario [Section titled “The shape — reuse su-116e7’s Hetzner harness, add a claim scenario”](#the-shape--reuse-su-116e7s-hetzner-harness-add-a-claim-scenario) The federation harness (`p2p-perf-tier3` + `hive-cross-machine.integration.test.ts`) already provisions real frames and ships the runtime. The claim E2E plugs into it: * **`claim-agent.ts`** — ONE Swarm as an OS process (the claim analog of `sync/hyperbee/perf/peer-child.ts`). It runs the **real** decentralized-claim machinery: `routeToAuthorityForHive` (argmin-device-pubkey election over an injected Hive presence roster), the real `HttpPeerRpcTransport` → `POST /api/authority/rpc` → `handleAuthorityRpc` (it serves that endpoint for ops routed to it when elected authority), fail-open on an unreachable authority, and a work-stealing claim loop. * **`claim-launcher.ts`** — `localClaimLauncher` (N child processes on loopback, the $0 path) and `sshClaimLauncher` (agents on real frames). A **slot** list, not a frame list, so you can place ≥3 Swarms across fewer frames (see the limit gotcha). * **`run-claim-dispatch.ts`** — the transport-agnostic orchestrator: build the roster, launch, `go`, kill the authority, collect completions, `reconcileAll`, and compute the verdict (no-starvation / no-double-complete-after-reconcile / determinism / exactly-once). * **`swarm-claim-dispatch.integration.test.ts`** — the $0 local-parity run (always) + the cred-gated real-Hetzner run. ## Gotcha 1 — the bench frame is PG-less; use the in-memory store via the seam [Section titled “Gotcha 1 — the bench frame is PG-less; use the in-memory store via the seam”](#gotcha-1--the-bench-frame-is-pg-less-use-the-in-memory-store-via-the-seam) A `p2p-perf-tier3` bench frame deliberately runs only `node --import tsx` against the hyperbee substrate — **there is no Postgres on it** (`bench-bootstrap.ts` emits no embedded-pg; the runtime-pack test even asserts the script never contains `embedded-pg`). The SQL claim store (`work-item-claims.ts`) needs `getOrgPg()`, so it cannot run there. The claim store is reached only through the `WorkItemClaimCoordinator` **seam** (`work-item-claim-authority-ops.ts`, whose own header says “tests inject a fake (or a real-PG-backed) coordinator”) plus the authority op’s `local` leg. So the agent binds an **`InMemoryWorkItemClaimStore`** (`work-item-claim-mem-store.ts`) through that seam. Only the *persistence* leg is swapped; the election, RPC, fail-open, and reconcile all run for real cross-machine. Don't let the in-memory store drift The in-memory store’s lease semantics (free-grant / steal-lapsed / extend-own / conflict-on-live; owner+claim\_id-checked heartbeat & release) are pinned identical to the SQL store by `work-item-claim-mem-store.integration.test.ts`, which runs the SAME sequences against BOTH and compares the decisions. The SQL store’s own authority-fronted serialization stays proven on real PG by `work-item-claims-two-instance.integration.test.ts` (N=2) + `work-item-claim-reconcile.integration.test.ts`. In-mem-on-frames + that coverage * the parity test = full picture, zero per-frame PG provisioning. Importing `work-item-claims.ts` transitively imports `@papercusp/db-org`, but that import is side-effect-free (the org PG client is lazy) — the agent boots fine on a PG-less frame. The local-parity child boots the SAME import chain, so it’s the canary: if it boots, the frame will too. ## Gotcha 2 — the authority-kill must be PROGRESS-GATED, not a fixed delay [Section titled “Gotcha 2 — the authority-kill must be PROGRESS-GATED, not a fixed delay”](#gotcha-2--the-authority-kill-must-be-progress-gated-not-a-fixed-delay) The first instinct — `sleep(killAfterMs); kill()` — is **fragile and was wrong**. A fixed 4 s delay let the authority complete its whole fair share and then die *late*; because a killed agent’s result is discarded, those items showed up as **starved**, and the survivors had already quiet-broken before the kill so they **never failed open** (`failOpen:0`, 6 items starved — observed live on the first real run). The fix: the orchestrator waits for the **authority to report ≥2 completions** (the agent emits a progress line on every completion) and kills *then*. The kill reliably lands while the survivors are still claiming — so they fail open and, because their own stores are empty for the authority’s items, they reclaim the WHOLE backlog (no starvation), with the expected tolerated double-claims that `reconcileAll` resolves to one deterministic winner. A `killAfterMs` cap remains only as a fallback. Lesson: **gate a mid-run kill on an observed progress signal, never on wall-clock — machine speed varies and you’ll race the work loop.** ## Gotcha 3 — the Hetzner account caps at 2 servers → 3 Swarms over 2 frames [Section titled “Gotcha 3 — the Hetzner account caps at 2 servers → 3 Swarms over 2 frames”](#gotcha-3--the-hetzner-account-caps-at-2-servers--3-swarms-over-2-frames) This account’s Hetzner Cloud **server limit is 2** (`createServer` 403 `resource_limit_exceeded` on the 3rd). “≥3 Swarms across instances” is still satisfied by placing the **authority alone on frame 0** and the **two survivors on frame 1** (distinct ports; the agent’s port is an argv marker so `pkill -f 'claim-agent.ts <port>'` kills exactly one co-located agent). Killing frame 0’s agent partitions the survivors from the authority across a real machine boundary — every cross-machine dynamic P-013 wants. Raise `CLAIM_E2E_FRAMES` (after raising the account limit) and the placement degrades to one Swarm per distinct VM automatically. ## How to run it [Section titled “How to run it”](#how-to-run-it) 
```bash
# $0 local parity (always runs, no creds):
cd packages/operator-core
npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts \
  lib/deployment/swarm-claim-dispatch.integration.test.ts -t "local parity"


# Paid real-Hetzner run (≥3 Swarms over real frames; ~8 min, well under $0.50; DESTROYS always):
export HCLOUD_TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/hcloud-token)
export HETZNER_SSH_KEY_ID=113417406
export HETZNER_SSH_IDENTITY_FILE=$HOME/.ssh/papercusp-latitude-frame
export HETZNER_E2E_SERVER_TYPE=cpx31
npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts \
  lib/deployment/swarm-claim-dispatch.integration.test.ts -t "REAL Hetzner"
# ALWAYS verify 0 leaked VMs after:
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $HCLOUD_TOKEN" https://api.hetzner.cloud/v1/servers
```
 The creds live where the federation harness’s do — see [`hetzner-cross-machine-federation-harness`](/internal/docs/agent-insights) (the memory) / `p2p-performance-suite`. `provisionBenchFleet` sweeps leftover frames at start and `teardownAll()` runs in a `finally` (it fires on assertion failure too), so a failed run still cleans up — but verify anyway. ## Proven [Section titled “Proven”](#proven) * **$0 local parity** — 3 Swarms, real loopback HTTP authority RPC: no-kill ⇒ exactly-once (zero double-claims, no starvation, no fail-open); kill-authority ⇒ fail-open observed, deterministic reconcile, no starvation, no surviving double-completion. * **Real Hetzner (paid, 2026-06-09)** — 3 Swarms across 2 cpx31 frames in `ash` (authority isolated on frame 0). The survivors’ claims crossed the real machine boundary to the authority (remote-authority RPCs), the authority was killed mid-run, the survivors failed open, `reconcileAll` resolved every contested item to a single deterministic winner, and the whole backlog was completed (no starvation). **0 leaked VMs** after.

# SwarmBench integration + the gateway's OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions path

> How SwarmBench (decentralized swarm coordination) plugs into external-bench via makePoolBacklogDriver — and the reusable finding that the Max-OAuth gateway exposes an OpenAI chat-completions endpoint, so any OpenAI-SDK harness can drive opus.

Two things the next agent will want — one reusable across suites, one SwarmBench-specific. ## REUSABLE: the gateway speaks OpenAI chat-completions, not just Anthropic [Section titled “REUSABLE: the gateway speaks OpenAI chat-completions, not just Anthropic”](#reusable-the-gateway-speaks-openai-chat-completions-not-just-anthropic) The Max-OAuth gateway (`:8788` / `:8799`, key `sk-papercusp-gateway`) exposes **`POST /v1/chat/completions`** in OpenAI format, in addition to the Anthropic `/v1/messages` path. A probe with the OpenAI shape returns a proper `chat.completion` object (`choices[0].message.content`). So **any harness built on the OpenAI SDK** (`AsyncOpenAI`, litellm’s openai provider, etc. — SwarmBench, tau2, many others) can drive opus by simply pointing its `api_base` at `http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1` and `model` at `claude-opus-4-8`. **No openai→anthropic shim is needed.** The **framing requirement carries over**: the FIRST system message must be the Claude Code identity (`"You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude."`) or you get the bogus `rate_limit_error` regardless of budget (the same Max-OAuth gotcha as the Anthropic path — [max-oauth-first-system-block-must-be-claude-code-identity](/internal/docs/agent-insights/max-oauth-first-system-block-must-be-claude-code-identity)). For an OpenAI-format call, put the identity in (or prepend it to) the `system` role message. `:8799` is the quiet account (often free); `:8788` is the paced one — either works, both honor the framing. **Cost/latency caveat:** an opus call through the gateway inside a multi-round sim is *slow* — a SwarmBench scenario at N agents × R rounds is N×R sequential-ish opus calls and a tiny pilot can take many minutes. Budget generously, run small, and treat full sweeps as owner-gated. ## SwarmBench-specific: how it plugs in [Section titled “SwarmBench-specific: how it plugs in”](#swarmbench-specific-how-it-plugs-in) Vendored at `~/.papercusp/bench-harnesses/swarmbench` (RUC-GSAI/YuLan-SwarmIntell, MIT) with a `.venv` (`numpy<2 scipy colorama pulp openai`). The integration: * **`swarmbench_run.py`** (in the vendored repo) runs ONE scenario to its deterministic sim score and prints a single `SWARMBENCH_RESULT_JSON\n{...}` line. Modes = the swarm-control topology = the ARM: * `random` — no LLM (deterministic; the mechanics spike + unit-test shape). * `openai` — SwarmBench’s NATIVE decentralized flow: each agent an independent OpenAI-compatible call. This is the **`su-independent`** arm (peer self-organization, local view only). * `queen` / `queen-random` — **control-inversion**: a custom loop gathers all agents’ AGGREGATED LOCAL obs (`env.obs(agent)` per agent — NOT `env.obs(None)`, which is the global grid and would *cheat* the local-only premise, D-001) and one coordinator decides all N actions. This is the **`hive-realqueen`** arm. * **`swarmbench-live.ts`** = the `RunSwarmSim` port (shells the python, parses the result; injected exec for tests). **`swarmbench-backlog.ts`** = the driver on the generic `makePoolBacklogDriver` (one scenario = one `perTask` → canonical `HiveBacklogResult`, sim score on `attempt.armMeta`) + `buildSwarmBenchReport` (per-(task,arm) mean±SE + the decentralized-vs-centralized **topology delta**). Same pattern as `metr-hcast-backlog.ts` — see [non-diff-bench-arm-via-pool-backlog-driver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/non-diff-bench-arm-via-pool-backlog-driver). * **Task-set** is programmatic (task × grid × num\_agents × seed × view\_size) — `swarmbench-pilot` (cheap) vs `swarmbench` (the expensive full 5-task × 10-agent × 100-round sweep, gated). Scores are CONTINUOUS, not pass/fail — the headline is the mean score + the arm delta, never a pass-rate. ## Running it: two mandatory robustness fixes + the contention asymmetry [Section titled “Running it: two mandatory robustness fixes + the contention asymmetry”](#running-it-two-mandatory-robustness-fixes--the-contention-asymmetry) Live full-sweep findings (plan D-001) — applicable to ANY in-sim, multi-round opus harness: * **Bound the per-agent retry + add a no-op fallback.** SwarmBench’s upstream `Agent.decision` is `while True: try: to_action(brain.generate()) except: retry` — an UNBOUNDED retry that HANGS the whole sim under gateway rate-limiting. The brain must catch, retry a few times, then return a safe `ACTION: STAY` (degrade, don’t deadlock). * **Lower the OpenAI client call timeout.** `framework/llm.py` hardcodes `timeout=3600` — a non-responsive (saturated) gateway then hangs *one hour per call*, stalling the sim. Set \~90s so a hung call fails fast → retry → STAY → the round proceeds. * **The decentralized arm is gateway-starved under fleet contention.** The `su-independent` arm fires **N concurrent calls/round** (10 agents × 100 rounds); against a gateway the SWE-Pro xbench fleet has saturated, rounds stall and it banks \~0 real scenarios while flooding the shared gateway. The `hive` queen (**1 aggregated-local call/round**) is gateway-efficient and completed 15/15 with real data. **So run the call-heavy decentralized arm in a QUIET gateway window (low fleet load), not concurrently with the fleet.** This is an infra asymmetry (centralized = fewer calls = robust to shared rate limits), not a SwarmBench-intrinsic result — label it as such. Queen-arm scores from the real run: Flocking 5.0±0.58 (genuine coordination), Pursuit 0.67, Foraging/Synchronization/Transport 0. ## The honest framing (don’t skip) [Section titled “The honest framing (don’t skip)”](#the-honest-framing-dont-skip) SwarmBench is coordination-NATIVE (the score *is* collaboration quality; a single agent can’t shortcut it) and unsaturated — so it’s the right suite to demo multi-agent value, unlike metr-hcast (which opus-4.8 saturated). But the “hive” arm is a SwarmBench-specific aggregated-local coordinator, **not** the production Queen-over-backlog (D-005). Report it as a coordination-topology A/B on opus-4.8 — *does centralizing decentralized-local info beat peer self-organization* — not as “our production Queen ran SwarmBench”. Plan: `benchmark-suite-swarmbench-2026-06-17`.

# notifySyncInvalidate's 90-second dedupe window

> Identical (name, args) notifies fired within 90s are silently suppressed at the source. Per-tick / heartbeat notifies will surprise you. Carry distinguishing args or data to bypass.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args?, data?)` has a **90-second source-side dedupe window**. Two notifies with identical `(name, args, data)` fired within that window: the second one is silently dropped before `pg_notify` runs. The dedupe now lives in the **generic** invalidation bus (`libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts`, `@papercusp/sync/server`), not in the operator’s `sync-sse.ts`. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` is now a thin wrapper that injects the operator’s PG transport into `createInvalidationBus()` and re-exports `notifySyncInvalidate` (= `bus.notifyInvalidate`) unchanged — the path moved from `apps/operator/lib/sync-sse.ts` → `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` and the mechanism was generalized, but the contract is identical. The constant: 
```ts
const DEFAULT_DEDUPE_WINDOW_MS = 90_000;  // 90 seconds (opts.dedupeWindowMs override)
```
 This sits IN the producer, before the channel write. SSE subscribers never see the dropped event. There’s no log line; the suppression is intentional. ## Why it exists [Section titled “Why it exists”](#why-it-exists) The 60-second `harness-fs-watcher` reconcile sweep upserts every (slug, panel) row every minute even when nothing changed. Without this guard, the operator fires \~80 no-op notifies per minute and the dashboard’s panels refetch in lockstep, which renders as constant flicker. The window is sized just over the reconcile interval so a *real* per-minute change still gets through (the preceding no-op notify falls out of the dedupe map by then). ## When this is a footgun [Section titled “When this is a footgun”](#when-this-is-a-footgun) You add a new heartbeat / per-tick notify expecting clients to refetch every tick: 
```ts
// every 5 seconds (this is wrong):
setInterval(() => {
  void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.recent').catch(() => {});
}, 5_000);
```
 Result: clients refetch ONCE, then nothing for 90 seconds. The 17 dropped notifies in between go nowhere. You spend an hour wondering why the UI is stale. ## How to bypass the dedupe (when you actually want every notify) [Section titled “How to bypass the dedupe (when you actually want every notify)”](#how-to-bypass-the-dedupe-when-you-actually-want-every-notify) The dedupe key hashes `(name, args, data)`. Vary any of them per call: 
```ts
// Option 1: include the timestamp in args
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.heartbeat', { ts: Date.now() });


// Option 2: include a sequence number
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.heartbeat', { seq: ++heartbeatSeq });


// Option 3: carry the actual data payload (data-bearing notifies
// hash the data into the dedupe key, so a NEW row set passes
// through naturally)
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.recent', undefined, latestRows);
```
 For data-bearing notifies the dedupe documentation says: > Notifies with a `data` payload are never dedupe’d — they carry actual content and the receiver acts on them, not just refetches. That’s not quite right: data-bearing notifies ARE dedupe’d, but the data hash is in the key, so a different payload bypasses. Identical payloads (rare but possible) still dedupe. ## How the dedupe map lives [Section titled “How the dedupe map lives”](#how-the-dedupe-map-lives) 
```ts
const recentNotifies = new Map<string, number>();
```
 **Update (post-generalization):** the dedupe map is now a plain module-scoped `Map` captured in the `createInvalidationBus()` closure (`libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts`). It is **no longer pinned to `globalThis.__syncNotifyDedupe`** — that idiom existed to survive Turbopack/Next HMR, and the operator no longer runs the bus inside the Next dev request path (operator is a Vite SPA + Hono host; the Hono host runs under `tsx` with no HMR). The bus is a single long-lived instance created once at module load, so a closure Map is sufficient. (A stale `delete globalThis.__syncNotifyDedupe` line still lingers in `sync-sse.test.ts` cleanup but is a no-op against the closure Map.) `ensure-schema.ts` — the other place this idiom was used — has since been removed entirely (schema is migrations-only now). ## The PG-trigger producer (P-018) does NOT use this dedupe [Section titled “The PG-trigger producer (P-018) does NOT use this dedupe”](#the-pg-trigger-producer-p-018-does-not-use-this-dedupe) The PG trigger `emit_change_notify` writes to the same `sync_invalidate` channel but **does not** go through `notifySyncInvalidate`. It calls `pg_notify` directly from the trigger function. So the 90s dedupe applies only to app-code notifies. This is fine in practice: the trigger fires on real PG writes, not on heartbeats. If an app write triggers the PG row update AND calls `notifySyncInvalidate`, the trigger fires first (synchronous inside the txn), the app-code notify second; identical (name, args) collisions get caught by the consumer-side `last-event-id` semantics * the listener’s own internal handling. ## Capacity [Section titled “Capacity”](#capacity) `recentNotifies` is bounded — when it exceeds 200 entries, `pruneNotifyCache` walks the map and drops entries older than the 90s window. Cheap GC; no unbounded growth on long-lived processes. 200 is sized for \~one notify per (panel, slug, phase) across registered harnesses. If you blow past it you’re probably also hitting other problems. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — operator wiring; `libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts` — the dedupe/bus implementation * [Adding a reactive table](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-reactive-table) — when to use `notifySyncInvalidate` vs the PG trigger * [Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) — the consumer side * [Sleep-mode shared-checkout discipline](/internal/docs/agent-insights/sleep-mode-shared-checkout) — companion ops doc

# useSyncMutate optimism is WebSocket/Zero-only — inert on the SSE desktop

> @papercusp/sync's useSyncMutate applies optimistically only through the Zero client, which exists only on the WebSocket transport. Zero is retired and the desktop ships on SSE, so useSyncMutate degrades to the plain REST fallback there — no optimistic apply. Hand-roll optimism in the hook (apply → reconcile → rollback).

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `@papercusp/sync` exposes an eager-mutation seam — `useSyncMutate(path, restFallback)` (`libs/generic/sync/src/SyncContext.ts`). Its docstring promises that the mutator “runs OPTIMISTICALLY through the Zero client (instant local apply, then server reconcile / rollback).” That is true **only on the WebSocket transport**, where a Zero client exists: 
```ts
// SyncContext.ts — resolveMutator returns the Zero custom-mutator if one is
// registered; otherwise the call takes restFallback (a plain fetch).
const fn = resolveMutator(mutate, path);
if (fn) return (await fn(args)) as R;   // optimistic — WS/Zero only
return restFallback(args);              // REST — every other transport
```
 Two facts make that optimistic path **dead on the shipping target**: 1. **Zero is retired** (`CLAUDE.md`, `libs/zero-harness`). No new Zero mutators are registered, so `resolveMutator` returns `null`. 2. **The desktop ships on SSE**, not WebSocket — browser WS is a dev fallback (`apps/operator/providers/HarnessSyncProvider.tsx`). With no Zero client, `useSyncMutate` deterministically takes `restFallback`. So on the desktop, `useSyncMutate` is **behaviour-identical to a bare `fetch`** — the write round-trips and the UI only updates when the server’s `notifySyncInvalidate` pushes the new rows back over SSE. There is no free optimistic apply. ## Why it bites [Section titled “Why it bites”](#why-it-bites) A mutation wired through `useSyncMutate` (or a raw POST) **feels laggy**: the control doesn’t reflect the change until the round-trip completes. This reads as “is it polling?” — it isn’t; it’s just the absence of optimism. Reaching for `useSyncMutate` “to get optimism for free” does **not** fix it on the desktop. ## Fix — hand-roll optimism in the hook [Section titled “Fix — hand-roll optimism in the hook”](#fix--hand-roll-optimism-in-the-hook) Apply the predicted state locally for instant feedback, then reconcile with the server’s authoritative response (or roll back on failure). The SSE invalidation still refreshes any derived data afterward. 
```ts
const prev = state;
if (optimistic) setState(optimistic);          // instant
try {
  const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body });
  const j = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok || !j.ok) throw new Error(j.error);
  setState(j.value ?? fallback);                // reconcile with server truth
} catch (e) {
  if (optimistic) setState(prev);               // roll back
  toast.error(...);
}
```
 Reference implementation: `apps/operator-vite/src/components/adv/use-account-override.ts` (the owner’s session-now Force/Exclude account override — the levers flip instantly, reconcile on the POST response, roll back on error). Pin it with a tiny render-a-harness test that holds the POST open to observe the optimistic window and asserts rollback on failure (`use-account-override.test.tsx`). A real “library-level optimism on the post-Zero transports” layer would be its own project; until then, optimism is the call site’s job.

# A best-effort sync resolver over a raw-SQL table must degrade SILENTLY on a missing table

> A console.warn in a resolver's catch trips vitest-fail-on-console in the structural "every registered name dispatches" test — because that test runs the GENERATED schema, which lacks raw-SQL tables that only boot-apply via migration. Suppress the expected 42P01.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) If you add a **best-effort** `useSyncQuery` resolver (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`) that reads a table which is **not in the generated drizzle schema** — i.e. a table that lives in raw SQL and only exists after its migration boot-applies (the gym/apiary/hive-eval-style sibling slices) — do **not** `console.warn` in the catch on the missing-table case. A warn there reddens the green gate. ## Why it bites [Section titled “Why it bites”](#why-it-bites) The sync-resolver has a structural unit test, `index.test.ts` → *“every registered name dispatches without TypeError”*, that resolves **every** registered query name. It runs against the **generated schema** (the drizzle/`pull-schema` output), which does **not** include raw-SQL tables that boot-apply via migration. So your resolver’s read throws `42P01 undefined_table`, your catch `console.warn`s, and `vitest-fail-on-console` turns that warn into a test failure → operator-core red → the whole fleet’s deploy is blocked. The trap is subtle because the obvious sibling to copy — `learning.apiary` — *also* `console.warn`s in its catch and is green. The difference is only that `beekeeper_instances` **is** in the generated schema, so apiary’s read succeeds (returns `[]`) and never warns. A brand-new raw-SQL table is not in the schema, so yours throws and warns.
