# Architecture

> How a production Papercusp binary is laid out, what it spawns at startup, and how the browser webview finds the operator server.

## Two repos, two stages [Section titled “Two repos, two stages”](#two-repos-two-stages) 
```plaintext
~/papercupai-workspace/
├── papercup/                 ← the operator (Vite SPA + Hono host + libs)
│   ├── apps/operator-vite/   ← @papercusp/operator-vite — the TanStack-Router SPA UI (:3055 dev)
│   └── apps/operator/        ← @papercusp/web — the Hono host (bin/hono-host.ts, :3070), serve entry (bin/serve.ts), + lib/app page bodies
└── papercusp-desktop/        ← the Tauri shell (Rust)
    └── src-tauri/            ← main.rs + tauri.conf.json — produces the .deb/.dmg/.msi
```
 `papercusp-desktop` is the wrapper. It bundles the operator as a single esbuild-bundled `serve.mjs` **sidecar** (built by `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` into `src-tauri/sidecar/`) and ships the Rust binary + sidecar in one installer. Per plan `operator-core-headless-serve-2026-06-04`, the desktop is an **embedder of `papercusp serve`**: `serve.mjs` owns the whole operator lifecycle (embedded Postgres, migrations, the Hono host, the discovery files); Rust just spawns it and points the webview at it. ## What a Tauri production build does at startup [Section titled “What a Tauri production build does at startup”](#what-a-tauri-production-build-does-at-startup) `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` `setup()` (production branch): 1. **Pick a free port hint** (e.g. `19210`) and a separate PG port hint — these are cold-start *hints*; the real ports are resolved later from discovery. 2. **Spawn `code-server`** (the bundled VS Code for the web) on a free port, and surface its URL to the sidecar via `PAPERCUSP_CODE_SERVER_URL`. (Debug builds also start an MCP bridge plugin bound to `127.0.0.1`.) 3. **Spawn the `serve.mjs --ensure` sidecar** as one child process. `serve` then owns everything PG/operator: it starts real embedded PostgreSQL (`wal_level=logical`) on its own free port, runs migrations, writes `~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json`, runs `runBootstrap()` (which starts the endpoint-IPC server + writes `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json`), and starts the Hono host bound to `127.0.0.1:<port>`. `--ensure` reuses an already-healthy operator under the same HOME instead of double-booting. 4. **Poll `~/.papercusp/operator.json`** (`wait_for_operator`, up to 120s for a first boot that pays `initdb` + full migration replay) until the pid is alive **and** the port accepts TCP. The **real** port comes from this file — `--ensure` reuse may land on a different port than the cold-start hint. 5. **`eval()` an init script into the webview** setting `window.__papercuspBase` / `window.__papercuspAppBase` / `window.__PAPERCUSP_TAURI__` and dispatching a `papercusp:base` event. The webview opens on the bootstrap page (`papercusp-desktop/web/index.html`, referenced by `main.rs`) that: 1. Waits for `window.__papercuspBase` (re-applied if the page-load drops it) 2. Polls `<base>/api/desktop/preflight` until ready 3. Navigates to the real operator UI (`tauri.conf.json`’s `frontendDist` is `http://127.0.0.1:3070` — the initial document the packaged build loads, which nothing serves on a user machine; `main.rs` navigates the window to the app origin immediately, and pre-discovery the custom-protocol handler serves the bundled SPA statics until `serve` is healthy. `frontendDist` is **not** a `../web` path.) With the `papercusp://` **custom protocol** on (default, shipped 2026-06-01), the real app loads from `papercusp://localhost/…` (forwarded to the loopback sidecar), so the webview opens **zero** HTTP connections. With `PAPERCUSP_DESKTOP_CUSTOM_PROTOCOL=0` it falls back to the HTTP `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` origin. Either way, `/api` fetches + EventSource ride **endpoint-IPC** (resolved from `endpoint-ipc.json`) to escape libsoup’s 6-socket pool, falling back to HTTP if the socket isn’t up. Tauri’s IPC (`invoke()`) works alongside because the page is in a Tauri webview. ## What dev mode does instead [Section titled “What dev mode does instead”](#what-dev-mode-does-instead) A debug build (`cfg!(debug_assertions) == true`) makes `main.rs` `setup()`: 1. **Skip the `serve.mjs` spawn entirely** — the developer is expected to run the operator dev stack separately. `beforeDevCommand` brings up this session’s **own working-tree Hono host** on `:3270` (see below); it does **not** start the Vite SPA, and it does **not** touch `:3070` (owned by the systemd green-release operator). 2. **Start the tauri-agent-tools dev bridge** (debug-only, localhost-only, token-authenticated) and, on Linux, auto-grant `getUserMedia` 3. **Open devtools automatically** (WebKitGTK doesn’t reliably wire Ctrl+Shift+I) 4. Webview loads the `devUrl` from `tauri.conf.json` (`http://127.0.0.1:3270`); `/api` fetches ride endpoint-IPC re-read from `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json` (written by the externally-run operator), with graceful HTTP fallback while it’s down ### Two dev modes: `npm run dev` (default, nohmr) vs `npm run dev:hmr` [Section titled “Two dev modes: npm run dev (default, nohmr) vs npm run dev:hmr”](#two-dev-modes-npm-run-dev-default-nohmr-vs-npm-run-devhmr) The **default** `npm run dev` is `bin/desktop-dev-nohmr`: it overrides `devUrl` to `http://127.0.0.1:3270` and pins `PAPERCUSP_DEV_API_TARGET=3270`, pointing the webview at this session’s own working-tree Hono host (a static SPA bundle, **no** HMR socket). nohmr is the default deliberately — this checkout is edited by a fleet of agents at once, and a Vite HMR server would reload the webview on every fleet edit / dep re-optimization (the “window constantly refreshes” problem), plus its `ws://localhost:3055/?token=…` HMR socket competes with SSE for libsoup’s 6-connection budget. The cost is a manual reload (Cmd-R / Ctrl-R) to pick up new work. `npm run dev:hmr` is the explicit opt-in: it overrides `devUrl` to `http://localhost:3055`, the bare Vite HMR server (which has **no** operator of its own — its `/api` proxies to the green operator on `:3070`). So a default dev Tauri window is a Tauri webview pointed at the working-tree Hono host on `:3270`; only `dev:hmr` points it at the live Vite dev server on `:3055`. Production is the same UI code but served from the bundled sidecar on a private port. (`papercusp-desktop`’s `beforeDevCommand` runs `bin/dev-operator-ifneeded.sh`, which starts **only** the working-tree Hono host — `bin/hono-host.ts` on `:3270`, PTY WS on `:3274` — if it isn’t already up.) ## Where the operator code lives in a prod bundle [Section titled “Where the operator code lives in a prod bundle”](#where-the-operator-code-lives-in-a-prod-bundle) After `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` (which esbuild-bundles the operator into `src-tauri/sidecar/`) followed by `tauri build` (`= npm run build` in `papercusp-desktop/` — note `beforeBuildCommand` is empty, so the sidecar build is a **separate** step): 
```plaintext
/usr/lib/Papercusp/                          # Linux .deb install root
├── papercusp-desktop                        # main Tauri binary
└── sidecar/                                 # bundled as a Tauri resource (sidecar/**/*)
    ├── serve.mjs                            # one esbuild-bundled ESM operator entry — main.rs spawns `node serve.mjs --ensure`
    ├── db-sql/                              # bundled SQL migration files
    ├── node_modules/                        # externalized native deps only (node-pty, @papercusp/embedded-postgres-server + its @embedded-postgres/<plat> binary, …)
    ├── code-server/                         # the bundled code-server
    └── bin/
        ├── node                             # bundled Node v24 runtime (Tauri prepends bin/ to the sidecar's PATH)
        ├── omp
        └── gh
```
 Embedded Postgres is no longer a separate sidecar directory — `serve.mjs` resolves the `@papercusp/embedded-postgres-server` package (with its platform binary) out of `sidecar/node_modules/` and runs PG in-process. `zero-cache` is **not** shipped (the desktop sidecar serves SSE itself; `zero-cache-server` bundling was removed 2026-06-06 per SP1 C5, after the operator’s `/api/zero-harness/sse` PG LISTEN/NOTIFY path had already replaced the Zero WS transport on desktop on 2026-05-07). Mac is the same shape inside `Papercusp.app/Contents/Resources/`. Windows under `C:\Program Files\Papercusp\` (where the sidecar is routed through WSL). ## The bundled Node binary (`bundled_path_env`) [Section titled “The bundled Node binary (bundled\_path\_env)”](#the-bundled-node-binary-bundled_path_env) `main.rs` has a `bundled_path_env()` helper that builds a `PATH` with the shipped `sidecar/bin/` directory (containing `node`, `omp`, `gh`) prepended. **Every node-based spawn runs through it** rather than relying on `which node`, because GUI-launched apps inherit `$PATH = /usr/bin:/bin` on macOS — Homebrew’s `node`, `nvm` Node, etc. won’t be visible. Without this, the packaged process can’t find `node` at all (the Linux clean-room test VM caught exactly this — see [VMs](/internal/docs/build-system/vms)), and `pg_dump`/`libpq` discovery would break on Mac. ## The embedded-PG discovery file [Section titled “The embedded-PG discovery file”](#the-embedded-pg-discovery-file) On boot, **`serve.mjs`** (not `main.rs` anymore) writes `~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json`. The actual shape is a single `url` field (the admin URL) plus diagnostics — there is **no** separate `adminUrl`/`appUrl`, and `startedAt` is epoch milliseconds (`Date.now()`), not an ISO string: 
```json
{
  "url": "postgresql://harness_admin:...@127.0.0.1:20721/papercusp",
  "port": 20721,
  "pid": 877130,
  "startedAt": 1747140960000
}
```
 The generic resolver reads the `url` field (the admin URL); the other fields are diagnostics. It also writes `~/.papercusp/operator.json` (the Hono host pid + port that `main.rs` polls) and `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json` (the IPC socket path). Three rules: * The operator reads PG discovery via `getHarnessAdminUrl()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/embedded-pg-discovery.ts`. **Never hard-code `:5432` or `:16534` anywhere** — always resolve through this helper. The central connection resolver in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/connection.ts` already does this; new code should call the helper. * The discovery files are **owned by `serve`**: it writes them atomically on boot and removes `operator.json`/`embedded-pg.json` on the way down. `serve --ensure` also makes same-HOME double-launches converge on one operator rather than fighting over the file. * Native PG (`:5432`) is for Restart / paperclip / marketplace **and** is what this dev box’s operator runs against (`apps/operator/.env.local` pins a `:5432/papercusp` `DATABASE_URL`). The **ship** target is embedded-pg, but on the standing dev box there is **no** `papercusp_legacy`/`papercusp_native_backup` rename — `papercusp` on `:5432` is alive and in use. Code must keep working under embedded-pg regardless, so resolve through `getHarnessAdminUrl()` rather than assuming either topology. ## What gets *built* vs. what gets *shipped* [Section titled “What gets built vs. what gets shipped”](#what-gets-built-vs-what-gets-shipped) * **Built** but **not shipped**: the Vite SPA’s intermediate output, `target/debug/`, `node_modules/.cache/`. The auditor (`papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh`) scans the *installer* contents, not the build directory. * **Built and shipped** but **not loaded at runtime in prod**: `web/index.html` only runs during the brief bootstrap; `tauri.conf.json`’s `devUrl` is dev-only and never read in a release binary. * **Built and shipped and active**: everything under `sidecar/`. `serve.mjs` is spawned at boot (and owns embedded PG in-process); `code-server` is spawned alongside it; both run for the lifetime of the Tauri window. ## A note on Linux WebKit quirks [Section titled “A note on Linux WebKit quirks”](#a-note-on-linux-webkit-quirks) WebKitGTK is what wry uses on Linux, and it has a few recurring quirks the desktop works around: * **`localhost` vs `127.0.0.1`** — WebKitGTK may resolve `localhost` to `::1` while the sidecar binds IPv4 loopback, which fails the bootstrap’s preflight fetch. `main.rs` deliberately hands the webview a `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` base, not `localhost`. * **libsoup’s 6-socket pool** — the webview’s `/api` fetch + EventSource are routed over endpoint-IPC (Unix socket) instead of HTTP precisely to escape this limit. See the discovery-file handoff above. * **getUserMedia denied by default** — `main.rs` auto-grants media permission on Linux so the operator’s voice / wake-word / ElevenLabs paths work without a `NotAllowedError`. > Historical note: the old “duplicate dashboard” + “access control checks CORS spam” bugs were Next.js-era artifacts (a Next error overlay double-mounting the layout, and wildcard CORS headers in `next.config.js`). Both that machinery and `next.config.js` are gone now that the operator is a Vite SPA served by the Hono host, so those specific fixes no longer apply.

# TypeScript Layers

> The four-layer model — core / host / routes / client — and the inert tsconfig scaffold under apps/operator/layers/ that names them. The scaffold (Phase 6a) was dropped 2026-06-14; the boundary is now enforced physically by the package split.

Status — dropped 2026-06-14 This scaffold (Phase 6a) was **dropped** per owner decision P-004 in [host-architecture-2026-05-20-v2](https://github.com/papercusp/papercusp/blob/main/apps/operator/docs/plans/host-architecture-2026-05-20-v2.md). Next has been removed and `apps/operator/app/api` is empty (zero `route.ts` files, `_hono/` deleted); the client moved to `apps/operator-vite`. The core/host/client boundary is now enforced **physically** by the package split (`tooldef` / `@papercusp/host-platform` / `operator-core` vs `apps`), so the tsconfig-projects layering described below is no longer planned — a `tsc`-projects scaffold would only fight Vite aliasing and duplicate the package boundary. The tsconfigs under `apps/operator/layers/` remain as inert scaffolding, and the route-migration narrative (Phase 4) below was superseded wholesale. Read the rest as design intent, not a live migration path. ## What this is [Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is) The original design split `apps/operator/` into four compile units. Each one is a tsconfig with its own `include` glob, and the layers reference each other in a one-directional dependency graph. The build invariant was: nothing in `core` can import from `host`, `routes`, or `client`; nothing in `host` can import from `routes` or `client`; etc. That invariant is now satisfied by the package split rather than by these tsconfigs (see the status banner). The partition is **scaffolded but empty**. The four layer tsconfigs exist under `apps/operator/layers/` with `include: []`. `tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json` resolves cleanly but checks no files. The original plan was for files to migrate into a layer’s `include` glob as the route-migration work (Phase 4) and the layering-enforcement work (Phase 6b) progressed — but **that migration is no longer expected** (see the status banner above). Phase 4 was superseded, and the layering-scaffold phase (6a) was dropped because the boundary is already enforced by the package split. This was by design — the alternative was to glob up the existing tree and lie about which files belong where. The layers describe a **target** that the package split (`tooldef` / `@papercusp/host-platform` / `operator-core` vs `apps`) now realizes directly, without these include globs ever being populated. ## The four layers [Section titled “The four layers”](#the-four-layers) 
```plaintext
                  ┌─────────┐
                  │  core   │
                  └────┬────┘
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼              ▼             ▼
   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────┐
   │  host   │   │  client  │   │ routes  │
   └────┬────┘   └──────────┘   └────┬────┘
        │                            │
        └────────► routes ◄──────────┘
                  (via host)
```
 ### core [Section titled “core”](#core) **What lives here:** typed business logic with no host coupling. `defineTool` handlers (the host-clean ones), the endpoint system’s pipeline + dispatch stack, schemas, pure helpers, type definitions. **What may be imported:** anything from `libs/*`, `packages/*`, and host-clean third-party packages (`zod`, `date-fns`, `postgres`, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, etc.). **What may NOT be imported:** * `next/*` * `node:fs`, `node:child_process` directly (use `@papercusp/host-platform` instead) * DOM types implicitly * React If you find yourself wanting to reach for `node:fs` in core code, the answer is to take a `HostPlatform` parameter (or call `getHostPlatform()`) — see [host-platform](/internal/docs/build-system/architecture) coverage in the host-platform package source. The `HostPlatform` interface, `getHostPlatform()`, `registerHostPlatform()`, and `desktopHostPlatform` already live in the standalone `@papercusp/host-platform` package (`libs/host-platform/src/`, wired into `apps/operator` as a `file:` dependency), so the host abstraction `core` depends on is a real package boundary today — not a future tsconfig include. That existing physical boundary is precisely why the layer scaffold below was deemed redundant. ### host [Section titled “host”](#host) **What lives here:** host-specific glue that the desktop needs but a future web host might not. `desktopHostPlatform`’s body (which already lives in `libs/host-platform/src/desktop.ts`, not under `apps/operator`), IPC bridge code (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/`), embedded-PG discovery, plugin runtime (`packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts`), FS watchers, background sweepers, socket lifecycle. **What may be imported:** `core`, anything in `libs/*` and `packages/*`, Node stdlib (`node:fs`, `node:child_process`, `node:net`, etc.). **What may NOT be imported:** `next/*` (Next-specific request/response shapes); React. ### routes [Section titled “routes”](#routes) **What lives here:** transport-shaped code — thin shims that map an HTTP request into a `core` or `host` function call. As originally drafted this meant Next route handlers (`app/api/.../route.ts`) and the Hono routers. Neither shape survives in the live tree: Next has been removed, `apps/operator/app/api` is empty (zero `route.ts` files), and `_hono/` was deleted — the Hono routers now live under `apps/operator/bin/` (`host-app.ts`, `hono-host.ts`, etc.), referenced internally by the logical name `_hono/app.ts`. The `~245`-route surface this layer was meant to receive no longer exists. **What may be imported:** `core`, `host`, Hono types (and, when Next was still present, `next/*` request/response shapes). **What may NOT be imported:** React; client-only browser APIs. A handler that holds non-transport state (cookies, cost caps, feature locks, transcript persistence) is A1-class — it stays as a substantive shim and doesn’t migrate to a `defineTool` projection. See [agent-policies §endpoint-system migration](/internal/docs/agent-policies) for the audit axes. ### client [Section titled “client”](#client) **What lives here:** React components, hooks, transport-adapter polyfills (`packages/operator-core/lib/transport-adapters/`), Zero client wiring, client-side state. **What may be imported:** `core`, `react`, `next/link`, `next/navigation` (client APIs), DOM types, browser-only third-party packages. **What may NOT be imported:** * `node:fs`, `node:child_process` (server-only) * `next/headers`, `cookies()` (server-only) * Database clients (`postgres`, drizzle) * Anything in `host` (the client doesn’t run on the host) ## How to run the layered build [Section titled “How to run the layered build”](#how-to-run-the-layered-build) 
```bash
npx tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json
```
 Exit code 0 with no output means all four layers’ include globs resolved + every cross-layer reference is satisfied. Today this trivially succeeds because every `include` is empty. Had files moved in (Phase 4, Phase 6b), the build would have started checking them and a violation — say, a file in `client/include` importing `host/some-thing` — would surface as a `tsc --build` error. That migration was dropped (P-004); the include globs stay empty. ## What this scaffold doesn’t do [Section titled “What this scaffold doesn’t do”](#what-this-scaffold-doesnt-do) * **No enforcement.** Phase 6a (this) shipped the structural slots only. Phase 6b would have added ESLint `no-restricted-imports` rules + dependency-cruiser, gated on Phase 4 disentangling routes from `core` first. Both are moot now — 6a was dropped and 6b never started. * **No code moves.** The four `include` arrays are `[]` and stay that way; the boundary is enforced by the package split instead. * **No replacement of the app tsconfig.** `apps/operator/tsconfig.json` is what the IDE consumes; it’s untouched. The layered build is a parallel surface that runs independently. ## How a file would have been added to a layer [Section titled “How a file would have been added to a layer”](#how-a-file-would-have-been-added-to-a-layer) This was the intended procedure before P-004 dropped the scaffold; it never ran at scale. When a route migration (Phase 4) determined that a handler was host-clean and projectable, the worker would: 1. Move the handler file to its target location (often `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/<feature>/<name>.ts` — that directory is real and now holds the migrated handlers). 2. Add the file’s path to the appropriate layer’s `include` glob in `apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.core.json` (or `host.json`, etc.). 3. Run `tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json` locally; address any reported violations before committing. In practice the handler moves (step 1) happened — `agent-tools/<feature>/<name>.ts` is populated — but the include-glob registration (step 2) never did, because the package split already enforces the boundary that step 3 was meant to catch. ## When this was revisited [Section titled “When this was revisited”](#when-this-was-revisited) The original trigger was: when ≥75% of the `app/api/*/route.ts` files had been audited (the Phase 4 milestone), or when an enforcement violation appeared that the scaffold should have caught. Neither happened on that path — Phase 4 was superseded by the endpoint-unification + hono-elimination arcs (`app/api` is now empty), and on 2026-06-14 the owner dropped Phase 6a outright (P-004). The tsconfigs stay as inert scaffolding. Sister doc: the [host-platform](https://github.com/papercusp/papercusp/tree/main/libs/host-platform) interface that `core` and `host` share, and [agent-policies §endpoint-system migration](/internal/docs/agent-policies) for the per-route audit rules.

# Privacy audit (PostHog leak scanner)

> The V1 ship contract, how bin/audit-bundle.sh enforces it, and how to extend it for future leak categories.

## The V1 contract [Section titled “The V1 contract”](#the-v1-contract) A freshly installed production binary must: 1. Make **zero network requests** to `flags.papercuspai.com` under any usage. 2. Resolve every feature flag to its `FLAG_DEFAULTS` ship value with `source: "defaults"` — i.e. the flag-eval server must not reach out to PostHog. The flag *values* themselves are no longer all-off: under the current **alpha flags-default-ON policy** a clean install serves the bundled defaults, and a large majority of them ship `true` (e.g. `papercusp-the-hive`, `papercusp-video-channels`, `papercusp-voice-channels`). What the contract guarantees is that those values come from the baked-in `FLAG_DEFAULTS` with no network call — not that they are uniformly `false`. The deliberately-off subset (unverified / destructive / security / dark) includes `papercusp-cloudflare-publish`, `papercusp-harness-phases`, `papercusp-design`, `papercusp-testing` (which now also gates the Oracle — the separate `papercusp-oracle` key was folded into it by owner ask 2026-06-10), `papercusp-improvement-auto-implement`, and `papercusp-inbox-durable-escalations`. (There is no `papercusp-snapshots` flag — SNAPSHOTS was retired in `retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`; the reproducible clone is now the ungated `InstanceSpec`.) Both must hold without anyone configuring anything post-install. ## How the system already enforces it [Section titled “How the system already enforces it”](#how-the-system-already-enforces-it) `packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-config.ts` resolves the active PostHog configuration in this priority order: 1. **Env vars** — `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_HOST`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_PERSONAL_KEY`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_TESTING_FEATURES` 2. **Discovery file** — `~/.papercusp/posthog.json`. The personal API key is read from the `personalApiKey` field *inside that one file*; there is no separate `posthog-personal.json` discovery file (any prose mention of one is stale). 3. **Default** — testing-features disabled → the `/api/flags/bootstrap` layer returns `source: "defaults"` `packages/operator-core/lib/flag-bus.ts` only initializes the PostHog client when `isTestingFeaturesEnabled() === true`. So on a clean install (no env vars, no discovery files), the PostHog SDK never starts for the **flag-eval path**. **Zero flag-network requests by construction.** ### Two-track design [Section titled “Two-track design”](#two-track-design) Privacy reasoning here has to separate two PostHog consumers: * **Server-side flag evaluation** (`posthog-config.ts` / `flag-bus.ts`) stays `unconfigured` / `null` on a clean install — no SDK, zero outbound flag requests, every flag served from the bundled `FLAG_DEFAULTS`. * **Browser telemetry** (`telemetry-flush.ts`, the desktop `telemetry-config` route) consumes the **bundled public defaults** (`POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS` — see below), so a user’s opt-in *alone* enables forwarding. It only fires after explicit opt-in (default off). `libs/flags/src/types.ts` exports `FLAG_DEFAULTS`, baked into the bundle. Under the alpha **flags-default-ON** policy most flags default `true`; only a deliberate subset (unverified / destructive / security / dark) defaults `false`. On a clean install these baked values are exactly what’s returned — the privacy guarantee is the *absence of a flag-network call*, not a uniform-off value set. ### Bundled public PostHog defaults [Section titled “Bundled public PostHog defaults”](#bundled-public-posthog-defaults) Every public build also bundles `POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS` (`packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-public-defaults.ts`): the public `host` (`https://flags.papercuspai.com`) and an anonymous-capture `phc_` projectKey (`phc_tnwKu5QTgaHi6hyrHwA3EUQFKhskJES4c4zAzHCUrPFv`). This is a deliberate loosening of the original “zero PostHog references in the artifact” V1 contract (`mac-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11` D-010): the key is a read-only/anonymous-capture client credential (it cannot read events or mutate flag definitions), shipped so a user’s opt-in is the only step needed to forward telemetry — no “drop a JSON file” dance. The write-side keys (`personalApiKey`, `webhookSecret`) are *never* bundled. Because that one public key now legitimately appears in every artifact, the auditor was patched to mask it before scanning (see below). ## What the auditor scans for [Section titled “What the auditor scans for”](#what-the-auditor-scans-for) `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh` **FAILs** an artifact only if it contains a real PostHog secret — a `phx_` or `phc_` key followed by 30+ alphanumeric/underscore chars: 
```plaintext
phx_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}
phc_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}
```
 These are `REGEX_NEEDLES`. Placeholders like `phx_xxx` or path/prose references (`posthog.json`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY`) deliberately do **not** match — earlier versions used those literal strings as needles and false-positived on source/docs/code, so the literal `NEEDLES` array is now empty. **The one allowed exception:** the bundled public projectKey (`POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS.projectKey`, kept in the script as `PUBLIC_PROJECT_KEY` and synced to `posthog-public-defaults.ts`) is `sed`-masked out of every candidate file *before* the regex runs. A file whose only `phc_`/`phx_` match is that public key therefore does **not** fail; any **other** `phc_`/`phx_` key — especially a write-side `phx_` personal key — still FAILs. So the contract the auditor now enforces is “no PostHog secret *other than* the deliberately-public anonymous-capture key.” It also has **soft `WARN_NEEDLES`** that surface (but do *not* fail) when the browser SDK is in the bundle: 
```plaintext
node_modules/posthog-js/
posthog-js@
```
 `posthog-js` is dynamic-imported only when the user opts into telemetry (default off), so its presence isn’t a leak per se — but a hostile fork could strip the opt-in gate, so it’s worth flagging. WARN, not FAIL. Documentation paths (`content/docs`, any `/docs/` path segment, `*.mdx`, `*.md`, `*.rsc`, prerendered `app/docs/*.html`) are excluded from the FAIL scan via an `exclude_re` so legitimate prose mentions of the needles don’t trip it. ## Supported artifact formats [Section titled “Supported artifact formats”](#supported-artifact-formats) 
```plaintext
.deb         → dpkg-deb -x
.rpm         → rpm2cpio | cpio -idm  (falls back to 7z)
.dmg         → hdiutil attach  (on Linux: 7z)
.msi         → 7z x
.exe (NSIS)  → 7z x
.AppImage    → ./Artifact --appimage-extract
directory    → copied + scanned in place (useful for an unpacked Papercusp.app or the sidecar/ dir)
```
 If `7z` (or `hdiutil`/`rpm2cpio`) isn’t available for a given format, the script WARNs and scans the artifact as a raw binary blob instead. Extraction goes into a `mktemp -d` and is `rm -rf`’d on exit. ## Usage [Section titled “Usage”](#usage) 
```sh
bin/audit-bundle.sh path/to/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
bin/audit-bundle.sh /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x86_64.dmg \
                    /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi \
                    /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe
```
 Exit codes: * `0` — all clean (`OK: N/N artifacts clean`) * `1` — at least one artifact had a match, or a named artifact was not found. A missing/`not found` artifact is counted as a failure (`FAIL: <artifact> (not found)`), and the exit-1 summary line reads `FAIL: N of M artifacts contain PostHog leaks`. * `2` — usage error ## /admin integration [Section titled “/admin integration”](#admin-integration) Three integration points: 1. **Inside each prod-build command** (Linux, Mac, Windows): the build script runs the auditor on its own output before declaring success. A bundled leak fails the build. 2. **Standalone “Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks” card** — re-runs against the local `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/{deb,rpm}` artifacts plus any `.dmg`/`.msi`/`.exe` in `/home/marsh-office/`. 3. **CI-equivalent local check** — `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh` can be called from any context; consider adding it to a pre-release script if/when one exists. ## Verified-clean status (2026-05-13) [Section titled “Verified-clean status (2026-05-13)”](#verified-clean-status-2026-05-13) All four currently-built artifacts pass: 
```plaintext
Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb       (700 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x86_64.dmg      (460 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi   (375 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe   (268 MB)  OK
```
 ## Extending the scanner [Section titled “Extending the scanner”](#extending-the-scanner) If a new “must not ship in prod” secret pattern is identified, edit `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh`. Prefer a **regex** that matches only the real secret (long random suffix), not a placeholder or path reference: 
```sh
REGEX_NEEDLES=(
  'phx_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}'
  'phc_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}'
  # add new secret-shaped patterns here
)
```
 For a literal-string match, add to the (currently empty) `NEEDLES` array — but be careful: literal needles like `posthog.json` false-positive on source/docs/code, which is exactly why they were removed. For a “this code is present but gated” signal that should surface without failing the build, add to `WARN_NEEDLES`. Then run the standalone audit card to verify existing artifacts before declaring the new policy enforced. ## Why this isn’t an AST / behavioral scan [Section titled “Why this isn’t an AST / behavioral scan”](#why-this-isnt-an-ast--behavioral-scan) The bundles are gigabytes of compiled JS, minified output, native binaries, postgres data files, etc. A `grep -rlF`/`grep -rlE` over the extracted tree is fast (\~5–10s per artifact). The auditor uses **regex** needles tuned to match only real secrets (a `phx_`/`phc_` key with a long random suffix) so it doesn’t false-positive on placeholders or prose — rather than parsing the JS, which would be slow and brittle against minification. ## What the auditor does NOT catch [Section titled “What the auditor does NOT catch”](#what-the-auditor-does-not-catch) * **Behavioral leaks**: code that hardcodes `flags.papercuspai.com` and calls `fetch()` regardless of `isTestingFeaturesEnabled()`. The auditor scans for embedded *secrets*, not for the SDK’s runtime behavior. Defense: the build chain validates `flag-bus.ts`’s gating discipline; no code outside that file should touch PostHog endpoints. * **Same-host PostHog instance accidentally pointing prod traffic somewhere it shouldn’t**. Defense: see the V1 contract — even with a wrong host, the client must not start. * **Telemetry from other sources** (Tauri’s auto-update, OS crash reporters). These are separate trust decisions documented elsewhere. If you need to validate behavioral guarantees, see [verification](/internal/docs/build-system/verification) — that page covers the live-run smoke test (`curl /api/flags/bootstrap`, `ss -tnp | grep flags.papercuspai`) that catches behavioral leaks.

# Proposal — shared desktop build kit (@papercusp/tauri-release-kit)

> Abstracting the Linux/Mac/Windows Tauri build+release pipeline into a shared library usable by both papercusp and myapp. Design, seam contract, migration.

## The ask [Section titled “The ask”](#the-ask) Can the cross-platform (Linux / macOS / Windows) desktop build + release pipeline be abstracted into a generalized shared library that **both papercusp and myapp** use? **Short answer: yes — the release *orchestration* generalizes cleanly; the *sidecar build* does not and must stay a per-app injected seam.** That split is the whole design. ## What the pipeline does today [Section titled “What the pipeline does today”](#what-the-pipeline-does-today) The canonical tree is the **`papercup/papercusp-desktop/` git submodule** (v0.0.2). It builds three platform families, all driven from `bin/`: | Layer | Driver | Where it runs | | --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Linux `.deb` / `.AppImage` / `.rpm` (x86\_64, opt. arm64) | `bin/release-local.sh` → `tauri build` | dev host, locally | | macOS universal `.dmg` | `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` → `tauri build --target universal-apple-darwin` | macOS VM over SSH (`:2222`) | | Windows `.msi` + NSIS `.exe` | `bin/build-windows-on-vm.sh` → `win-build.ps1` | Windows VM over SSH (`:2223`); WSL2 runtime distro from `scripts/build-rootfs.sh` | `bin/release-local.sh` is the spine. Its steps: 1. **Version bump** across `package.json`, `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`. 2. **Build the sidecar** (`bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh`, \~1,070 lines). 3. **`tauri build`** per target — Tauri does native bundling + minisign signing in one shot, keyed by `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH`. 4. **Generate `latest.json`** (the auto-updater manifest) — maps `{platform → {url, signature}}` against the GitHub release download URL. 5. **Commit + tag + push** (`desktop-vX.Y.Z[-channel]`). 6. **`gh release create/upload`** (idempotent, `--prerelease` for alpha/beta). ## The core insight: two layers, only one generalizes [Section titled “The core insight: two layers, only one generalizes”](#the-core-insight-two-layers-only-one-generalizes) The pipeline is **release orchestration** wrapped around a **sidecar build**, and they generalize very differently: * **Release orchestration is domain-free.** Version bump, the `tauri build` target matrix, signing, `latest.json` generation, `gh release` upload, and the Mac/Windows **VM SSH orchestration** know nothing about what the app *is*. This is the shareable half. * **The sidecar build is wildly app-specific.** Papercusp’s `build-desktop-sidecar.sh` is **\~1,070 lines** bundling the operator UI + harness + orchestrator + MCP server + node-pty + embedded-postgres + pgvector * external binaries (omp, gh, MinGit, node) + a WSL rootfs tarball. MyApp’s `apps/desktop/scripts/build-sidecar.mjs` is **\~42 lines** of esbuild over one `serve.ts`. There is nothing to share here — it must be an **injected step**. So the library owns the *dance*; each app supplies a `buildSidecar()` plugin and a config object. ### Generic vs injected boundary [Section titled “Generic vs injected boundary”](#generic-vs-injected-boundary) | Concern | Generic (in the kit) | Injected per-app (seam) | | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | Version bump | ✅ field-path-driven updater | which files/fields | | `tauri build` matrix | ✅ Linux x64/arm64, Win cross, Mac universal | which targets enabled | | Signing | ✅ already an env-var seam | key path / passphrase | | `latest.json` / updater manifest | ✅ generator | GH download base URL | | `gh release` create/upload | ✅ idempotent driver | owner/repo, tag pattern, channel→prerelease | | Mac/Windows **VM orchestration** | ✅ SSH/SCP/rsync boilerplate | VM host/port/user/key, build dir | | WSL rootfs builder | ✅ Docker bootstrap algorithm | pkg list, output path | | **Sidecar build** | ❌ stays per-app | the whole `buildSidecar()` impl | | App metadata | ❌ | name, id, bundle targets, category, publisher | ## Where it would live, and how it’s consumed [Section titled “Where it would live, and how it’s consumed”](#where-it-would-live-and-how-its-consumed) MyApp already consumes the shared `@papercusp/*` libs (`@papercusp/sse`, `@papercusp/sync`, `@papercusp/ui-primitives`, `@papercusp/embedded-pg-discovery`, …) via workspace `*` deps — and **those `*` deps resolve to git submodules**: myapp’s `workspaces` maps `@papercusp/sync` → its local `libs/sync`, which is a submodule of the shared `Papercusp/sync` repo (the same repo papercup vendors at `libs/generic/sync`). So the kit should follow that **same shared-submodule pattern**: > **`@papercusp/tauri-release-kit`** — a standalone repo (like `Papercusp/sync`) vendored as a submodule by **both** papercup (`libs/generic/tauri-release-kit`) and myapp (`libs/tauri-release-kit`), exposing (a) a typed `TauriReleaseConfig` + programmatic API and (b) a thin `bin/` CLI. Each app adds a small `release.config.ts` + a `bin/release` wrapper. > **Build it in-tree first, extract to a shared repo second.** Per CLAUDE.md a domain-free lib *starts* as `libs/generic/<name>` — which is exactly where it lives now (feature-complete, 56 tests green). Promoting it to a standalone repo > > * submodule (so myapp can vendor it) is the bridge step, and it’s **owner-gated** (it creates a GitHub repo + rewrites two `.gitmodules`). A git-submodule of the whole desktop tree was considered and rejected: myapp deliberately does not submodule papercusp, and the desktop *shells* legitimately differ (myapp builds its own SPA + a tiny sidecar; papercusp serves operator-vite + the heavy sidecar). Sharing the **kit** (logic), not the **shell** (the Tauri app), is the right grain. ### Seam contract (shipped — `libs/generic/tauri-release-kit/src/types.ts`) [Section titled “Seam contract (shipped — libs/generic/tauri-release-kit/src/types.ts)”](#seam-contract-shipped--libsgenerictauri-release-kitsrctypests) The shipped `TauriReleaseConfig` (authoritative source: `types.ts`): 
```ts
export interface TauriReleaseConfig {
  appName: string;              // "Papercusp"
  appId: string;                // "com.papercusp.desktop"
  root: string;                 // desktop app root (where src-tauri/ lives)
  repo: { owner: string; name: string };
  version: string;              // e.g. "0.2.1"
  channel: Channel;             // 'alpha' | 'beta' | 'stable'
  versionFiles: VersionFile[];  // [{path, kind: 'json'|'cargo-toml'}]
  targets: TargetKey[];         // flat array: ['linux-x86_64', 'macos-universal', …]
  signing: SigningConfig;       // { keyPath, passwordEnv? }
  buildSidecar: BuildSidecar;   // ← the injected seam: (ctx: SidecarContext) => Promise<void>
  latestJsonUrl: (a: { tag: string; name: string }) => string;
  tagFor?: (version: string, channel: Channel) => string;   // override default tag scheme
  classifyArtifact?: (path: string) => PlatformKey | null;  // override artifact→platform mapping
  vm?: Partial<Record<TargetKey, VmConfig>>;  // per-target SSH frame (Mac/Windows)
}
```
 `buildSidecar` is the firewall: papercusp wires in its 1,070-line bash; myapp wires in its esbuild. The kit never knows the difference. ## Migration order [Section titled “Migration order”](#migration-order) 1. **Canonicity (resolved — P-002).** Three desktop trees exist: * `papercup/papercusp-desktop/` — **submodule, v0.0.2, CANONICAL** (has the release + VM build scripts). The kit’s papercusp adoption targets this. * `papercupai-workspace/papercusp-desktop/` — standalone, v0.0.1, **stale**; it lives *outside* the papercup repo, so it can’t be retired from here — flagged for owner cleanup. * `papercup/libs/papercusp/apps/desktop/` — a v0.0.1 second app, but `branding.md` references it as a deliberate “secondary in-repo desktop app” (icon-pack mirror), so it is **not** auto-deleted — whether to retire it is an owner judgment call, not a safe autonomous removal. Net: canonical is recorded; no destructive deletes were made (both non-canonical trees are either out-of-repo or referenced). 2. **Extract the kit** behind the seam; **papercusp adopts it first** — its `bin/release-local.sh` becomes a thin wrapper over the kit. Prove byte-identical (or intentionally-improved) artifacts. 3. **MyApp adopts second** — add `release.config.ts` + `buildSidecar` (its esbuild) + a `bin/release`, giving myapp the Linux/Mac/Windows release flow it currently lacks entirely. ## MyApp adoption (ready once the kit is a shared submodule) [Section titled “MyApp adoption (ready once the kit is a shared submodule)”](#myapp-adoption-ready-once-the-kit-is-a-shared-submodule) The kit is already proven app-agnostic — a second-app-shaped config runs through `runRelease` unchanged (proven by the kit’s app-shape test). Once the kit is vendored into myapp as `libs/tauri-release-kit`, myapp adds two files (and nothing in the kit changes): 
```ts
// apps/desktop/bin/release.config.ts (myapp)
export function makeMyAppConfig({ version, channel }): TauriReleaseConfig {
  return {
    appName: 'MyApp',
    appId: 'com.myapp.desktop',
    root: DESKTOP_ROOT,
    repo: { owner: 'my-org', name: 'myapp' },
    version, channel,
    versionFiles: [
      { path: 'package.json', kind: 'json' },
      { path: 'src-tauri/tauri.conf.json', kind: 'json' },
      { path: 'src-tauri/Cargo.toml', kind: 'cargo-toml' },
    ],
    targets: ['linux-x86_64'],            // its tauri.conf ships deb+appimage
    signing: { keyPath: '~/.myapp/signing/myapp.key' },
    buildSidecar: async ({ root, ports }) => {       // the seam: ~42-line esbuild
      await ports.exec.run('npm', ['run', 'build:spa'], { cwd: root });
      await ports.exec.run('node', ['scripts/build-sidecar.mjs'], { cwd: root });
    },
    latestJsonUrl: ({ tag, name }) =>
      `https://github.com/my-org/myapp/releases/download/${tag}/${name}`,
  };
}
```
 `apps/desktop/bin/release.ts` is the *same* thin CLI as papercusp’s. Every difference is config — appId, repo, bundle targets, and the sidecar seam (myapp’s esbuild vs papercusp’s 1,070-line bash). This hands myapp the version-bump + `latest.json` + gh-release + auto-updater flow it has **none** of today. ## Risks & timing [Section titled “Risks & timing”](#risks--timing) * ⚠ **The release scripts are being actively stabilized right now.** The `windows-public-release-readiness-2026-06-25` drive (and the Mac drive) are editing `build-windows-on-vm.sh`, Authenticode signing, and the WSL rootfs as of this writing. Refactoring mid-cut risks destabilizing a live public release. Safest sequencing: extract **after** that release lands, **or** scope a first pass to the **stable Linux x86\_64 core only** (the part not in flux) and prove it on both apps before touching the VM paths. * The sidecar seam must be drawn carefully — papercusp’s bundling pulls \~1GB of external binaries with platform-specific exclusions (omp/code-server dropped on Windows for NSIS size limits); these stay entirely on papercusp’s side of the seam. ## Open questions (for owner) [Section titled “Open questions (for owner)”](#open-questions-for-owner) 1. Go now, or after the public-release drive stabilizes? 2. Full kit (incl. VM orchestration) vs Linux-core-first slice? 3. `libs/generic/` npm package (recommended) vs a standalone `Papercusp/tauri-release-kit` repo?

# Verifying a build

> How to smoke-test each platform end-to-end before declaring the artifact good to ship.

## Pre-flight check (any platform) [Section titled “Pre-flight check (any platform)”](#pre-flight-check-any-platform) Re-run the auditor on every artifact: 
```sh
papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh \
  papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_universal.dmg \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe
```
 Or click **Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks** in `/admin`. (The `.dmg` is the `universal-apple-darwin` artifact — `Papercusp_0.0.1_universal.dmg`, not `x86_64`.) Should print `OK: 4/4`. If any FAIL, **stop** — the artifact must not ship. *** ## Linux .deb verification [Section titled “Linux .deb verification”](#linux-deb-verification) ### 1. Install + launch [Section titled “1. Install + launch”](#1-install--launch) 
```sh
sudo dpkg -i papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
papercusp
```
 Or click **Install + launch Linux .deb** in `/admin`. Expected: a brief bootstrap page, then the window navigates to the operator UI within \~5–15s (a first boot pays `initdb` + migrations inside `serve.mjs`, so allow longer). Title bar “Papercusp”. If it stays stuck on the bootstrap page, the sidecar never reached the preflight-ready state → check the serve logs. ### 2. Verify no discovery files leaked [Section titled “2. Verify no discovery files leaked”](#2-verify-no-discovery-files-leaked) 
```sh
sudo useradd -m papercusp-verify
sudo -u papercusp-verify ls -la ~papercusp-verify/.papercusp/ 2>&1
```
 Expected: `No such file or directory`. The bundle never created the file. ### 3. Flag bootstrap silent [Section titled “3. Flag bootstrap silent”](#3-flag-bootstrap-silent) 
```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3055/api/flags/bootstrap | jq
```
 Wait — the prod binary doesn’t serve on `:3055`. The sidecar (`node serve.mjs`) picks a free port, which it records in `~/.papercusp/operator.json` (the authoritative source). Read it from there, or grep the listener. 
```sh
PROD_PORT=$(jq -r .port ~/.papercusp/operator.json)
# Fallback if operator.json isn't present:
# PROD_PORT=$(ss -tnlp | awk '/serve\.mjs|node/{split($4,a,":"); print a[2]}' | sort -u | grep -v 3055 | head -1)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:${PROD_PORT}/api/flags/bootstrap | jq
```
 Expected — a `source: "defaults"` payload whose `flags` object carries the **full** flag map. `getAllFlags` builds it via `resolveWithDefaults`, which spreads every key in `FLAG_DEFAULTS` (libs/flags/src/types.ts), so on a clean install you get **all \~101 flag keys**, not a handful. Many of them legitimately default `true` (51 of the keys default on, 50 off), so a clean install showing lots of `true` flags is correct, not a leak. A representative excerpt: 
```json
{
  "flags": {
    "papercusp-cloudflare-publish": false,
    "papercusp-harness-phases": false,
    "papercusp-design": false,
    "papercusp-testing": false,
    "papercusp-the-hive": true,
    "papercusp-video-channels": true,
    "papercusp-voice-channels": true
    // …all remaining flag keys, each at its FLAG_DEFAULTS value
  },
  "evaluatedAt": 1234567890,
  "source": "defaults"
}
```
 `source` must be `"defaults"` (the only other values are `"posthog"` and `"override"`). A `"posthog"` source on a clean install means PostHog config leaked in. Don’t diff against a fixed key list — verify each value against `FLAG_DEFAULTS` in `libs/flags/src/types.ts` (the authoritative full map). Two things to know when comparing: (1) the payload contains **every** flag key, so a verifier expecting a short fixed list will falsely flag a correct install; (2) `getAllFlags` runs the stored PG override row through `resolveWithDefaults`, which **drops retired/unknown keys** — e.g. `papercusp-oracle` (folded into `papercusp-testing` by owner ask 2026-06-10) and the long-gone `SNAPSHOTS` key (retired in `retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`; the reproducible clone is now the ungated InstanceSpec) will never appear even if the stored row still carries them. (`papercusp-templates` / `papercusp-marketplace` were likewise retired — distribution lives in the ungated Cupboard.) ### 4. No outbound PostHog traffic [Section titled “4. No outbound PostHog traffic”](#4-no-outbound-posthog-traffic) 
```sh
sudo ss -tnp | grep -E "flags.papercuspai|posthog"
```
 Expected: empty. ### 5. Embedded PG discovery [Section titled “5. Embedded PG discovery”](#5-embedded-pg-discovery) 
```sh
cat ~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json
cat ~/.papercusp/operator.json
```
 Expected: JSON with a non-5432 port (both files written by `serve.mjs`). **Confirms the desktop spawned its own embedded PG, didn’t talk to native `:5432`.** ### 6. Feature data loads [Section titled “6. Feature data loads”](#6-feature-data-loads) In the app, navigate to **Harness → sheets**. The Feature Queue panel should populate with features (not empty). No errors in the DevTools console. ### 7. Closed-flag routes really 404 [Section titled “7. Closed-flag routes really 404”](#7-closed-flag-routes-really-404) 
```sh
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:${PROD_PORT}/design
```
 Expected: `404`. The V1 contract requires `notFound()` to return real HTTP 404, not a 200-page-with-404-content. ### 8. Cleanup [Section titled “8. Cleanup”](#8-cleanup) 
```sh
sudo dpkg -r papercusp
sudo userdel -r papercusp-verify
```
 *** ## macOS .dmg verification [Section titled “macOS .dmg verification”](#macos-dmg-verification) ### 1. Install [Section titled “1. Install”](#1-install)

 Or via Settings → Apps → Papercusp → Uninstall. *** ## FAIL criteria (any platform) [Section titled “FAIL criteria (any platform)”](#fail-criteria-any-platform) | Symptom | Means | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | A real PostHog key (`phx_…` / `phc_…`) found by `audit-bundle.sh` inside the install | Secret leaked into bundle — **must** rebuild | | `/api/flags/bootstrap` returns `source: "posthog"` on a clean install | PostHog config (env var or discovery file) made it through — leak | | A flag value disagrees with `FLAG_DEFAULTS` in `libs/flags/src/types.ts` on a clean install | Default ship-state violated — leak. (Note: 51 flags default `true`, so a clean install with many `true` flags is **correct** — only a *mismatch* against `FLAG_DEFAULTS` is a leak.) | | A retired key (e.g. `papercusp-oracle`, `papercusp-snapshots`) appears in the payload | `resolveWithDefaults` should have dropped it — stored override row leaking retired keys | | `ss -tnp` shows connection to `flags.papercuspai.com` | App phoning home in clean-install state — leak | | Window stuck on the bootstrap page (never navigates off `web/index.html`) | The sidecar never became ready — check the preflight handshake / serve logs | | `embedded-pg.json` / `operator.json` missing, or app connects to `:5432` | Embedded PG didn’t bootstrap (`serve.mjs` owns this) | | Sheets harness shows 0 features when the API returns features | Feature loading broken | | Window shows the **dev** server’s app (URL has `:3055`) | The webview pointed at the dev server instead of the bundled sidecar — rebuild | *** ## A self-contained checklist [Section titled “A self-contained checklist”](#a-self-contained-checklist) Copy this and run top to bottom: 
```sh
# 1. Auditor pass
papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh \
  papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_universal.dmg \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi \
  /home/marsh-office/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe


# 2. Linux install + launch + smoke
sudo dpkg -i papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
setsid /usr/bin/papercusp >/dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null &
sleep 15
PORT=$(jq -r .port ~/.papercusp/operator.json)
echo "operator port: $PORT"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/api/flags/bootstrap" | jq .source       # → "defaults"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/design"  # → 404
sudo ss -tnp | grep -E "flags.papercuspai|posthog" || echo "no posthog traffic ✓"


# 3. Cleanup
pkill -KILL papercusp
sudo dpkg -r papercusp
```
 When every line is green, the artifact is ship-ready for that platform.

# VMs (Mac + Windows + Linux test)

> SSH access, sudo credentials, port maps, disk-sizing notes, the Windows-VM survival kit, and the Linux clean-room test VM.

## Inventory [Section titled “Inventory”](#inventory) | VM | Host process | SSH port | Display | Inside-VM repo path | | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **macOS Sonoma** (x86\_64) | `qemu-system-x86_64 ... mac_hdd_ng.img` | `2222` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5930` | rsync’d `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop` (the in-VM `~/papercupai/papercusp-desktop` checkout is legacy/broken — see below) | | **Windows 11** | `qemu-system-x86_64 ... windows_hdd.qcow2` | `2223` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5931` | `C:\Users\User\papercupai\papercusp-desktop` | | **Linux test** `clean` (Ubuntu 24.04) | `qemu-system-x86_64 … run/<name>/overlay.qcow2` (via `scripts/linux-test-vm/vmctl`) | `2224` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5932` | n/a — installs the packaged `.deb` (no checkout) | | **Linux fed** `fed-a`/`fed-b` (Ubuntu 24.04) | same golden image, +2nd NIC on `pcusp-fedbr0` (via `bin/vm-federation.sh`) | `2225`/`2226` | SPICE `127.0.0.1:5933`/`5934` | n/a — two-machine federation testing | The **Mac** and **Windows** VMs exist only to *produce* their platform’s Tauri bundle. The **Linux test** VM is different in kind — it *consumes* the built `.deb`, fresh-installing it on a pristine Ubuntu to validate the shipped artifact (and to act as a separate machine for federation testing). Day-to-day operator dev (`:3055`) and Linux builds still run entirely on the host. ## Linux test VM (clean-room: fresh-install + federation) [Section titled “Linux test VM (clean-room: fresh-install + federation)”](#linux-test-vm-clean-room-fresh-install--federation) Unlike the build VMs, this is a **disposable Ubuntu 24.04 clean-room** for testing the packaged `.deb` in true isolation — driven by **`papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm/vmctl`**, not a hand-rolled boot script. It exists for (1) **fresh-install testing** the real `.deb` on a pristine machine, and (2) acting as a **separate machine** for shared-harness / federation testing. Plan: `linux-test-vm-and-federation-2026-06-04`. * **Scripts (versioned):** `papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm/` — `vmctl`, `boot-vm.sh`, `cloud-init/`, `lib/common.sh`. * **Images (outside the repo, never committed):** `~/papercup-linux-test-vm/` — `images/golden.qcow2` + per-instance `run/<name>/overlay.qcow2`. SSH key `~/.ssh/papercup-vm-linux` (auto-generated on first `provision`). * **Base:** Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image + a *minimal X stack* (openbox via getty-autologin + `startx`) — deliberately **not** GNOME (which fails to register its session on the qxl GPU) and with **no** preinstalled webkit, so `apt install ./Papercusp.deb` pulls the WebKitGTK runtime from scratch (a truer fresh install). 
```sh
cd papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm
./vmctl provision            # one-time: build the golden image (~10–15 min)
./vmctl up clean             # boot a pristine overlay
./vmctl install clean        # scp newest .deb in + apt install (the fresh-install test)
./vmctl verify clean         # assert deps/PG/operator/window + screenshot → PASS/FAIL
./vmctl gui clean            # (run yourself) open a SPICE viewer to click around
./vmctl reset clean          # wipe back to a pristine overlay
./vmctl down clean           # power off
```
 `install` defaults to the newest `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_*_amd64.deb` (pass a path to override). `verify` checks: package installs (dpkg), `apt-get -s check` confirms no missing/broken dependencies, binary `ldd`-resolves, app process up, embedded Postgres running, operator responds **on its dynamic port** (parsed from the app log — *not* a fixed `:3070`), and captures a window screenshot via the qemu monitor (`screendump`). Artifacts land in `run/<name>/verify/`. Tunables: `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_RAM_MB`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_CPUS`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_DISK`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_HOME`. **It earns its keep.** The first fresh-install run caught that the shipped `.deb` had **no database** on a clean machine: the node-based sidecar spawns in `src-tauri/src/main.rs` used a bare `Command::new("node")` while the packaged process PATH has no `node` — fixed by routing all three spawns through the bundled-node PATH (`bundled_path_env`) like `spawn_sidecar` does. The dev box hides this because it always has `node` on PATH, which is exactly why a clean VM is necessary. (Plan decision D-009.) This is the **historical** (pre-refactor) shape of the bug: the embedded-Postgres + zero-cache process management has since moved **into `serve.mjs`** (`apps/operator/bin/serve.ts`), and `zero-cache-server` is no longer shipped — so the `spawn_embedded_postgres_server` / `spawn_zero_cache_server` functions no longer exist in `main.rs`. The bundled-PATH discipline still applies to the surviving `serve.mjs` spawn. ### Two-machine federation (Phase 2) [Section titled “Two-machine federation (Phase 2)”](#two-machine-federation-phase-2) The same VMs double as **separate machines** for cross-machine federation testing — proving the packaged `.deb` federates (a write on one machine lands in the other’s PG) over a real OS + real network hop, not just loopback. Driven by **`papercusp-desktop/bin/vm-federation.sh`**, which reuses the one-box smokes’ assertion core (`bin/lib/federation-asserts.sh`, D-003) over an SSH driver. 
```sh
cd papercusp-desktop
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --dht=testnet --net=bridge   # primary: fed-a ↔ fed-b
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=1                               # host instance ↔ fed-a VM
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --net=socket                 # rootless (no sudo) fallback
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --no-reset --skip-install    # fast iteration (reuse overlays)
```
 * **Network (D-016):** every fed VM keeps its slirp NIC (internet/SSH/SPICE) and gets a **second** NIC on host bridge `pcusp-fedbr0` (`10.77.0.0/24`, host `10.77.0.1`) with a static guest IP — no dnsmasq/NAT. The host runs a `hyperdht/testnet` advertised on the bridge IP; both VMs set `PAPERCUSP_DHT_BOOTSTRAP` to it → deterministic discovery over a real hop. `--net=socket` is a rootless dual-NIC fallback (qemu socket L2, exactly two VMs). * **Identities:** `papercupai` / `aviynw` via per-instance `GH_TOKEN` (resolved by `gh-token.ts`); `gh` + `postgresql-client` are apt-installed in each VM as driver prereqs. * **Up-front `.deb` gate (P-011):** a static grep of the packaged `serve.mjs` (the sidecar boot entry; `host.mjs` is retired) asserts it carries `PAPERCUSP_DHT_BOOTSTRAP` support + `[swarm]` logs (landed 2026-06-02), failing fast on an older `.deb` that would silently use the public DHT. **Status (verified 2026-06-07, unattended runs on a current `.deb`):** the harness proves everything up to the holepunch boundary in **both modes** — `--vms=2` *and* `--vms=1` reach fresh-install, clean embedded-PG boot on a fresh `initdb`, write-free share (`state:"booted"` both sides), and **cross-machine swarm-join** (both identities announcing on the same topic + DHT). Neither reaches the bidirectional merge, and the boundary is now fully classified: hyperdht **holepunch does not complete between any two endpoints on ONE physical host** — VM↔VM *and* host↔VM both sit at `conns=0` in raw-hyperswarm tests (same topic, same bridge-advertised bootstrap, working UDP both directions), so neither the single-NIC+NAT candidate nor the host’s no-NAT network position rescues it (plan D-017/D-018). `--dht=public` (P-012) is **INCONCLUSIVE** by same-host NAT hairpin, per the plan’s D-004 best-effort caveat — though both peers do announce on the real public DHT through slirp. The full bidirectional-merge acceptance needs **truly separate machines** — and that gate was **discharged on Hetzner (2026-06-08, plan D-019)**: the Tier-3 p2p-perf suite on two separate Hetzner cpx31 VMs over the public DHT got `peer_connected` on both peers, cross-region append→visible p95 = 950.5 ms, and a real NAT holepunch (`punches=1 relaySuccess=0`) — positively confirming the single-host `conns=0` wall is a topology artifact (no second physical box needed; the cloud-deployment layer provides the separate machines on-demand). It was further confirmed **cross-region** (ash↔hil: append→visible p95 = 1115.5 ms over real transcontinental WAN) and — via `bin/deb-hetzner-federation.sh` — for the **shipped `.deb` itself** (two Hetzner VMs, the `.deb`’s headless sidecar, `peer_connected` + bidirectional `origin=remote` merge over the public DHT). (These last two results are recorded in the agent-insight below; the `linux-test-vm-and-federation-2026-06-04` plan’s decision log ends at D-019, so they have no D-020/D-021 plan citation.) The finding, the clean-machine traps the harness flushed out (slirp-subnet, embedded-PG boot race, the sidecar port-grep race, embedded-pg-refuses-root, and the bundled `pgvector` needing the 24.04 toolchain), and the Hetzner discharge are in the agent-insight [VM federation harness](/internal/docs/agent-insights/vm-federation-separate-machine-proof). ## SSH commands [Section titled “SSH commands”](#ssh-commands) 
```sh
# Mac
ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1
# Windows
ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1
```
 Inside the Mac VM, `sudo` password is `aviweiss`. Windows VM has no sudo concept; `User` has admin rights. ## Booting them [Section titled “Booting them”](#booting-them) ### Mac VM [Section titled “Mac VM”](#mac-vm) 
```sh
systemctl --user start papercup-vm-mac.service     # the supported path
```
 The unit runs **`boot-sonoma-durable.sh`** (32 GB RAM, `Type=forking` + `PIDFile=qemu.pid`, QMP control socket at `OSX-KVM/qmp.sock`, logs in `OSX-KVM/logs/qemu-current.log`, graceful QMP `system_powerdown` on stop). \~60–120s to SSH-ready. ⚠ Do **not** launch `boot-sonoma.sh` for routine boots — it is the *installer-media* variant (16 GB, attaches `BaseSystem.img`, currently a macOS Tahoe installer) and was the cause of the 2026-06-11 service crash-loop split-brain. If SSH is dead and the service can’t bind SPICE `:5930`, an orphaned qemu probably holds the ports and may be parked at the OpenCore boot picker — recover it via QMP, never `pkill`: [mac-vm-qmp-recovery](/internal/docs/agent-insights/mac-vm-qmp-recovery). To view the desktop: `remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5930`. ### Windows VM [Section titled “Windows VM”](#windows-vm) 
```sh
cd ~/windows-vm
nohup bash boot-windows.sh > /tmp/win-boot.log 2>&1 &
```
 \~90s to SSH-ready. (To get a desktop window in one shot, `~/windows-vm/launch-vm-and-viewer.sh` boots the VM and opens `remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5931`.) ## Resource specs (current; tunable in the boot scripts) [Section titled “Resource specs (current; tunable in the boot scripts)”](#resource-specs-current-tunable-in-the-boot-scripts) | | macOS VM | Windows VM | | ------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | | RAM | 32 GB (was 16; Xcode + Rust eats RAM) | 32 GiB (was 8 GB pre-2026-05-12) | | vCPUs | 8 (`-smp 8`: 4 cores × 2 threads) | 16 | | Disk | 120 GB qcow2 (grown from 80 on 2026-05-13) | `windows_hdd.qcow2`, \~120 GB qcow2 | | Cache | writeback | writeback | | Net | virtio-net-pci | e1000 | | Storage | AHCI | AHCI | ## Disk discipline [Section titled “Disk discipline”](#disk-discipline) Tauri builds are huge. A clean Mac build typically consumes: * \~5 GB Rust target dir (`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/`) * \~3 GB npm cache (`~/Library/Caches/`) * \~1.5 GB built node\_modules * \~500 MB intermediate `.dmg` staging * \~10 GB Xcode CoreSimulator runtimes (if you build iOS at all) **Pre-build check** the user reflexively runs: `df -h /` on each VM. If `<10 GB` free, clean up before kicking off a build — mid-build ENOSPC is a hard failure and leaves a broken-half state. The macOS VM has been on the verge of full multiple times. Safe deletes when desperate: 
```sh
# iOS simulator runtimes (recreatable in Xcode → Settings → Platforms)
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices/*    # device instances only
# spm cache
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/SourcePackages/
# Rust target (forces clean rebuild but reclaims ~3-5 GB)
rm -rf ~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target
```
 The canonical Mac build does **not** use the in-VM `~/papercupai/papercusp-desktop` checkout — that one is a legacy/broken tree (its git was historically corrupt; don’t resurrect it, per the mac-desktop-release-readiness plan). `build-mac-prod` instead `rsync`s the canonical tree into an isolated `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup` and builds there, so that’s the target worth clearing. The Linux host (\~40-50 GB free typical) doesn’t hit ENOSPC during builds but the Rust target dir there does grow to \~5 GB. ## Node version pinning [Section titled “Node version pinning”](#node-version-pinning) Both VMs run **nvm + Node 22** for the build-time `npm install` + `tauri build`. (This is separate from the *bundled* runtime that ships inside the artifact — `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` vendors Node **v24** into `sidecar/bin/node`.) Node 20 hangs / errors during `npm install`. 
```sh
# In either VM:
nvm install 22       # one-time
nvm use 22           # every shell
```
 The **`build-mac-prod`** `/admin` command pins Node 22 via `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` (which sources `~/.nvm/nvm.sh` and runs `nvm use 22`). The **`build-windows-prod`** command instead runs a PowerShell script (`win-build.ps1`) — bash `nvm` doesn’t apply there, so that script handles its own Node pinning. If you SSH into the Mac VM manually, don’t forget `nvm use 22`. ## npm `--legacy-peer-deps` is required [Section titled “npm --legacy-peer-deps is required”](#npm---legacy-peer-deps-is-required) The workspace’s peer-dep tree has unresolvable conflicts that make `npm install` hang **silently with 0% CPU** in modern npm. **Always pass `--legacy-peer-deps`** for installs done in the build context. The /admin scripts do this; if you do manual installs in either VM, you must too. ## Mac VM environment quirks [Section titled “Mac VM environment quirks”](#mac-vm-environment-quirks) * **Bundled-Node PATH**: GUI-launched apps on macOS inherit `$PATH = /usr/bin:/bin` — Homebrew Node, nvm Node, brew-installed `pg_dump` / `libpq` are all invisible. `main.rs:bundled_path_env()` builds a `PATH` with the shipped `sidecar/bin/` (node/omp/gh) prepended, and every node-based spawn (the `serve.mjs` sidecar + `code-server`) runs through it. **If you add a new spawn**, route it through the same helper. * **Gatekeeper**: the DMG is unsigned. First launch will be blocked. The install-mac-dmg `/admin` command strips quarantine via `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Papercusp.app`. If launching by hand, you’ll need to do this too. ## Windows VM crashes routinely [Section titled “Windows VM crashes routinely”](#windows-vm-crashes-routinely) The Windows VM crashed **6+ times during a single build session** (2026-05-13). Symptoms: SSH hangs indefinitely, `qemu-system-x86_64` process disappears, `/tmp/win-boot.log` last line is a kernel power error. **Recovery procedure** (this happens often enough it’s worth automating; for now do it manually): 
```sh
# Verify dead
ps -ef | grep -v grep | grep "qemu.*windows_hdd"   # → should be empty


# Restart
cd ~/windows-vm && nohup bash boot-windows.sh > /tmp/win-boot.log 2>&1 &


# Wait ~90s
sleep 90 && ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1 'echo ok'


# Re-run the build (it'll resume from incremental Rust cache if not corrupted)
```
 The Rust target dir in the Windows VM survives crashes — it’s qcow2 + AHCI writeback so a few seconds of write-back data may be lost, but cargo’s atomic incremental graph handles this gracefully. If a build was mid-`tauri build` when the VM crashed, you may need to delete and recreate `C:\Users\User\papercusp-desktop\src-tauri\binaries\embedded-postgres-server-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.exe` — `tauri-bundler` doesn’t always recover cleanly from in-place sidecar binary writes when the process disappears mid-write. Symptom: `failed to remove symlink ... os error 5`. ## Why builds don’t run in containers [Section titled “Why builds don’t run in containers”](#why-builds-dont-run-in-containers) The Tauri team’s MSI tooling (`wix`) requires Windows, and Apple’s code-signing tooling requires macOS. We don’t currently sign builds (the audit pipeline assumes unsigned binaries) but the Mac build does need to be a Darwin host for `cargo` to cross-compile to `x86_64-apple-darwin`. So the VMs aren’t replaceable by Linux containers without a substantial cross-compile setup. ## Build cancellation [Section titled “Build cancellation”](#build-cancellation) The `/admin` build commands run via `bash -lic`. Closing the SSE stream (Stop button or browser close) sends `SIGTERM` to the whole process group — which cleanly terminates the local `npm` and `tauri build` invocations on the host, but the SSH-driven Mac/Windows builds **continue running inside the VM** even after SIGTERM kills the SSH client. To actually cancel a Mac/Windows build mid-flight, SSH in separately and `pkill -f "tauri build\|cargo"`.

# The layered agent-liveness model

> How Papercusp decides an agent is alive — supervision, stream activity, dispatch beats, coord beats — which consumers read which legs, and why the sweep never prods processes directly.

Shipped by `agent-liveness-heartbeat-hardening-2026-06-12` (after the stale-claims sweep and EI-348). This page is the one mental model; the per-module docs live in the source headers it links. ## The four signals, robustness-ordered [Section titled “The four signals, robustness-ordered”](#the-four-signals-robustness-ordered) | # | Signal | Written by | Semantics | Covers a long no-tool-call turn? | | - | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | | 1 | **Supervision heartbeat** — `spawned_agents.heartbeat_at` | The host that OWNS the process: the operator’s nursery loop (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts ensureSpawnHeartbeatLoop`) for bees; the psu launcher’s supervisor beat (`scripts/psu-launcher.mjs startSupervisorBeat` → the bootstrap-su heartbeat endpoint) for interactive sessions | ”I hold this process handle and it is alive” | **Yes** | | 2 | **Stream activity** — `spawned_agents.last_output_at` (bees, mig 233) · pty discovery-file `lastOutputAt` (psu pty sessions) | The runner’s in-process stdout/stderr listeners (`dbos/orchestrator-runner.ts onOutputActivity`); the pty host’s activity tracker (`scripts/psu-pty-host.mjs makeActivityTracker`) | “The agent emitted bytes just now” — *generating*, not merely alive | Yes, and it distinguishes generating from wedged | | 3 | **Dispatch beat** — `coord_presence.last_active_at` AND `.heartbeat_at` via `touchActivity` | The projected-tool dispatch seam (`projected-tool-deps.ts recordInvocationImpl` → `agent-tools/coordination/dispatch-heartbeat.ts`), throttled per owner | ”The agent made ANY platform tool call recently” — the per-edit lock hook traffic alone keeps an actively-editing session warm | No (but such turns also make no edits) | | 4 | **Coord beat** — `coord_presence.heartbeat_at` | `coord:declare-intent`, `coord:inbox` reads | ”The agent touched the coordination layer recently” | No | A projected dispatch IS genuine activity, so leg 3 beats via `touchActivity` (bumps `last_active_at` *and* `heartbeat_at`, presence-v2 D-003) — distinct from the pure keepalive `touchHeartbeat` (leg 1’s 60s supervisor beat) which bumps `heartbeat_at` only. Both are no-ops when no presence row exists, so one-shot HTTP callers never mint roster rows. Two invariants: * **A signal is written by whoever can actually observe it.** The sweep/roster never `kill -0`s processes: it’s same-host-only, session agents have no PID (`coord_presence.pid` is null for HTTP MCP clients), and alive ≠ progressing — a wedged process passes `kill -0` forever. Supervision heartbeats ARE process-prodding, done by the process-owner and projected into PG where every host can read them. * **Annotate, don’t suppress** (plan D-002) — for the badge and for attended / non-bee sessions: stream-activity staleness flags a `possibly_wedged` candidate for humans/the Queen (`fleet:tree`, `isPossiblyWedged` in `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts`) without feeding claim release, so an attended-but-quiet session keeps its claims. **The exception is a supervised local bee under the now-shipped wedge auto-reaper** (D-006, flag `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP` default ON): a bee whose stream is silent past 30min IS reaped — `reapWedgedLocalSpawns` (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts`) durably cancels it via `cancelSubtree`, which DOES release its work-item and plan-item claims (`claimsReleased` / `planClaimsReleased` in `fleet/nursery.ts`) before the local abort. For a wedged bee, then, stream-activity staleness (leg 2) feeds claim release; absence of any observed output is still never treated as a wedge. ## Which consumers read which legs [Section titled “Which consumers read which legs”](#which-consumers-read-which-legs) | Consumer | Legs read | Where | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Stale-claims sweep (releases `taken_by` of dead holders) | 1 + 3/4 (presence OR nursery, alias-aware per mig 225) | `work-items-stale-claims.ts` | | Spawn reclaim (frees ceiling slots of dead-host spawns) | 1, plus same-host pid-alive as a keep-alive override (EI-85) | `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` | | Colony roster / Sessions view | best of 1 (nursery join, pid-alive definitive) and 3/4 (presence) — EI-348 | `adv-roster.ts mergeRosterEntries` | | Wedge badge (`possibly_wedged`) | 1 fresh AND 2 stale | `fleet:tree` → `isPossiblyWedged` | | Wedge auto-reaper (cancels + releases claims of supervised bees silent past threshold) | 1 fresh AND 2 stale | `fleet/operator-spawn.ts reapWedgedLocalSpawns` (flag `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP`, default ON) | **The rule for new consumers: read the strongest leg available for the agent class, not just presence.** EI-348 was exactly a consumer reading only leg 3/4 for agents whose truth lived in leg 1. For bees, legs 1 and 2 are not two independent timers: the nursery heartbeat loop (`ensureSpawnHeartbeatLoop`) is one tick on `SPAWN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS` that (a) bumps `heartbeat_at`, (b) write-throughs `last_output_at` for streams that moved since the last persist (`GREATEST`-monotonic, P-008 — zero extra write cadence), and (c) runs the wedge auto-reaper. The runner’s `onOutputActivity` only records the in-process stream timestamp; this tick is what persists it. ## The supervisability boundary [Section titled “The supervisability boundary”](#the-supervisability-boundary) Processes our infrastructure launches are fully supervisable: fleet bees (operator children) and psu sessions (the launcher stays parent in both the plain and managed-pty paths; the pty host additionally sees every byte). The remainder — a bare `claude` launched outside psu, remote claude.ai/code sessions, desktop embedded chat — can only be observed through their platform traffic (legs 3/4). That is why the dispatch beat exists and ships enabled. ## Tuning knobs [Section titled “Tuning knobs”](#tuning-knobs) * `DISPATCH_BEAT_INTERVAL_MS` (45s) — `dispatch-heartbeat.ts` * `SUPERVISOR_BEAT_MS` (60s) — `psu-launcher.mjs` * `SPAWN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS` (60s) — `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` * `ACTIVITY_PERSIST_MS` (15s, pty discovery write-through) — `psu-pty-host.mjs` * `WEDGE_SILENT_MS` (10min, badge threshold) — `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` * `WEDGE_REAP_SILENT_MS` (30min, env `PAPERCUSP_WEDGE_REAP_MS`, reaper threshold — distinct from and longer than the badge’s) — `fleet/operator-spawn.ts` * `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP` flag (default ON, D-006) — `libs/flags/src/types.ts` * Liveness windows: `LIVE_MS` 60s / `STALE_MS` 10min (`liveness.ts`) · claim-sweep grace `STALE_CLAIM_GRACE_MS` 10min (`work-items-stale-claims.ts`)

# Checkpoints and facts — the durable carry surfaces

> The memory layers that carry agent state across turns, wakes, compactions, and successors — work-item checkpoints, loop checkpoints, standing facts, and where each is stored and re-injected.

Agents are transient; work is not.
