Each entry in `state-snapshot.openCards[]` is an `OpenCardSnapshot`: it carries `correlationId`, `prompt`, `presentation`, `fallbackText`, `allowDecline`, `report`, `createdAt`, and `dataSchemaJson`. The `dataSchema` is **not** shipped as a Zod object — the server serializes it to JSON Schema (the required `dataSchemaJson` field) so the renderer can read the schema without a Zod runtime. The default adapter is Zod 4’s `toJSONSchema` (`zod-to-json-schema@3` produced empty output for Zod 4 schemas), with the `$schema` key stripped. ## API [Section titled “API”](#api) 
```ts
interface CardSpec<TSchema extends ZodTypeAny> {
  /** Human-readable prompt. Voice surfaces read this verbatim. */
  prompt: string;


  /** Zod schema for the response payload. Validated server-side. */
  dataSchema: TSchema;


  /** Visual presentation hint. Voice surfaces ignore. */
  presentation?: CardPresentation;


  /** Plain-text fallback for voice / MCP-elicitation bridge. */
  fallbackText?: string;


  /** Wall-clock timeout. Rejects with {action:'cancel'} if user does not respond. */
  timeoutMs?: number;


  /** Per-run idempotency key. Same key returns cached response within the run. */
  idempotencyKey?: string;


  /** When false, the renderer hides the Skip affordance. Default true. */
  allowDecline?: boolean;


  /**
   * Optional structured body block (the shared `ReportBlock` two-tier
   * plan→item shape from `@papercusp/chat-protocol`) rendered between the
   * prompt and the options. Copied verbatim onto the wire snapshot.
   */
  report?: ReportBlock;


  /**
   * Fired synchronously once the card is registered, with the freshly-minted
   * `correlationId` and the run/workspace it's scoped to. Lets a caller link
   * the live card to an external durable record (e.g. an inbox / coord
   * escalation). NOT called on an idempotency-cache hit (no card is
   * registered), and any throw is swallowed — it never breaks the card flow.
   */
  onCard?: (info: { correlationId: string; runId: string; workspaceId: string }) => void;
}


type CardResponse<TSchema extends ZodTypeAny> =
  | { action: 'submit';  payload: z.infer<TSchema> }
  | { action: 'decline'; reason?: string }
  | { action: 'cancel' };
```
 ### Submit payload shape by presentation [Section titled “Submit payload shape by presentation”](#submit-payload-shape-by-presentation) The renderer wraps the user’s response into a per-kind payload shape: | Presentation | Submit payload | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | `radio`, `checkbox` | `{ picks: [optionId, ...] }` | | `text` | `{ value: string }` | | `date` | `{ value: string }` *(ISO `yyyy-mm-dd`)* | | `slider` | `{ value: number }` | Your `dataSchema` must match the payload shape. For a single-select radio with two options, that’s typically `z.object({ picks: z.tuple([z.enum(['x','y'])]) })`. For a date, `z.object({ value: z.string().date() })`. The server validates the inbound payload against `dataSchema` before resolving the handler’s promise. ### `presentation` shapes [Section titled “presentation shapes”](#presentation-shapes) 
```ts
type CardPresentation =
  | { kind: 'radio';    options: CardOption[]; voiceAnswerable?: boolean }
  | { kind: 'checkbox'; options: CardOption[] }
  | { kind: 'text';     placeholder?: string; multiline?: boolean }
  | { kind: 'date';     min?: string; max?: string }
  | { kind: 'slider';   min: number; max: number; step?: number };


interface CardOption {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  hint?: string;
  style?: 'default' | 'primary' | 'danger';
}
```
 `voiceAnswerable` on the `radio` variant is the opt-in that makes a radio card answerable **by voice**: when `true`, voice surfaces expose the option set for spoken answering. It defaults to off, and every other presentation kind stays announce-only on voice regardless. ## Response actions [Section titled “Response actions”](#response-actions) | `r.action` | Meaning | When | | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `submit` | User picked. `r.payload` validated against `dataSchema`. | User clicked Submit / chose a single option. | | `decline` | User explicitly skipped. | User clicked Skip (only available when `allowDecline ≠ false`). | | `cancel` | Run cancelled, workspace switched, or `timeoutMs` fired. | Out-of-band — user did not respond. | The handler picks one branch for each. `decline` is for “this card isn’t relevant, but keep running.” `cancel` always means the entire run is going away. Single-select choice cards may also include **navigational** (non-terminal) options — clicking one opens a sub-surface (e.g. a chat thread or a log view) and leaves the card live instead of answering it. This is a renderer-local `navigate` action: it does **not** POST to `/card-response` and never resolves the `ctx.askUser` promise, so it has no `r.action` branch on the handler side. ## What ctx.askUser is **not** [Section titled “What ctx.askUser is not”](#what-ctxaskuser-is-not) * **Not a tool call.** It happens *inside* a tool handler. The model sees the tool as one unit of work that returned a value. * **Not on the event channel.** `ctx.emit('card', …)` is rejected at register time — `'card'` is a reserved event name to prevent plugins from intercepting other tools’ askUser flow on the wire. * **Not available when the transport is one-shot.** When `ctx.askUser` is undefined (no `runId` in context — e.g. a non-streaming HTTP caller hitting a tool directly), the handler should detect this and either return an error or pick a default. ## Lifecycle [Section titled “Lifecycle”](#lifecycle) 
```plaintext
                 (1) tool handler awaits ctx.askUser(spec)
                                │
                                ▼
              (2) card-correlator registers a UUID correlationId,
                  publishes state-snapshot with openCards[+correlationId]
                                │
                                ▼
              (3) transport ships state-snapshot to client
                                │
                                ▼
              (4) renderer reads openCards[head], shows AskChoiceCard
                                │
                                ▼
              (5) user clicks → POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/card-response
                                │
                                ▼
              (6) card-correlator: validate payload, resolve deferred,
                  publish state-snapshot with openCards[-correlationId]
                                │
                                ▼
              (7) handler continues with the response value
```
 If the run aborts at any point, every open card under the run is resolved `{action:'cancel'}`. If the user switches workspaces, every open card in the **leaving** workspace is resolved `{action:'cancel'}` via the `onWorkspaceSwitch` hook. `POST /api/workspaces/switch` captures `leaving = reg.current` *before* writing the new current, then fires `dispatchWorkspaceSwitch(leaving)` so the card-correlator’s `cancelPendingCardsForWorkspaceSwitch(leaving)` resolves every deferred under that workspace; the state-channel drops all snapshots in the same pass. ## Cancelling an entire run [Section titled “Cancelling an entire run”](#cancelling-an-entire-run) A user can dismiss every pending card under a run with one click. The chat surface (`PendingCardsBar`) renders a “Cancel” button alongside the head card. Click → `POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/run-cancel`: 
```plaintext
POST /api/operator/conversations/:convId/run-cancel
Cookie: <session>
Content-Type: application/json


{ "runId": "<run-uuid>", "workspaceId": "<workspace-id>" }
```
 The server calls `cancelPendingCardsForRun(runId)` — every pending card’s deferred resolves `{action:'cancel'}`. Tools awaiting those cards see cancel and (typically) throw an “operation cancelled” error that the dispatcher catches. Same auth + rate-limit contract as `/card-response`: session-cookie required (401 if missing), 30 RPS per session user, 404 on cross-workspace runId. The client-side `PendingCardsBar` also optimistically dismisses ALL cards from the cancelled run (not just the head) — even if the SSE state-snapshot update is delayed, the local UI clears immediately. ## Auth, defense in depth, rate limit [Section titled “Auth, defense in depth, rate limit”](#auth-defense-in-depth-rate-limit) The `/card-response` endpoint requires a session cookie (401 if missing). Beyond that, the card-correlator validates `expectedWorkspaceId` against the card’s stored workspace — even if a caller bypasses the session check, cross-workspace replay returns 404 (`card not found`). Rate limit: **30 RPS per session user**, sliding window. Bursts past that return 429. The bucket key is the session’s user id (not the caller-supplied `workspaceId`, which is untrusted) so a single workspace-hopping client cannot evade the limit. ## Client-side companion: `askUserLocal` [Section titled “Client-side companion: askUserLocal”](#client-side-companion-askuserlocal) For render-time-only prompts that never cross the wire (tab pickers, settings dialogs, “are you sure?” confirmations): 
```ts
import { askUserLocal } from '@/lib/chat-cards/ask-user-local';


const r = await askUserLocal({
  prompt: 'Switch to a new chat?',
  dataSchema: z.object({ choice: z.enum(['yes', 'no']) }),
  presentation: { kind: 'radio', options: [...] },
});
```
 Same `CardSpec` / `CardResponse` types. Different transport: a global subscriber registry in the React tree. To **render** an `askUserLocal` prompt, mount a `LocalCardHost` somewhere in the React tree: 
```tsx
import { LocalCardHost } from '@/app/_components/chat/LocalCardHost';


function MyLayout() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* …app chrome… */}
      <LocalCardHost />
    </>
  );
}
```
 `LocalCardHost` subscribes to the `askUserLocal` registry on mount, queues incoming cards, and reuses the same `AskChoiceCard` / `InputCard` renderer dispatch as `PendingCardsBar` (so cards look identical regardless of which path emitted them). The operator chat sidebar already mounts one `LocalCardHost`; without any host mounted, every `askUserLocal` call immediately resolves `{action:'cancel'}`. `askUserLocal` and `ctx.askUser` are **not interchangeable**. Use `ctx.askUser` when the prompt is in flight inside a tool execution; use `askUserLocal` when the prompt is purely a UI affordance. ## Idempotency [Section titled “Idempotency”](#idempotency) 
```ts
const r = await ctx.askUser({
  prompt: '...',
  dataSchema: ...,
  idempotencyKey: 'pick-flavor',
});
```
 If the tool reaches this point again within the same `runId` (e.g. re-entrant flow), the cached response is returned without re-prompting. Keys are scoped per-run — two different runs ask independently. ## Timeouts [Section titled “Timeouts”](#timeouts) `timeoutMs` is on the card, not the tool. The card’s deferred is resolved `{action:'cancel'}` when the timeout fires; the handler decides what to do next. The tool’s own `timeoutSec` is independent — it aborts the entire run, which cascades cancel to every open card under it. ## State retention across reconnects [Section titled “State retention across reconnects”](#state-retention-across-reconnects) `state-snapshot` for a `runId` is retained for 5 minutes after the run ends (success or abort). A late reconnect within that window receives the final snapshot. Past 5 minutes the entry is GC’d. ## Limitations [Section titled “Limitations”](#limitations) * **In-process only.** The PENDING map lives in the operator’s Node process. Dev-mode HMR drops it; a server restart drops it. v1 accepts this — the same bound applies to `/turn-answer` today. PG-backed persistence is a v1.x follow-up. * **One card visible at a time.** The renderer shows `openCards[0]`; additional concurrent cards queue behind it with an indicator. This avoids the multi-card chat-surface cliff. If you need a multi-question flow, prefer one card with a multi-field `dataSchema` instead of multiple sequential `ctx.askUser` calls. * **No bidirectional state sync.** `ctx.publishState` handles server-to-client state (snapshot-only in v1; JSON-Patch deltas deferred to v1.1). The reverse (client-edits-server-state) is not in scope — it’s the same shape as a regular tool call, which already covers that direction. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * [Function-as-truth](./function-as-truth.mdx) — how `defineTool` projects to every transport. * [Voice modality](./voice-modality.mdx) — how cards collapse to plain text on voice surfaces. * Plan: `apps/operator/docs/plans/bespoke-card-improvements-2026-05-13.md`

# Function-as-truth

> The architectural decision that makes the rest of the system work. Why the function comes first, the manifest second, the transports last.

## The decision [Section titled “The decision”](#the-decision) The function is the source of truth. The manifest declares which transports project it. The framework auto-mounts both HTTP and MCP without per-tool route code. This is *not* “HTTP-first wrapped by MCP.” It’s not “MCP-first wrapped by HTTP.” Both transports are equal-weight projections of one underlying function. ## What that means in practice [Section titled “What that means in practice”](#what-that-means-in-practice) A tool author writes this: libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/index.ts 
```ts
export const tools: PluginToolMap = {
  pack: async (input, ctx) => {
    const result = await ctx.spawn('repomix', ['--stdout', ...]);
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: result.stdout }] };
  },
};
```
 And this: 
```json
// libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/papercusp.json (excerpt)
{
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "pack",
      "description": "Pack a project into a single LLM-friendly document.",
      "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "target_dir": { "type": "string" } } },
      "capabilities": ["compute:exec:repomix"],
      "roles": ["worker", "scoper", "architect"],
      "rolesQuota": { "worker": { "perChunk": 1 }, "architect": { "perRun": 5 } },
      "timeoutSec": 120
    }
  ]
}
```
 That’s it. No route file. No `app/api/plugins/repomix/pack/route.ts`. The framework reads the manifest, finds the matching `tools.pack` handler, registers it in the projected-tool registry, and the catch-all routes do the rest. Projection is name-derived by default: a tool with no `expose` block projects onto both transports under the dotted MCP name `<plugin>.<tool>` (e.g. `repomix.pack`) and the HTTP path `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`. The optional `expose.{http,mcp}` block overrides those names/paths or restricts a tool to a single transport (registration requires at least one of `expose.http` / `expose.mcp` when the block is present) — that’s the concrete meaning of “the manifest declares which transports project it.” A new caller — UI, agent over MCP, or another module — gets the function with all gating and telemetry intact. ## The pivot away from per-route code [Section titled “The pivot away from per-route code”](#the-pivot-away-from-per-route-code) Before this design we had \~50 hand-written `app/api/agent-mcp/*/route.ts` files. Each one re-implemented its own auth check, its own JSON parse, its own try-catch, its own logging, its own error mapping. They drifted: some returned 500 where they should have returned 401; some forgot RLS scoping; some accepted GET when only POST made sense; some had quotas, most didn’t. The function-as-truth approach replaces all that with a single dispatcher (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts`). A new tool inherits correct behavior because there’s only one place that behavior is defined. ## Why we didn’t just generate routes from the manifest at build time [Section titled “Why we didn’t just generate routes from the manifest at build time”](#why-we-didnt-just-generate-routes-from-the-manifest-at-build-time) We considered codegen — read the manifests, emit one route file per tool. We chose dynamic catch-all routes instead because: * **No build step.** Adding a tool is editing a manifest + restarting the host. Codegen would mean re-running a generator and committing generated files; the next agent edit always clashes. * **Single dispatcher invariant.** With codegen, behavior diverges if anyone hand-edits a generated file. Dynamic routing forces all tools through the same code path. * **Plugin hot-reload is possible.** A new plugin registered at runtime appears in the catch-all on next request. Codegen would require a rebuild. * **About 10 lines of routing magic.** The Hono catch-all routes (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` and `…/agent-tools/catchall.ts`, serving `/api/plugins/*` and `/api/agent-tools/*`) look up the tool by path in the registry at request time. No magic, easy to debug. The trade is one extra registry lookup per request. Compared with auth + RLS + database I/O, it’s noise. ## Why we kept mcp-handler [Section titled “Why we kept mcp-handler”](#why-we-kept-mcp-handler) We use Vercel’s `mcp-handler` library as the MCP transport. We do not rebuild `StreamableHTTPTransport`. The bridge between two existing transports (mcp-handler for MCP, Hono route handlers for HTTP) is \~150 lines, both share the same `dispatchProjectedTool`, both populate the same `UnifiedToolContext`. Building our own MCP transport would have been weeks of work for no win. ## What “decoupling” actually means in our codebase [Section titled “What “decoupling” actually means in our codebase”](#what-decoupling-actually-means-in-our-codebase) Three rules a function must follow to be projection-ready: 1. **No transport awareness.** A function does not know whether it’s serving HTTP or MCP. It does not read headers, it does not write `Response` objects. It receives `(input, ctx)` and returns `ToolResult` or throws. 2. **Cancel via `ctx.signal`.** If a function does long work it watches `ctx.signal.aborted` and bails. Both transports thread the abort signal through the dispatcher’s timeout mechanism. 3. **Progress via `ctx.progress()`.** Optional. If called, MCP transport emits `notifications/progress`; HTTP SSE emits an `event: progress` line. No transport branching in the function. When you migrate a route, you’re really doing two things: (a) writing the function in this shape, (b) deleting the legacy route. The MCP-callable part is automatic. ## The six known tool shapes [Section titled “The six known tool shapes”](#the-six-known-tool-shapes) After the foundation pivot we shipped four plugins to validate the model. The fifth (MCP-proxy) shipped in the revive-plugin-system arc (2026-06-04) as the GitNexus bridge. The sixth (interactive-card) was originally a render-only emergent pattern but consolidated into a first-class framework primitive (`ctx.askUser`) in the bespoke-card-improvements arc (2026-05-13). Each shape stresses a different corner: | Shape | Example | What it stresses | | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Subprocess single-tool | `repomix.pack` | `ctx.spawn`, capability `compute:exec:*`, large output to scratch dir | | HTTP fetch with optional secret | `fetch_plus.fetch_clean` | `ctx.secret` returning null, capability `http:fetch:<host>` | | Subprocess multi-tool | `code2prompt.diff` + `code2prompt.pack` | Two tools sharing a manifest, dynamic templates | | HTTP fetch with required secret | `firecrawl.scrape` + `extract` + `map` | Three tools sharing a manifest, `secrets:read:<NAME>`, JSON-schema-driven extraction | | **MCP-proxy plugin** | `gitnexus-bridge` (GitNexus wrapper) | Forwards to an external MCP server. Implements `getDynamicTools()` so the proxy enumerates the child’s `tools/list` at register time instead of hard-coding. May set `discoveryTimeoutMs` (default \~10s; gitnexus uses 30s) because a cold child-process probe can exceed the default budget; the plugin host caps the whole discovery sweep at 60s, tools registered before the cap stay live, and a slow probe drains errors into plugin-host status. | | **Interactive card** | `chat:ask_choice` | Tool calls `ctx.askUser(spec)` and blocks until the user submits/declines/cancels. The card travels on the **state channel** (`state-snapshot` SSE), not the per-tool event ring buffer — so reconnect-resilient by construction. Handler returns the user’s response value, not echoed args. See [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx). | If your work doesn’t fit one of those shapes, stop and discuss before inventing a seventh. See [Operations → When to stop and ask](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/operations#when-to-stop-and-ask). ### Interactive-card conventions [Section titled “Interactive-card conventions”](#interactive-card-conventions) For tools that pause execution to ask the user something via the chat sidebar: 1. **Call `ctx.askUser(spec)`** — the handler blocks on a deferred Promise. The card-correlator registers a `correlationId`, the state-channel publishes a snapshot containing the card, and the SSE stream ships it to subscribed clients. The handler resumes with `r.action` ∈ `'submit' | 'decline' | 'cancel'` and a Zod-validated `r.payload`. 2. **No client-side `renderToolCard` registry.** The chat surface (`PendingCardsBar`) reads `openCards` straight from the `state-snapshot` SSE and renders the appropriate component (`AskChoiceCard`, `InputCard`) keyed off `presentation.kind`. There’s nothing per-tool to register — adding a new card-emitting tool just calls `ctx.askUser`; no client code changes. 3. **Persistence** — `state-snapshot` payloads are in-process for the run’s lifetime + a 5-min reconnect window. Past 5 min the snapshot GCs. The handler’s *return value* (after `ctx.askUser` resolves) is persisted as a normal `assistant` turn in `operator_turns` if the caller is an LLM agent. 4. **Voice modality** — voice surfaces don’t render cards. If a card-emitting tool runs during a voice turn, the operator-converse SSE forwarder appends each card’s `fallbackText` to the spoken response (gated on `body.modality === 'voice'` to prevent cross-conversation leak). Voice users still can’t *send* a structured `/card-response` payload — they’d have to click via the chat surface. See [Voice modality → Cards on voice](./voice-modality.mdx#cards-on-voice--fallbacktext). 5. **Naming** — use the `chat:` namespace for tools whose only purpose is to ask via card (e.g. `chat:ask_choice`, plus future siblings like a hypothetical `chat:ask_text`). Today `chat:ask_choice` is the only shipped card-emitting tool; free-text input isn’t a distinct server tool — it rides the `InputCard` presentation kind of an ask\_choice-style card. `ui:` namespace is for browser-control side-effect tools (`ui:dispatch`) that don’t produce a server return value. 6. **Reserved event name** — `'card'` is rejected at register time (`registerProjectedTool` throws). Plugins cannot intercept the askUser flow by declaring `events: { card: ... }`. ## Where the model is *not* the right answer [Section titled “Where the model is not the right answer”](#where-the-model-is-not-the-right-answer) * **Bidirectional audio streams** (voice WSS, agent ↔ user mid-call audio). Those go through the ElevenLabs Conv AI integration, not the endpoint system. The `(input, ctx) → ToolResult` shape *does* support mid-run question/answer via `ctx.askUser` (server publishes a card on the state channel; the handler awaits a deferred until the user clicks) and LLM token streams via `ctx.emit`. What it does NOT support is a long-lived bidirectional audio/binary channel — those need WebRTC or raw WebSockets. * **File uploads >5MB.** The dispatcher is JSON-in / JSON-or-SSE-out. Multipart isn’t wired. * **Browser-state actions.** Things like “expand left panel” or “set voice mode.” Those don’t have a server-side function to project; they’re client commands. Use `ui:dispatch` instead. * **Anything that needs a real bearer principal *and* is callable by spawned agents.** Today, agents pass URL spawn context — no bearer. The HMAC-signed URL scheme provides workspace/role attribution but doesn’t carry an enforceable capability set. If a tool genuinely needs principal-bound capabilities and agent-callability, that’s separate auth work.

# Gating

> The ordered gates every tool call runs through — signature, default-deny, roles, capabilities, capability-envelope, RBAC, harness, quota, resource authorization, declarative preconditions, timeout — and the error codes they emit.

## The gates, in order [Section titled “The gates, in order”](#the-gates-in-order) Every projected tool call runs through `tryBuildSpawnContext` → `dispatchProjectedTool` and faces these gates in order. The first one that fails short-circuits with the matching error code. The dispatch-stack gates are defined once in `DEFAULT_DISPATCH_STACK` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts`); signature verification runs earlier, in `tryBuildSpawnContext`. 
```plaintext
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 0. Signature verification (per-spawn)           │  → request_rejected: spawn_sig_<reason>
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Default-deny (opt-in; off by default)        │  → ungated (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Role allowlist (agent role vs tool.roles)    │  → role_not_allowed (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Capability check (principal capabilities)    │  → unauthorized (401) | missing_capability (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. Capability envelope (per-role "may at all")  │  → capability_denied (enforce mode only)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5. RBAC role requirement (tool.requireRoles)    │  → missing_role (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 6. Harness-required gate                        │  → harness_required (400)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 7. Per-window quota                             │  → quota_exceeded (429)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 8. Resource authorization (tool.authorize)      │  → authorization_denied (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 9. Declarative preconditions (tool.requires)    │  → precondition_failed (412)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 10. Per-tool timeout (during execution)         │  → timeout (504)
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
 If every gate passes, the function runs. Whatever it returns or throws is recorded with one of the post-execution statuses (`ok`, `error`, `timeout`). Gates **1, 5, 8** and the **authorization audit trail** are the [RFC tooldef-auth](/internal/docs/spec/plan-format) layer: a fail-closed default-deny posture, declarative RBAC roles, resource-level “can THIS principal act on THIS resource”, and an audit event for every authz decision. Gate **4** (capability envelope) is the [agent-capability-confinement](/internal/docs/spec/plan-format) layer (B-06 / P-012). Gates 0, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 are the original coarse checks. Each is detailed below. ## Signature verification (gate 0) [Section titled “Signature verification (gate 0)”](#signature-verification-gate-0) Before any other gate fires, the dispatcher verifies the per-spawn URL’s HMAC signature. A worker that rewrites `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` produces an `invalid_signature` and is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_invalid_signature`. The attempt is persisted to `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` for on-call review. This check is **not** wired into `tools/list` — listing returns what the *claimed* role would see, so an agent can introspect what tools exist before invoking. Verification happens at `tools/call`. The `?superuser=1` door bypasses this check entirely; it has its own loopback + bearer envelope. See [Superuser mode](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/superuser-mode). Full scheme, reason codes, rotation, and observability live in [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing). ## Default-deny (gate 1) [Section titled “Default-deny (gate 1)”](#default-deny-gate-1) A **fail-closed posture**: when the host sets `deps.defaultDeny`, a tool that declares **no gate at all** — no capabilities, no agent `roles`, no `requireRoles`, no `authorize` hook — is denied as `ungated` (403) unless it is explicitly marked `public: true` (the `[AllowAnonymous]` equivalent). The *engine* default is off (the legacy allow-by-omission posture), but **the Papercusp host turns it ON** — `PROJECTED_DEPS` in `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts` sets `defaultDeny: true` (audited 2026-05-31). It currently denies nothing registered, because every first-party `defineTool` (which *requires* a `capability`) and every bundled plugin tool already declares a gate; it’s the fail-closed floor for a future / third-party tool that forgets to. It is **not bypassable** by `GateBypass` — an ungated tool is a declaration gap regardless of caller, so the fix is to declare a gate or mark it `public`. `defineTool` *requires* a `capability`, so every first-party built-in tool already declares a gate and is never `ungated`. The posture exists to catch plugin / direct `registerProjectedTool` registrations that forgot to gate themselves. Since `defaultDeny` is already on, re-verify before/after installing a plugin by running `listUngatedProjectedTools()` (with the full registry loaded) — an empty result means nothing is silently denied; anything it returns must declare a gate or be marked `public`. ## Role allowlist (gate 2) [Section titled “Role allowlist (gate 2)”](#role-allowlist-gate-2) Tools declare `roles[]` — the **agent**-role allowlist (worker / scoper / architect / …), checked against `ctx.role` from the URL spawn param. This is orchestration gating, distinct from the RBAC role requirement below. 
```jsonc
{
  "roles": ["worker", "scoper", "architect"]
}
```
 A `validator` calling this tool gets: 
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "role_not_allowed",
    "message": "Role \"validator\" cannot call tool \"plugin.tool\" (allowed roles: worker, scoper, architect)"
  }
}
```
 HTTP status: 403. The check only runs when *both* `tool.roles` and `ctx.role` are set, and is skipped when `GateBypass.role` is set. Tools without `tool.roles` skip this check. ## Capability check (gate 3) [Section titled “Capability check (gate 3)”](#capability-check-gate-3) Built-in tools declare a single capability string per tool. When a request arrives with a bearer token, the framework resolves it to a principal with a `Set<string>` of granted capabilities. The dispatcher checks `tool.capabilities[]` ⊆ `principal.capabilities`. Two distinct failure modes: * **No principal at all** (no bearer or invalid bearer) → `unauthorized` (401). The wrapper around legacy `defineTool` handlers throws `UnauthorizedToolError`; the dispatcher catches it and maps to 401. * **Principal present but missing the required capability** → `missing_capability` (403). The check is skipped when there is no principal (the agent path gates via the role allowlist instead) or when `GateBypass.capability` is set. Plugin tools have `capabilities[]` declared too, but they’re descriptive-only today — used by the Intel UI and tooling, not enforced. ## Capability envelope (gate 4) [Section titled “Capability envelope (gate 4)”](#capability-envelope-gate-4) A cheap, static, **per-role “may this caller do X *at all*”** gate (agent-capability-confinement B-06 / P-012). It runs right after the capability check (both are cheap capability gates) and before the costlier RBAC / authorize / precondition gates. Unlike gate 3 (which asks “does this principal hold the capability”), the envelope asks “is this tool even *inside* the envelope of what this role is ever allowed to reach”. It is **host-supplied** through `deps.checkCapabilityEnvelope` and is a **no-op when unwired** (no port ⇒ behavior-neutral). Papercusp wires it via `PROJECTED_DEPS.checkCapabilityEnvelope`, but it is in **OBSERVE / shadow mode by default** today: the `CAPABILITY_ENVELOPE` flag defaults to **off** (`libs/flags/src/types.ts`), which means *observe-only* — the evaluator runs and annotates the decision-ledger posture but **never blocks**. Enforcement only begins when the flag is flipped on (the B-18 arming act). * **Within envelope** → `allow`, pass. * **Beyond envelope, flag off (default)** → `observe` — logged/annotated, call proceeds. * **Beyond envelope, flag on** → `deny` with error code `capability_denied`. * **Evaluator throws** → **fail-open** (`return null`, call proceeds) — the OS sandbox is the containment backstop, so an evaluator bug must never wedge the fleet (matches the quota gate’s fail-open-on-error posture). * **Exempt callers** — SU / power-user / non-fleet / roleless principals are exempt; the evaluator returns no verdict and the gate no-ops. Note the HTTP mapping caveat: `capability_denied` has **no explicit case** in `statusForErrorCode`, so over HTTP it currently falls through to the default **500** (see the table below) — likely itself a defect, since it is a 403-class authz denial. ## RBAC role requirement (gate 5) [Section titled “RBAC role requirement (gate 5)”](#rbac-role-requirement-gate-5) A tool declaring `requireRoles` is callable only by a principal whose **RBAC `roles`** (`principal.roles`) include at least **one** of them (any-of). This is the typed, declarative, audited replacement for ad-hoc `requireAdminKey` / `requireStaff`-style checks. 
```jsonc
{ "requireRoles": ["staff", "admin"] }   // caller must hold staff OR admin
```
 `principal.roles` is a **distinct axis** from `kind` (how the caller authenticated), from `capabilities` (OAuth-scope-like grants), and from the agent `roles` allowlist above (which is checked against `ctx.role`, not the principal). * **Principal holds a required role** → pass. * **Principal lacks every required role, or there is no principal (anonymous)** → `missing_role` (403). The gate is **fail-closed**: a role requirement can’t be satisfied without an identity. * Skipped when `GateBypass.role` is set — a superuser passes RBAC role gates as it passes the agent-role allowlist. Every denial emits an authorization audit event (see below). ## Harness-required gate (gate 6) [Section titled “Harness-required gate (gate 6)”](#harness-required-gate-gate-6) A tool declaring `harness: 'required'` (a ctx-only harness-scoped tool — one with no slug arg, so `ctx.harnessSlug` is its only harness source) is rejected with `harness_required` (400) when no harness is in scope. “No harness in scope” means `ctx.harnessSlug` is unset/empty **or** the literal `'*'` wildcard sentinel — the superuser “no harness picked” case (a harness that is present-but-unselected), not only a missing slug (`if (slug && slug !== '*') return null`). This gate **fails closed even for privileged callers** by default, because a `harness: 'required'` tool genuinely can’t function without a harness; the point is to return the uniform “harness required” hint rather than push the failure into the handler. There is a narrow explicit dispatcher escape hatch, `GateBypass.harness`, but the normal superuser/power-user mapping does not set it. ## Per-window quota (gate 7) [Section titled “Per-window quota (gate 7)”](#per-window-quota-gate-7) A window is a counter scoped by `(workspace, tool, role, window_key)` against `harness_shared.tool_invocations`. The window key depends on role (the Papercusp policy in `packages/agent-mcp/src/quota-policy.ts`, wired via `PROJECTED_DEPS.computeQuotaWindow`): * **Worker** → `chunk:<chunkId>` (resets per chunk; capped by `perChunk`) * **Power-user session** (`?power_user=1`) → `power-user:<uiClientId>` (the `auth_session_id`; capped by `perRun`) — a power-user MCP call gets a fresh `runId` per request, so a run-keyed window would never accumulate; it keys on the stable session instead. * **Anyone else** → `run:<runId>` (resets per orchestrator run; capped by `perRun`) `tool_invocations` rows that count against quota have `status='ok'` only. Failures (`error`, `timeout`, `quota-exceeded`, `role-not-allowed`) don’t consume a slot, so a tool that returns 500 doesn’t burn the budget. Manifest declares the limit per role: 
```jsonc
{
  "rolesQuota": {
    "worker":    { "perChunk": 1 },
    "architect": { "perRun": 5 },
    "scoper":    { "perRun": 3 }
  }
}
```
 When a call exceeds, the dispatcher returns: 
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "quota_exceeded",
    "message": "Tool \"plugin.tool\" exceeded quota (1/1) in window \"chunk:Q1\"",
    "meta": { "tool": "plugin.tool", "role": "worker", "windowKey": "chunk:Q1", "used": 1, "limit": 1 }
  }
}
```
 HTTP status: 429. Skipped when `GateBypass.quota` is set. ### Quota under concurrency [Section titled “Quota under concurrency”](#quota-under-concurrency) Five simultaneous requests with `perChunk=1` produce one ok and four `quota-exceeded`. This holds in practice because Node’s event loop serializes through the JS code paths and the first INSERT lands before the others reach `readQuotaState`. There is a theoretical TOCTOU window: all five readers could see `count=0` before any of them inserts. Closing this rigorously would require a PG advisory lock or `INSERT ... RETURNING` with a check constraint. Today the soft guarantee is good enough for the workloads the framework handles. If you have a tool where a one-call-over-quota bug is catastrophic, file an issue. ### Don’t quota reads [Section titled “Don’t quota reads”](#dont-quota-reads) Read-only tools (`roles:list`, `snapshots:get`) shouldn’t have a `rolesQuota`. Quotas exist for: external API spend, PG write bursts, subprocess fan-out. Counting every read produces noise without protection. ## Resource authorization (gate 8) [Section titled “Resource authorization (gate 8)”](#resource-authorization-gate-8) The coarse gates above answer “may this *kind* of caller use this tool”. The `authorize` hook answers the **fine-grained** question the others can’t express: “may THIS principal act on THIS *resource*” (ownership / ReBAC / ABAC). 
```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'orders:get',
  capability: 'orders:read',
  authorize: ({ principal, input }) =>
    input.ownerId === principal?.slug
      ? { allow: true }
      : { allow: false, reason: 'not the owner' },
  // …
});
```
 It runs **after** the coarse gates and **before** the handler, **fail-closed** (a throw denies → `authorization_denied`), and is **additive** — a tool with no `authorize` skips this gate entirely. Because it runs in-process with the tool’s `ctx`, it can load the resource it needs to decide (“authorize close to the data”) and can return `obligations` (e.g. a row filter) for list endpoints rather than checking each row. The framework is the **policy-enforcement point**; it ships the contract (`AuthzQuery` / `AuthDecision` / `PolicyDecisionPoint`, plus a trivial `ownerOnly` helper) and **no policy engine** — the decision is the host’s, supplied as an in-process closure or by delegating to an external PDP (OPA / Cedar / OpenFGA / Cerbos / an AuthZEN engine). ### Break-glass: `GateBypass.policy` [Section titled “Break-glass: GateBypass.policy”](#break-glass-gatebypasspolicy) Unlike the role/capability/quota bypasses, the resource-`authorize` gate is **not** skipped by them — resource ownership is a separate decision a host opts out of explicitly, per call, via `GateBypass.policy` (default off). And even then **the bypass is audited**: skipping the hook still emits an authz audit event recording the bypass. Break-glass best practice is “policy-governed *and* mandatorily logged” — a bypassed check that isn’t logged is the silent super-admin the standard forbids. ## Declarative preconditions (gate 9): `requires:` [Section titled “Declarative preconditions (gate 9): requires:”](#declarative-preconditions-gate-9-requires) The **preInvoke mirror of `emits:`** (autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05 D-006). A tool declares `requires: [ToolRequireSpec, …]` — each spec a declarative condition (a `@papercusp/rules` MatchMap / `all`/`any`/`not` combinator over `{ tool, args, ctx, state }`) that must **hold** for the call to proceed, plus a response when it doesn’t: * `{ error }` — **reject** the call with `precondition_failed`. * `{ fire, then: 'retry' }` — **auto-correct, visibly**: fire a corrective tool through the host’s injectable `deps.firePrecondition` port (Papercusp wires it to the same dispatch path reactions use — auth-gated, audited, cause-chained), re-resolve state, re-evaluate **once**, and reject if it still fails. 
```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'autoloop:status',
  // The former in-handler `if (!slug) throw` guard, lifted (the proof migration):
  requires: [{
    id: 'harness-slug',
    when: { any: [
      { 'args.harnessSlug': { truthy: true } },
      { 'ctx.harnessSlug':  { truthy: true } },
    ]},
    error: 'autoloop:status — harness slug required (passed or in spawn ctx)',
  }],
  // …
});
```
 Host state enters through the spec’s optional `state(args, ctx)` resolver (re-resolved before the retry); conditions are **declarative only** — there is deliberately no JS-predicate hatch here, because inspectability/serializability is the point of the lift. Everything fails **closed**: a throwing resolver, a malformed condition, a missing fire port, or a failed retry all deny. Denials and auto-corrections are audited with `gate: 'precondition'` through the same `deps.auditAuth` sink as gates 5/8 (first-try passes are not audited — they’re the overwhelmingly common case). It runs **after** `authorize` — a corrective fire must only happen for an authorized caller, and a functional gap must not mask an auth denial — and **before** `timeout` (it’s a gate; no timers or buffers exist yet on the deny path). **What belongs in `requires:`:** *functional* preconditions — an arg/scope shape the handler can’t proceed without, a resumable resource that a corrective fire can fix (the reject/auto-correct/delete choice is D-006’s safety-vs-convenience judgment: auto-correct ergonomic preconditions visibly; reject ones the caller must fix; delete artificial ones instead of migrating them). ### Safety invariants are EXCLUDED by design (D-007) [Section titled “Safety invariants are EXCLUDED by design (D-007)”](#safety-invariants-are-excluded-by-design-d-007) **`requires:` must never absorb a safety invariant.** The rule (autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild D-007): *the operator proposes, the gate disposes* — an agent gets maximal agency **inside** a small set of hard, coded guardrails it cannot reason past. A safety gate in a declarative rule table is a safety gate an agent (or a rule edit) can weaken; these stay imperative, fail-closed, audited **code**. The inventory (verified 2026-06-05): | Gate | Where (imperative code) | Audit sink | Bypass | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Don’t-deploy-on-red** | `apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts` (ready advances only on green) + `deploy-cli.ts` (refuses un-green targets) | coord broadcast per checkpoint/deploy | `--force` / `--deploy-commit` — loudly audited (`🚨 FORCED un-green deploy`) | | **Protected-paths** | `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/improvements/policy.ts` `classifyImprovement()` — glob patterns route protected surfaces to the human queue | tier decision in the improvements digest/queue | none (kind-graduation only widens `auto` kinds, never the protected paths) | | **Budget / quota caps** | `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/budget-enforcement.ts` (row-locked atomic budget check, fail-closed) + `orchestrator-loop.ts` `SAFETY_CEILING` (hard constant; blueprint `dispatch.safetyCeiling` may only tighten) + the quota gate (7) above | `tool_invocations` (quota); `BudgetExceededError` carries detail | quota: `GateBypass.quota`; budget/ceiling: none | | **Auth perimeter** | gates 0–5 + 8 above (`dispatch-stack.ts`, `tryBuildSpawnContext`) | `harness_shared.tool_authz_log` + `spawn_sig_verification_failures` | per-gate `GateBypass`, `policy` bypass audited | | **No-double-allocate** | `work-items.ts` atomic CAS (`UPDATE … WHERE taken_by IS NULL`), `orchestrator/feature-claim.ts` append-only claim log, `authority/lock-authority.ts` | `harness_shared.claim_audit` (won/lost/timeout/error) | none — atomic by construction | None of the five flows through `@papercusp/rules`, the event-reaction tables, or `requires:` — and that’s load-bearing, not an accident. When migrating a hardcoded guard to `requires:` (or a reaction to `emits:`), first ask: *is this gate’s failure mode harm?* If yes, it stays code. ## The authorization audit trail [Section titled “The authorization audit trail”](#the-authorization-audit-trail) Gates **5** (RBAC), **8** (authorize), and **9** (preconditions), plus every `GateBypass.policy` bypass, emit an `AuthAuditEvent` through the optional `deps.auditAuth` sink. What each emits differs: * **Gate 5 (RBAC role requirement)** audits **denials only** — the pass path returns without an emit; only the missing-role branch records `decision: 'deny'`. * **Gate 8 (authorize)** is the one that audits **every allow, deny, *and* bypass** — its allow path, deny path, and the `GateBypass.policy` break-glass all emit. * **Gate 9 (preconditions, `gate: 'precondition'`)** audits both **denials** and **successful auto-corrections** (the auto-correct allow on a `{ fire, then: 'retry' }` spec); first-try passes are not audited. The Papercusp host persists them to `harness_shared.tool_authz_log` (`packages/operator-core/lib/tool-authz-audit.ts`), a security-decision stream distinct from the login-scoped `auth_audit_log` and the per-call `tool_invocations` telemetry. It answers “show me every denial / every break-glass bypass / everything this principal was denied”. ## Per-tool timeout (gate 10) [Section titled “Per-tool timeout (gate 10)”](#per-tool-timeout-gate-10) Each manifest entry has `timeoutSec` (default 60). The dispatcher creates an `AbortController`, hands `controller.signal` to the function as `ctx.signal`, and aborts after the configured time. Functions doing long work should watch `ctx.signal.aborted` and bail. A timed-out call gets: 
```json
{
  "error": { "code": "timeout", "message": "tool \"plugin.tool\" exceeded timeout of 60s" }
}
```
 HTTP status: 504. The `tool_invocations` row records `status='timeout'`. ## The whole error code → HTTP status table [Section titled “The whole error code → HTTP status table”](#the-whole-error-code--http-status-table) For HTTP transport, `statusForErrorCode` in `libs/generic/tooldef-http/src/http-projection.ts` maps: | Error code | HTTP | Source | | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `ungated` | 403 | Default-deny on; tool declares no gate and isn’t `public` | | `unauthorized` | 401 | Built-in tool, no bearer / invalid bearer | | `role_not_allowed` | 403 | Agent role not in the tool’s allowlist | | `missing_capability` | 403 | Principal missing required capability | | `capability_denied` | 500 (no explicit case; falls to default) | Capability-envelope gate denied (enforce mode). The missing 403-class case means this authz denial is currently surfaced as a 500 over HTTP | | `missing_role` | 403 | Principal missing a required RBAC role (`requireRoles`) | | `harness_required` | 400 | `harness:'required'` tool with no harness in scope | | `quota_exceeded` | 429 | Window count ≥ limit | | `authorization_denied` | 403 | The tool’s `authorize` hook denied (or threw → fail-closed) | | `precondition_failed` | 412 | A declarative `requires:` precondition failed (after the auto-correct retry, when one was declared) | | `invalid_input` | 400 | Function threw a typed input-validation error | | `timeout` | 504 | AbortController fired before function returned | | `unknown_tool` | 404 | No projection registered at this path/name | | `method_not_allowed` | 405 | HTTP method not in `expose.http.methods` | | anything else | 500 | Function threw an unhandled error → `handler_error` | For MCP transport, errors are returned as a normal `tools/call` result with `isError: true` and a `content[].text` describing the error. There’s no JSON-RPC-level rejection — the MCP spec puts tool errors in the result envelope. ## A worked example [Section titled “A worked example”](#a-worked-example) Here’s what happens when a `worker` tries to call `firecrawl.scrape` with `chunk=Q1` for the second time: 1. **Default-deny.** On in Papercusp (`defaultDeny: true`), but `firecrawl.scrape` declares a role allowlist, so it’s gated → pass. 2. **Role check.** `firecrawl.scrape.roles = [scoper, architect, operator, reviewer, debugger, worker]`. Worker is in. Pass. 3. **Capability check.** Plugin tool — no principal — skipped. 4. **Capability envelope.** `CAPABILITY_ENVELOPE` flag off (default) → observe mode: the evaluator may annotate the decision-ledger posture but never blocks → pass. 5. **RBAC role requirement.** No `requireRoles` → skip. 6. **Harness gate.** Not `harness:'required'` → skip. 7. **Quota check.** Window `chunk:Q1`, role `worker`. Manifest says `worker: { perChunk: 2 }`. Read state: `count=1` (the first call already landed as ok). 1 < 2, pass. 8. **Resource authorization.** No `authorize` hook → skip. 9. **Preconditions.** No `requires:` declared → skip. 10. **Timeout.** AbortController set to 60s. 11. **Execute + record.** `scrape` runs, completes in 800ms; insert `tool_invocations` row with `status='ok', duration_ms=800`. Same call a third time: gates 1–6 pass/skip as before, then the quota check reads `count=2`, `2 ≥ 2`, **fails**, inserts a quota-exceeded row, returns 429 with `message: "Tool \"firecrawl.scrape\" exceeded quota (2/2) in window \"chunk:Q1\""` (the role lives in `meta`, not the message). ## Where the dispatcher lives [Section titled “Where the dispatcher lives”](#where-the-dispatcher-lives) `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts` defines `DEFAULT_DISPATCH_STACK` — the one ordered list these checks run in; `dispatch-projected.ts` drives it. If you find yourself wanting to add a custom gate inside a tool function, you’re probably making a mistake. The dispatcher is the canonical place for cross-cutting concerns.

# Operations

> Day-to-day workflows for the endpoint system. Hot reload, host refresh, common failure modes, and when to stop and ask.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`. ## After every plugin manifest or handler edit [Section titled “After every plugin manifest or handler edit”](#after-every-plugin-manifest-or-handler-edit) 
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/host/refresh
```
 The projection registry is module-level state. HMR is unreliable for it. If you don’t refresh after editing a plugin, you’re testing stale code and you won’t know. The endpoint returns the host status: 
```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "status": {
    "loaded": 15,
    "errors": 2,
    "plugins": [...],
    "loadErrors": [...]
  }
}
```
 `errors=2` is the steady-state baseline (two unrelated pre-existing manifest issues). If you push a change and `errors` goes up, your edit broke discovery — read the `loadErrors[]` list. ## Where the registry lives [Section titled “Where the registry lives”](#where-the-registry-lives) Three module-level Maps in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts`: * `REGISTRY` — keyed by `mcp:<name>` or `http:<path>`, value is the full `ProjectedTool` * `BY_MCP_NAME` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for `tools/call` lookups * `BY_HTTP_PATH` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for the catch-all routes These are populated at startup as a side effect of: 1. Importing `@papercusp/agent-mcp` — every `defineTool(...)` auto-registers into the registry (PR 0c.D extension). 2. The first call to `getPluginHost()` — runs `loadPlugins({ projectDir, harnessSlugs, globalPluginsDir })`, then `registerPluginTools(loaded)` walks each plugin’s `toolDefinitions[]` and calls `registerProjectedTool` per entry. `registerPluginTools` is **idempotent** for same-plugin re-registration: it calls `unregisterProjectedToolsForPlugin(pluginName)` first, then re-registers. This means `/api/plugins/host/refresh` works correctly without producing collision errors. **Cross-plugin collisions still throw** — two different plugins claiming the same MCP name fails with `ToolRegistrationError`. ## Discovery sources [Section titled “Discovery sources”](#discovery-sources) `loadPlugins` searches in this order: 1. `<projectDir>/plugins/<name>/` — for in-repo bundled plugins. The operator wires this via `findBundledPluginsParent()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts`. In dev, `projectDir` isn’t an arbitrary repo root: `findBundledPluginsParent()` walks up looking for `libs/papercusp/plugins` and returns `libs/papercusp` itself, so source #1 is concretely `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`. In installed builds where that path doesn’t exist it returns `null` and this source is skipped. 2. `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugins/<name>/` — per-harness plugins. 3. `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/<name>/` — globally installed plugins. Dedupe by `plugin.name` with priority `project > harness > global`. So if you have both `libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/` and `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/repomix/`, the in-repo one wins. This is why you don’t need to symlink plugins into `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/` during development. Just put them in `libs/papercusp/plugins/` and they’ll be discovered. ## Hot-reload watcher [Section titled “Hot-reload watcher”](#hot-reload-watcher) `watchPluginsForReload` (in `plugin-host-runtime.ts`) sets up a debounced fs.watch over the global-plugins directory. The match regex is `/papercusp\.json$|\/index\.(?:m?js|ts)$|\/dist\/index\.js$/`, so it triggers on changes to `papercusp.json`, `index.js`, `index.mjs`, `index.ts`, or `dist/index.js`. On a hit, it calls `_resetPluginHostForTests()` which clears the host cache; next request to the host re-runs discovery. **Gotcha:** a compiled `index.cjs` entry is **not** matched (the regex covers `index.js`/`.mjs`/`.ts` and `dist/index.js`, but not `.cjs`). Editing a `.cjs` entry won’t trigger auto-reload — POST `/api/plugins/host/refresh` manually. It’s gated behind `PAPERCUSP_DEV_PLUGIN_WATCH=1`. Off by default because filesystem-watch overhead is unwanted on shared hosts. Turn it on for plugin development if you don’t want to keep curling `/api/plugins/host/refresh`. ## Migrations on the system PG [Section titled “Migrations on the system PG”](#migrations-on-the-system-pg) The embedded-postgres-server has a migration runner that walks `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/*.sql` on boot and applies missing files via `harness_shared.schema_migrations`. The native system PG (`localhost:5432`) **used to have no equivalent boot hook** — every new SQL file required a manual `psql -f` plus a manual `schema_migrations` INSERT, and a missed migration could silently go dark. That gap is closed: `applyPendingMigrationsAtBoot()` (`packages/operator-core/lib/db-boot-migrate.ts`) now runs the **same idempotent runner** against the operator’s admin DB on host boot. It’s wired into `apps/operator/bin/host-bootstrap.ts` and **awaited before the boot-gate flips**, so a new SQL file is auto-applied on the next operator restart on the native box. Two caveats: * **It runs only on the primary host.** The boot apply sits inside the `PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS`-gated block. A secondary host (`PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=0`) **skips** boot migrations entirely — so if you’re on a secondary host, a brand-new migration may still need manual application. * **It’s log-and-continue, not fail-loud.** A migration that fails to apply is logged + coord-broadcast and left pending (retried next boot) rather than halting the shared dev-api. So a broken migration won’t wedge boot — but it also won’t have applied. Manual application is the fallback when auto-apply hasn’t happened (you don’t want to restart, or you’re on a secondary host): 
```bash
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -f libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/048-my-table.sql


PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -tAc "SELECT to_regclass('harness_shared.my_table')"
```
 If your tool depends on a table that doesn’t exist, the queries throw, the dispatcher catches and continues, the tool returns 200 with `output` text — and your quota tracking + telemetry are silently dead until the migration applies. **Verify with `to_regclass` before testing the tool.** ## Common failure modes [Section titled “Common failure modes”](#common-failure-modes) ### Tool returns 404 `unknown_tool` after a manifest edit [Section titled “Tool returns 404 unknown\_tool after a manifest edit”](#tool-returns-404-unknown_tool-after-a-manifest-edit) You forgot to refresh. `curl -X POST /api/plugins/host/refresh`. Or HMR wiped the registry. Same fix. ### Tool returns 200 but `tool_invocations` is empty [Section titled “Tool returns 200 but tool\_invocations is empty”](#tool-returns-200-but-tool_invocations-is-empty) Two likely causes: 1. **Workspace GUC not set.** The HOST\_EXTRAS.deps insert calls `SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)` — but if the request didn’t include `?workspace=<id>`, `ctx.workspaceId` is `undefined`, and the insert silently fails. Make sure the test request has the workspace param. 2. **Migration not applied.** The table doesn’t exist. See above. ### Tool returns 500 `handler_error` [Section titled “Tool returns 500 handler\_error”](#tool-returns-500-handler_error) The function threw an unhandled error. Check the `tool_invocations.error_message` for that call. If the message is `spawn <bin> ENOENT`, the binary isn’t installed on the machine running the operator (e.g. `code2prompt` not present in dev). Either install it or skip that tool. ### Tool returns 401 `unauthorized` for a tool you expected to work without bearer [Section titled “Tool returns 401 unauthorized for a tool you expected to work without bearer”](#tool-returns-401-unauthorized-for-a-tool-you-expected-to-work-without-bearer) You wrote a built-in (`defineTool(...)`) when you needed a plugin. Built-ins require `ctx.principal`; agents over MCP only have URL spawn context, no bearer. Move the tool to `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`. ### `/api/plugins/host/refresh` shows error count > 2 [Section titled “/api/plugins/host/refresh shows error count > 2”](#apipluginshostrefresh-shows-error-count--2) Something in your manifest broke discovery. The response body has `loadErrors[]` — read it. Common causes: `name` collision with an existing tool from a different plugin; `expose.mcp.name` missing the namespace separator (must contain `.` or `:`); orphan handler (manifest declares `tools[].name = 'foo'` but `index.ts` has no `tools.foo` export). ### Tool works on MCP but returns “ctx.X is unset” on HTTP [Section titled “Tool works on MCP but returns “ctx.X is unset” on HTTP”](#tool-works-on-mcp-but-returns-ctxx-is-unset-on-http) The HTTP catch-all needs the same `ctx.spawn` / `ctx.secret` / `ctx.projectDir` resolvers as MCP. Check that the plugins catch-all (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts`) builds its `HttpToolHostExtras` with `spawn` (`pluginSpawnImpl`), `secret` (`secretImpl`/`makeSecretResolver`), and `resolveHarnessPaths`. If it doesn’t, that’s a regression of audit-2/3 fixes. ### Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don’t see it [Section titled “Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don’t see it”](#tool-works-on-dev-but-agents-in-spawned-subprocesses-dont-see-it) Check the orchestrator’s `.mcp.json` URL. In dev (`NODE_ENV=development`) it should point at `http://localhost:3055/api/sse`; in prod, `http://localhost:3070/api/sse`. Override with `PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_URL` if neither default applies. ### Search-provider env vars don’t reach spawned agents [Section titled “Search-provider env vars don’t reach spawned agents”](#search-provider-env-vars-dont-reach-spawned-agents) The orchestrator’s `invoke()` path (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`) decrypts search-provider keys from PG via `buildSearchProviderSpawnEnv` (`spawn-env-from-pg.ts`) and attaches them to `InvokeContext.extraSpawnEnv`. They land in every `invoke()` call’s spawn env. The operator harness-launch path does this independently: `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-launch.ts` calls `buildSpawnEnv` from `packages/operator-core/lib/search-provider-credentials.ts`. Both paths are wired; if a worker doesn’t see `TAVILY_API_KEY` etc., the keys aren’t in PG (check `harness_shared.operator_search_provider_credentials`) or the encryption key is missing (`~/.papercusp/db-encryption-key`). ## Spawn-signing admin endpoints [Section titled “Spawn-signing admin endpoints”](#spawn-signing-admin-endpoints) The HMAC signing scheme (see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing)) ships with two admin routes for incident response and observability. Both are gated `auth: { trust: ['trusted'] }` — the gate is the **trust tier**, not the bearer specifically. The documented loopback + superuser-bearer is the canonical way an operator obtains a `trusted` principal (a valid superuser bearer on a loopback request resolves to `kind: 'system'`, `trust: 'trusted'`), but any other `trusted` principal (e.g. a process-internal/system caller) also passes the gate. ### Rotate the signing key [Section titled “Rotate the signing key”](#rotate-the-signing-key) 
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```
 Rotates the PG row **and** bumps the operator’s in-process cache. Every in-flight signed URL fails its next call with `invalid_signature`. The orchestrator must re-spawn affected workers. Wrapper script: `bun run rotate:spawn-key`. ### Read the verification audit log [Section titled “Read the verification audit log”](#read-the-verification-audit-log) 
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl "http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/failures?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```
 Query params: `limit` (max 1000, default 100), `since` (ISO timestamp), `reason` (filter). Returns `{ rows, summary: { byReason, window } }`. A non-zero rate of `invalid_signature` outside explicit test runs is a real signal. Correlate `claimed_spawn` with orchestrator spawn IDs to identify the culprit. ## When to stop and ask [Section titled “When to stop and ask”](#when-to-stop-and-ask) You should stop and ask before doing any of these: * The component you want to wrap doesn’t fit one of the four shipped plugin shapes (subprocess single-tool, HTTP+optional-secret, subprocess multi-tool, HTTP+required-secret-with-schema). Don’t invent a fifth shape; the function-as-truth design doc lists which patterns are blessed. * You want to extend the manifest contract with a new field. Each existing field corresponds to a dispatcher behavior; adding one is an architecture decision, not a cleanup. * You hit one of the known open issues and need to work around it. The workaround usually masks a real bug — better to surface it and get the framework fix. * The handler signature you’d want isn’t `(input, ctx) => ToolResult`. The framework can’t accommodate exotic shapes. If you want a callback-based contract, a multi-response stream, or anything else non-request/response, it doesn’t belong here. * You’re tempted to delete a route a UI surface still fetches from. **Always grep for UI callers first.** The legacy Next app-router routes are gone — `apps/operator/app/api` is now an empty leftover directory with no `route.ts` files anywhere under `apps/operator`; everything is now a `defineTool` route under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes`, served at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`. The migration is complete, but the rule stands for any route you’re about to remove: switch UI URLs in the same PR, and delete only when zero callers remain. ## Per-tool migration checklist [Section titled “Per-tool migration checklist”](#per-tool-migration-checklist) When you’re moving an existing route to the endpoint system, run through this list. Each step is mandatory; skip any and you ship a broken tool: 1. Grep for UI callers of the legacy route. Decide replace-with-redirect or full-delete. 2. If new PG schema, write the SQL file in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/` and apply it manually. 3. Write the typed function with no transport awareness. 4. Write the manifest entry. JSON Schema directly. No `zodToJsonSchema`. 5. `curl` the HTTP transport. Verify status code + body shape. 6. `curl` the MCP transport. Verify the same. 7. `psql` the telemetry row. Verify `status='ok'` and `app.workspace_id` was set. 8. Quota smoke test: fire perChunk+1 → second is 429. 9. Role gate smoke test: wrong role → 403. 10. `curl /api/plugins/host/refresh`. Confirm error count unchanged. 11. Delete the legacy route in the same commit (only if step 1 said zero UI callers). 12. Submodule commit first if you touched `libs/papercusp/`, then bump the parent’s submodule pointer in a second commit. ## Per-turn commit discipline [Section titled “Per-turn commit discipline”](#per-turn-commit-discipline) When you’re working across the operator app and the `libs/papercusp/` submodule: * Commit the submodule first. * Bump the parent’s submodule pointer in a second commit. Otherwise the parent commit references a submodule SHA that isn’t pushed and the next agent sees a broken checkout. This is observed-from-experience guidance; multiple agents have shipped half-broken trees by inverting the order.

# Overview

> One function, three transports — what the endpoint system is and why we built it this way.

## The one-line version [Section titled “The one-line version”](#the-one-line-version) You write **one typed function**. The framework projects it onto: * An **HTTP route** at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` (or `/api/agent-tools/<tool>` for built-ins) * An **MCP `tools/call` entry** under `<plugin>.<tool>` (or `<scope>:<verb>` for built-ins) * An **in-process call** any TypeScript caller can `await` directly You declare exposure, role allowlist, capabilities, and quotas in a manifest. The framework handles auth gating, role enforcement, quota windows, telemetry persistence, streaming progress, and per-spawn URL context — none of which you write per tool. ## Why “endpoint system” not “MCP migration” [Section titled “Why “endpoint system” not “MCP migration””](#why-endpoint-system-not-mcp-migration) The first instinct was to call this an MCP migration. That framing is wrong. **The function is the source of truth.** HTTP and MCP are projections of it. Once a function is decoupled from any specific transport, all three callers — your dashboard, an AI agent over MCP, another module in the same Node process — get it for free, with the same auth/role/quota/telemetry behavior. The hard part isn’t writing the MCP wrapper. The hard part is pulling a function out of its current transport-coupled form so that the wrapper *can be* generated. The “MCP-callable” part is the smallest-and-easiest consequence of that decoupling. ## What this gets you [Section titled “What this gets you”](#what-this-gets-you) * **No duplicated route+handler code.** A new feature is one typed function plus six lines of manifest. Both the dashboard and the agent get it. * **Single test surface.** You test the function. Both transports inherit correct behavior because they both go through the same dispatcher. * **Uniform observability.** Every invocation lands in `harness_shared.tool_invocations` with role, window key, status, duration, output size — regardless of transport. You can answer “which agents called which tools when” without per-route instrumentation. * **Uniform gating.** Role allowlist, capability check, and per-window quota all enforce in the same dispatcher. Adding a new sensitive tool means setting `roles: ["operator"]` + `rolesQuota: { operator: { perRun: 5 } }` and you’re done. * **Stream-or-not, no rewrite.** A function that calls `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` automatically gets MCP `notifications/progress` events on the MCP transport and SSE events on the HTTP transport. No transport-specific wiring. * **Token-efficient by default.** A function returns structured `data`; the dispatcher serializes it in the most compact format the data’s shape allows (TOON for arrays, lossless JSON otherwise) — agents read ≈ −20–35% fewer tokens on list results with no change to how they call. Declaring `result: <schema>` unlocks CSV + MCP `outputSchema` advertisement. See [Transports → Result formats](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/transports). ## What this is not [Section titled “What this is not”](#what-this-is-not) * Not a replacement for SSE chat, WebSocket voice, or anything else that holds a long-lived bidirectional connection. Those stay on dedicated routes; the endpoint system is for request → response (with optional streamed progress). * Not a way to expose your dashboard to the public internet. The trust model is **loopback bind + HMAC-signed per-spawn URL params** (see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing)), suitable for local dev + Tauri desktop. Off-loopback exposure needs a real principal/auth layer in front, since same-UID code can still read the signing key from PG. * Not a generic RPC framework. The contract is narrow on purpose: `(input, ctx) => ToolResult`. Trying to make it accommodate exotic shapes (callbacks, multi-response, file uploads >5MB) defeats the point of having one function as truth. ## The route projection — `defineTool` also defines plumbing [Section titled “The route projection — defineTool also defines plumbing”](#the-route-projection--definetool-also-defines-plumbing) Not every endpoint is an agent tool. The browser, the desktop shell, an orchestrator, a webhook — they call **routes**: HTTP plumbing that must *not* appear in the agent tool catalog. `defineTool` produces those too. `defineTool` accepts a **route-shaped** input — discriminated by the `method` field — and returns a `RouteDefinition` instead of a `ToolDefinition`: 
```ts
defineTool({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/desktop/version',
  auth: 'public',                    // or a PrincipalRequirements gate
  input: z.object({ verbose: z.coerce.boolean().optional() }), // optional
  handler(req, ctx) {                // Web-standard Request in, Response out
    return Response.json({ version: '…' });
  },
});
```
 A route runs through the same cross-cutting machinery — auth, input validation, timeout, telemetry, uniform errors — but it is **not** projected onto the MCP catalog. `tools/list` never sees it; an agent cannot call it. That guarantee is what keeps plumbing out of the agent surface. Two route-level knobs tune that machinery. A route defaults to a **30s wall-clock timeout** — a wedged handler aborts; pass `timeoutSec: null` to disable the watchdog for long-lived SSE/streaming routes whose handler legitimately outlives any fixed budget. Telemetry defaults to `sampleRate: 1` (record every call); lower it (`0..1`) for high-frequency polled routes, or set `0` to never record. Route files import `defineTool` directly — the former `defineRoute` alias was **removed** when the primitives were unified (Phase E6, `endpoint-unification-2026-05-21`). A route is *declared* with `defineTool` and *mounted* host-side by `registerRoute` (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/`). ### Paired-phone routes — `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` + `cors` [Section titled “Paired-phone routes — auth: { kind: \['device'\] } + cors”](#paired-phone-routes--auth--kind-device---cors) A route reachable from the paired phone declares the device-JWT auth gate and opts into cross-origin reachability — there is no implicit folding: 
```ts
defineTool({
  method: 'POST', path: '/device/heartbeat',
  auth: { kind: ['device'] },        // gate on the device-JWT principal
  cors: true,                        // CORS allowlist (paired-device + tauri + localhost)
  handler(req, ctx) { /* ctx.principal is the device */ },
});
```
 `cors: true` mounts the shared CORS middleware (OPTIONS preflight + headers); `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` makes the route-stack reject anything that doesn’t resolve to a device principal. Paired-phone routes live under `/api/device/*`. Built-in tools are reachable from the phone for free — the device JWT is a bearer token, and the `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all resolves it like any other. ## Two channels at a glance [Section titled “Two channels at a glance”](#two-channels-at-a-glance) A tool handler has two outbound channels available, projected uniformly across transports: | Channel | API | Wire | Replay on reconnect | | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | | **Events** | `ctx.emit('name', payload)`, `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` | typed SSE events / MCP notifications | Ring buffer (T2.2), bounded by `replayBufferSize` | | **State** | `ctx.askUser(spec)`, `ctx.publishState(snapshot)` | `state-snapshot` SSE on `/api/operator/state-snapshot` | Current snapshot only — replay does not re-prompt | Cards (`ctx.askUser`) and tool state (`ctx.publishState`) live on the state channel because they’re not append-only — a reconnecting client wants the latest answered/unanswered card state, not history of every snapshot. The two installs have different conditions: `ctx.askUser` is installed whenever the call has a `workspaceId + runId` (always present for HTTP-projected calls), but `ctx.publishState` is installed only when the tool *also* declares a `state` schema. A tool with no `state` schema gets `ctx.publishState === undefined` even on an HTTP-projected call — publish snapshots from a state-shaped tool, and use `ctx.emit` otherwise. See [ctx.askUser](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/ask-user) and [state-shaped tools](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/state-tools). ## How it’s packaged [Section titled “How it’s packaged”](#how-its-packaged) The endpoint system started life inside `@papercusp/agent-mcp`. It has since been **carved into a host-agnostic engine plus thin adapters** (plan `papercusp-tooldef-extraction-2026-05-29`), so the same dispatcher can be used outside Papercusp: | Package | Role | | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **`@papercusp/tooldef`** | The engine — `defineTool`, the registry, the dispatch pipeline, the state/card/replay channels, OpenAPI assembly, core types. **Zero host-coupled deps**: no PG / Next / `@restart`. Its only `@papercusp/*` deps are three host-agnostic `libs/generic/` libs (`chat-protocol`, `result-encoding`, `rules`). Validator-agnostic ([Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev)); every host-specific rule is injected (table below). | | **`@papercusp/tooldef-http`** | The HTTP transport adapter (`handleHttpToolRequest` / `…Streaming`). Resolves a request → tool, builds the ctx from `X-Papercusp-*` headers, dispatches. Depends only on the engine + `@papercusp/sse`. | | **`@papercusp/ipc-endpoint-server`** | The IPC (unix-socket) transport adapter. IPC exposure is **opt-in per tool** via `expose: { ipc: true }` in `defineTool` — unlike HTTP + MCP, which project automatically. | | **`@papercusp/tooldef-mcp`** | The MCP transport bridge primitives — generic `mcp-handler` `extra` extractors (`bearerFromExtra` / `urlFromExtra` / `headersFromExtra`) plus a projected-dispatch→MCP-result mapper (extracted under P-031). The host-specific auth + spawn-context assembly stays in the host route layer. | | **`@papercusp/agent-mcp`** | The **Papercusp host adapter** — supplies the injected deps (PG-backed quota/telemetry, the role config, quota-window policy, capability→tier table, gate-bypass mapping) and re-exports the engine + HTTP surface so existing import sites are untouched. The **generic MCP-bridge glue** now lives in `@papercusp/tooldef-mcp`; only the host-specific spawn-context auth and HMAC spawn *verification* stay in the operator route layer (`packages/operator-core/lib/spawn-signing.ts`, wired in the transport `_mcp-handler`). | Everything Papercusp-specific is a **host-injected seam** with a generic engine default: | Concern | Seam | Engine default | | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | | Roles | augment the `RoleRegistry` interface → shapes `AgentRole` | `string` (any role) | | Quota window + ceiling | `DispatchProjectedDeps.computeQuotaWindow(ctx, roleQuota)` | run-scoped / `perRun` | | Capability → tier | `setCapabilityTierResolver` (read via `tierFor`) | `'low'` | | Gate bypass (privileged callers) | `ctx.gateBypass { role?, capability?, quota? }` | absent ⇒ all gates enforce | | Schema validation | `args` / `state` / card `dataSchema` typed `StandardSchemaV1`; `standardValidate` | any Standard Schema validator | | Schema → JSON Schema | `setJsonSchemaAdapter` (read via `toJsonSchema`) | Zod 4 `toJSONSchema` | | Quota / telemetry I/O | `DispatchProjectedDeps.readQuotaState` / `recordInvocation` | no-ops | | Transaction handle | `ToolContext<Tx = any>` | `any` | The engine is provably standalone — see `libs/generic/tooldef/examples/standalone-inprocess.ts` (registers + dispatches a tool importing **only** `@papercusp/tooldef`).
