This lets you toggle a flag at runtime on a dev box with no PostHog and no restart — a stored override **beats** the evaluated/default value (`stored beats evaluated`). The presets clear these: applying either preset calls `clearAllFlagOverrides()`, so the V1 ship state truly returns to the bundled defaults rather than leaving a stale PG override in place. (Overrides are filtered through `resolveWithDefaults`, so retired keys like `papercusp-oracle` can never leak back into a client payload.) ## The two-knob model [Section titled “The two-knob model”](#the-two-knob-model) There are two things that need to be set to enable a feature for a user: **Knob 1 — `testingFeatures` in `~/.papercusp/posthog.json`** A single boolean. `true` → operator phones home to PostHog and reads live flag definitions. `false` (default) → operator never contacts PostHog and uses bundled defaults. This is the per-machine privacy toggle. **Knob 2 — individual flag values in PostHog** The actual per-flag on/off switches. Only consulted when `testingFeatures: true`. With `testingFeatures: false`, PostHog values are irrelevant; the operator never reads them. Combined behavior: | `testingFeatures` | PostHog value | Effective | | ----------------- | ------------- | ------------------------- | | `false` (default) | any | `false` (bundled default) | | `true` | `false` | `false` | | `true` | `true` | `true` | You can’t get a flag to evaluate `true` without `testingFeatures: true`. That’s the privacy moat. ## How to flip flags [Section titled “How to flip flags”](#how-to-flip-flags) ### Through the admin UI [Section titled “Through the admin UI”](#through-the-admin-ui) Open **Admin → Features** (`/admin/features`). You’ll see: 1. **Preset row** — two one-click buttons: * **🚀 V1 Production** → sets `testingFeatures: false`. Operator stops contacting PostHog. Cuts stay cut. PostHog values are left untouched (irrelevant). * **🧪 Full testing** → sets `testingFeatures: true` + flips every flag in `ALL_FLAG_KEYS` to `active=true` with `rollout_percentage: 100`. Everything on. 2. **Master switch** — the `testingFeatures` toggle with a status pill (`on` / `off`) and its current source (`discovery-file`, `discovery-file-opt-out`, `env`, `unconfigured`). 3. **Per-flag toggles** — every flag in `ALL_FLAG_KEYS` listed with its raw key. Only the original V1 cut-set (\~11 flags) carries a friendly label + blurb, resolved through the lexicon (`flagLabels(t)` / `flagBlurbs(t)`); the remaining \~90 flags display their raw key (`labels[key] ?? key`). Toggles are disabled (greyed) when `testingFeatures` is off — turn that on first. Every toggle round-trips through the operator’s HTTP endpoints, which: * Persist the change (discovery file for `testingFeatures`, PostHog API for individual flags) * Invalidate the in-process PostHog config cache * Re-init the flag backend if `testingFeatures` was just turned on * Publish a `flag_changed` event on the in-process SSE bus Other open tabs subscribed to `/api/flags/stream` reflect the change **instantly** — the admin endpoint calls `publishFlagChange()` on the in-process SSE bus before responding, which fans out to every connected tab. ### Through the PostHog UI [Section titled “Through the PostHog UI”](#through-the-posthog-ui) `https://flags.papercuspai.com` is the authoritative dashboard. Admins can flip flags, edit rollout percentages, target specific users/cohorts, view history. The operator’s admin UI is a convenience layer over the PostHog API. **Propagation when flipped directly in PostHog UI**: the operator’s `posthog-node` SDK polls flag definitions every 10 seconds (`featureFlagsPollingInterval: 10_000`), so flips made outside the admin UI take up to \~10s to reflect. There’s no upstream webhook from PostHog → operator: PostHog’s REST-hooks system is Zapier-locked + deprecated, and its Hog-functions system only fires on analytics events (flag updates are activity-log entries, not events). 10s polling is the documented behavior; if you need instant flips, use `/admin/features`. Use this when you need targeting (cohort A/B, gradual rollout) beyond the binary on/off the admin UI exposes. ### Through MCP [Section titled “Through MCP”](#through-mcp) For agents: | Tool | Capability | Action | | ------------ | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `flags:list` | `intel:read` | Lists all flags with current values (mirrors `/api/flags/bootstrap`). | | `flags:get` | `intel:read` | Reads a single flag value. | | `flags:set` | `audit:write` | Flips a flag in PostHog. Requires a `reason` arg (≥8 chars). Writes an audit row (`action='flag:set'`) in `harness_shared.audit_log`. | All three are defined under `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/flags/`. `flags:set` is exposed to the `operator` / `architect` roles; the read tools `flags:list` / `flags:get` are exposed more widely — to `operator`, `architect`, `debugger`, **and `bee`**. `flags:set` runs with `profile: 'engineer'` and `crossWorkspace: true`: its only PG write is the no-workspace operator `audit_log` INSERT (on the admin handle), which is why it isn’t a workspace-scoped RLS write. `flags:set` writes both `active` and `filters.groups[].rollout_percentage` so the binary on/off semantics work as expected — see “Bug 1” in the [Wire-up gotchas](#wire-up-gotchas) section for why. ### Through env vars [Section titled “Through env vars”](#through-env-vars) For CI and ephemeral overrides: | Env var | Effect | | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_HOST` | Override the host. Must be paired with `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY`. | | `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY` | Override the project key. | | `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_PERSONAL_KEY` | Override the personal API key. Defaults to `KEY` if not set. | | `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_TESTING_FEATURES` | Set to `"true"` to flip the master switch on without touching the discovery file. | Env vars are checked **before** the discovery file. They never get written into the desktop binary at build time — that would defeat the privacy contract. There is also a **per-flag** dev override, independent of PostHog: `PAPERCUSP_FLAG_<KEY>=1` (or `=true`) flips a single flag on without configuring PostHog at all. The key is uppercased with `-`→`_` — e.g. `PAPERCUSP_FLAG_PAPERCUSP_DESIGN=1`. This override beats test overrides / PostHog / defaults and is applied to both the single-flag `getFlag()` path and the all-flags bootstrap payload (so `useFlag()` sees it too). Useful in dev for exercising a gated feature (e.g. running the Oracle, which gates on `papercusp-testing` — `PAPERCUSP_FLAG_PAPERCUSP_TESTING=1`) when PostHog isn’t configured. ## How flags are enforced [Section titled “How flags are enforced”](#how-flags-are-enforced) Each cut feature has gating at multiple layers; the goal is that no path — direct URL, deep-link, command palette, API call, MCP tool — surfaces a cut feature when its flag is off. ### Route layer (TanStack Router, operator-vite SPA) [Section titled “Route layer (TanStack Router, operator-vite SPA)”](#route-layer-tanstack-router-operator-vite-spa) The operator frontend is the Vite SPA (Next.js is retired). Gated routes call `requireFlag(FLAGS.X)` in their `beforeLoad`; the helper (`apps/operator-vite/src/lib/require-flag.ts`) `loadFlags()`-then-`throw notFound()` if the flag is off, which renders the root route’s `notFoundComponent`: 
```tsx
// apps/operator-vite/src/routes/design/$slug.tsx
import { FLAGS } from '@papercusp/flags';
import { requireFlag } from '../../lib/require-flag';


export const Route = createFileRoute('/design/$slug')({
  beforeLoad: () => requireFlag(FLAGS.DESIGN),
  component: DesignSlugPage,
});
```
 `loadFlags()` is idempotent + cached in `@papercusp/flags/client`, so every gated route’s `beforeLoad` shares a single fetch. (The old page-side `requireFlag()` was a Next Server-Component gate using `next/navigation`’s `notFound()`; it was removed with the Next→Vite migration — `finish-next-removal-2026-06-01`.) ### Nav layer [Section titled “Nav layer”](#nav-layer) Nav / settings-sidebar entries are wrapped in `useFlag(FLAGS.X) && …`. `useFlag` comes from `@papercusp/flags/client` (a synchronous read of the cached bootstrap payload that re-renders on SSE flag-change events): 
```tsx
import { useFlag } from '@papercusp/flags/client';
import { FLAGS } from '@papercusp/flags';


const designFlag = useFlag(FLAGS.DESIGN);
// …
{designFlag ? <DesignLauncher /> : null}
```
 ### Component layer (defense-in-depth) [Section titled “Component layer (defense-in-depth)”](#component-layer-defense-in-depth) Modal panels like `<DesignPanel>` use `useQueryState` for their open/closed state, so anyone can deep-link `?design=true` and trigger a render. The render conditions additionally check the flag: 
```tsx
{showDesign && activeSlug && designEnabled && (
  <DesignPanel … />
)}
```
 Command-palette entries that would open these panels are similarly gated: 
```tsx
if (designEnabled) cs.push({ id: 'design', … });
```
 ### API route layer [Section titled “API route layer”](#api-route-layer) API routes are now Hono `endpoint-route` handlers (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/**`), each authored with `defineTool({ method, path, … })`. The `gateApiRoute(req, key)` helper (`packages/operator-core/lib/require-flag.ts`) returns a 404 `Response` when the flag is off, or `null` to continue: 
```ts
import { FLAGS } from '@papercusp/flags';
import { gateApiRoute } from '../../../require-flag';


async handler(req) {
  const blocked = await gateApiRoute(req, FLAGS.DESIGN);
  if (blocked) return blocked;
  // …handler logic…
}
```
 For a whole route group (Oracle, harness tests), the gate is checked per handler against `getFlag(FLAGS.X, 'system')` and returns 404 when off (see `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/oracle/index.ts`). Note the Oracle group gates on `FLAGS.TESTING` — the Oracle is dark unless `papercusp-testing` is on (the `papercusp-oracle` key was folded into `TESTING`, see the flag table above): 
```ts
async function oracleEnabled(): Promise<boolean> {
  const { getFlag } = await import('@papercusp/flags/server');
  const { FLAGS } = await import('@papercusp/flags');
  return getFlag(FLAGS.TESTING, 'system');
}
```
 ### MCP tool layer [Section titled “MCP tool layer”](#mcp-tool-layer) Each gated MCP tool checks the flag at registration time and at runtime. Tools that are off-gated don’t register their schema; agents can’t call what isn’t there. ### Configuration [Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration) The single source of truth for which surfaces each flag gates is **not** documented in code comments — it’s expressed in the gating itself. `grep -rln "FLAGS.DESIGN" apps/operator` is the canonical answer. ## File structure [Section titled “File structure”](#file-structure) The system lives in three places: | Path | What | | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `libs/flags/` | The package. Types + defaults (`src/types.ts`), server SDK wrapper (`src/server.ts`), client cache + `useFlag` (`src/client.ts`), test overrides (`src/test.ts`). Exported as `@papercusp/flags` (+ `/server`, `/client`, `/test`). | | `packages/operator-core/lib/flag-bus.ts` | In-process pub/sub + boot-time backend init. Wraps the `@papercusp/sse` channel. | | `packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-config.ts` | Discovery-file resolver + `fs.watch` auto-reload. The env → file → unconfigured fallback lives here. | | `packages/operator-core/lib/require-flag.ts` | The server-side `gateApiRoute` helper used by Hono route handlers. | | `apps/operator-vite/src/lib/require-flag.ts` | The SPA `requireFlag` (TanStack `beforeLoad` → `notFound()`). | | `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/flags/*` | The Hono handlers: `bootstrap`, `stream`, `webhook`, `testing-features`, `set`, `preset`, `dashboard-url`. | | `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/flags/*` | The MCP tools: `list`, `get`, `set`. | | `apps/operator/app/admin/features/FeaturesAdmin.tsx` | The admin UI component, mounted by the SPA route `apps/operator-vite/src/routes/admin/features.tsx`. | ## HTTP API [Section titled “HTTP API”](#http-api) | Method + path | Body | Returns | | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `GET /api/flags/bootstrap` | — | `{ flags: { [key]: bool }, evaluatedAt, source }`. The client’s main read endpoint. | | `GET /api/flags/stream` | — | SSE stream of `flag_changed` events. Used by the React client to refresh after flips. | | `POST /api/flags/webhook` | PostHog webhook payload | Auth header `X-Papercusp-Webhook-Secret`. Publishes a `flag_changed` event on the SSE bus. | | `GET /api/flags/testing-features` | — | `{ testingFeatures: bool, source }` | | `POST /api/flags/testing-features` | `{ enabled: bool }` | Writes the discovery file, resets the in-process config cache, re-inits the flag backend. | | `POST /api/flags/set` | `{ key: FlagKey, enabled: bool }` | PATCHes the flag in PostHog. Sets `active` + `rollout_percentage` (100 or 0). | | `POST /api/flags/preset` | `{ name: 'production' \| 'testing' }` | Atomic preset apply (loopback-guarded). `production` writes `testingFeatures: false`; `testing` sets `testingFeatures: true` + flips every flag in `ALL_FLAG_KEYS` on. | | `GET /api/flags/dashboard-url` | — | Returns the PostHog UI URL for deep-linking out of the admin page. | All of these are Hono `endpoint-route` handlers (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/flags/*`) authored via `defineTool({ method, path, auth, … })` and served by the operator’s bundled Hono host on `:3070`. They split across two declarative auth tiers: * **`auth: 'public'`** — `bootstrap`, `stream`, `webhook`, `dashboard-url`, and the **GET** half of `testing-features`. “Public” opts the route out of principal auth; `webhook` then authenticates via the shared-secret header. * **`auth: 'loopback'`** — the flag-mutating routes `set` and `preset`, plus the **POST** half of `testing-features`. This is the auth-tier Wave 1 declarative tier (`ENDPOINT_AUTH_TIERS`): loopback is enforced at the dispatch chokepoint (a non-loopback `Host` → 403), **not** by a hand-called `requireLoopbackOr403` in the handler body. The earlier in-handler `requireLoopbackOr403` sites were converted to the declared tier. ## How a flag flip propagates [Section titled “How a flag flip propagates”](#how-a-flag-flip-propagates) 
```plaintext
1. User clicks toggle in /admin/features.
   └─> POST /api/flags/set { key, enabled }


2. Handler invokes setFlag(key, enabled) in @papercusp/flags/server.
   └─> GET  flags.papercuspai.com/api/projects/@current/feature_flags/?search=<key>
       PATCH flags.papercuspai.com/api/projects/@current/feature_flags/<id>/
       body: { active, filters.groups[0].rollout_percentage }


3. Handler publishes 'flag_changed' on the in-process flag bus.
   └─> SSE channel @papercusp/sse fan-out.


4. Every open tab connected to /api/flags/stream gets the event.
   └─> The client calls loadFlags() → GET /api/flags/bootstrap.


5. The operator's posthog-node SDK has its own 10s polling interval.
   Either the SDK's local cache is already fresh (rare — flips are
   pushed via the bus) or it refreshes on its next poll.


6. All useFlag() reads re-render via the client's flag-stream subscription.
```
 End-to-end: a flag flip typically reflects in the UI within 1–2 seconds for client-rendered components, and on next navigation for server-rendered pages. **If the flip came from PostHog UI directly** (not the admin UI), the operator skips steps 1–4 entirely and only learns about the change when its 10s SDK polling refreshes. The SSE fan-out is admin-UI-only. ## Discovery-file auto-reload [Section titled “Discovery-file auto-reload”](#discovery-file-auto-reload) `packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-config.ts` installs an `fs.watch` on `~/.papercusp/`. Any write to `posthog.json` (manual edit, secret rotation, bin-helper script) invalidates the in-process config cache and triggers `reinitFlagBackend()`: * If `testingFeatures` flipped on → the PostHog SDK is initialized (or re-initialized with the new key) * If `testingFeatures` flipped off → the PostHog SDK is torn down; subsequent flag reads return `FLAG_DEFAULTS` * Either way, a `flag_changed` SSE event is broadcast so connected tabs refetch Net effect: edit the discovery file → operator picks it up within \~50ms, no restart needed. ## The admin UI architecture [Section titled “The admin UI architecture”](#the-admin-ui-architecture) The Admin section is structured as separate operator-vite SPA routes per tab (not in-page state): * `/admin/features` → `<AdminShell title="Features"><FeaturesAdmin /></AdminShell>` — the flag console (`apps/operator-vite/src/routes/admin/features.tsx`; the `FeaturesAdmin` component still lives at `apps/operator/app/admin/features/FeaturesAdmin.tsx`, imported via the SPA’s `@/app` alias). * Sibling tabs (`/admin/git`, `/admin/dbos`, …) follow the same `<AdminShell>` pattern. `AdminShell` is the chrome (header with title + tabs). Each tab is a TanStack `<Link>` so navigations are full route transitions; the URL is the source of truth for the active tab (no `useState`). The `/admin/*` routes are intentionally not linked from the nav — reach them by URL. The flag-mutating endpoints behind them (`/api/flags/set`, `/api/flags/preset`) enforce loopback server-side via the declarative `auth: 'loopback'` tier (the `ENDPOINT_AUTH_TIERS` chokepoint), **not** an in-handler `requireLoopbackOr403` call; the route itself is **not** flag-gated (an earlier `FLAGS.ADMIN` gate was removed — and that key no longer exists in `FLAGS`). ## Wire-up gotchas [Section titled “Wire-up gotchas”](#wire-up-gotchas) Three bugs surfaced during the initial wire-up that future contributors should know about. All are fixed in `main` but the explanations are worth keeping. ### Bug 1: `setFlag` only flipped `active` [Section titled “Bug 1: setFlag only flipped active”](#bug-1-setflag-only-flipped-active) PostHog flags have a hierarchical evaluation: `active` is the master switch, but `filters.groups[].rollout_percentage` decides which fraction of users see it. The original `setFlag` only PATCHed `active`. Flags were created with `rollout_percentage: 0`, so even `active: true` evaluated `false` for every user. Fix: `setFlag` now PATCHes both `active` and `rollout_percentage` (100 when enabling, 0 when disabling). For binary on/off semantics that’s correct; for gradual rollouts use the PostHog UI directly. ### Bug 2: SDK missing `personalApiKey` [Section titled “Bug 2: SDK missing personalApiKey”](#bug-2-sdk-missing-personalapikey) `initFlagBackend` initially constructed the `posthog-node` client with only `projectKey` and `host`. Without `personalApiKey`, the SDK can’t fetch flag definitions and falls back to remote evaluation (per-call `/flags/` endpoint hits, slower and different semantics). Fix: pass `personalApiKey` + set `featureFlagsPollingInterval: 10_000`. The SDK now polls flag definitions every 10s and evaluates locally — sub-millisecond per call, no per-request network. ### Bug 3: One-shot `booted` latch in flag-bus [Section titled “Bug 3: One-shot booted latch in flag-bus”](#bug-3-one-shot-booted-latch-in-flag-bus) `packages/operator-core/lib/flag-bus.ts` had `let booted = false` at module scope, set to `true` after the first `bootIfNeeded()` call. The intent was “init the PostHog client once at startup.” But if `testingFeatures` was off at startup and got flipped to `true` later, the latch had already fired, so no init ever happened. Fix: added `reinitFlagBackend()` which the `testing-features` and `preset` endpoints call after writing the discovery file. The latch is now a debounce, not a guard against re-init. ## Testing [Section titled “Testing”](#testing) The flag system has a test override hook: 
```ts
import { setFlagOverridesForTest } from '@papercusp/flags/test';


beforeEach(() => {
  setFlagOverridesForTest({
    [FLAGS.DESIGN]: true,
    [FLAGS.TESTING]: false,
  });
});
```
 When overrides are set, the server’s `getAllFlags()` returns them directly with `source: "override"`, bypassing PostHog entirely. Tests don’t need to mock the SDK or run a real PostHog instance. This is the live way to neutralize flag state in tests — consumers include `packages/operator-core/lib/lexicon/configure.test.ts`, the `@papercusp/flags` server suites, and `apps/operator/bin/host-spa.test.ts`. (`PAPERCUSP_FLAG_<KEY>` env overrides win over test overrides, so clear them if a test relies on the override map.) ## Common operations [Section titled “Common operations”](#common-operations) ### ”Flip everything on for a dev session” [Section titled “”Flip everything on for a dev session””](#flip-everything-on-for-a-dev-session) Admin → Features → **🧪 Full testing**. Or: 
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/flags/preset \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"testing"}'
```
 ### “Go back to V1 ship state” [Section titled ““Go back to V1 ship state””](#go-back-to-v1-ship-state) Admin → Features → **🚀 V1 Production**. Or: 
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/flags/preset \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"production"}'
```
 ### “Verify the ship state on a freshly built binary" [Section titled ““Verify the ship state on a freshly built binary"”](#verify-the-ship-state-on-a-freshly-built-binary) 
```bash
# On a clean install, before any admin opt-in:
curl -s http://localhost:3055/api/flags/bootstrap | jq


# Expected: source="unconfigured", every flag at its FLAG_DEFAULTS value
# (cut-for-V1 flags false; alpha default-on flags true — see the table above)
```
 ### "Add a new flag” [Section titled “"Add a new flag””](#add-a-new-flag) 1. Add the key + default to `libs/flags/src/types.ts` (`FLAGS` + `FLAG_DEFAULTS`). **In alpha, the `FLAG_DEFAULTS` entry for a flag you create alongside the feature is `true`** — finished work ships active; the flag exists so the owner can switch it off (or cut it for ship), not to ship the feature dark. Default `false` only for genuinely incomplete/unsafe work or an explicit owner-requested dark launch — and then surface the pending flip in the plan + completion report. 2. If you also define the flag in the PostHog UI at `flags.papercuspai.com`, match the bundled default (`active: true`, `rollout_percentage: 100` for an alpha default-on flag). Key must match the TS string exactly. 3. *(Optional)* Add a friendly label/blurb in `apps/operator/app/admin/features/FeaturesAdmin.tsx`. There are **no** `FLAG_LABELS`/`FLAG_BLURBS` constants — labels and blurbs are built at render through the lexicon-bound functions `flagLabels(t)` / `flagBlurbs(t)` (so the displayed names follow the active `THE_HIVE` brand pack). These cover only the original V1 cut-set (\~11 flags); every other flag falls back to its raw key in the admin per-flag list (`labels[key] ?? key`). Skipping this step just means your flag shows its raw key — the admin list still renders and toggles it. 4. Gate the actual surfaces — pages with `requireFlag`, nav entries with `useFlag`, API routes with `gateApiRoute`, MCP tools with the same. 5. `tsc --noEmit` on the operator to confirm no surface forgot the gate. ### ”Discover what a flag gates” [Section titled “”Discover what a flag gates””](#discover-what-a-flag-gates) 
```bash
grep -rln "FLAGS.DESIGN" apps/operator
```
 The gating sites are the documentation.

> The built-in harness blueprints — each a declarative harness shape (work-item kind, spine decider, roles, dispatch policy, gates). Generated from the blueprint.yaml source of truth.

Part of `starlight-projection-generators-2026-06-05` (Brief 29). # Blueprint catalog [Section titled “Blueprint catalog”](#blueprint-catalog) A **blueprint** is a harness’s declarative shape — its work-item kind, the role spine the engine routes work through (`deriveNext`), its dispatch/concurrency policy, and its finalize gates. # Generated API & lib reference (projection site)

> The operator HTTP/tool API and the libs/generic TypeDoc API rendered as a browsable human site, projected directly from code. Built on demand via npm run docs:preview; additive to the hand-written docs, replacing none of them.

Two parts of this reference are **projected directly from code**, not hand-written — so they never drift. They are **additive**: they document surfaces that never existed as hand-authored pages, and they replace none of the conceptual, spec, design, or runbook docs in this site. * **Operator API** — every HTTP-exposed `defineTool` projected into an OpenAPI 3.1 spec (`npm run gen:openapi`) and rendered with [`starlight-openapi`](https://starlight-openapi.vercel.app/). * **Lib API** — the borrowable `libs/generic/*` libraries’ public TypeScript API, rendered with [`starlight-typedoc`](https://starlight-typedoc.vercel.app/) from the same entry points `npm run gen:lib-api` resolves. This is the human half of the “two independent projections of one source” design (`docs-and-memory-as-projections-2026-06-05` D-004): the agent form is served directly from code over the `docs:*`/MCP surface, and this site is the parallel human view of the **same** artifacts. ## Building & browsing it [Section titled “Building & browsing it”](#building--browsing-it) The render is **generated on demand**, behind a `DOCS_PREVIEW` build, so it is not baked into the default docs build (which stays fast and free of the operator-core registry import + the multi-lib TypeDoc run). To build and browse it: 
```bash
# from the repo root
npm run docs:preview          # gen:openapi + DOCS_PREVIEW=1 astro build -> dist-preview
npm run docs:preview:serve    # serve it; open the printed URL
```
 Then browse: * **`/internal/docs/preview/api`** — the Operator API reference (one page per operation). * **`/internal/docs/preview/lib-api`** — the libs/generic TypeScript API. ## Don’t hand-edit it [Section titled “Don’t hand-edit it”](#dont-hand-edit-it) These pages are a **projection**. Edits go to the source — the code (for the API/lib surface) or the plans/insights (for rationale) — never to the generated output, which is overwritten on every build.

# Role & persona registry

> The built-in agent roles (AGENT_ROLES) joined with their spawn personas. Generated from role-config.ts + the harness persona files.

> **Generated — do not edit by hand.** Run `npm run gen:doc-projections` (or `npm run gen:doc-role-registry`). Source: `scripts/gen-doc-role-registry.ts`. Part of `starlight-projection-generators-2026-06-05` (Brief 29). # Role & persona registry [Section titled “Role & persona registry”](#role--persona-registry) A **role** is what kind of agent a spawn is. `AGENT_ROLES` is the runtime source of truth for the built-in role ids (tool `roles:` allowlists, `byRole` guidance, quotas); a role’s **persona** is its spawn prompt at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/<id>/prompts/<role>.md` (the `base` library is the universal one). Not every role has a persona (operator/oracle are chat surfaces), and many personas are blueprint deciders/helpers that are not themselves `AGENT_ROLES` entries. Sources: `packages/agent-mcp/src/role-config.ts` (52 built-in roles) + `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/*/prompts/*.md` (56 personas). ## Built-in roles (`AGENT_ROLES`) [Section titled “Built-in roles (AGENT\_ROLES)”](#built-in-roles-agent_roles) These ids appear in tool `roles:` allowlists, `rolesQuota` keys, and `byRole` guidance overrides. # Distribution trust posture

> The v1 trust model for distributing harnesses, blueprints, plugins, tool-packs, and learning-packs through the Cupboard — why forking/installing pulls a supply-chain surface, how capability-gating + install-consent contain it, why instruction-carrying kinds are review-gated, what we defer, and what's out of scope.

The **Cupboard** is one storefront with five listing kinds, each with a different consumer action and a different trust surface: | Kind | Action | Pulls code? | Trust surface | | --------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `harness` | **join** | No — joins a Hypercore swarm by topic | Peer/membership trust ([shared harnesses](/internal/docs/security/shared-harnesses)) | | `blueprint` | **fork** | **Yes** — clones the project remote + any bundled plugin code | Supply chain + review gate (this page) | | `plugin` | **install** | **Yes** — installs a distributable plugin (a pack *with* a runtime) | Supply chain (this page) | | `tool-pack` | **install** | **Yes** — installs a runtime-less code-tool pack, registering MCP tools | Supply chain (this page) | | `learning-pack` | **install** | No code — seeds curated learnings into a hive’s shared memory | Injected agent context + review gate (this page) | > The `snapshot` kind was **retired** (`retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`, D-005). It is no longer in `LISTING_KINDS`, `normalizeListingKind` returns `null` for it, and Cupboard migration 008 deletes every snapshot row and drops `snapshot` from the `listing_kind` CHECK constraint — no current worker code can serve a snapshot listing. References below are to its successors (blueprint for the fork path). This page is the trust posture for the kinds that either **pull code** — forking a blueprint, installing a plugin or tool-pack — or **inject agent context** — a learning-pack. It records the v1 decision (`harness-blueprint-distribution-2026-06-03`, **P-009 / D-007 / D-009**) and, importantly, what is **deferred** and what is **out of scope**. ## The supply-chain surface [Section titled “The supply-chain surface”](#the-supply-chain-surface) Forking a blueprint pulls the project remote *and any plugin code it bundles*; installing a plugin or tool-pack pulls code directly. A `tool-pack` is a runtime-less code-tool pack that registers MCP tools (`provides_tools`), so it sits on the same supply-chain surface as a plugin. Plugin code runs in the operator’s plugin host with access to host services (tasks, secrets, fetch, compute). **Unconstrained, that is a classic supply-chain risk** — a published listing could ship a plugin that reads secrets or exfiltrates over the network. A `learning-pack` pulls *no executable code*, but it injects curated learnings into a hive’s shared memory — i.e. content that lands in agent context. That is a different risk (prompt injection), addressed by the review gate below rather than by capability-gating. ## v1 posture: capability-gate + install-consent [Section titled “v1 posture: capability-gate + install-consent”](#v1-posture-capability-gate--install-consent) The v1 containment for the **code-pulling** kinds is the **existing two-tier plugin capability model** — we reuse it rather than inventing a distribution-specific mechanism (D-009). A plugin capability is usable **iff it is in BOTH tiers**: 1. **Tier 1 — manifest.** The plugin’s `capabilities[]` (manifest) declares what it *could* use. Format `namespace:action[:resource]` (`tasks:read`, `http:fetch:*.youtube.com`, `secrets:read:YT_API_KEY`). 2. **Tier 2 — install-consent.** At install/enable the operator presents those caps to the user, who grants a subset. The grant set is stored in `harness_shared.plugin_capability_grants` (originally Migration 051, now in `000-baseline.sql`) and loaded at plugin init. The gate is `hasCapability(ctx, cap)` in [`packages/plugin-loader/src/capabilities.ts`](https://github.com/Papercusp/plugin-loader) — it ANDs the manifest set with the granted set (both wildcard-aware). The grants store + loader live in the operator core (`lib/plugin-grants.ts` · `getGrantsForPluginInHarness`, and `lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts` · `loadGrantedCapsSafe`; post-carve these are `@papercusp/operator-core`). Caution `loadGrantedCapsSafe` returns `undefined` — not an empty array — when there are **zero** grants for a `(plugin@version, harness)` pair (no consent flow has run yet, or Postgres is unreachable with no legacy file present) and on any read error. That `undefined` is stored verbatim into the runtime’s grant state, and `hasCapability` treats `granted === undefined` as the **legacy single-tier (manifest-only)** path. So the operator runtime is *not* unconditionally on the two-tier path: until grants exist for a plugin, or if the grants read fails, it falls back to manifest-only for that plugin. The deliberate revoke path deletes specific caps (leaving a non-empty set), so an explicit user-revoke is *not* confused with “no grants yet”. The dangerous egress surfaces are gated at the boundary a forked plugin actually hits: `makeFetchProxy` rejects any host not covered by an `http:fetch:<host>` capability, and `makeSecretsProxy` rejects any `secrets:read:<NAME>` not granted. ### Fork inherits the parent’s grants [Section titled “Fork inherits the parent’s grants”](#fork-inherits-the-parents-grants) Forking does **not** silently re-prompt or degrade a plugin to manifest-only on first invocation. `copyGrantsToNewHarness` (`lib/plugin-grants.ts`) copies every `(plugin, version, capability)` grant from the source harness to the new one under the target slug, `granted_by='system'`, `reason='fork from <sourceSlug>'` (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so a re-fork doesn’t duplicate). The fork inherits its parent’s capability decisions rather than starting from no grants. ### Backfill for already-enabled plugins [Section titled “Backfill for already-enabled plugins”](#backfill-for-already-enabled-plugins) At operator boot, `backfillGrantsFromEnabledPluginsAndLegacyFile` **silently grants** each currently-enabled plugin its full manifest-declared cap set (`granted_by='system'`, `reason='enabled-plugins.json backfill'`) so existing harnesses don’t break on first reload after the two-tier rollout. A legacy `~/.papercusp/granted-capabilities.json` file is a **read-only fallback** that is also replayed verbatim. The practical consequence: the consent prompt is for *new* installs — already-enabled plugins are backfilled with their declared caps rather than re-prompted retroactively. Users can revoke any backfilled cap from the consent UI afterward. ### Server-capability invocation (palette) [Section titled “Server-capability invocation (palette)”](#server-capability-invocation-palette) The desktop palette’s server-capability path (`lib/capabilities/invoke.ts` · `paletteInvokeGuard` → `invokeServerCapability`; post-carve `@papercusp/operator-core`) runs **with no gate bypass for trust/role**: it is a plain loopback `operator` principal, a server-side §3 admission re-check refuses non-eligible tools, and destructive/high-risk tools require an explicit `confirmed:true`. Every call is audited. (See D-007 in the source.) ## Review gate for instruction-carrying kinds [Section titled “Review gate for instruction-carrying kinds”](#review-gate-for-instruction-carrying-kinds) Capability-gate + install-consent covers **code-egress** risk (fetch/secrets) — it does **not** cover **prompt-injection** risk from content that lands in agent context. So the two **instruction-carrying** kinds now carry a **pre-publication review gate**: * A **learning-pack** injects curated learnings into a hive’s shared memory. * A **blueprint** runs agent roles. `REVIEW_POLICY_KINDS = ['learning-pack', 'blueprint']`. At publish, a listing of one of these kinds lands `review_status='pending'` (every other kind, and every pre-008 row, is `'approved'`). Pending/rejected listings are **excluded from public list and read** — only the publisher can read their own pending listing (via `GET /:id` with auth), and operators triage them through `/admin`. A non-owner request for a non-approved listing returns 404. An operator approval (or rejection, with a surfaced reason) flips the status. Pure code kinds — `plugin` and `tool-pack` — are **not** review-gated; they keep install-consent + reactive moderation (reports → unlist). The split is by risk type: code kinds are contained by the capability gate at runtime; instruction kinds have no analogous runtime gate, so they’re held for human review before they’re publicly visible. ## Publisher trust signals (Cupboard worker) [Section titled “Publisher trust signals (Cupboard worker)”](#publisher-trust-signals-cupboard-worker) The Cupboard worker (`apps/operator-public`) surfaces *advisory* publisher signals on each listing — they inform, they do not hard-gate (a provisional listing is **not** an ownership claim): * **Publisher-collaborator signal** — the publisher’s GitHub permission on the bound repo at publish time (`publisher_permission`, Migration 002; `derivePublisherPermission`). The browse card shows “collaborator” vs “not a collaborator”. A non-collaborator who can merely read a public repo reads as `read`. * **Channel-2 device attestation** — an optional device-key to GitHub-login gist binding (Migration 003), verified/revoked by the hourly indexer. * **Operator ban-list** — `banned_publisher_pubkeys`; a banned publisher device pubkey’s listings are filtered from browse and 404 on detail. * **Private repos are rejected** at publish; all listings are public. These are the same signals harness listings already carried — the storefront merge applies them uniformly across all listing kinds (every kind is project-remote-backed in v1). ## Deferred (D-009) — acceptable because there are no users yet [Section titled “Deferred (D-009) — acceptable because there are no users yet”](#deferred-d-009--acceptable-because-there-are-no-users-yet) * **Plugin signing.** No cryptographic signature on plugin code. Note that a **review gate is no longer fully deferred**: the instruction-carrying kinds (blueprint, learning-pack) are now pre-publication review-gated (above). What remains deferred is review/curation for the **pure code kinds** (plugin, tool-pack), which keep install-consent + reactive moderation as their floor, and cryptographic signing for all kinds. Capability-gate + install-consent (code kinds) and the review gate (instruction kinds) are the floor; signing raises it later. Revisit before there are real users installing third-party listings. ## Out of scope here (D-012) [Section titled “Out of scope here (D-012)”](#out-of-scope-here-d-012) * **Producer-side trust** — collaborator push-access to the papercupai project remote (who may *publish/contribute to* a project), as opposed to consumer-side trust (what a *forked/installed* plugin may *do*, this page). That surface is owned by the [project-centric rethink](/internal/docs/spec) and the distributed-coordination plans (`distributed-coordination-shared-harness-2026-06-04`). ## Summary [Section titled “Summary”](#summary) | Concern | v1 | | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Live listing kinds | `harness`, `blueprint`, `plugin`, `tool-pack`, `learning-pack` (snapshot retired) | | Forked/installed plugin capability | manifest ∩ user-consented grant (`hasCapability`) when grants present; manifest-only fallback when grants absent/unreadable | | Consent record | `plugin_capability_grants` (baseline.sql; was Migration 051) | | Fork capability inheritance | parent grants copied `granted_by='system'` (`copyGrantsToNewHarness`) | | Already-enabled plugins | manifest caps backfilled at boot (`granted_by='system'`); legacy JSON read-only fallback | | Network / secret egress | per-host / per-name capability via fetch+secrets proxies | | Instruction-carrying kinds | pre-publication review gate (`blueprint`, `learning-pack` land `pending`, hidden until operator-approved) | | Palette server-capability | §3 re-check, confirm-for-destructive, no trust bypass, audited | | Publisher trust | advisory signals (collaborator perm, device attestation, ban-list); private repos rejected | | Signing | deferred (D-009); review deferred only for pure code kinds | | Producer-side push trust | out of scope (D-012) |

# Shared harnesses

> The trust and security model for peer-to-peer shared harnesses — how identity, authorization, membership, and revocation work, what we borrow from other P2P systems, and the tradeoffs we accept intentionally.

Partially built — model is being implemented in phases This page records the security model for **shared harnesses** (the peer-to-peer, multi-engineer sync substrate), the research it rests on, and the tradeoffs we are choosing **intentionally**. The model below is the agreed direction, tracked in the design memo `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-trust-model-2026-05-31.md`. Sections marked **Today** describe the original (2026-05-31) insecure state; **Recommended** describes the target. **Build-state update (2026-06-13).** The substrate trust layer is now substantially built: **per-log admission** (signed announce + GitHub-anchored `verifyBinding` attestation), **revocation** (`revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list, gated on a live GitHub repo-admin check), and **identity attestation** (`verifyAttestation`) are all wired. Crucially, a confirmation audit (P-017, plan `shared-hive-hardening-2026-06-13`) verified that the model’s load-bearing invariant — **every decision-bearing fact re-derives from GitHub at the point of action** — holds across all current call sites. See [The advisory-vs-trusted boundary](#the-advisory-vs-trusted-boundary) for the verified call-site table. Per-op signing (Phase 2 below) remains a defense-in-depth future enhancement, not a shipped gate — the shipped model is **per-log** admission, so an admitted peer’s ops are trusted wholesale (the accepted equivocation tradeoff), which is why the GitHub re-derivation invariant is what actually carries the safety. **Build-state update (2026-06-25).** Read admission is intentionally **not** a repo-collaborator permission gate. The pure decider in `sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts` admits a log only after announce signature verification, GitHub-gist attestation verification, and the `revoked_pubkeys` veto. Boot adds two Hive-specific scope wideners: an already-known Hive member can be admitted from the local `hive_members` projection via `trustedHiveMemberDeviceAdmission`, and a same-Hive cross-member announce whose membership has not federated yet is buffered as `pending` and retried within the boot grace window. GitHub collaborator/admin permission remains the authority for repo binding, revocation actions, push/PR/merge, and shipped verification; it is not the swarm read-admission allow-list. ## What a shared harness is [Section titled “What a shared harness is”](#what-a-shared-harness-is) A shared harness lets several engineers collaborate on one coding project. Shared state — the **feature queue, pull-request status, the contributor list, and feature “claims”** — syncs peer-to-peer over the Holepunch stack and is projected into each peer’s local Postgres: * **Hyperswarm** — DHT peer discovery. The swarm **topic = `sha256("papercusp-substrate-v1:gh:<github_repository_id>")`**, derived from the *public* GitHub repo id, so it is **discoverable, not a secret**. `gh:<repository_id>` is only one of several topic bindings: the shipped multi-engineer (**Hive**) substrate is keyed by **`hive:<hive_pubkey>`**, which *replaces* the per-repo slug as the top-level federation unit (a Hive’s Swarms all join this one topic), with `local:<workspace_id>/<slug>` for pre-binding/private dev and an explicit `topic:<hex>` carrier so a link-joiner lands on the owner’s exact Hive topic rather than re-deriving a `gh:` topic that wouldn’t match. * **Hypercore** — one Ed25519-signed append-only log per device. * **Model B peer-log** — one single-writer Ed25519 log per device + a read-merge over the others (`sync/hyperbee/peer-log.ts`). This **replaced** the earlier multi-writer **Autobase** design; Autobase mentions below are the historical survey/analysis, not the shipped substrate (P-024 truth fix). Identity is anchored to **GitHub**: each device holds an Ed25519 keypair in the OS keychain. The OAuth `GET /user` channel is a **local self-attestation only — it is never part of remote admission**. Remote admission (post write-free-join) proves the `device_pubkey ↔ github_user_id` binding entirely from a **device-signed announce** plus `verifyAttestation` on a **public GitHub gist** — the gist pins `owner.id === github_user_id`, the body’s `device_pubkey`, and a device signature. There is **no device-signed commit** anywhere in the code: the old shared-repo contributor-file channel was removed in the write-free-join work. The single most important fact: **the authority for the one thing that truly matters — merging code — is GitHub itself.** PRs merge through the GitHub REST API with a real user token, so GitHub’s write-access and branch-protection rules are enforced regardless of anything that happens on the swarm. ## The trust problem [Section titled “The trust problem”](#the-trust-problem) Original 2026-05-31 state: the substrate was wide open Replicated Autobase ops were **not signed, authenticated, or authorized on receipt** — the only admission check was a schema-version filter. Because the swarm topic is derivable from the public repo id, **any peer who could reach the DHT could join and write forged feature/PR/contributor/claim rows into every other peer’s local database.** The designed defenses (an admission step gated on the two-channel binding, a `revoked_pubkeys` drop-list) existed on paper but had **no production callers**. **Update (2026-06-13):** admission is now wired (Model B per-log: signed announce + GitHub-anchored `verifyBinding` + `revoked_pubkeys` veto — see `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts`), so a peer is admitted only on a verified GitHub-anchored attestation, not by mere DHT reachability. What remains **intentionally** unbuilt is **per-op** signature verification at projection time: once a peer is admitted, its ops are projected wholesale (the accepted equivocation tradeoff). The forged-advisory-row surface is therefore narrowed to *already-admitted* peers and, per the verified invariant below, **no decision-bearing action acts on those rows without re-deriving from GitHub**. Keep two threat models separate: * **Untrustworthy local user** — every local API route is `auth: 'public'` (127.0.0.1 only). It trusts whoever is on the desktop. Fine for a single-user desktop; not a shared-machine model. * **Untrustworthy swarm peer** *(the serious one)* — public topic + unsigned ops means a peer can poison every other peer’s local DB/UI. This is what the security layer exists to contain. A code audit (2026-05-31) confirmed that **GitHub is the only authorization actually enforced today.** Everything Papercusp layers on top — the feature state machine, the PR “trusted authors” gate, the `completion_ref` “shipped ✓” verifier, contributor identity signatures, and substrate op-auth — is currently dead code, unwired, or self-asserted. ## How other systems solve it [Section titled “How other systems solve it”](#how-other-systems-solve-it) A three-pass survey of production P2P / local-first / decentralized systems. They converge on a small primitive set: **sign every replicated write and verify it on receipt; gate membership cryptographically; anchor identity to keys or an external authority; and accept that true deletion is impossible in an append-only log.** | System | Identity anchor | Per-op authorization | Membership / removal | Verdict for Papercusp | | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Hypercore** | per-device Ed25519 key (our model) | signed merkle tree per log (integrity, single-writer) | — | **Maps** — proves you authored *your* log, not that you’re allowed | | **Autobase** | — | **none built in**; *“optimistic blocks should self-verify in the apply handler”* | `addWriter`/`removeWriter` are app calls inside `apply` | **Maps / confirms the gap** — per-op verification is the app’s job | | **Hyperswarm / HyperDHT** | connecting peer’s Noise key | Noise authenticates the *connection*, not ops | only `firewall(remotePublicKey)` | **Maps / confirms threat** — public topic; connection-auth ≠ op-auth | | **blind-pairing** (Keet) | invite secret | candidate signs with invite key; member verifies | admit-by-invite; app-evaluated `userData` | **Partial** — a ready admission handshake; put the GitHub proof in `userData` | | **Radicle** *(closest analog)* | self-sovereign `did:key` (opposite of ours) | **signs every write** (`refs/rad/sigref`); **rejects invalid before storing**; signed collaborative objects | delegate threshold/quorum | **Mechanism maps, anchor doesn’t** — proves the sign-and-verify-before-store pattern | | **Radicle COBs** | content-addressed | exposes each change’s author → filter a bad author at view-build | filter at materialization | **Maps** — our `revoked_pubkeys` is this *local projection filter*, not network rejection | | **Kleppmann (BFT-CRDT)** | — | **signatures necessary but NOT sufficient** — a signed *equivocation* breaks version vectors | a replicated ACL must itself be a BFT CRDT | **Decisive** — don’t try to make advisory state Byzantine-trustworthy | | **Keyhive / BeeKEM** (Ink & Switch) | **deliberately excludes** identity binding | capability chains + per-op Ed25519 sig; BeeKEM needs only **causal** order → fits Autobase | coordination-free removal with **real post-compromise security** | **Authz maps; complements (≠ replaces) the GitHub binding** — see [Keyhive](#does-keyhivebeekem-fit-our-stack) | | **MLS / RFC 9420** | — | TreeKEM epoch chain | needs **one linear chain of agreed Commits**; concurrent commits fork a DAG it can’t merge | **Does not map** over Autobase’s concurrent merge | | **Keybase** *(two-channel analog)* | per-user signed **sigchain**; key↔GitHub via a GitHub-hosted signed proof | each link signed, `seqno` + `prev` hash | revocation = a **signed revoke link**; sibkeys for device-loss recovery | **Maps — improves the binding**: model two-channel as a signed link; revoke-as-signed-statement beats a side-list | | **Sigstore / SLSA / in-toto** | short-lived **OIDC** identity (Fulcio) | keyless sig + **Rekor transparency log**; in-toto/DSSE | no revocation (short-lived certs); compromise caught by **monitoring** | **Partial — provenance pattern**: a signature proves *authenticated-at-a-time*, **not** authorization or “good.” Confirms “shipped” must be **GitHub-derived** | | **AT Proto `did:plc`** | hybrid: self-cert keys + a directory | signed repo commits | **rotation-key priority list + 72h recovery window** | **Partial — recovery lesson**: for us, GitHub *is* the recovery anchor | | **Nostr NIP-05** | pubkey ↔ `name@domain` via a `.well-known` file | per-event Schnorr sig | — | **Partial** — a GitHub-hosted well-known file is a lighter binding variant | | **Secure Scuttlebutt** | per-identity signed append-only feed (≈ Hypercore) | every message signed | **invite + follow-graph** bounds replication & Sybils | **Partial — admission analog**: Hive membership + revocation bounds shared-hive replication; GitHub permission is reserved for decision-bearing actions | ### The decisive constraints [Section titled “The decisive constraints”](#the-decisive-constraints) 1. **Autobase will not authenticate ops for us** — per-op signing and `addWriter` gating are *our* code, in the `apply`/projection seam. 2. **Signatures are necessary but not sufficient** (Kleppmann) — a validly-admitted-then- malicious writer can sign false or *equivocating* rows. Full Byzantine resilience needs a hash-DAG causal layer we are **not** going to build. 3. **True removal / post-compromise security is impossible in an append-only multi-writer log** — a revoked writer’s signed ops persist and replicate; “removal” means every honest peer drops them at projection time. 4. **A provenance signature proves authentication-at-a-time, not authorization or quality** (Sigstore) — so the trustworthy “shipped” signal must come from GitHub’s *merge state*, not a self-reported receipt. 5. **GitHub already enforces the only hard authorization that matters.** This is the escape hatch from the unsolved Byzantine-CRDT access-control problem. ## Does Holepunch provide its own solution? [Section titled “Does Holepunch provide its own solution?”](#does-holepunch-provide-its-own-solution) Mostly the **building blocks**, not a turnkey access-control product: * **Hypercore** signs each log for free. * **Autobase** gives a writer set with `addWriter`/`removeWriter`, but **you** write the per-op check and the admission policy in `apply`. * **blind-pairing-core** (what Keet actually uses) is a real cryptographic invite/pairing handshake — admit-by-possession-of-invite-secret. This is Holepunch’s native admission answer. * **Hyperswarm** gives Noise-encrypted connections + a coarse `firewall(remotePublicKey)` reject hook. What Holepunch deliberately leaves to the app: fine-grained capabilities (read/write/admin), **identity binding** (always app-layer — our GitHub anchor), and **post-compromise security on removal** (`removeWriter` stops new appends; it is not key-rotation/PCS). Of those, the only one we actually need is identity binding — which no library provides. **So the plan builds on Holepunch’s native primitives**: per-op signature verification + GitHub-anchored `addWriter` (via blind-pairing, GitHub proof in `userData`) + a `revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list. ## Does Keyhive/BeeKEM fit our stack? [Section titled “Does Keyhive/BeeKEM fit our stack?”](#does-keyhivebeekem-fit-our-stack) Compatible *in principle*, but **not native and arguably overkill**: * **It fits the ordering model** — BeeKEM needs only a *causal* order, which Autobase provides. It’s the only post-compromise-secure option that works over a concurrent-merge log (MLS does not). * **But it’s an Automerge-ecosystem Rust library** (the `beekem` crate), not a Holepunch component. Adopting it means embedding that crate and running its control ops over Autobase — an unsupported combination, and it is **pre-alpha, unaudited, BeeKEM not formally proven**. * **It couples authorization with *encryption*** (it’s a continuous group key agreement). Our substrate data is plaintext to swarm members today; BeeKEM means encrypting group state with key rotation — a large shift that *buys* post-compromise security but is more than advisory data needs. * **It still doesn’t solve identity** — Keyhive defers human-identity binding to “a future layer above,” i.e. our GitHub anchor regardless. ## Recommended model — GitHub is the authority of record [Section titled “Recommended model — GitHub is the authority of record”](#recommended-model--github-is-the-authority-of-record) 1. **Authority of record = GitHub.** Every *decision-bearing* fact (did it merge, who has write access, real PR status, who is a contributor) is **re-derived from GitHub at the point of action** — never trusted from a peer. 2. **Peer-synced rows = advisory cache** (fast/offline UI), explicitly untrusted. 3. **Per-op Ed25519 signing + verify-on-receipt** in the Autobase `apply`/projection path — *defense-in-depth / UX integrity*, not the authority of record. **Sign sequence + freshness, not just content** (Radicle’s 2026 replay-CVE lesson). 4. **GitHub-anchored log admission** — signed announce + GitHub gist attestation verifies the device identity; `revoked_pubkeys` denies known-bad devices. Hive scope is then narrowed/widened by signed `harness_slug`, local `hive_members`, and pending retry for membership propagation. This is not a collaborator permission gate. 5. **Identity binding = a Keybase-style signed link** — the GitHub-hosted device-signed proof is the cross-check that lets any peer detect a rewritten identity; revocation is a *signed* statement, not just a side list. 6. **Device-key rotation/recovery is GitHub-rooted** — losing a device means re-running the two-channel binding from the new device; the old key goes on `revoked_pubkeys`. GitHub (the account) plays `did:plc`’s “higher-authority key” recovery role. 7. **“Shipped”/provenance = GitHub-derived** — read merge state from GitHub; optionally record it as a signed in-toto-style attestation. Do **not** build a Rekor-style transparency log — GitHub already is the authority and stores attestations. (This also means the `completion_ref` “shipped” signal should be GitHub-derived, not a self-reported peer receipt.) 8. **Sybil/admission = verified GitHub identity plus Hive membership/revocation.** The swarm topic is public, so unauthenticated devices are filtered by signed announce + gist attestation; shared-Hive cross-member scope is filtered by `hive_members`; and `revoked_pubkeys` is the hard local blocklist. The GitHub collaborator graph is still consulted at decision points that need repo authority, but it is not the read-admission allow-list. 9. **Do not** adopt MLS or build a Byzantine-CRDT ACL. ### The advisory-vs-trusted boundary [Section titled “The advisory-vs-trusted boundary”](#the-advisory-vs-trusted-boundary) The central decision: which synced surfaces are advisory vs must-re-derive-from-GitHub. | Synced surface | Advisory (peer-supplied cache)? | Decision-bearing → re-derive from GitHub? | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Feature queue / status | yes — display & coordination | a “shipped” decision → GitHub merge state | | PR status | yes — display | merge / approval authority → GitHub | | Contributor list | yes — display | ”is X a real contributor / has write access” → GitHub collaborators | | Feature claims | yes — coordination/UX only | (advisory by nature; no hard authority needed) | | Completion / “shipped ✓“ | no | **GitHub-derived only** | Anything in the right column must never be acted on from peer state alone. ### Confirmation pass — 2026-06-13 (P-017): every decision-bearing fact re-derives [Section titled “Confirmation pass — 2026-06-13 (P-017): every decision-bearing fact re-derives”](#confirmation-pass--2026-06-13-p-017-every-decision-bearing-fact-re-derives) The shipped substrate uses **per-log** admission: a peer is admitted on a verified signed-announce + GitHub-anchored attestation, after which its ops are trusted **wholesale** into the projection (no per-op authz — the accepted equivocation tradeoff). That is safe **iff** every decision-bearing fact re-derives from GitHub at the point of action. A call-site audit (plan `shared-hive-hardening-2026-06-13`, P-017) confirmed this invariant holds across **all** authorization-bearing consumers of peer-synced state — there is **no gap**. The federated tables are `contributors`, `queue` / `features-by-id` (→ `harness_features_consolidated`), `working-set`/`claims`, `presence`, plans, and coord; the table below enumerates every site that *acts* on one (display-only reads omitted). PR state is **not** federated: `harness_feature_prs` was reclassified `sync:'none'` (EI-479) — it is GitHub-derived and re-polled per-machine, so Postgres is the local store-of-record and federation is redundant; it has no projection producer and is not a registered projection tag. (This is why the auto-merge row below correctly reads the `Pr` object from a live GitHub poll, not from a federated row.) | Call-site | Authorization decision | Reads | Re-derives from GitHub? | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · `claimBinding` | claim a repo binding (needs maintain/admin) | local cache + **live** `getRepoPermission` | **Yes** — `getRepoPermission(owner,repo,login)` at point of action | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · `supersedeBinding` | supersede a binding (needs admin) | local cache + **live** `getRepoPermission` | **Yes** — live permission check, admin required | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · claimant re-verify sweep | demote a claimant who lost write access | cached claimants | **Yes** — per-claimant live permission check | | `sync/hyperbee/revoke-contributor.ts` | revoke a contributor’s device key | `contributors` row | **Yes** — `repos.get → permissions.admin` gate before any write | | `sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts` (+ `boot.ts`) | admit a peer’s log to the substrate | signed announce + local Hive membership projection | **Yes** — announce-sig verify + `verifyBinding` (GitHub-hosted attestation); `revoked_pubkeys` veto; same-Hive scope uses `hive_members` / pending retry, not repo collaborator permission | | `harness/fork-pr-on-feature-pass.ts` | fork-PR vs direct-push mode on feature pass | local pipeline pass event | **Yes** — **live** `getPermission` (fork iff `read`/`none`) | | `pr-host/auto-merge.ts` · `tryAutoMerge` → `host.merge` | merge a PR | `Pr` object from **GitHub** poll (`PrHost`/`github.ts`) | **Yes** — PR state read live from GitHub; merge enforced by GitHub write-access + branch protection | | `pr-host/auto-approve.ts` · `tryAutoApprove` | post an approving review | **local** `trusted_authors` + GitHub PR author | **N/A** — trust list is local config (not federated); approval still doesn’t bypass GitHub’s merge authority | | `harness/completion-ref-verifier.ts` | stamp the “shipped ✓” verified tier | `completion_ref` on the feature row | **Yes** — `git ls-remote <remote> <sha>` (GitHub native auth) confirms the SHA is on the remote | | `dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts` · `reconcileDoneStatus` | flip a feature `validating`/`in_progress → passed` | `harness_features_consolidated.status` (federated) | **N/A — advisory.** Fires only from the **local** orchestrator’s own pipeline reaching an unblocked DONE (`outcome==='done'`); a peer’s forged row cannot make the local pipeline run a feature to DONE. `passed` is internal pipeline coordination, **not** a “shipped”/authz fact — every downstream effect (push/PR/merge) is independently GitHub-gated. (Completion-integrity update, `fleet-backlog-lessons-2026-07-01` P-001/WI-1542: the same local-only write now also stamps `terminal_owner='system:dbos-orchestrator-finalize'` and a `terminal_completion_ref` — an auditability fix for the genuine-completions metric, not a change to who may write or to the trust boundary.) | | `contributors` / `claims` / `queue` / `working-set` readers (claim avatars, status badges, queue UI) | display & coordination only | federated rows | **N/A** — advisory by design; gate no action | **Why the federated feature `status` is not a gap (the one row worth tracing).** `harness_features_consolidated.status` *is* a federated projection target (tag `features-by-id`), so an admitted peer can write a `status` value into another peer’s PG. But no authorization decision acts on it: a forged `status='shipped'` does not earn the verified ✓ badge (that re-derives via `git ls-remote`), and `reconcileDoneStatus` only closes the `validating`/`in_progress`→`passed` loop (the `in_progress` case was added 2026-06-17 for coding-harness bees that skip the validator step) as the **local** pipeline’s own terminal verdict on a feature it actually executed — it cannot be driven by a peer-supplied row; terminal-failure states (failing/deprecated) are left untouched. The real “did it ship” authority remains GitHub’s merge state, and code only lands through GitHub’s write-access + branch-protection. This is the security doc’s own placement of “feature queue / status” in the **advisory** column, confirmed at the code level. **Verdict:** the wholesale-trust-of-admitted-peer model is sound **because** the re-derivation invariant is universal. No remediation needed; P-017 closed `done`. ### Revocation chokepoints (built) [Section titled “Revocation chokepoints (built)”](#revocation-chokepoints-built) Two revocation mechanisms are wired beyond the `revoked_pubkeys` admission drop-list: * **PR auto-approve and auto-merge refuse a revoked contributor’s PR up front.** A PR whose author is a revoked Hive contributor is denied (action `skipped_revoked`) **before** the trust / checks / approval gates — the strongest deny, **overriding the trust list** (it holds even for an author otherwise in `trusted_authors`). The live chokepoint resolves it via `isHiveContributorRevoked` and passes it into both `tryAutoApprove` and `tryAutoMerge`. * **Owner-revocation of another contributor** (`revokeContributorViaGithub`) is gated on a **live GitHub repo-admin** check (`repos.get → permissions.admin`) — the harness-owner authority. It works by unioning the target’s device pubkeys into the **owner’s own** contributor-row `revoked_pubkeys` and publishing it (the old “delete the `user/<id>` branch” lever became a no-op under write-free join, and an admin cannot delete another user’s attestation gist). Because `load-revoked-pubkeys` **unions `revoked_pubkeys` across all contributor rows** for the harness, that block federates via the owner’s log and is honored by every peer’s admission union. ## Accepted-insecurity tradeoffs [Section titled “Accepted-insecurity tradeoffs”](#accepted-insecurity-tradeoffs) Under this model we **deliberately accept**: 1. **Public, discoverable topic** — swarm spam/DoS is *mitigated* (firewall + admission), not prevented. 2. **Advisory rows can be injected by an admitted identity** — read admission proves identity and Hive membership, not truth. An admitted-then-malicious writer can still inject signed-but-false advisory rows (equivocation). Mitigation: nothing decision-bearing acts on it without GitHub re-derivation. 3. **No true removal / no post-compromise security** in the append-only log — revocation is best-effort projection filtering; the data persists and replicates. 4. **Sybil resistance is mostly delegated to GitHub identity plus Hive membership** — identity = GitHub account, bounded by the gist attestation and GitHub’s account-creation friction; cross-member shared-Hive writes also require a current `hive_members` device row or they remain pending/dropped. 5. **Per-op signatures don’t defeat a signed equivocator** (Kleppmann) — accepted because state is advisory and GitHub-re-derived; we explicitly do not build a BFT-CRDT ACL. 6. **Identity binding inherits GitHub account integrity** — a compromised GitHub account is a compromised identity (the same trust root as the merge authority, so not a new exposure). 7. **Local API stays loopback-trusted** — a single-user-desktop model, not a shared machine. ## Phased implementation [Section titled “Phased implementation”](#phased-implementation) * **Phase 1 — make peer state advisory + re-derive from GitHub.** Highest value, lowest risk; neutralizes the forgery surface for anything that matters. Resolves `completion_ref` as a GitHub-derived “shipped” signal. * **Phase 2 — per-op Ed25519 signing + verify-on-receipt** in the `apply`/projection path (sign seq + content); drop unverifiable ops at projection. * **Phase 3 — GitHub-anchored `addWriter` admission** (two-channel proof in blind-pairing `userData`) + `revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list; model the binding as a signed link. * **Phase 4 — only if a threat model demands real PCS** — Keyhive/BeeKEM membership. ## Sources & method [Section titled “Sources & method”](#sources--method) Three deep-research passes (web search → fetch primary sources → adversarial verification), \~9M tokens. Passes 1–2 (50 claims verified): Holepunch repos, Radicle (Heartwood + `radicle-cob` + LWN), ForgeFed, Kleppmann (PaPoC’22 + keynote), Ink & Switch Keyhive notebook, RFC 9420/9750 + DMLS drafts. Pass 3 (Keybase, Sigstore/SLSA, `did:plc`, Nostr, SSB): primary-sourced but the workflow’s vote-tally step crashed, so those rows are extracted-not-triple-verified; the two most decision-relevant (Sigstore threat model, `did:plc` recovery) were re-confirmed by direct fetch. Full per-claim detail lives in the design memo `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-trust-model-2026-05-31.md`.

# Sharable infrastructure plan

> The design — now largely shipped — for letting plugin configuration carry reproducible share semantics and arbitrary infrastructure provisioning, so a fork can stand up a complete working stack.

## What problem this solves [Section titled “What problem this solves”](#what-problem-this-solves) The snapshot export/fork system has been retired This section’s premise — that a harness snapshot is **exported** and **forked** as a tarball — is no longer current. The snapshot-EXPORT/fork system (`@papercusp/export-state`, the `snapshots:*` tools, `/api/snapshots/*`, and the Cupboard `kind=snapshot` fork-source) was retired on **2026-06-09** to `_retired/snapshot-system/`, and migration `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/199-drop-snapshot-index.sql` dropped the `snapshot_index` table (verified applied to the live database). The one job that survived — the *reproducible clone* — is now a lightweight **InstanceSpec** descriptor `{ blueprintRef, repoSha, deploymentConfig, genome }` (`packages/operator-core/lib/instance-spec/`, with `instance:capture|boot|clone` tools), **not** a forkable tarball. The share-semantics and provisioning mechanisms described below still shipped (into the plugin SDK + substrate); read the captured-state list and the “fork a snapshot” flow as the *historical* motivation that produced them, not as a live tarball pipeline. The original motivation: a harness snapshot used to capture — * The harness’s project files (code, docs, prompts) * The harness’s database state (the `harness_<slug>` schema name is still correct — see `packages/operator-core/lib/scaffold-harness-schema.ts` — but it is no longer captured/restored by a snapshot export) * Per-harness plugin configs (raw JSON in `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugin-configs/`) * The set of enabled plugins (`enabled-plugins.json`) When a user **forked** that snapshot, they got a fully working harness — *as long as* the underlying infrastructure already existed. Concretely: * If the original harness deployed to a Cloudflare Pages project, the forker has to manually create their own Cloudflare account + token + Pages project + paste credentials before the `cloudflare-pages` plugin’s actions work. * If the original harness pushed to a GitHub repo, the forker has to manually create a PAT + a target repo before `github-repo` works. * If the original harness used a hypothetical `aws-lambda` plugin to deploy serverless functions, the forker has to manually create the Lambda + IAM role + API gateway… none of which is captured by today’s snapshot. This makes “publish a working harness template” significantly harder than it should be. Two changes close the gap: 1. **Per-field share semantics** — plugins declare which config fields are sharable (default), which are private to the publisher (must be re-supplied), and which are credentials (must be re-authorized via OAuth or paste). The snapshot exporter respects these flags. 2. **Build scripts** — plugins can ship an executable `setup` script that the substrate runs (with full visibility) on the fork-er’s host to provision the plugin’s required infrastructure. Symmetric `teardown` and `verify` scripts cover uninstall and health-check. Both changes preserve the snapshot system’s current safety properties (no secret leakage; no silent code execution) while extending what a snapshot can encapsulate. ## Vision: standing up a complex clone [Section titled “Vision: standing up a complex clone”](#vision-standing-up-a-complex-clone) The user-visible flow the share-semantics + provisioning pieces were built to enable — illustrated here against a complex stack like `ecommerce-stripe-aws-cloudflare`. (The “fork a snapshot tarball” entry points named below predate the [snapshot-export retirement](#what-problem-this-solves); the connect-accounts and approve-provisioning steps are the parts that shipped.) 
```text
Forking ecommerce-stripe-aws-cloudflare → my-store
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────


  1.  Fork project files       …………………………………………………………… ✓ done (instant)
  2.  Restore harness DB schema ……………………………………………………… ✓ done (1.2s)
  3.  Apply redacted plugin configs ……………………………………………… ✓ done (instant)
  4.  Connect external accounts:


      ☐ GitHub      [ Connect with GitHub ]      ←  OAuth, no token paste
      ☐ Stripe      [ Connect with Stripe ]      ←  OAuth
      ☐ AWS         [ Paste access keys… ]       ←  no OAuth — paste
      ☐ Cloudflare  [ Paste API token… ]         ←  no OAuth — paste


  5.  Approve and run provisioning scripts:


      ☐ aws-lambda          provision-aws.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 Lambda function, 1 API Gateway, 1 IAM role
            Estimated cost: $0–5/mo
      ☐ stripe-webhooks     provision-stripe.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 webhook endpoint, 1 Stripe restricted-key
      ☐ cloudflare-pages    provision-cloudflare.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 Pages project, 1 custom domain binding


      ☐ I trust this snapshot's publisher (papercupai)


      [ Approve all & run ]    [ Run one at a time ]
```
 After step 5, the harness is genuinely ready to run. Every credential the user provided is theirs; every cloud resource was provisioned with their explicit approval; the audit log preserves what ran. ## Two-part proposal [Section titled “Two-part proposal”](#two-part-proposal) This plan is split across two complementary mechanisms. They’re orthogonal — either could ship without the other — but together they’re what unlocks shareable arbitrary infrastructure. | Part | What it does | Read more | | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | **Build scripts** | Plugins declare `provision.{setup,teardown,verify}` scripts that the substrate runs on the host with full visibility, capturing output and tracking created resources for cleanup. | [Build scripts](./build-scripts) | | **Share semantics** | Plugins flag each `configSchema` field as `secret` (credential, stripped on snapshot) / `shareable: false` (publisher-specific identifier, stripped) / default (config that travels with the snapshot). | [Share semantics](./share-semantics) | | **OAuth integration** | The substrate provides a generic OAuth helper so plugins can mark a credential field as `oauth: { provider, scopes }` and users get a “Connect” button instead of a paste field. | [OAuth integration](./oauth-integration) | ## Implementation status [Section titled “Implementation status”](#implementation-status) The two-part proposal above is **largely shipped**. What landed, where it lives, and which proposed fields stayed design-only: **Build scripts / provision lifecycle — shipped.** The runner and OS-level sandbox live at `packages/operator-core/lib/provision/` (`runner.ts`, `sandbox.ts` for bwrap, plus `audit-log.ts`, `trust-store.ts`, `network-policy.ts`, `single-user.ts`, `hashes.ts`, a WAL `state-store.ts`, and the `runtime/lib.sh` `papercusp_record_resource` FIFO bridge). It runs as a durable DBOS workflow (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/provision-workflow.ts`, gated by `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_PROVISION`, default-on), and three first-party plugins ship `provision/` scripts (`cloudflare-stack` and `github-repo` ship the full `{setup,teardown,verify}.sh` trio; `cloudflare-pages` ships only `verify.sh`). Per \[\[plugin-system-hive-port-2026-06-11]] P-010, the shipped `ProvisionScript` type carries `path` / `timeoutSec` / `runAt` plus consent-dialog fields `displayName` / `description`; the proposed `network`, `writesState`, and `requiresInteractive` fields **stay design-only** and are not in the SDK. `PluginProvision` additionally carries `cloudProvider`, `allowedHosts`, `skipReprovisionOnPatch`, and `auditLogCapMb`. **OAuth integration — shipped.** The substrate lives at `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/` (`state.ts` for HMAC-signed URL state + single-use nonce, `providers.ts` with the hand-written GitHub provider, `token.ts` with the `getOAuthToken` Promise-cache that dedupes concurrent refreshes and retries once on 401, `storage-fs.ts`), exposes `/api/oauth/start|callback|verify-paste`, and offers `ctx.oauth.token(provider)` (refreshing \~5 minutes before expiry). See `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/README.md`. OAuth was rolled in-house — the `arctic` library mentioned below was **not** adopted as a dependency. Additional providers (Slack/Linear/Notion/Jira) remain V2 (`// V2: slack, linear, notion, jira providers.` in `providers.ts`). **Share semantics — shipped at the SDK contract.** The plugin SDK declares the per-field flags `secret` / `snapshotPolicy` / `shareable` / `oauth` / `aliases` on `configSchema`, plus top-level `provision`, `oauth`, and `versionPin` (`packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts`). Note the exporter that *consumed* these flags rode the now-retired snapshot-export system; the flags themselves remain the live contract. ## What this plan does NOT change [Section titled “What this plan does NOT change”](#what-this-plan-does-not-change) To set scope expectations: * **The plugin loader contract** — plugins still ship as a manifest + JS entry + capability declaration. Scripts are an *additional* lifecycle surface, not a replacement. * **The capability gate** — actions and hook handlers still run inside the DI sandbox with `secrets:read:*` / `http:fetch:*` enforcement. Build scripts are a separate, opt-in escape hatch with their own consent flow, not a backdoor around the gate. * **The harness contract** (§3 of the spec) — fresh-context roles, structured state, atomic checkout, etc. all unchanged. * **The CLI surface** — `papercusp install` (live — `libs/papercusp/packages/cli/src/papercusp.ts`) and `papercusp plugin enable` (live — `plugin-cli.ts`, `cmdPluginEnable`) keep their current commands; new flags get added without renames.
